title: Science, Class 8
subject: Science
description: NCERT Grade 8 Science, chapter by chapter.

chapters.title: Exploring the Investigative World of Science
chapters.summary: In this chapter: wonder and the spirit of investigation; from microbes to forces; pressure, particles and mixtures; light, living systems and earth’s balance.

lessons.title: Wonder and the spirit of investigation

activities.prompt: What helps us turn a wondering question into an investigation?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: The spirit of investigation
activities.body: Science begins when you wonder and ask simple “Why?” and “How?” questions. Focused questions help you investigate carefully. You can design experiments to answer your questions and make observations. Observations are things you notice. They help improve your understanding. Scientific ideas may change slowly as exploration opens new questions. Curiosity helps you move towards the unknown. Good investigation balances careful observation with creative thinking.
keyPoints: Wonder and questions begin science.
Focused questions support careful investigation.
Observations improve understanding.
Good investigation balances observation and creative thinking.
activities.explanation: Curiosity helps you ask useful questions and explore new ideas.

activities.prompt: Why does one paper boat carry a toy farther than another?
steps: The child asks a focused question, because focused questions guide careful investigation.
The child tests both boats alike, because experiments answer focused questions.
The child watches closely, because observations improve understanding.
Therefore, the child should explore further, because deeper exploration opens new questions.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.title: A good beginning
activities.prompt: Which question best begins a scientific investigation?
options: What colour is my lunchbox?
Why does this plant grow upwards?
Can I finish my game sooner?
Which shirt should I wear today?
activities.explanation: A “Why?” question seeks an explanation about the world.

activities.title: Connecting ideas
activities.prompt: Match each idea with a helpful action.
activities.explanation: Questions, experiments and observations each support scientific investigation.

activities.title: Careful investigation
activities.prompt: Focused questions help us investigate more ______.
activities.hint: This word describes work done with close attention.
activities.explanation: Focused questions guide investigations with greater care.

activities.title: Learning through science
activities.prompt: What should science education teach pupils?
options: How to avoid new questions
How to copy old answers
How to find new facts
How to stop exploring
activities.explanation: Science education should help pupils discover and find new facts.

activities.title: Investigation steps
activities.prompt: Put these investigation steps in order.
activities.explanation: You begin with wonder and progress through careful investigation.

activities.title: Choosing an investigation plan
activities.prompt: Which plan is best for investigating a question?
options: Plan carefully and notice what happens.
Guess without noticing any clues.
Use a focused question and design an experiment.
Copy an old idea without testing it.
activities.explanation: A focused question and experiment support careful investigation.

activities.prompt: One child compares two paper bridges. Which question guides a careful investigation?
options: Why does one bridge hold more weight than the other bridge?
Why can paper be useful for making many different things?
What kinds of bridges can people build using only paper?
Which bridge looks strongest to a child who sees it?

why.Why can paper be useful for making many: This is too broad because it does not compare one clear cause.
why.What kinds of bridges can people build u: This asks for examples instead of explaining the difference between bridges.
why.Which bridge looks strongest to a child: This mistakes a bridge's looks for evidence about why it holds more.

activities.explanation: This is a clear question that an experiment can investigate.

activities.prompt: A surprising result raises another question. What should the child do next?
options: The child should explore the new question with another careful test.
The child should stop because the first answer is already complete.
The child should repeat the first test without asking any new questions.
The child should accept the first result and ignore the surprise.

why.The child should stop because the first: One answer does not mean deeper exploration has no more questions.
why.The child should repeat the first test w: Repeating without a new question does not explore the surprise.
why.The child should accept the first result: Ignoring surprising evidence weakens the child's understanding.

activities.explanation: New questions can open deeper exploration, so the child should keep investigating.

activities.prompt: A child asks, “Which paper boat carries a toy better?” Which plan is fairest?
options: Test both boats the same way, then compare what happens.
Test one boat twice, then choose the better-looking result.
Change every part of both boats, then compare only their looks.
Guess from one boat, then avoid watching the other boat.

why.Test one boat twice, then choose the bet: Testing one boat twice cannot compare the two different boats.
why.Change every part of both boats, then co: Changing many parts removes a clear link between cause and result.
why.Guess from one boat, then avoid watching: A guess without observations cannot answer the child's question.

activities.explanation: The same test gives observations that can fairly compare the boats.

activities.prompt: “My guess feels right, so it must be a fact.” What is missing before accepting it?
options: An observation or experiment that can check the guess.
A stronger feeling that makes the guess seem more certain.
A longer story that explains why the guess feels right.
A prettier name that makes the idea sound more scientific.

why.A stronger feeling that makes the guess: A stronger feeling still does not show how to find new facts.
why.A longer story that explains why the gue: A story cannot replace observations that check the idea.
why.A prettier name that makes the idea soun: A name cannot show whether observations support the idea.

activities.explanation: Facts need to be found through investigation, not feeling alone.

activities.prompt: A scientist only records results and never imagines explanations. What should change?
options: Creative thinking that balances careful observations and possible explanations.
More guesses without watching results or checking any ideas.
A quick answer that leaves no room for deeper questions.
A fixed idea that prevents new questions and deeper exploration.

why.More guesses without watching results or: Unchecked guesses do not improve understanding through observation.
why.A quick answer that leaves no room for d: A quick answer can stop the deeper exploration that brings new questions.
why.A fixed idea that prevents new questions: A fixed idea prevents ideas from changing as exploration goes deeper.

activities.explanation: Good investigation balances careful observation with creative thinking.

activities.prompt: One question is answered, but curiosity remains. What is best next?
options: Ask a new focused question and explore it carefully.
Stop searching because one question now has an answer.
Change the old question so the new answer seems certain.
Repeat the answered question without learning anything new.

why.Stop searching because one question now: One answer does not remove every question from deeper exploration.
why.Change the old question so the new answe: Changing the question to fit an answer does not find new facts.
why.Repeat the answered question without lea: Repeating an answered question does not explore what remains unknown.

activities.explanation: Curiosity moves the child toward the unknown through new questions.

lessons.title: From microbes to forces

activities.prompt: How can tiny microbes and mighty forces change the way we live?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: A journey through science
activities.body: Microbes are so small that you cannot see them. Some help us digest food or produce medicines. Others cause infections. Nutritious food, exercise, medicines and vaccines help you stay healthy. Electric current makes everyday activities easier. It can keep you warm and help motors work. Forces can speed up, slow down, or change the direction of moving objects. Pressure spreads force over an object.
keyPoints: Some microbes help us, while others harm us.
Electric current has heating and magnetic effects.
Forces change motion, while pressure spreads force.
activities.explanation: This lesson connects health, electricity, forces, and pressure.

activities.prompt: A child has an electric toy. The room is cold. What can current do?
steps: Electric current is useful because it makes everyday activities easier.
The toy can work because the current's magnetic effect helps motors work.
The child can stay warm because the current's heating effect provides warmth.
So current can help both the toy and the child.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.title: Invisible helpers
activities.prompt: Which helpers can help us digest food or produce medicines?
options: Microbes
Magnets
Brakes
Forces
activities.explanation: Some microbes are invisible helpers that help us digest food or produce medicines.

activities.title: Help from current
activities.prompt: Electric current helps make many everyday activities ______.
activities.hint: Think about what electric current does for us.
activities.explanation: Electric current makes many everyday activities easier.

activities.title: Join each idea
activities.prompt: Match each idea with its correct meaning or use.
pairs: Describes force spread over an object
activities.explanation: These pairs match each idea with what it does.

activities.title: Motors at work
activities.prompt: Which effect of electric current helps motors and machines work?
options: Magnetic effect
Heating effect
Braking effect
Pressure effect
activities.explanation: The magnetic effect of electric current helps motors and machines work.

activities.title: Follow the lesson
activities.prompt: Put these lesson topics in the order shown in your lesson.
activities.explanation: The lesson moves from microbes and health to current, forces, and pressure.

activities.title: Spread of force
activities.prompt: A force is spread over an object. Which word describes this?
options: Pressure
Heating
Magnetism
Braking
activities.explanation: Pressure describes how force is spread over an object.

activities.prompt: Some invisible helpers can produce medicines. A factory uses them. Why are they there?
options: To help make the medicine.
To help digest the food.
To cause a new infection.
To create electric current.

This confuses making medicine with digesting food.
This confuses helpful helpers with microbes that cause infections.
This confuses microbes with electric current.

activities.explanation: This matches the helpers' role in producing medicines.

activities.prompt: Some microbes can harm us by causing infections. A child has an infection. What may be true?
options: A harmful microbe caused it.
A helpful medicine caused it.
A helpful vaccine caused it.
An electric current caused it.

This mistakes a health helper for the cause of an infection.
This mistakes a health helper for the cause of an infection.
This confuses an infection with the effect of electric current.

activities.explanation: Some microbes can cause infections in people.

activities.prompt: Electric current has a heating effect. A cold room needs warmth. What can this effect do?
options: It can keep the room warm.
It can keep the room cold.
It can run the room's motor.
It can spread pressure around.

This reverses the warming effect of electric current.
This confuses heating with the magnetic effect that helps motors.
This confuses heating with the spreading of force over an area.

activities.explanation: The heating effect of current can keep us warm.

activities.prompt: Electric current has a magnetic effect. A mixer has a motor. What can this effect do?
options: It can help the motor work.
It can keep the motor cold.
It can make the food digest.
It can cause pressure in food.

This confuses the magnetic effect with the heating effect.
This confuses the motor's action with microbes that help digestion.
This confuses the magnetic effect with force spread over food.

activities.explanation: The magnetic effect of current helps motors and machines work.

activities.prompt: Braking shows how forces affect moving objects. A bicycle moves forward. What happens when its brake is pressed?
options: The bicycle slows down.
The bicycle speeds up.
The bicycle keeps its speed.
The bicycle changes direction.

This confuses braking with a force that speeds up movement.
This overlooks the braking force acting on the bicycle.
This confuses slowing down with changing direction.

activities.explanation: Braking uses a force that slows down the moving bicycle.

activities.prompt: Pressure describes how force is spread over an object. The same force acts over a smaller area. What happens?
options: The pressure becomes greater.
The pressure becomes smaller.
The pressure stays the same.
The pressure becomes electric.

This reverses what happens when the same force is spread more tightly.
This overlooks that changing the spread changes pressure.
This confuses pressure with electric current.

activities.explanation: Spreading the same force over a smaller area makes pressure greater.

lessons.title: Pressure, particles and mixtures

activities.prompt: Why do pressure, particles, and mixtures behave in such different ways?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: How pressure and particles are connected
activities.body: Pressure differences can make winds. A small difference in pressure can create a gentle breeze. A stronger difference can create strong winds. Everything around us is made of tiny particles. These particles cannot move much in solids, but can move freely in gases. Elements are pure substances. Compounds contain two or more elements bonded together. Mixtures are combinations that can be separated physically.
keyPoints: Pressure differences can create gentle breezes or strong winds.
Solid particles cannot move much, but gas particles move freely.
Elements, compounds and mixtures have different properties.
activities.explanation: This lesson connects pressure, particle movement and the different kinds of substances.

activities.title: Heat the water

tasks.then: Below 0 degrees water is ice: its particles can only jiggle in place.
At 100 degrees water boils and its particles fly apart as steam.

activities.takeaway: Heating gives particles more energy: held in place in ice, sliding in water, flying apart as steam.
activities.explanation: Heating gives particles more energy: held in place in ice, sliding in water, flying apart as steam.

activities.prompt: Two places have a small pressure difference. What can happen between them, and why?
steps: Because the pressure difference is small, a gentle breeze can form.
Gas particles move freely, so they can move between the places.
That particle movement explains why a gentle breeze forms.
A stronger pressure difference could instead create strong winds.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.prompt: What can a small difference in pressure create?
options: A gentle breeze
Strong winds
A daily safety plan
An agricultural change
activities.explanation: A small difference in pressure can create a gentle breeze. Strong winds need a stronger difference.

activities.prompt: Elements are ______ substances.
activities.hint: This word shows that an element has no other substance mixed with it.
activities.explanation: Elements are pure substances. A compound contains two or more elements bonded together.

activities.prompt: Which example is a solution?
options: An element in its pure form
Two elements bonded together
A combination separated physically
Sugar dissolving in tea
activities.explanation: Sugar dissolving in tea is an example of a solution. The other options describe elements, compounds or mixtures.

activities.prompt: Match each idea with its correct description.
activities.explanation: Each pair joins an idea with its description from the lesson.

activities.prompt: Compounds contain two or more ______ bonded together.
activities.hint: Pure substances that can join together form compounds.
activities.explanation: Compounds contain two or more elements bonded together. Elements are pure substances.

activities.prompt: Put these steps in order to show how particle study helps us.
items: Learn that everything is made of tiny particles.
Understand why water boils at a certain temperature.
activities.explanation: First, learn about tiny particles. Then study them to understand water's boiling temperature.

activities.prompt: One place has a small pressure difference. Another has a stronger pressure difference. What can happen?
options: The first can have a breeze; the second can have strong winds.
The first can have strong winds; the second can have a breeze.
Both places can have strong winds after the pressure change.
Neither place can have any wind or breeze after the change.

why.The first can have strong winds; the sec: This swaps the outcomes for small and strong pressure differences.
why.Both places can have strong winds after: This wrongly suggests both differences create strong winds.
why.Neither place can have any wind or breez: This wrongly suggests no pressure difference can create moving air.

activities.explanation: A small difference gives a breeze; a stronger difference gives strong winds.

activities.prompt: A storm reaches a town and farm. A child says only farming is affected. What is wrong?
options: The storm can also affect daily life and safety.
The storm can stop particles moving in solids.
The storm can make pure elements appear.
The storm can physically separate every mixture.

why.The storm can stop particles moving in s: This confuses storm effects with particle movement in solids.
This confuses storm effects with the formation of elements.
why.The storm can physically separate every: This confuses storm effects with physical separation.

activities.explanation: Storms and cyclones affect daily life and safety as well as farming.

activities.prompt: A teacher mixes sugar and sand. Which action can separate the mixture again?
options: Use a physical method to separate both parts.
Bond both parts into one new compound.
Change both parts into pure elements.
Turn both parts into one pure element.

Bonding would join the parts instead of separating the mixture.
Changing parts into elements is not physical separation.
A physical separation does not turn a mixture into an element.

activities.explanation: Mixtures can be separated physically, so this method keeps them separable.

activities.prompt: Sugar is stirred into tea until it cannot be seen. What has happened?
options: The sugar has dissolved and formed a solution.
The sugar has bonded and formed an element.
The tea has bonded and formed a compound.
The sugar has stopped moving in the tea.

why.The sugar has bonded and formed an eleme: Bonding elements together forms a compound, not a pure element.
why.The tea has bonded and formed a compound: Dissolving sugar in tea does not bond the tea into a compound.
Dissolving spreads sugar through tea rather than stopping its movement.

activities.explanation: Sugar dissolving in tea is an example of a solution.

lessons.title: Light, living systems and Earth’s balance

activities.prompt: How does light connect living things and the balance of our home?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: Light and Moon phases
activities.body: Light can reflect from flat and curved mirrors. It bends when it passes through lenses. Corrective glasses help many people see clearly. Rough surfaces and the Moon also reflect light. The Moon’s illuminated part changes with the positions of Earth, Moon, and Sun. These changes produce visible phases. Living organisms and their environments form ecosystems that support life on Earth.
keyPoints: Light reflects from mirrors and rough surfaces.
Corrective glasses help many people see clearly.
Moon phases come from changing positions.
activities.explanation: Light reflects and bends, while Moon phases come from changing positions.

activities.prompt: Why does the Moon look different? How can its changing shapes help people?
steps: The Moon’s illuminated part changes as Earth, Moon, and Sun change positions.
Those position changes produce the visible phases of the Moon.
People once used those changing phases to create the first calendars.
So, the Moon’s changing phases can help make calendars.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.title: Living systems and Earth’s balance
activities.body: Living organisms and their environments form complex patterns of relationships. These relationships form ecosystems, which support life on Earth. Earth lies at a perfect distance from the Sun. Earth’s atmosphere provides the oxygen we breathe. Human activities can cause small changes in Earth’s temperature.
keyPoints: Living organisms and environments form relationships.
Ecosystems support life on Earth.
Human activities can cause small temperature changes.
activities.explanation: Ecosystems support life, and Earth’s atmosphere provides oxygen.

activities.prompt: What happens when light passes through a lens?
options: It bends.
It reflects.
It makes oxygen.
It changes ecosystems.
activities.explanation: Light bends when it passes through a lens.

activities.prompt: Rough surfaces can reflect light.
activities.explanation: Rough surfaces reflect light, just like the Moon does.

activities.prompt: Corrective ______ help many people to see clearly.
activities.hint: They help your eyes see clearly.
activities.explanation: Corrective glasses help many people to see clearly.

activities.prompt: Match each thing with what the lesson says happens.
activities.explanation: Lenses bend light, and rough surfaces reflect it. Ecosystems support life. Earth’s atmosphere provides oxygen.

activities.prompt: What do relationships between living organisms and environments form?
options: Ecosystems that support life on Earth.
Ecosystems that remove all oxygen from Earth.
Ecosystems that block all sunlight from Earth.
Ecosystems that cause only large temperature changes.
activities.explanation: These relationships form ecosystems that support life on Earth.

activities.prompt: Human activities can cause only large changes in Earth’s temperature.
activities.explanation: Human activities can cause small changes in Earth’s temperature.

activities.prompt: How were the first calendars created?
options: Using the Moon’s phases.
Using Earth’s atmospheric oxygen.
Using light bending in lenses.
Using changes in ecosystem relationships.
activities.explanation: Humans used the Moon’s phases to create the first calendars.

activities.prompt: Earth, Moon, and Sun change places. What happens to the Moon’s shape?
options: The illuminated part changes, producing visible phases.
The illuminated part stays fixed, producing no phases.
The Moon stops reflecting light during these changes.
The Moon’s light bends through lenses in space.

why.The illuminated part stays fixed, produc: It wrongly assumes the illuminated part never changes.
why.The Moon stops reflecting light during t: It confuses the Moon’s phases with a loss of reflection.
why.The Moon’s light bends through lenses in: It wrongly uses lens bending to explain Moon phases.

activities.explanation: Changing positions change the illuminated part and create Moon phases.

lessons.sceneCaption: This diagram connects the Moon’s visible phases with its revolution and rotation around Earth.

lessons.title: Investigating a puffing puri

activities.prompt: What helps a puri puff up just right?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: How a puri puffs up
activities.body: A puri puffs up when you place it in hot oil. You can investigate this in a home kitchen. Start with curiosity and ask a scientific question. Change one thing at a time, such as dough thickness or oil temperature. Then observe or measure the puffing time. Keep notes of everything you see and sense. This careful method is called systematic investigation.
keyPoints: A puri puffs up in hot oil.
Change one thing at a time and measure the difference.
Keep notes and follow a systematic investigation.
activities.explanation: Curiosity starts a scientific investigation. Careful questions, changes, measurements, and notes help you learn more.

activities.prompt: Does dough thickness or oil temperature change how quickly a puri puffs up?
steps: Ask if thickness changes puffing time, because investigation starts with a question.
Change only thickness, because each test should change one thing.
Keep oil temperature the same, because thickness is the only change.
Record times and observations, because fewer seconds show faster puffing.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.prompt: What happens when you place a puri in hot oil?
options: It puffs up.
It stays flat.
It becomes smaller.
It turns cold.
activities.explanation: A puri puffs up in hot oil. You can observe this change during your investigation.

activities.prompt: A home kitchen can be used for simple scientific experiments.
activities.explanation: True. A home kitchen can be used for simple scientific experiments.

activities.prompt: You want to test the oil temperature. What should you keep the same?
options: the dough thickness and size
the oil temperature
the seconds needed to puff up
the notes you keep
activities.explanation: Change only the oil temperature. Keep the dough thickness and size the same.

activities.prompt: Match each item with its matching description.
activities.explanation: Each pair shows a change or measurement. These help you investigate the puri.

activities.prompt: Put these investigation steps in order.
items: Identify what you can change or control
Change one thing at a time
activities.explanation: The order moves from curiosity to a question, then a test and measurement. Change only one thing at a time.

activities.prompt: What is the careful method called when you follow these investigation steps?
options: an unplanned investigation
systematic investigation
an unfinished investigation
a careless investigation
activities.explanation: This careful method is called systematic investigation. It includes questioning, controlling changes, measuring, and keeping notes.

activities.prompt: A child changes the dough thickness and keeps the oil temperature the same. What should be measured?
options: Seconds until each puri puffs up.
Seconds before the oil becomes hot.
Thickness of the dough after it puffs.
Temperature of the dough before frying.

This times the oil's heating, not the puri's puffing.
This records dough after puffing, not the puffing time.
This measures the dough's start, not its puffing time.

activities.explanation: This measures the change in puffing time.

activities.prompt: A child wants to test whether oil temperature affects puffing time. Which plan is fairest?
options: Change oil temperature; keep dough thickness and size the same.
Change dough thickness; keep oil temperature the same.
Change oil temperature and dough thickness together.
Change oil temperature and dough size together.

why.Change dough thickness; keep oil tempera: This changes the wrong factor and does not test oil temperature.
why.Change oil temperature and dough thickne: This changes two factors, so the cause cannot be found.
why.Change oil temperature and dough size to: This also changes dough size, so the cause cannot be found.

activities.explanation: This changes only oil temperature and controls the dough.

activities.prompt: During a test, both dough thickness and oil temperature change. What problem does this cause?
options: The two changes cannot be tested fairly on their own.
The puri will certainly fail to puff up.
Both puris will certainly puff up at once.
These changes will always make the puri puff faster.

This wrongly assumes two changes will stop puffing.
why.Both puris will certainly puff up at onc: This wrongly assumes two puris will puff at once.
why.These changes will always make the puri: This wrongly assumes two changes always speed up puffing.

activities.explanation: This follows the rule that only one thing changes.

activities.prompt: Which set of notes best supports a puri experiment?
options: Puffing times, oil temperature, dough thickness, and all observations.
Only the final puffing time, with no other observations.
Only how many puris looked tasty in the hot oil.
No measurements or observations, only a final guess.

why.Only the final puffing time, with no oth: This leaves out other observations and the changed factors.
why.Only how many puris looked tasty in the: This counts looks instead of measuring the puffing time.
why.No measurements or observations, only a: This uses a guess instead of keeping evidence.

activities.explanation: This records measurements and everything seen or sensed.

activities.prompt: One child asks a question, changes one thing, measures the result, and keeps notes. Why is this a systematic investigation?
options: One change is tested, and the result is checked and recorded.
This mistake thinks the place alone makes the method careful.
This mistake thinks changing many things makes a fair test.
This mistake thinks a question is not needed for investigation.

why.This mistake thinks the place alone make: This mistake thinks the place alone makes the method careful.
why.This mistake thinks changing many things: This mistake thinks changing many things makes a fair test.
why.This mistake thinks a question is not ne: This mistake thinks a question is not needed for investigation.

activities.explanation: This changes one thing and checks and records the result.

activities.context: A pupil watching a simple activity wondered why it behaved differently each time. Instead of accepting the first guess, the pupil asked a focused “Why?” and “How?” question, then designed an experiment to test it. Careful observation led to a new result and another question. The pupil also tried a creative idea, showing that investigation can grow as deeper exploration opens new questions.
activities.prompt: If the new result raises another question, what should the pupil do next?
options: Turn the new question into a focused inquiry and test it with a designed experiment.
Stop investigating because the first experiment already produced a result.
Choose an easier question without making any further observations.
Use only the creative idea and leave careful observation out of the investigation.

why.Stop investigating because the first exp: A result does not mean that every question has been answered.
why.Choose an easier question without making: Changing the question merely to make it easier avoids deeper exploration.
why.Use only the creative idea and leave car: Good investigation needs both careful observation and creative thinking.

activities.explanation: The new question should guide another careful investigation.

activities.context: A pupil watching a simple activity wondered why it behaved differently each time. Instead of accepting the first guess, the pupil asked a focused “Why?” and “How?” question, then designed an experiment to test it. Careful observation led to a new result and another question. The pupil also tried a creative idea, showing that investigation can grow as deeper exploration opens new questions.
activities.prompt: If careful observation and a creative idea suggest different explanations, what would be the best way to continue?
options: Balance careful observation with creative thinking while investigating the question.
Accept whichever explanation was thought of first and ignore the other.
Follow only the observation and reject every creative possibility.
Follow only the creative idea and make no further observations.

why.Accept whichever explanation was thought: The first idea should still be tested rather than accepted automatically.
why.Follow only the observation and reject e: Observation provides important information that should not be ignored.
why.Follow only the creative idea and make n: Creative ideas also need careful investigation.

activities.explanation: Good investigation combines observation with imagination.

activities.prompt:
Assertion (A): A focused question helps a pupil investigate more carefully.
Reason (R): The pupil made the broad wonder into a focused question before designing an experiment.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.
activities.explanation: The focused question directly guides the investigation, so the reason explains the statement.

activities.prompt:
Assertion (A): Scientific ideas never need to change after deeper exploration.
Reason (R): Deeper exploration can open new questions and lead to ideas changing slowly.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.
activities.explanation: Deeper exploration can change ideas, so the statement is false while the reason is true.

activities.prompt: Explain how wonder can lead a pupil towards a scientific investigation.
activities.answer: Wonder begins when a pupil asks a simple “Why?” or “How?” question. A focused question makes the investigation clearer and helps the pupil decide what to examine. The pupil can then design an experiment to answer the question. During the experiment, observations can improve understanding and may lead to new questions. Curious pupils must be willing to take flight towards the unknown, while good investigation balances careful observation with creative thinking. As exploration goes deeper, scientific ideas may change slowly, so the process does not end with the first result.
points: Science begins with wonder and simple questions.
Focused questions support careful investigation.
Experiments and observations help answer questions.
Curiosity, observation, and creative thinking support investigation.
activities.explanation: Compare your answer with the points a marker looks for.

activities.prompt:
Assertion (A): Some microbes can cause infections.
Reason (R): Some invisible helpers help us digest food or produce medicines.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.
activities.explanation: Both statements are true, but the reason does not explain why microbes can cause infections.

activities.prompt:
Assertion (A): Braking can show how a force slows a moving object.
Reason (R): Forces can make objects speed up, slow down or change direction.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.
activities.explanation: The reason explains that slowing a moving object is an effect of force.

activities.prompt: Explain the difference between the heating effect and the magnetic effect of electric current.
activities.answer: The heating effect and magnetic effect of electric current have different uses. The heating effect can keep us warm, so it relates to warmth. The magnetic effect helps motors and machines work, so it relates to their operation. These effects should not be confused with braking or pressure. Braking shows a force slowing a moving object, whereas pressure describes how force is spread over an object.
points: The heating effect can keep us warm.
The magnetic effect helps motors and machines work.
The two effects have different uses.
Braking and pressure concern the effects of force.
activities.explanation: Compare your answer with the points a marker looks for.

activities.context: A coastal town is preparing for a possible storm. A small difference in pressure has made a gentle breeze, but the difference is becoming stronger. Farmers worry because storms and cyclones influence farming and safety. In a home there, sugar dissolves in tea, illustrating the lesson's solution example. The particles in the gas around the town are able to roam freely.
activities.prompt: What would be a likely next result if the difference in pressure became stronger?
options: Strong winds could develop, with risks to farming and safety.
A gentle breeze would remain the most likely result.
The effect would be limited to farming, with no effect on safety.
The wind would become weaker because stronger pressure differences reduce movement.

why.A gentle breeze would remain the most li: This overlooks the stated effect of a stronger pressure difference.
why.The effect would be limited to farming,: Storms and cyclones affect safety as well as agriculture.
why.The wind would become weaker because str: The relationship between pressure difference and wind strength has been reversed.

activities.explanation: A stronger pressure difference can create strong winds, and storms can affect farming and safety.

activities.context: A coastal town is preparing for a possible storm. A small difference in pressure has made a gentle breeze, but the difference is becoming stronger. Farmers worry because storms and cyclones influence farming and safety. In a home there, sugar dissolves in tea, illustrating the lesson's solution example. The particles in the gas around the town are able to roam freely.
activities.prompt: Which particle fact best supports the movement of air in this case?
options: Particles in the gaseous state can move freely.
Particles in the gaseous state are nearly fixed, like particles in solids.
Particles can move only in pure substances, not in gases.
A pressure difference can create wind without involving particle movement.

why.Particles in the gaseous state are nearl: Particles in solids cannot move much, unlike particles in gases.
why.Particles can move only in pure substanc: The stated fact allows particles to move in gases, even though a gas is not a pure substance.
why.A pressure difference can create wind wi: The case connects pressure differences with particle movement rather than separating them.

activities.explanation: The fact about free movement in gases supports moving air.

activities.prompt:
Assertion (A): A small difference in pressure can create a gentle breeze.
Reason (R): Particles can move freely in gases, allowing pressure differences to produce moving air.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.
activities.explanation: Both statements are true, and the movement of gas particles explains how a pressure difference can create a breeze.

activities.prompt: Explain how differences in pressure and the movement of particles are connected, and why a stronger pressure difference matters in the case.
activities.answer: A small difference in pressure can create a gentle breeze, while a stronger difference can create strong winds. This is possible because everything around us is made of tiny particles, and particles can move freely in gases. The gas around the town therefore contains particles that can move. When the pressure difference grows stronger, strong winds may develop. This matters because storms and cyclones affect farming, safety, and daily life.
points: A small pressure difference can create a gentle breeze.
A stronger pressure difference can create strong winds.
Gas particles can move freely.
Strong winds and storms can affect farming and safety.
activities.explanation: Compare your answer with the points a marker looks for.

activities.context: A student is planning a classroom display about light. The display includes a flat mirror, a curved mirror, a lens, and a rough wall. Light rays reflect from both kinds of mirror, and light bends when it passes through the lens. The rough wall also reflects light. The student draws the Moon’s illuminated part at different positions of Earth, Moon, and Sun. These changes produce the Moon’s visible phases, which humans used to create the first calendars.
activities.prompt: The student shines light onto the rough wall instead of the lens. What should happen next?
options: The light would bounce from the rough wall.
The light would bend as it crosses the rough wall.
The light would make the wall’s illuminated part change.
The light would pass through the wall without changing direction.

why.The light would bend as it crosses the r: Bending occurs when light passes through a lens.
why.The light would make the wall’s illumina: The Moon’s changing illumination is not caused by a rough wall.
why.The light would pass through the wall wi: The wall is described as reflecting light, not transmitting it.

activities.explanation: Rough surfaces reflect light.

activities.context: A student is planning a classroom display about light. The display includes a flat mirror, a curved mirror, a lens, and a rough wall. Light rays reflect from both kinds of mirror, and light bends when it passes through the lens. The rough wall also reflects light. The student draws the Moon’s illuminated part at different positions of Earth, Moon, and Sun. These changes produce the Moon’s visible phases, which humans used to create the first calendars.
activities.prompt: The student wants to make an early calendar based on the display. What should the student use?
options: The Moon’s pattern of changing illumination.
The oxygen in Earth’s atmosphere.
The light reflected from the classroom’s rough wall.
The bending of light through corrective glasses.

Atmospheric oxygen is not the changing pattern used for those calendars.
why.The light reflected from the classroom’s: Reflection from the rough wall does not produce the Moon’s phases.
why.The bending of light through corrective: Corrective glasses help vision but do not provide the lunar pattern used in calendars.

activities.explanation: Humans used the Moon’s phases to create the first calendars.

activities.prompt:
Assertion (A): The visible phases of the Moon change as the positions of Earth, Moon, and Sun change.
Reason (R): The Moon’s illuminated part changes with those positions, producing the visible phases.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.
activities.explanation: The reason directly explains why the visible phases change.

activities.prompt:
Assertion (A): Earth’s atmosphere provides the oxygen people breathe.
Reason (R): Human activities can cause small changes in Earth’s temperature.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.
activities.explanation: Both statements are true, but temperature changes do not explain how the atmosphere provides oxygen.

activities.prompt: Explain the difference between how light behaves at a mirror and how it behaves at a lens.
activities.answer: Light rays reflect from flat and curved mirrors. When light reaches a lens, however, it bends as it passes through. The difference is therefore between reflection from a surface and bending during passage through a lens. Corrective glasses help many people to see clearly, while rough surfaces and the Moon also reflect light. This comparison shows that mirrors and rough surfaces reflect light, whereas a lens bends it as the light passes through.
points: Mirrors reflect light rays.
Both flat and curved mirrors reflect light.
A lens bends light that passes through it.
Rough surfaces reflect light, while corrective glasses help people see clearly.
activities.explanation: Compare your answer with the points a marker looks for.

activities.context: In a home kitchen, a family becomes curious about why one rolled puri takes longer to puff up than another. They write a scientific question: “Does dough thickness affect the time taken to puff up?” They plan to change only the thickness of the rolled dough while keeping its size and the oil temperature the same. They measure how many seconds each puri takes to puff up, and they keep notes of everything they see and sense.
activities.prompt: What should the family do to test the effect of dough thickness without mixing it with another change?
options: Change only the thickness and keep the size and oil temperature the same.
Change the thickness and oil temperature together while keeping the size the same.
Change only the oil temperature and keep the thickness and size the same.
Change the thickness, size, and oil temperature together in one investigation.

why.Change the thickness and oil temperature: Changing two things would make the effect difficult to identify.
why.Change only the oil temperature and keep: Oil temperature would be a second change.
why.Change the thickness, size, and oil temp: Changing everything together would not show which change mattered.

activities.explanation: Changing only thickness follows the rule for a good experiment.

boss.title: Chapter challenge: Exploring the Investigative World of Science

activities.title: Changing Ideas
activities.prompt: What can happen when deeper exploration opens new questions?
options: Scientific ideas may keep changing
All questions will disappear
Experiments become unnecessary
New facts stop appearing
activities.explanation: Deeper exploration can open new questions. Our scientific ideas may change as we explore further.

activities.title: Living Connections
activities.prompt: What do relationships between organisms and their environments form?
options: Complex ecosystems
Electric motors
Strong winds
Chemical compounds
activities.explanation: These relationships form ecosystems. Ecosystems support life on Earth.

activities.prompt: Particles can move freely in solid materials.
activities.explanation: Particles cannot move much in solids. They can move freely in gases.

activities.prompt: Both rough surfaces and the Moon reflect light.
activities.explanation: Yes. Rough surfaces and the Moon both reflect light.

activities.title: Spread of Force
activities.prompt: Pressure describes how ______ is spread over an object.
activities.hint: Think about what causes pressure.
activities.explanation: Pressure tells us how force is spread over an object.

activities.title: Science Connections
activities.prompt: Match each idea from the chapter to its correct meaning.
activities.explanation: These ideas connect living things, electricity and pressure. Each pair shows an important link.

activities.title: How Moon Phases Appear
activities.prompt: Put these Moon ideas in order.
items: Earth, Moon and Sun are in different positions.
These changes produce the visible phases.
activities.explanation: Different positions change the Moon’s illuminated part. These changes produce the visible Moon phases.

chapters.title: The Invisible Living World
chapters.summary: In this chapter: seeing the invisible world; inside a cell; cell shapes and levels of organisation; microorganisms and a cleaner environment.

lessons.title: Seeing the Invisible World

activities.prompt: How can we see a whole hidden world through a tiny lens?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: A Hidden World of Tiny Things
activities.body: Your eyes cannot see objects that are too small. Tools such as magnifying glasses and microscopes help us see tiny things. A microscope reveals a hidden world of tiny living creatures. All plants and animals are called organisms. The first lens was shaped like a lentil seed. Later, scientists made more powerful lenses. A flask of water can even work like a magnifying glass.
keyPoints: Human eyes miss objects below a certain size.
Magnifying glasses and microscopes reveal tiny things.
All plants and animals are organisms.
activities.explanation: These ideas explain how people see a hidden world of tiny things.

activities.prompt: Can a flask full of water help me read tiny print?
steps: My eyes cannot see objects below a certain size.
A flask filled with water can work like a magnifying glass.
Magnifying glasses help people see tiny things.
Therefore, the flask can help me see tiny print more clearly.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.title: Great Lenses Reveal Tiny Creatures
activities.body: Robert Hooke’s microscope made things look 200 to 300 times bigger. In 1665 CE, he published his book Micrographia. He also saw small spaces in cork cells. Antonie van Leeuwenhoek made lenses for more useful microscopes. These tools helped people explore a hidden world of tiny living creatures.
keyPoints: Hooke published Micrographia in 1665 CE.
His microscope made things look 200 to 300 times bigger.
Leeuwenhoek made lenses for more useful microscopes.
activities.explanation: These tools revealed tiny living creatures that human eyes could not see.

activities.prompt: Human eyes can see every object, however small.
activities.explanation: Human eyes cannot see objects below a certain size. Tools help us see them.

activities.prompt: The first lens was shaped like a lentil seed.
activities.explanation: The first lens had a shape like a lentil seed.

activities.prompt: All plants and animals are called ______.
activities.hint: This word includes both plants and animals.
activities.explanation: All plants and animals share the name organisms.

activities.prompt: What can a flask filled with water work like?
options: A magnifying glass
A microscope
A cork cell
A tiny creature
activities.explanation: A flask filled with water can work like a magnifying glass.

activities.prompt: Match each clue with the correct detail.
activities.explanation: The pairs identify Hooke’s book, date, microscope, cork observation, and Leeuwenhoek.

activities.prompt: Whose microscope could make things look 200 to 300 times bigger?
options: Robert Hooke's microscope
Antonie van Leeuwenhoek's microscope
The first lens
The water flask
activities.explanation: The lesson states that Hooke’s microscope could magnify things 200 to 300 times.

activities.prompt: Put the steps in order from an unseen object to a hidden discovery.
items: An object below a certain size
Use a magnifying glass or microscope
Reveal a hidden world of tiny living creatures
activities.explanation: This order moves from something unseen to the tiny living creatures revealed.

activities.prompt: The first lens looked like a lentil seed. A tiny object still cannot be seen. What should scientists try next?
options: Use a water flask, because it always works better than any lens.
Stop using lenses, because human eyes can already see tiny things.
Make the lenses more powerful, because tiny viewing needs better tools.
Keep the lenses unchanged, because every tiny object is already visible.

why.Use a water flask, because it always wor: This wrongly treats a helpful water lens as better than every lens.
why.Stop using lenses, because human eyes ca: This wrongly ignores that eyes cannot see objects below a certain size.
why.Keep the lenses unchanged, because every: This wrongly assumes human eyes can see objects below the usual size limit.

activities.explanation: Scientists later made lenses more powerful to improve tiny viewing.

activities.prompt: Tiny creatures hide in clear water. What tool can show them?
options: Use a microscope, because it revealed a hidden world of tiny creatures.
Use the first lens, because it reveals every hidden living creature.
Use ordinary eyes, because hidden creatures are always easy to see.
Use a book, because printed pages show living creatures better.

why.Use the first lens, because it reveals e: This wrongly assumes the earliest lens was as useful as later microscopes.
why.Use ordinary eyes, because hidden creatu: This wrongly ignores the size limit of human eyes.
why.Use a book, because printed pages show l: This wrongly treats printed words as a tool for seeing actual creatures.

activities.explanation: The microscope revealed the hidden world of tiny living creatures.

lessons.sceneCaption: Hooke’s detailed flea illustration revealed a hidden world too small for unaided eyes.

lessons.title: Inside a Cell

activities.prompt: What are the tiny parts inside a cell?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: The Main Parts of a Cell
activities.body: A cell is a complex structure with many specialised parts. It has three main parts: the cell membrane, cytoplasm and nucleus. The membrane encloses the cytoplasm and nucleus. The cytoplasm contains many other parts and compounds. The nucleus controls cell activities and growth. Most life processes take place in the cytoplasm.
keyPoints: The three main parts are the cell membrane, cytoplasm and nucleus.
The nucleus controls cell activities and growth.
Most life processes take place in the cytoplasm.
activities.explanation: The cell membrane encloses the cytoplasm and nucleus.

activities.prompt: A child sees a firm onion peel and a green leaf. What explains both?
steps: The rectangular onion cells fit together because they are closely arranged.
The onion peel feels firm because the cell wall gives strength.
Green parts get their colour because chloroplasts contain chlorophyll.
So plant cells have separate parts for support and colour.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.prompt: Which description matches onion peel cells?
options: Rectangular and close together
Round and far apart
Triangular and neatly spaced
Oval and widely spread
activities.explanation: Onion peel cells are rectangular. They are also closely arranged.

activities.prompt: The cell membrane encloses the cytoplasm and the ______.
activities.hint: This part controls the activities and growth of a cell.
activities.explanation: The cell membrane encloses both the cytoplasm and the nucleus.

activities.prompt: Cheek cells form the inner lining of your mouth.
activities.explanation: Cheek cells form the inner lining of your mouth.

activities.prompt: Match each cell part with its job.
pairs: Gives a plant cell rigidity and strength
Stores substances and helps keep shape
activities.explanation: The nucleus controls activities and growth. The membrane encloses the cytoplasm and nucleus. The wall gives strength, and the vacuole stores substances.

activities.prompt: Which part contains many other parts and compounds of the cell?
options: Cytoplasm
Nucleus
Cell wall
Vacuole
activities.explanation: Cytoplasm contains many other parts and compounds of the cell.

activities.prompt: Plant cells contain tiny rod-shaped parts called ______.
activities.hint: These tiny parts are found inside plant cells.
activities.explanation: These tiny rod-shaped parts in plant cells are called plastids.

activities.prompt: A plant cell loses part of its cell wall. What happens next?
options: It will become less rigid and strong.
It will gain more rigidity and strength.
It will store more substances inside.
It will control more cell activities.

This mistake thinks losing the wall would add strength.
This mistake mixes up the cell wall with the vacuole.
This mistake mixes up the cell wall with the nucleus.

activities.explanation: The cell wall gives plant cells rigidity and strength.

activities.prompt: A cell's nucleus is damaged. What is most likely to happen?
options: Its growth and activities may be affected.
Its stored substances may all disappear.
Its cell wall may become weaker.
It may lose all of its chlorophyll.

This mistake mixes up nucleus control with vacuole storage.
This mistake mixes up nucleus control with cell wall strength.
This mistake mixes up nucleus control with chlorophyll colour.

activities.explanation: The nucleus controls the activities and growth of a cell.

activities.prompt: A plant cell's vacuole cannot store substances well. What happens next?
options: It may not keep its shape well.
It may lose control of its growth.
It may gain more cell wall strength.
It may make much less chlorophyll.

This mistake confuses vacuole storage with nucleus control.
This mistake confuses shape keeping with cell wall strength.
This mistake confuses vacuole storage with chlorophyll making.

activities.explanation: The vacuole stores substances and helps the cell keep its shape.

activities.prompt: Chloroplasts contain chlorophyll. Why is blaming cell walls for green wrong?
options: Chlorophyll in chloroplasts makes plants green.
Strength in cell walls makes plants green.
Control by the nucleus makes plants green.
Storage in vacuoles makes plants green.

why.Strength in cell walls makes plants gree: This mistake confuses cell wall strength with green colour.
why.Control by the nucleus makes plants gree: This mistake confuses nucleus control with green colour.
This mistake confuses vacuole storage with green colour.

activities.explanation: Chlorophyll in chloroplasts makes plants green.

lessons.sceneAlt: A microscopic view of onion epidermal cells.
lessons.sceneCaption: Microscopic view of onion epidermal cells.

lessons.title: Cell Shapes and Levels of Organisation

activities.prompt: Why do cells have different shapes, and how do they work together?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: How Cells Are Organised
activities.body: Cell shape, size and structure help cells perform specific jobs. Inner cheek cells are thin and flat, while nerve cells carry messages. Muscle cells push food down the food pipe. Stomach cells can make digestive juices and acid. Plant cells can be rectangular, elongated, oval or tube-like. Some long plant cells carry water. Similar cells form tissues. Tissues form organs. Organs form organ systems. Organ systems together make an organism.
keyPoints: Cell shape, size and structure help specific functions.
Different cells have different jobs.
Similar cells form tissues, organs, organ systems and organisms.
activities.explanation: Each cell shape suits a job, and cells work together in larger groups.

activities.prompt: How is a complete organism organised from its very first cell?
steps: A multicellular organism begins as one egg cell, showing its first cell.
Similar cells form a tissue, so cells with one kind work together.
Different tissues form an organ, so one organ joins different tissue kinds.
Organs work together in organ systems; all systems make a complete organism.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.title: Inner Cheek Cells
activities.prompt: What shape are inner cheek cells?
options: Thin and flat
Rectangular and tube-like
Elongated and oval
Nerve and muscle
activities.explanation: Inner cheek cells are described as thin and flat in your lesson.

activities.title: Join the Tissues
activities.prompt: Different tissues come together to form a ______.
activities.hint: Choose a short word.
activities.explanation: Different tissues join together to make an organ.

activities.title: Cells and Their Work
activities.prompt: Match each cell with its shape or function.
pairs: Push food down the food pipe
activities.explanation: Each pair shows a cell and its stated function or shape.

activities.title: An Organ System
activities.prompt: Which group works together as an organ system?
options: Several organs
Different tissues
A group of similar cells
Cell shapes and sizes
activities.explanation: An organ system is formed when several organs work together.

activities.title: Levels of Organisation
activities.prompt: Put the levels of organisation in the correct order.
items: A group of similar cells forms a tissue.
Several organs work together as an organ system.
activities.explanation: Cells form tissues, organs, organ systems and finally a complete organism.

activities.title: The Complete Organism
activities.prompt: What do all organ systems together make?
options: A complete organism
An organ system
An organ
A tissue
activities.explanation: All organ systems working together make a complete organism.

activities.prompt: A plant must move water through its body. Which cell shape fits this job best?
options: A long, tube-like plant cell shape.
A short, oval plant cell shape.
A wide, rectangular plant cell shape.
A thin, flat inner cheek shape.

Oval cells may occur, but they are not linked to water carrying.
Rectangular cells may occur, but water carrying is not linked to them.
Thin flat cells are inner cheek cells, not water-carrying plant cells.

activities.explanation: Long plant cells can carry water throughout the plant.

activities.prompt: Similar cells form a tissue. Different tissues form an organ. What comes next?
options: Several organs work together in an organ system.
One similar cell forms a tissue.
Different tissues form a single organ.
One egg cell forms an organism.

This describes the earlier step from cells to a tissue.
This describes the earlier step from tissues to an organ.
This describes the beginning of a multicellular organism.

activities.explanation: Several organs working together form an organ system.

activities.prompt: All organ systems work together. Which two facts describe the result?
options: It is a complete organism that began as one egg cell.
It is a tissue that began as one nerve cell.
It is an organ that began as many organs.
It is an organ system that began as one tissue.

why.It is a tissue that began as one nerve c: A tissue contains similar cells, and it is not made of all systems.
why.It is an organ that began as many organs: An organ comes from tissues, not from many organs.
why.It is an organ system that began as one: An organ system has several organs, not one tissue.

activities.explanation: All organ systems make a complete organism, which begins as one egg cell.

lessons.sceneCaption: Human inner-cheek cells viewed through a microscope.

lessons.title: Microorganisms and a Cleaner Environment

activities.prompt: How can tiny organisms help us keep our environment cleaner?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: Meet the Microorganisms
activities.body: Microorganisms are tiny living organisms with only one or very few cells. Bacteria and Amoeba are examples. Some fungi and algae have many cells. They live in water, soil, air and inside our bodies. A microscope magnifies them 100 to 400 times. Fungi and bacteria can slowly turn plant waste into nutrient-rich manure.
keyPoints: Microorganisms can have one cell or many cells.
They live in water, soil, air and bodies.
Fungi and bacteria can make manure from plant waste.
activities.explanation: Some microorganisms have one cell, while others have many cells.

activities.prompt: Why might a soil suspension look empty even though it contains tiny creatures?
steps: A soil suspension can contain tiny creatures, so it may not look empty.
Our eyes miss these creatures because they are too small to see.
A microscope helps because it magnifies microorganisms 100 to 400 times.
Therefore, a microscope can reveal life hidden from ordinary sight.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.title: Tiny Helpers
activities.body: Fungi and bacteria can slowly turn plant waste into manure with useful nutrients. Bacteria in our intestine help us digest food. Microorganisms differ in shape, size and structure. Some have one cell, while some fungi and algae have many cells. They live in water, soil, air and inside our bodies. A microscope magnifies them 100 to 400 times.
keyPoints: Bacteria help us digest food.
Microorganisms differ in shape, size and structure.
Plant waste can become nutrient-rich manure.
activities.explanation: Bacteria can help digestion, while fungi and bacteria can make manure.

activities.prompt: Amoeba is a unicellular microorganism.
activities.explanation: The lesson names Amoeba as a unicellular microorganism.

activities.prompt: Match each thing with what the lesson says it does or is.
pairs: Multiply after entering a living cell
activities.explanation: Each pair connects a thing with its role. Bacteria and fungi slowly make manure from plant waste.

activities.prompt: Fungi and bacteria can slowly turn plant waste into nutrient-rich ______.
activities.hint: This nutrient-rich material comes from plant waste.
activities.explanation: The lesson says fungi and bacteria slowly turn plant waste into manure.

activities.prompt: Which pair are unicellular microorganisms?
options: Fungi and algae
Bacteria and Amoeba
Water and soil
Viruses and cells
activities.explanation: Bacteria and Amoeba are both unicellular microorganisms.

activities.prompt: All microorganisms are multicellular.
activities.explanation: Bacteria and Amoeba are unicellular. Some fungi and algae are multicellular.

activities.prompt: A gardener leaves plant waste. Which group can slowly turn it into nutrient-rich manure?
options: Bacteria and Amoeba
Water and soil
Fungi and bacteria
Algae and viruses
activities.explanation: Fungi and bacteria can slowly turn plant waste into nutrient-rich manure.

activities.prompt: You look at clear pond water and see nothing. What could a microscope show?
options: Microorganisms too small for your eyes to see.
Bacteria and fungi living only inside our bodies.
Amoeba and algae living only in the soil.
Plant waste turning into nutrient-rich manure there.

why.Bacteria and fungi living only inside ou: This mistake mixes up the places where microorganisms live.
why.Amoeba and algae living only in the soil: This mistake gives microorganisms only one possible habitat.
why.Plant waste turning into nutrient-rich m: This mistake describes waste changes instead of tiny living things.

activities.explanation: This is right because water can contain tiny microorganisms.

activities.prompt: A child sees one microorganism. Which observation shows it is multicellular?
options: Several cells are visible inside the microorganism.
Only one cell is visible inside the microorganism.
Its shape changes while the microorganism moves.
It lives in water and cannot be seen directly.

why.Only one cell is visible inside the micr: This mistake confuses unicellular and multicellular microorganisms.
why.Its shape changes while the microorganis: This mistake treats different shapes as proof of many cells.
why.It lives in water and cannot be seen dir: This mistake uses a habitat instead of the number of cells.

activities.explanation: This is right because a multicellular microorganism has more than one cell.

activities.prompt: To compare soil suspension with plain water, what is the fairest test?
options: Use equal samples and the same microscope magnification.
Use more soil suspension and a stronger microscope.
Use plain water and look with a weaker microscope.
Use equal samples but change magnification for each.

why.Use more soil suspension and a stronger: This mistake changes two things at once during the test.
why.Use plain water and look with a weaker m: This mistake compares only plain water and changes the magnification.
why.Use equal samples but change magnificati: This mistake keeps samples equal but changes the magnification.

activities.explanation: This is right because equal samples and one magnification keep the test fair.

lessons.title: Microorganisms in Our Food

activities.prompt: What might make dough puff up and milk turn tangy?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: Microorganisms at Work
activities.body: Yeast is a microorganism and belongs to the fungi group. It grows well in warm conditions. Yeast respires and breaks down food to release energy. Carbon dioxide bubbles make dough soft and fluffy. Yeast also produces a little alcohol, which changes the dough’s smell. Lactobacillus helps ferment batter for foods such as idli and dosa. Rhizobium lives in swollen nodules on legume roots and makes nitrogen from the air useful for plants.
keyPoints: Yeast belongs to the fungi group.
Lactobacillus helps ferment batter.
Rhizobium makes nitrogen useful for plants.
activities.explanation: Microorganisms help change food and help plants use nitrogen.

activities.prompt: Why does dough puff up and smell different after it rests?
steps: Yeast grows well in warm conditions, so warm dough helps it grow.
It respires and breaks down food, releasing energy.
Carbon dioxide forms bubbles, making the dough soft and fluffy.
It also makes alcohol, so the dough smells different.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.title: Yeast’s Group
activities.prompt: Which group does yeast belong to?
options: Fungi
Bacteria
Plants
Minerals
activities.explanation: Yeast belongs to the group of microorganisms called fungi.

activities.title: A Microorganism
activities.prompt: Yeast is a microorganism.
activities.explanation: Yes. Yeast is a microorganism.

activities.title: Fill the Group
activities.prompt: Yeast belongs to the group called ______.
activities.hint: This group includes mushroom-like organisms.
activities.explanation: Yeast belongs to the fungi group.

activities.title: Match the Work
activities.prompt: Match each microorganism with its work.
pairs: Carbon dioxide bubbles make dough soft and fluffy
Makes nitrogen from air useful for plants
activities.explanation: Each microorganism has a special job described in the lesson.

activities.title: What Happens in Dough
activities.prompt: Put these changes in order.
activities.explanation: Carbon dioxide bubbles help dough become soft and fluffy.

activities.title: Lactobacillus’s Food
activities.prompt: What does Lactobacillus feed on?
options: Milk sugar
Air nitrogen
Dough bubbles
Food energy
activities.explanation: Lactobacillus feeds on milk sugar and multiplies.

activities.title: Nitrogen for Plants
activities.prompt: Rhizobium makes nitrogen from the air less useful for plants.
activities.explanation: No. Rhizobium makes nitrogen from the air useful for plants.

activities.prompt: A baker leaves dough in a warm place. What will happen next?
options: The dough will rise and become soft and fluffy.
The dough will stay flat and become hard.
The dough will lose its bubbles and become dry.
The dough will release nitrogen for nearby plants.

why.The dough will stay flat and become hard: This ignores that yeast grows well and makes dough fluffy.
why.The dough will lose its bubbles and beco: Yeast makes bubbles rather than removing them from dough.
why.The dough will release nitrogen for near: Rhizobium, not yeast, traps nitrogen for plants.

activities.explanation: Warm conditions help yeast grow, and carbon dioxide makes bubbles.

activities.prompt: Dough smells different after resting with yeast. What caused the change?
options: Yeast produced a little alcohol in the dough.
Yeast trapped nitrogen from the air.
Yeast fed on milk sugar and multiplied.
Yeast released carbon dioxide into the dough.

Trapping nitrogen from air is Rhizobium's work.
Feeding on milk sugar describes Lactobacillus, not yeast.
why.Yeast released carbon dioxide into the d: Carbon dioxide forms bubbles rather than changing dough's smell.

activities.explanation: Yeast makes a little alcohol that changes dough's smell.

lessons.title: Microalgae and the Cell as Life’s Unit

activities.prompt: What can tiny cells do for us and for Earth?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: Meet Microalgae
activities.body: Microalgae live in water, soil, air and on trees. They use sunlight to make their own food. They produce more than half of Earth’s oxygen supply. Many animals that live in water eat them. Microalgae help clean water. Some are used as medicines. They can make biofuel. Spirulina is called a superfood because it has health benefits. You must conserve them to protect the environment.
keyPoints: Microalgae live in many places and make food using sunlight.
They produce more than half of Earth’s oxygen supply.
Spirulina has health benefits, so it is called a superfood.
activities.explanation: This is the big picture of microalgae and their uses.

activities.prompt: A pond has fewer microalgae, and aquatic animals are looking for food. What may happen?
steps: Microalgae are food for many aquatic animals, so their numbers affect food supply.
If their numbers fall, some aquatic animals may have less food.
Microalgae also help clean water, so fewer may mean less cleaning.
Therefore, conserving microalgae helps protect the environment.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.title: Cells Are Life’s Unit
activities.body: The cell is the unit from which living beings are made. Every living being has one cell or many cells. A unicellular organism has one cell and carries out every survival function in it. A multicellular organism has many cells that specialise and cooperate. Fungal cells have a cell wall, an outer layer, around the cell membrane. Bacteria have a nucleoid instead of a well-defined nucleus.
keyPoints: All living beings have one cell or many cells.
A unicellular organism carries out all survival functions in one cell.
Fungal cells have a wall around the membrane. Bacteria have a nucleoid.
activities.explanation: This connects cells with the different kinds of organisms.

activities.prompt: Microalgae can live on trees.
activities.explanation: Yes. Microalgae live in water, soil, air and on trees.

activities.prompt: What do microalgae use to make their own food?
options: water
sunlight
soil
air
activities.explanation: Microalgae use sunlight to make their own food.

activities.prompt: Microalgae produce more than ______ of Earth’s oxygen supply.
activities.hint: Think of a whole divided into two equal parts.
activities.explanation: Microalgae produce more than half of Earth’s oxygen supply.

activities.prompt: Match each group with its cell feature.
pairs: all survival functions in one cell
a cell wall around the cell membrane
a nucleoid instead of a well-defined nucleus
activities.explanation: A unicellular organism does everything in one cell. Fungal cells have a wall around the membrane. Bacteria have a nucleoid.

activities.prompt: Cells in multicellular organisms work separately and never cooperate.
activities.explanation: Cells in multicellular organisms specialise and cooperate with each other.

activities.prompt: Which pair of microalgae uses is correct?
options: clean water and biofuel
medicines and cell walls
nuclei and specialised cells
trees and cell membranes
activities.explanation: Microalgae help clean water and can be used to make biofuel.

activities.prompt: Microalgae make food using sunlight. Which test is fair?
options: Keep two ponds the same, but change only sunlight.
Keep two ponds the same, but change only soil.
Keep two ponds the same, but change only animals.
Keep two ponds the same, but change only water.

why.Keep two ponds the same, but change only: This changes soil too, so the test has two changes.
This changes animals too, so the test has two changes.
This changes water too, so the test has two changes.

activities.explanation: Correct: sunlight is the only thing changed.

activities.prompt: A pond loses many microalgae. What may happen to aquatic animals?
options: Some aquatic animals may have less food.
Some aquatic animals may have more food.
All aquatic animals may stop needing food.
Some aquatic animals may find cleaner water.

This reverses what happens when their food source falls.
why.All aquatic animals may stop needing foo: This wrongly treats less food as no need for food.
why.Some aquatic animals may find cleaner wa: This confuses cleaner water with a supply of animal food.

activities.explanation: Correct: many aquatic animals use microalgae as food.

activities.prompt: A farm makes biofuel from microalgae. What other benefit may happen?
options: The water may become cleaner during this process.
Aquatic animals may get more food after the harvest.
People may gain health benefits from this process.
Earth may gain more oxygen from this process.

why.Aquatic animals may get more food after: This wrongly assumes removal leaves more algae for animals.
why.People may gain health benefits from thi: This confuses biofuel making with using algae as supplements.
why.Earth may gain more oxygen from this pro: This wrongly assumes harvesting will increase oxygen production.

activities.explanation: Correct: microalgae help clean water and can make biofuel.

activities.prompt: People remove many microalgae from a pond. Why is this a problem?
options: It can harm animals and the environment.
It can make animals need less food.
It can stop oxygen production in the pond.
It can turn the pond completely clean.

This reverses the effect of losing an animal food source.
why.It can stop oxygen production in the pon: Fewer microalgae may reduce oxygen, not stop all production.
Removing algae may reduce water cleaning, not complete it.

activities.explanation: Correct: microalgae must be conserved to protect the environment.
