activities.context: At a school science lesson, a student looks at a tiny object that is too small to see clearly with the eyes alone. The teacher shows a magnifying glass and then a microscope. The lesson explains that the first lens was shaped like a lentil seed, that later lenses became more powerful, and that Hooke’s microscope made objects appear 200 to 300 times bigger. The student also learns that a flask filled with water can work like a magnifying glass.
activities.prompt: The teacher does not want to use the classroom microscope. What should the teacher do to help the student see the tiny object more clearly?
options: Use a water-filled flask as an enlarging lens.
Ask the classroom microscope to make the image smaller.
Look at the object with unaided eyes and expect a clearer image.
Use a lens shaped like a lentil seed and expect it to behave like the later powerful lenses.

why.Ask the classroom microscope to make the: A microscope helps by making objects look bigger.
why.Look at the object with unaided eyes and: Unaided eyes cannot see all tiny objects.
why.Use a lens shaped like a lentil seed and: The first lens’s shape does not give it the power of later lenses.

activities.explanation: A water-filled flask can work as a magnifying glass.

activities.context: At a school science lesson, a student looks at a tiny object that is too small to see clearly with the eyes alone. The teacher shows a magnifying glass and then a microscope. The lesson explains that the first lens was shaped like a lentil seed, that later lenses became more powerful, and that Hooke’s microscope made objects appear 200 to 300 times bigger. The student also learns that a flask filled with water can work like a magnifying glass.
activities.prompt: If scientists had not made lenses more powerful, what would likely have happened to the study of tiny living things?
options: Building and using useful microscopes for tiny living things would have been harder.
Scientists would have found it easier to see tiny living creatures without lenses.
Scientists would have needed no later improvements in lens power.
Scientists would have used water-filled flasks for every observation of living creatures.

why.Scientists would have found it easier to: Unaided eyes cannot see objects below a certain size.
why.Scientists would have needed no later im: If power had not improved, later improvements would have been needed.
why.Scientists would have used water-filled: Water-filled flasks could enlarge views but were not described as full microscopes.

activities.explanation: More powerful lenses helped make useful microscopes.

activities.prompt:
Assertion (A): Scientists later made lenses more powerful.
Reason (R): The later lenses kept exactly the same power as the first lens.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.
activities.explanation: The assertion is true, but the reason is false because later lenses became more powerful.

activities.prompt: Explain how improvements in lenses changed what people could see.
activities.answer: Human eyes cannot see objects below a certain size, so seeing tiny things required better tools. The first lens was shaped like a lentil seed. Later, scientists made lenses more powerful. Magnifying glasses and microscopes then helped people see tiny things, and the microscope revealed a hidden world of tiny living creatures. Hooke’s microscope made objects look 200 to 300 times bigger. These improvements allowed smaller details to become visible than unaided eyes could show.
points: States that eyes have a size limit
Explains that lens power increased
Mentions magnifying glasses and microscopes
Explains that a hidden world became visible
activities.explanation: Compare your answer with the points a marker looks for.

activities.context: A student looks at onion peel cells and sees many rectangular cells packed closely together. The student also collects cheek cells from the inner lining of the mouth. One onion cell shows a firm outer layer, while the cheek cell does not. Another plant-cell view shows tiny rod-shaped structures and green colour. The student draws the cells and asks which parts control growth, carry out life processes, and explain the green colour.
activities.prompt: If the firm outer layer of an onion cell became weaker, what would the student expect next?
options: The cell would lose some rigidity and strength.
The cell would control its growth less effectively.
The cell would carry out fewer life processes.
The cell would be less able to store substances.

why.The cell would control its growth less e: Control of activities and growth belongs to the nucleus.
why.The cell would carry out fewer life proc: Most life processes take place in the cytoplasm.
why.The cell would be less able to store sub: Storage of substances is helped by the vacuole.

activities.explanation: Supporting the cell is the job of the cell wall.

activities.context: A student looks at onion peel cells and sees many rectangular cells packed closely together. The student also collects cheek cells from the inner lining of the mouth. One onion cell shows a firm outer layer, while the cheek cell does not. Another plant-cell view shows tiny rod-shaped structures and green colour. The student draws the cells and asks which parts control growth, carry out life processes, and explain the green colour.
activities.prompt: What should the student predict if a plant cell's vacuole could no longer store substances?
options: The cell would have more difficulty keeping its shape.
The cell would become less rigid.
Its growth would be controlled less well.
It would carry out more life processes.

Rigidity and strength are provided by the cell wall.
why.Its growth would be controlled less well: The nucleus controls activities and growth.
Most life processes take place in the cytoplasm.

activities.explanation: The vacuole helps a plant cell keep its shape.

activities.prompt:
Assertion (A): A plant cell with a weaker cell wall would have less rigidity and strength.
Reason (R): The cell wall normally gives a plant cell rigidity and strength.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.
activities.explanation: Both statements are true, and the reason explains the assertion.

activities.prompt:
Assertion (A): Most life processes in a cell occur in the cytoplasm.
Reason (R): They occur there because the nucleus contains chlorophyll.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.
activities.explanation: The assertion is true, but chlorophyll is found in chloroplasts rather than the nucleus.

activities.prompt: How do the main parts of a plant cell help it carry out its functions?
activities.answer: The cell membrane encloses the cytoplasm and nucleus. The cytoplasm contains many other parts and compounds, and most life processes take place there. The nucleus controls the cell's activities and growth. The cell wall gives a plant cell rigidity and strength, while a vacuole stores substances and helps keep the cell's shape. Plant cells also contain tiny rod-shaped plastids. Chloroplasts contain chlorophyll, which makes plants green. Together, these specialised parts allow the cell to carry out processes, control activity, stay supported, store materials, and show green colour.
points: Describes the membrane, cytoplasm, and nucleus.
Explains the roles of the cell wall and vacuole.
Identifies plastids and the role of chloroplasts.
Shows how the specialised parts work together.
activities.explanation: Compare your answer with the points a marker looks for.

activities.prompt:
Assertion (A): Different tissues come together to form an organ.
Reason (R): Tissues contain groups of similar cells, and organs contain different tissues.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.
activities.explanation: Both statements are true, and the reason explains how tissues are organised into organs.

activities.prompt:
Assertion (A): Several organs working together form an organ system.
Reason (R): An organ system is made from only one kind of tissue.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.
activities.explanation: The assertion is true, but the reason is false because an organ contains different tissues.

activities.prompt: Explain how the case shows that cells can perform different functions.
activities.answer: The case shows that cells can have different specific functions. Muscle cells pushed the food down the food pipe, while some stomach cells produced digestive juices and acid. A cell’s shape, size and structure help it perform its function, so cells with different structures can do different jobs. These actions are part of the organism’s organisation. The case therefore links the work of individual cells with the larger levels of organisation, ending with all organ systems together making a complete organism.
points: Muscle cells push food down the food pipe.
Some stomach cells produce digestive juices and acid.
Shape, size and structure help cells perform functions.
Organ systems together make a complete organism.
activities.explanation: Compare your answer with the points a marker looks for.

activities.prompt:
Assertion (A): Bacteria and Amoeba are unicellular microorganisms.
Reason (R): They each consist of only one cell.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.
activities.explanation: Having only one cell explains why bacteria and Amoeba are called unicellular.

activities.prompt:
Assertion (A): All microorganisms are unicellular.
Reason (R): Some fungi and algae are multicellular microorganisms.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.
activities.explanation: The counterexample shows that not every microorganism has only one cell.

activities.prompt: Explain the difference between unicellular and multicellular microorganisms, using examples from the lesson.
activities.answer: Microorganisms are tiny living organisms, and some have only one cell or very few cells. Bacteria and Amoeba are unicellular microorganisms, meaning each has only one cell. Other microorganisms have many cells: some fungi and algae are multicellular microorganisms. Microorganisms also differ in their shape, size and structure. Therefore, they should not all be described as identical or as having the same number of cells.
points: Microorganisms are tiny living organisms.
Bacteria and Amoeba are unicellular.
Some fungi and algae are multicellular.
Microorganisms differ in shape, size and structure.
activities.explanation: Compare your answer with the points a marker looks for.

activities.context: A baker mixes dough and keeps it in a warm place so that yeast can grow well. The dough later becomes soft and fluffy, and its smell changes. In another kitchen, Lactobacillus helps ferment batter for idli and dosa. At the same time, Rhizobium bacteria live in swollen nodules on legume roots, where they trap nitrogen from the air and make it useful for plants.
activities.prompt: If the baker moves the dough from the warm place to a cool place, what should the baker expect?
options: Yeast would probably grow less well.
Yeast would probably grow better than before.
Yeast would probably grow at the same rate.
Yeast would probably grow much more quickly.

why.Yeast would probably grow better than be: Cooler conditions do not match the stated warm conditions for good growth.
why.Yeast would probably grow at the same ra: A change in temperature can affect how well yeast grows.
why.Yeast would probably grow much more quic: Faster growth would not be expected from the change described.

activities.explanation: Yeast is stated to grow well in warm conditions.

activities.context: A baker mixes dough and keeps it in a warm place so that yeast can grow well. The dough later becomes soft and fluffy, and its smell changes. In another kitchen, Lactobacillus helps ferment batter for idli and dosa. At the same time, Rhizobium bacteria live in swollen nodules on legume roots, where they trap nitrogen from the air and make it useful for plants.
activities.prompt: Why did the dough’s smell change?
options: Yeast produced a little alcohol.
Yeast produced carbon dioxide.
Lactobacillus fed on milk sugar.
Rhizobium trapped nitrogen from the air.

Carbon dioxide is responsible for bubbles in the dough.
Lactobacillus feeding on milk sugar does not explain this dough’s smell change.
Rhizobium traps nitrogen for plants rather than changing dough.

activities.explanation: Yeast produces a little alcohol that changes the dough’s smell.

activities.prompt:
Assertion (A): Yeast can grow well in warm conditions.
Reason (R): The dough was kept in a warm place, so yeast had suitable conditions to grow well.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.
activities.explanation: The warm conditions in the reason explain why yeast could grow well.

boss.title: Chapter challenge: The Invisible Living World

activities.prompt: Which shape was the first lens?
options: A lentil seed
A glass bead
A metal cup
A paper cone
activities.explanation: The first lens was shaped like a lentil seed.

activities.prompt: Hooke’s microscope could make things look 200 to 300 times bigger.
activities.explanation: Hooke’s microscope could make tiny things look 200 to 300 times bigger.

activities.prompt: Match each cell part with its job.
pairs: Gives a plant cell rigidity and strength
Helps store substances and keep its shape
activities.explanation: Each cell part has a special job. Together, the parts help the cell work.

activities.prompt: All plants and animals are called ______.
activities.hint: This word includes every living thing.
activities.explanation: All plants and animals are called organisms.

activities.prompt: Put these organisation levels in order.
items: Several organs form an organ system
All organ systems form an organism
activities.explanation: A tissue forms from similar cells. Organs contain tissues, and organ systems contain organs.

activities.prompt: Viruses multiply after they enter a living cell.
activities.explanation: Viruses need a living cell. They multiply after entering that cell.

activities.prompt: Rhizobium bacteria live in swollen ______ on legume roots.
activities.hint: These are small swellings on the roots.
activities.explanation: Rhizobium bacteria live in swollen nodules on legume roots.

activities.prompt: Match each microorganism with its role.
pairs: Makes dough soft and fluffy with bubbles
Ferments batter for idli and dosa
Slowly turn plant waste into manure
activities.explanation: Microorganisms can help food, digestion and farming. Each microbe has a different role.

activities.prompt: Which statement is true about microalgae?
options: They live only inside animal bodies.
They make their own food using sunlight.
They feed on milk sugar.
They live in swollen root nodules.
activities.explanation: Microalgae use sunlight to make food. They also produce more than half of Earth’s oxygen supply.

chapters.title: Health: The Ultimate Treasure
chapters.summary: In this chapter: lesson 1: what health really means; lesson 2: healthy lifestyle habits; lesson 3: a clean environment supports health; lesson 4: signs, symptoms and types of disease.

lessons.title: Lesson 1: What Health Really Means

activities.prompt: What does being healthy really mean?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: Health Means More Than Feeling Well
activities.body: Health is more than being free from disease. It includes physical, mental and social wellbeing. Positive feelings and strong relationships matter too. Ayurveda describes true health as balance between body, mind and surroundings. Daily and seasonal routines help maintain balance. Fresh wholesome food suited to the body supports health. Exercise, cleanliness, sleep and a calm mind help too. Yoga, meditation and mindfulness can also help.
keyPoints: Health includes physical, mental and social wellbeing.
Positive feelings and strong relationships matter.
Healthy habits and practices support balance.
activities.explanation: Health works like a balance between your body, mind and surroundings.

activities.prompt: A child feels unhappy and has few strong relationships, despite no illness. What should we understand?
steps: Health includes mental and social wellbeing, not only illness.
Feeling positive and having strong relationships also matter for health.
This child needs support for feelings and relationships, not only the body.
Therefore, health is incomplete without mental and social wellbeing.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.prompt: What does health include?
options: Physical, mental and social wellbeing
Only the absence of disease
Only physical wellbeing
Only food and exercise
activities.explanation: Health includes all three parts of wellbeing. It is not only the absence of disease.

activities.prompt: Ayurveda describes true health as balance between body, ______ and surroundings.
activities.hint: Think of the three parts of this balance.
activities.explanation: The three parts are body, mind and surroundings. Together, they describe true health.

activities.prompt: Which choice matches how healthy people usually live?
options: Neglect your body and keep a positive mindset
Care for your body and keep a positive mindset
Care for your body and keep a negative mindset
Neglect your body and keep a negative mindset
activities.explanation: Healthy people usually care for their body. They also keep a positive mindset.

activities.prompt: Match each part of health with its example.
activities.explanation: Your body, mind and relationships are all important parts of health.

activities.prompt: Which person shows health in the broadest sense?
options: A person with no disease but weak relationships and negative thoughts
A person who feels positive but cannot adjust well to peers
A person with strong relationships who adjusts well to peers
A person who adjusts well to peers but cannot handle difficulty
activities.explanation: Strong relationships and adjusting well to peers both support health. Healthy people can also handle difficult situations well.

activities.prompt: Following daily and ______ routines helps maintain balance.
activities.hint: Think of the two kinds of routines named in the lesson.
activities.explanation: Daily and seasonal routines both help maintain balance between body, mind and surroundings.

activities.prompt: A child exercises, eats fresh food, sleeps, and keeps a calm mind. What is this child most likely to do?
options: Perform tasks efficiently and handle difficult situations well.
Need support for every ordinary task during the day.
Adjust poorly to peers and other members of society.
Stay healthy only when illness is completely absent.

why.Need support for every ordinary task dur: This mistake thinks good habits do not help perform tasks efficiently.
why.Adjust poorly to peers and other members: This mistake confuses social adjustment with physical wellbeing.
why.Stay healthy only when illness is comple: This mistake treats absence of illness as the only sign of health.

activities.explanation: This is right because routines support overall wellbeing and efficient action.

activities.prompt: A student wants to test whether a daily routine supports balance. Which plan is fairest?
options: Keep one routine steady and compare wellbeing with usual days.
Change food, sleep, exercise, and cleanliness all at once.
Skip routines and judge health only by illness.
Use yoga alone and ignore food, sleep, and rest.

why.Change food, sleep, exercise, and cleanl: This mistake changes many things together, so the result is unclear.
why.Skip routines and judge health only by i: This mistake judges balance by illness alone and skips routines.
why.Use yoga alone and ignore food, sleep, a: This mistake treats yoga as a replacement for other healthy supports.

activities.explanation: This is right because changing one routine gives a clearer test.

lessons.sceneAlt: A mother practices yoga with her young child as part of their daily routine.
lessons.sceneCaption: Family yoga brings love and peace while including a young child in daily routines.

sceneCredit.text: Yoga en familia by Ximenabc, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons
sceneCredit.creator: Ximenabc

lessons.title: Lesson 2: Healthy Lifestyle Habits

activities.prompt: What are some simple habits that can help you feel healthy and strong?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: Habits That Help You Stay Healthy
activities.body: Staying healthy needs nutritious food, good hygiene and other healthy habits. A balanced diet includes plenty of fruits, vegetables and whole grains. Processed, fatty and sugary foods and drinks should be avoided. Stay active through play, walking, running or cycling. Limit screen time, spend more time in nature and get enough sleep. Practise yoga and simple breathing exercises regularly. Avoid tobacco, alcohol and addictive drugs.
keyPoints: Eat plenty of fruits, vegetables and whole grains.
Stay active and limit screen time.
Sleep enough and avoid harmful substances.
activities.explanation: Small healthy choices can help your body and mind.

activities.prompt: A child eats fast food every day and skips breakfast. The child wonders how to eat better. What should change?
steps: Fast food every day is unhealthy, so it should be avoided.
Breakfast should not be skipped because skipping meals is unhealthy.
Processed, fatty and sugary foods and drinks should be avoided.
Meals should include fruits, vegetables and whole grains because this makes a balanced diet.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.title: Stay Active
activities.prompt: Which activity helps you stay active?
options: Playing outdoors
Using a digital screen
Sleeping very late
Skipping breakfast
activities.explanation: Playing outdoors helps you stay active. Walking, running and cycling are good choices too.

activities.title: Outdoor Activity
activities.prompt: Children can stay active by playing ______, walking, running or cycling.
activities.hint: Think about the place where you can play outside.
activities.explanation: Outdoor play is one way to stay active.

activities.title: Choose a Balanced Lunch
activities.prompt: Which packed lunch best fits a balanced diet?
options: Fruit, vegetables and whole grains
Chips, sweets and a sugary drink
Fast food and salty snacks
Processed meals and fatty foods
activities.explanation: A balanced diet contains plenty of fruits, vegetables and whole grains. Avoid processed, fatty and sugary choices.

activities.title: Healthy Choices and Benefits
activities.prompt: Match each healthy choice with its benefit.
pairs: Helps your body and mind rest
activities.explanation: Healthy choices support activity, rest, regular meals and good nutrition.

activities.title: Improve Your Routine
activities.prompt: You spend too much time on screens and sleep very late. What should you change?
options: Play outside and get enough sleep
Use screens late and skip meals
Choose sugary drinks every day
Try tobacco, alcohol and drugs
activities.explanation: Outdoor activity helps you stay active. Enough sleep gives your body and mind time to rest.

activities.title: Screens and Nature
activities.prompt: Screen time should be ______, while time in nature should be increased.
activities.hint: Screens should not take up too much of your time.
activities.explanation: Limiting screen time and spending more time in nature supports healthy habits.

activities.prompt: The child has fruit, vegetables and whole grains for lunch. The child also has a sugary drink. What should the child leave out?
options: Leave out the sugary drink, because sugary drinks should be avoided.
Leave out the whole grains, because balanced meals need fewer foods.
Leave out the vegetables, because only fruit is needed each day.
Leave out the sugary drink, because it helps make the meal balanced.

why.Leave out the whole grains, because bala: This mistakes a balanced diet for eating fewer kinds of food.
why.Leave out the vegetables, because only f: This mistakes fruit for the only food a balanced diet needs.
why.Leave out the sugary drink, because it h: This wrongly treats sugary drinks as part of a balanced diet.

activities.explanation: Sugary drinks should be avoided, so the drink should be left out.

activities.prompt: Enough sleep gives the body and mind time to rest and recover. The child plans to sleep very late. What should the child do instead?
options: Sleep enough, because the body and mind need time to recover.
Sleep later, because more screen time can take the place of rest.
Skip breakfast, because a late night makes breakfast unnecessary.
Play outside, because outdoor play removes the need for sleep.

why.Sleep later, because more screen time ca: This mistakes screen time for rest, but too much screen time is harmful.
why.Skip breakfast, because a late night mak: This mistakes skipping breakfast for healthy timing, but meals should not be skipped.
why.Play outside, because outdoor play remov: This mistakes outdoor play for a replacement for sleep.

activities.explanation: Enough sleep gives the body and mind time to rest and recover.

activities.prompt: Playing outdoors helps the child stay active. The child has a free afternoon. What should the child choose?
options: Play an outdoor game, because playing outdoors helps the child stay active.
Watch a video game, because sitting indoors can still count as activity.
Use a mobile phone, because screens can replace the outdoor activity.
Sit quietly, because resting is another name for physical activity.

why.Watch a video game, because sitting indo: This mistakes sitting and watching for physical activity.
why.Use a mobile phone, because screens can: This mistakes screen use for outdoor activity.
why.Sit quietly, because resting is another: This mistakes quiet sitting for active play.

activities.explanation: Playing outdoors is a healthy way for children to stay active.

activities.prompt: The child says sugary drinks are healthy because they taste nice. What is wrong with the reason?
options: Taste does not show whether a sugary drink is healthy.
Taste proves that a sugary drink contains whole grains.
Taste proves that a sugary drink is a balanced meal.
Taste proves that a sugary drink should be drunk daily.

why.Taste proves that a sugary drink contain: This wrongly treats a balanced diet as containing whole grains in drinks.
why.Taste proves that a sugary drink is a ba: This wrongly treats a balanced drink as a balanced meal.
why.Taste proves that a sugary drink should: This wrongly assumes tasty drinks should be drunk daily.

activities.explanation: Taste alone cannot show healthiness, and sugary drinks should be avoided.

activities.prompt: The child eats fast food every day. The child wants healthier habits. What should the child change?
options: Eat fast food less often, because eating it daily is unhealthy.
Eat fast food more often, because daily meals should stay the same.
Eat fast food every day, because avoiding it can prevent balance.
Eat fast food every day, because a balanced diet includes junk food.

why.Eat fast food more often, because daily: This mistakes staying the same for making meals healthier.
why.Eat fast food every day, because avoidin: This wrongly suggests daily junk food can create balance.
why.Eat fast food every day, because a balan: This wrongly thinks a balanced diet includes junk food.

activities.explanation: Eating fast food every day is unhealthy, so it should be avoided.

activities.prompt: Yoga and simple breathing exercises should be practised regularly. The child wants a bedtime routine. Which plan best follows the facts?
options: Practise simple breathing exercises, then sleep enough.
Use digital screens, then sleep very late.
Skip breakfast, then practise yoga before school.
Drink sugary drinks, then use digital screens.

why.Use digital screens, then sleep very lat: Digital screens should be limited, and sleeping very late is unhealthy.
why.Skip breakfast, then practise yoga befor: Skipping breakfast is unhealthy, even if yoga is practised.
why.Drink sugary drinks, then use digital sc: Sugary drinks should be avoided, and too much screen time is harmful.

activities.explanation: Regular breathing exercises and enough sleep follow the healthy habit facts.

lessons.sceneCaption: Girls wash up after playing soccer, showing how sports can support healthy choices and empowerment.

lessons.title: Lesson 3: A Clean Environment Supports Health

activities.prompt: How does keeping our surroundings clean help our bodies and minds?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: Clean surroundings help us feel well
activities.body: Keeping ourselves and our surroundings clean helps us stay healthy. Clean air and water support good health. Dirty places may contain flies and mosquitoes. Air pollution from vehicles and factories can cause coughing or asthma. The Air Quality Index shows how clean the air is. Cleaner environments help us feel better. Happy time with friends and family supports healthy minds. Loneliness can make us feel unwell in clean places.
keyPoints: Clean air and water support good health.
Pollution and dirty places can harm health.
Clean surroundings and happy relationships support wellbeing.
activities.explanation: A clean environment supports both our bodies and our minds.

activities.prompt: Children live near rubbish, dirty water, and vehicle traffic. What should their community clean, and why?
steps: Unhygienic places may contain flies and mosquitoes, so rubbish needs cleaning.
Living in polluted areas may cause more sickness, so traffic needs attention.
Clean air and water support good health, so dirty ones need attention.
We should clean ourselves and our surroundings because this helps children stay healthy.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.title: Keeping clean
activities.prompt: What should we keep clean?
options: Keeping our surroundings clean
Keeping only our bodies clean
Leaving rubbish everywhere
Ignoring dirty places
activities.explanation: We should keep both ourselves and our surroundings clean. This helps us stay healthy.

activities.title: Polluted areas
activities.prompt: People living in polluted areas may fall sick more often.
activities.explanation: Polluted areas can affect health. People living there may fall sick more often.

activities.title: The Air Quality Index
activities.prompt: The Air Quality Index shows how ______ the air is.
activities.hint: Think about the quality of the air around you.
activities.explanation: The Air Quality Index shows how clean the air is.

activities.title: Causes and supports
activities.prompt: Match each cause or support with its partner.
activities.explanation: Pollution and dirty places can affect health. Happy time supports healthy minds.

activities.title: Body and mind
activities.prompt: A clean environment helps our bodies but does not support our minds.
activities.explanation: Clean surroundings help us stay healthy and feel better. Happy relationships also support healthy minds.

activities.title: A harmful chain
activities.prompt: Put the harmful chain in order.
activities.explanation: Vehicles and factories can cause air pollution. Air pollution can cause coughing or asthma.

activities.title: Feelings and health
activities.prompt: Someone feels unwell in a clean place. What may explain this?
options: Loneliness can make someone feel unwell
A clean place always prevents illness
Friends and family have no health effect
Clean air and water cause loneliness
activities.explanation: Loneliness or upset feelings can make us feel unwell, even in a clean place.

activities.prompt: Before a picnic, a family checks the Air Quality Index. Which choice is sensible?
options: Choose the spot with cleaner air because it supports health.
Choose the spot with dirtier air because it supports health.
Choose the spot with cleaner air because it causes coughing.
Choose the spot with dirtier air because it causes asthma.

why.Choose the spot with dirtier air because: This mistake treats dirty air as healthy.
why.Choose the spot with cleaner air because: This mistake confuses cleaner air with pollution that causes coughing.
why.Choose the spot with dirtier air because: This mistake confuses dirtier air with pollution that causes asthma.

activities.explanation: This is right because clean air supports good health.

activities.prompt: How can a class fairly test whether cleaner surroundings support health?
options: Compare sickness in cleaner and polluted areas.
Compare sickness in one clean area only.
Compare how clean two areas look.
Ask whether clean areas look nicer.

This mistake tests only one place, so it cannot compare surroundings.
This mistake judges appearance instead of health.
This mistake asks about looks instead of illness.

activities.explanation: This is right because it compares health in different environments.

lessons.sceneAlt: An environmental health officer observes Anopheles mosquitoes and larvae inside a container used for breeding mosquitoes.
lessons.sceneCaption: A health officer examines Anopheles mosquitoes and larvae in a container where mosquito eggs are grown.

lessons.title: Lesson 4: Signs, Symptoms and Types of Disease

activities.prompt: How can we notice illness, and why do some diseases spread?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: How Your Body Shows Disease
activities.body: Your body usually works in a certain way to keep you healthy. Feeling unwell may mean that something inside is not working properly. Pain, tiredness and dizziness are symptoms. A symptom is something you feel. A sign is something that can be seen or measured. A disease affects the normal working of your body or mind. Diseases are broadly divided into two main types by causes and spread.
keyPoints: Symptoms are felt; signs are seen or measured.
Diseases can affect the body or mind.
Communicable diseases can pass from one person to another.
activities.explanation: These ideas help you tell symptoms, signs and diseases apart.

activities.prompt: A child feels pain, tiredness, and dizziness during a body check. Which are symptoms, and what might be happening inside?
steps: The body usually works in a certain way to keep us healthy.
Pain and dizziness are symptoms because the child feels them.
The measured result is a sign because it can be measured.
Feeling unwell may mean a disease is affecting normal body work.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.title: Find the Symptom
activities.prompt: Which one is an example of a symptom?
options: Bacteria
Protozoa
Tiredness
Viruses
activities.explanation: Good choice! Tiredness is a symptom because a person feels it.

activities.title: Signs or Symptoms?
activities.prompt: A sign is something that a person feels.
activities.explanation: A symptom is felt. A sign can be seen or measured.

activities.title: Complete the Definition
activities.prompt: A disease affects the normal working of the body or ______.
activities.hint: Think of the two parts mentioned in the lesson.
activities.explanation: The answer is mind because diseases affect normal working of the body or mind.

activities.title: What Can Cause Disease?
activities.prompt: Which one can cause diseases?
options: Tiredness
Bacteria
Dizziness
Pain
activities.explanation: Bacteria can cause diseases. Pain, tiredness and dizziness are symptoms.

activities.title: Match the Health Words
activities.prompt: Match each description with the correct health word.
pairs: Something that can be seen or measured
Normal body or mind working affected
activities.explanation: Each description matches the definition given in the lesson.

activities.title: Other Causes of Disease
activities.prompt: Poor nutrition and unhealthy lifestyles can also cause diseases.
activities.explanation: The lesson says poor nutrition and unhealthy lifestyles can cause diseases.

activities.title: How Communicable Diseases Spread
activities.prompt: According to the lesson, how can communicable diseases spread?
options: Only through poor nutrition
By making organs work better
By causing symptoms such as pain
From one person to another
activities.explanation: Communicable diseases can pass from one person to another.

activities.title: Explain What Is Happening
activities.prompt: Someone feels unwell and has pain. Which explanation best fits?
options: Something may work properly; pain is a sign.
Something may not work properly; pain is a symptom.
Everything works properly; pain is a disease.
Something may not work properly; pain is a sign.
activities.explanation: Feeling unwell may mean something inside is not working properly. Pain is a symptom because it is felt.

activities.prompt: One child has a communicable disease. The children meet. What may happen?
options: The other child may catch the disease.
The other child must feel pain and dizziness.
The other child cannot catch this disease at all.
The first child caught the disease from the second.

why.The other child must feel pain and dizzi: This wrongly assumes that everyone must feel these two symptoms.
why.The other child cannot catch this diseas: This directly contradicts the meaning of a communicable disease.
why.The first child caught the disease from: This reverses the direction in which the disease passed.

activities.explanation: This is right because communicable diseases can pass between people.

activities.prompt: Bacteria can cause a disease. Can we tell that it passes between people?
options: Yes, all bacterial diseases are communicable.
Yes, bacteria always cause communicable diseases.
No, bacterial diseases can never pass between people.
No, these facts do not say that it passes.

why.Yes, all bacterial diseases are communic: This wrongly treats all bacterial diseases as communicable.
why.Yes, bacteria always cause communicable: This wrongly assumes that one cause group fixes how disease spreads.
why.No, bacterial diseases can never pass be: This wrongly assumes that bacterial diseases never spread.

activities.explanation: This is right because the facts do not connect bacteria with spread.

lessons.sceneAlt: A doctor uses a stethoscope to examine an adult woman while two other physicians observe in a clinic.
lessons.sceneCaption: A doctor examines a patient with a stethoscope while two other physicians observe.

sceneCredit.text: Doctor examines patient with stethoscope (2) by Unknown photographer, Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons
sceneCredit.creator: Unknown photographer

lessons.title: Lesson 5: How Communicable Diseases Spread

activities.prompt: How do tiny germs travel from one person to another?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: How Do These Diseases Spread?
activities.body: Communicable diseases are caused by pathogens. Pathogens can enter your body through the air you breathe. They may also enter through contaminated food or water. An infected person can spread them by coughing or sneezing. Direct contact, such as shaking hands, can spread them too. Some insects, including mosquitoes and houseflies, can spread pathogens.
keyPoints: All communicable diseases are caused by pathogens.
Pathogens enter through air, contaminated food, or contaminated water.
People and insects can spread pathogens.
activities.explanation: This shows the main ways that pathogens spread.

activities.prompt: A child drinks contaminated water and then coughs near a sibling. How can pathogens spread, and what should the family do?
steps: The water is contaminated, so pathogens may enter the child's body.
If the child is infected, coughing or sneezing can spread pathogens to the sibling.
Covering the mouth and nose while coughing helps protect others, so the child should do this.
Washing hands with soap and water helps remove pathogens, so the family should do this too.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.title: What Causes Communicable Diseases?
activities.prompt: What causes all communicable diseases?
options: Hand washing
Face mask
Pathogens
Covering coughs
activities.explanation: Good choice! Pathogens are the cause of all communicable diseases.

activities.title: A Route Into the Body
activities.prompt: Pathogens may enter through contaminated ______ or water.
activities.hint: Think of something that we eat.
activities.explanation: Nice thinking! Contaminated food and water can carry pathogens into the body.

activities.title: Clean Hands
activities.prompt: What helps remove pathogens from your hands?
options: Cover mouth and nose
Use soap and water
Wear masks in crowds
Cough into your hands
activities.explanation: Correct! Soap and water help remove pathogens from your hands.

activities.title: Ways That Pathogens Spread
activities.prompt: Match each source to the way it can spread pathogens.
pairs: Spread pathogens by an infected person
activities.explanation: Great matching! Each pair shows a way communicable diseases can spread.

activities.title: Protecting Other People
activities.prompt: An infected person coughs near other people. What should the person do?
options: Shake both hands
Share food with others
Use contaminated water
Cover mouth and nose
activities.explanation: Correct! Covering your mouth and nose helps protect nearby people.

activities.prompt: Pathogens can enter the body through the air we breathe. A child breathes in a room where an infected person coughs. What may happen?
options: Pathogens may enter the child's body through the breathed air.
Pathogens may enter through the food in the room.
Pathogens may enter through the child's clean hands.
Pathogens may enter through the child's mask.

why.Pathogens may enter through the food in: This mistake mixes up the air route with the food route.
why.Pathogens may enter through the child's: This mistake assumes clean hands are a way pathogens enter the body.
This mistake assumes a mask is a way pathogens enter the body.

activities.explanation: This is right because breathing in the air can bring pathogens into the body.

activities.prompt: Contaminated drinking water and food can spread some communicable diseases. A child drinks contaminated water. What may happen?
options: Pathogens may enter the child's body through the water.
Pathogens may enter through the child's clean hands.
Pathogens may enter through the soap used for washing.
Pathogens may enter through the mask on the child's face.

why.Pathogens may enter through the child's: This mistake assumes clean hands are a way pathogens enter the body.
why.Pathogens may enter through the soap use: This mistake assumes soap is a way pathogens enter the body.
why.Pathogens may enter through the mask on: This mistake assumes a mask is a way pathogens enter the body.

activities.explanation: This is right because contaminated water can carry pathogens into the body.

activities.prompt: Direct contact, such as shaking hands, can spread communicable diseases. Two people shake hands. What may happen?
options: A communicable disease may spread through the handshake.
A disease may spread through the air during the handshake.
A disease may not spread through the handshake.
A disease may spread only if both people cough.

why.A disease may spread through the air dur: This mistake believes air is the only way diseases spread.
why.A disease may not spread through the han: This mistake believes handshake contact cannot spread diseases.
why.A disease may spread only if both people: This mistake believes coughing is needed for diseases to spread by handshake.

activities.explanation: This is right because direct contact can spread communicable diseases.

activities.prompt: Insects such as mosquitoes and houseflies can spread pathogens. A housefly touches a child's food. What may happen?
options: Pathogens may spread from the housefly to the food.
Pathogens may spread from the food to the child's mask.
Pathogens may spread from the soap to the child's hands.
Pathogens may spread from the child's hands to the housefly.

why.Pathogens may spread from the food to th: This mistake reverses the possible spread from the insect to the food.
why.Pathogens may spread from the soap to th: This mistake wrongly suggests soap spreads pathogens to hands.
why.Pathogens may spread from the child's ha: This mistake reverses the possible spread from the insect to the food.

activities.explanation: This is right because insects can spread pathogens to food they touch.

activities.prompt: Wearing a mask in crowded places provides protection. A child must cough in a crowded place. What should the child do?
options: Cover the mouth and nose, and wear a mask.
Cover the mouth and nose, but do not wear a mask.
Wear a mask, but do not cover the mouth and nose.
Wash the hands instead of covering or wearing a mask.

why.Cover the mouth and nose, but do not wea: This mistake ignores the protection a mask provides in crowded places.
why.Wear a mask, but do not cover the mouth: This mistake ignores covering the mouth and nose while coughing.
why.Wash the hands instead of covering or we: This mistake believes handwashing can replace covering and mask protection.

activities.explanation: This is right because it uses both protections for coughing in crowded places.

lessons.title: Lesson 6: Preventing and Treating Disease

activities.prompt: How can we prevent diseases and help our bodies fight them?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: Understanding Disease
activities.body: Non-communicable diseases are linked with lifestyle, diet or environment. They are the most common cause of death in India. Deficiency diseases happen when the diet lacks particular nutrients. Diseases that continue for a long time are called chronic diseases. Immunity is your body's natural ability to fight diseases. Vaccines help prevent disease, but they do not cure it after illness begins. Antibiotics work only against bacterial infections.
keyPoints: Deficiency diseases result from missing nutrients.
Vaccines prevent disease but do not cure it.
Antibiotics work only against bacterial infections.
activities.explanation: These ideas help you protect yourself from disease.

activities.prompt: A child has a bacterial illness. What can treat it and prevent disease?
steps: Antibiotics can treat the bacterial illness because they work only against bacteria.
Vaccines can prevent disease before it starts because they are preventive.
A vaccine cannot cure the current illness because it does not treat disease after it begins.
Use antibiotics as prescribed because surviving bacteria can multiply and develop resistance.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.title: What Causes Deficiency Diseases?
activities.prompt: What can cause deficiency diseases?
options: A lack of particular nutrients
Unhealthy daily habits
Bacteria surviving treatment
An illness lasting for years
activities.explanation: Deficiency diseases result from a lack of particular nutrients in the diet.

activities.prompt: Deficiency diseases can develop when a diet lacks particular nutrients.
activities.explanation: Yes. Missing particular nutrients from the diet can cause deficiency diseases.

activities.title: When Do Antibiotics Work?
activities.prompt: Against which health problem do antibiotics work?
options: Bacterial infections
Deficiency diseases
Chronic diseases
Non-communicable diseases
activities.explanation: Antibiotics work only against bacterial infections.

activities.title: Using Antibiotics Safely
activities.prompt: Put the rules for using antibiotics in the order given in the lesson.
activities.explanation: Antibiotics should be used only when prescribed, in the correct dose and for the right duration.

activities.title: Health Words and Meanings
activities.prompt: Match each health word with its meaning.
pairs: Linked with lifestyle, diet or environment
The natural ability to fight diseases
Bacteria survive and multiply despite treatment
activities.explanation: Chronic diseases last a long time, while immunity helps the body fight diseases.

activities.title: Choosing the Right Antibiotic Use
activities.prompt: What should you do when taking an antibiotic?
options: Use it exactly as prescribed.
Start it without a prescription.
Take a smaller dose than prescribed.
Stop before the right duration.
activities.explanation: Use antibiotics only when prescribed, in the correct dose and for the right duration.

activities.prompt: Unhealthy diet, habits, and surroundings affect a person. Which conclusion is sound?
options: Non-communicable diseases may be linked, and they cause most deaths.
Deficiency diseases may be linked, and they cause most deaths.
Non-communicable diseases may be linked, but rarely cause death.
Communicable diseases may be linked, and they cause most deaths.

why.Deficiency diseases may be linked, and t: This confuses a nutrient shortage with the broader lifestyle and environment link.
why.Non-communicable diseases may be linked,: This reverses the fact that non-communicable diseases most commonly cause death.
why.Communicable diseases may be linked, and: This wrongly says communicable diseases cause more deaths than other diseases.

activities.explanation: These factors link to non-communicable diseases, India's most common cause of death.

activities.prompt: A child eats poorly, never exercises, and is overweight. What may develop?
options: Diabetes, because these habits and weight can lead to it.
A deficiency disease, because the diet may lack one nutrient.
Antibiotic resistance, because unhealthy habits make bacteria stronger.
Chronic disease, because these habits can make illness continue.

why.A deficiency disease, because the diet m: This focuses on a missing nutrient, but no nutrient shortage is described.
why.Antibiotic resistance, because unhealthy: Antibiotic resistance comes from bacteria surviving treatment, not unhealthy habits.
why.Chronic disease, because these habits ca: Chronic disease means lasting a long time, but that is not shown here.

activities.explanation: Diabetes can develop because unhealthy habits, inactivity, and being overweight are linked causes.

activities.prompt: An ill child receives a vaccine. What can the vaccine do?
options: It can prevent disease later, but it cannot cure this illness.
It will cure this illness, because vaccines use weakened pathogens.
It will cure this illness, because vaccines contain harmless pathogen parts.
It will prevent only bacterial infections, just like antibiotics.

why.It will cure this illness, because vacci: Vaccines may contain weakened pathogens, but they do not cure existing illness.
Harmless pathogen parts do not give a vaccine the power to cure illness.
why.It will prevent only bacterial infection: Antibiotics work only against bacteria, while vaccines work preventively.

activities.explanation: Vaccines are preventive and do not cure an illness after it begins.

activities.prompt: An infection is not caused by bacteria. What will antibiotics do?
options: They will not work, because they act only against bacteria.
They will cure it, because they work against every infection.
They will prevent it, because every infection needs antibiotics.
They may cure it faster if the prescribed dose is doubled.

why.They will cure it, because they work aga: This wrongly assumes antibiotics work against infections caused by non-bacteria.
why.They will prevent it, because every infe: This wrongly assumes every infection is bacterial and needs antibiotic treatment.
why.They may cure it faster if the prescribe: This ignores the rule to use only the correct prescribed dose.

activities.explanation: Antibiotics work only against bacterial infections, so this infection is not helped.

activities.prompt: A child stops antibiotics early when feeling better. What should happen?
options: The child should continue the prescribed dose for the full duration.
The child should stop whenever the illness feels better.
The child should double the dose to finish treatment sooner.
The child should use antibiotics whenever the child wants them.

why.The child should stop whenever the illne: This ignores the rule to use antibiotics for the full prescribed duration.
why.The child should double the dose to fini: This ignores the rule to take only the correct prescribed dose.

activities.context: A student feels low after difficult lessons and also has trouble sleeping. The student eats fresh wholesome food suited to their body constitution, exercises regularly, keeps clean, and follows a calm bedtime routine. When problems arise, the student talks with friends and peers. The student also practices yoga, meditation and mindfulness. After making these habits part of daily life, the student feels better and handles school challenges more easily.
activities.prompt: If the student stops exercising and replaces restful sleep with late-night screen use while keeping the food and calm-mind habits, what is most likely to happen?
options: Their overall wellbeing will improve because healthy food and a calm mind can replace exercise and restful sleep.
Their overall wellbeing may weaken because exercise and restful sleep also support overall wellbeing.
Their overall wellbeing will remain exactly the same because exercise and sleep are not part of health.
Their overall wellbeing will weaken only if a disease develops, because health means only the absence of disease.

why.Their overall wellbeing will improve bec: Healthy food and a calm mind support health, but they cannot replace exercise and restful sleep.
why.Their overall wellbeing will remain exac: Exercise and restful sleep are also important parts of a healthy daily life.
why.Their overall wellbeing will weaken only: Health includes physical, mental and social wellbeing, not only the absence of disease.

activities.explanation: Exercise and restful sleep support overall wellbeing.

activities.context: A student feels low after difficult lessons and also has trouble sleeping. The student eats fresh wholesome food suited to their body constitution, exercises regularly, keeps clean, and follows a calm bedtime routine. When problems arise, the student talks with friends and peers. The student also practices yoga, meditation and mindfulness. After making these habits part of daily life, the student feels better and handles school challenges more easily.
activities.prompt: What should the student do if a change in the season disrupts the daily routine?
options: Stop following daily and seasonal routines until the season changes again.
Resume daily and seasonal routines, including suitable wholesome food, exercise, cleanliness, restful sleep and a calm mind.
Keep only the food habit and stop exercise, sleep, cleanliness and calm-mind practices.
Use only meditation and ignore exercise, suitable food, restful sleep and cleanliness.

why.Stop following daily and seasonal routin: Daily and seasonal routines should not be abandoned simply because circumstances change.
why.Keep only the food habit and stop exerci: Food is essential, but it is not the only supportive habit.
why.Use only meditation and ignore exercise,: Yoga, meditation and mindfulness can support health, but they do not replace other essential practices.

activities.explanation: Following balanced routines and supportive habits helps maintain wellbeing.

activities.prompt:
Assertion (A): Healthy people can perform different tasks efficiently and handle difficult situations well.
Reason (R): Taking care of the body and keeping a positive mindset usually helps healthy people function well.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.
activities.explanation: Both statements are true, and caring for the body and maintaining a positive mindset help people function well.

activities.prompt:
Assertion (A): Following daily and seasonal routines helps maintain a balance between body, mind and surroundings.
Reason (R): This balance can be maintained without fresh wholesome food suited to the body constitution because food is not essential to health.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.
activities.explanation: The assertion is true, but the reason is false because suitable wholesome food is essential.

activities.prompt: Explain why health is more than simply the absence of disease.
activities.answer: Health includes physical, mental and social wellbeing, so it is not limited to whether a person has a disease. Taking care of the body, keeping a positive mindset and having strong relationships all contribute to health. Exercise, cleanliness, restful sleep, a calm mind and suitable wholesome food support overall wellbeing. These habits help a person perform tasks efficiently and handle difficult situations. Ayurveda also describes health as balance among body, mind and surroundings, which daily and seasonal routines help maintain.
points: Health includes physical, mental and social wellbeing.
Positive feelings and strong relationships are part of health.
Exercise, sleep, cleanliness, calm mind and suitable food support wellbeing.
Balance among body, mind and surroundings is important.
activities.explanation: Compare your answer with the points a marker looks for.

activities.context: A student often skips breakfast, eats fast food every day, drinks sugary drinks and spends much of the evening on a mobile phone. activities.prompt: The student keeps eating fast food every day and skipping breakfast but starts walking outdoors each day. Which conclusion best matches the lesson?

Since walking outdoors is healthy, the eating and meal-skipping habits are no longer a concern.
Because outdoor activity has been added, the student no longer needs enough sleep.
Since the student is active, daily fast food and skipped meals have become healthy habits.

why.Since walking outdoors is healthy, the e: Eating fast food every day and skipping meals remain unhealthy.
why.Because outdoor activity has been added,: The body and mind still need enough sleep to rest and recover.
why.Since the student is active, daily fast: Outdoor activity does not make junk food or skipped meals healthy.

activities.explanation: Healthy activity does not cancel unhealthy eating habits.

activities.context: A student often skips breakfast, eats fast food every day, drinks sugary drinks and spends much of the evening on a mobile phone. The student also sleeps very late and rarely plays outdoors. The student decides to improve the routine by eating balanced meals, limiting screen time, going outside for activity, sleeping enough and practising simple breathing exercises.

Because yoga and breathing are practised regularly, very late sleeping is no longer harmful.
The regular exercises mean the body and mind no longer need enough sleep.
Sleeping very late becomes healthy when breathing exercises are added.

why.The regular exercises mean the body and: The body and mind still need sleep for rest and recovery.
why.Sleeping very late becomes healthy when: One healthy habit cannot make an unhealthy sleep routine healthy.

activities.explanation: Yoga and breathing are healthy, but so is getting enough sleep.

activities.prompt:
Assertion (A): Limiting screen time is part of a healthy lifestyle.
Reason (R): Time in nature should be increased and time on mobile phones and digital screens should be limited.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.
activities.explanation: Both statements are true, and the reason explains why limiting screen time supports a healthy lifestyle.

activities.prompt:
Assertion (A): Eating fast food every day is an unhealthy habit.
Reason (R): A balanced diet should contain plenty of fruits, vegetables and whole grains.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.
activities.explanation: Both statements are true, but the reason does not directly explain why daily fast food is unhealthy.

activities.prompt: Explain why healthy lifestyle habits are important and what changes can support them.
activities.answer: Staying healthy requires nutritious food, good hygiene and other healthy habits. A balanced diet should contain plenty of fruits, vegetables and whole grains, while processed, fatty and sugary foods and drinks should be avoided. Children can stay active through outdoor play, walking, running or cycling. Limiting screen time, increasing time in nature and getting enough sleep also support health. Regular yoga and breathing exercises, good hygiene, and avoiding tobacco, alcohol and addictive drugs are also important parts of a healthy routine.
points: Healthy living requires nutritious food, good hygiene and other healthy habits.
A balanced diet contains plenty of fruits, vegetables and whole grains.
Screen time should be limited and time in nature increased.
Enough sleep, regular exercise and avoiding harmful substances support health.
activities.explanation: Compare your answer with the points a marker looks for.

activities.context: A girl lives in a polluted neighbourhood where pollution comes from vehicles and factories. Rubbish lies outside, and flies and mosquitoes are often seen nearby. activities.prompt: If pollution from the vehicles and factories around her home decreases, what might happen?
options: The air-quality reading may improve, and her coughing might lessen.
The air-quality reading may improve, but her coughing would certainly increase.
Her coughing might lessen, but people in her area would then fall sick more often.
Her loneliness would disappear, but the air-quality reading would remain poor.

why.The air-quality reading may improve, but: B: Cleaner air would not be expected to increase coughing.
why.Her coughing might lessen, but people in: C: Cleaner surroundings should not make people fall sick more often.
why.Her loneliness would disappear, but the: D: Cleaner air does not automatically remove loneliness.

activities.context: A girl lives in a polluted neighbourhood where pollution comes from vehicles and factories. Rubbish lies outside, and flies and mosquitoes are often seen nearby. She has begun coughing. Although she keeps her room clean and spends happy time with her family, she still feels unwell when she is lonely or upset.
activities.prompt: What should she do to support both her physical and emotional health?

Keep rubbish outside, avoid checking air quality, and stay alone whenever possible.
Only clean her room, because wider surroundings and feelings never affect health.
Focus on air quality alone, since loneliness cannot influence health.

why.Keep rubbish outside, avoid checking air: B: Rubbish and isolation could worsen health and feelings.
why.Only clean her room, because wider surro: C: Cleaning only the room ignores dirty surroundings and emotional health.
why.Focus on air quality alone, since loneli: D: Air quality matters, but loneliness can also affect how someone feels.

activities.prompt:

Reason (R): Air pollution from vehicles and factories can cause coughing or asthma.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.

activities.explanation: Both statements are true, and pollution-related illness explains why polluted areas may have more sickness.

activities.prompt:
Assertion (A): A clean environment guarantees that nobody will ever feel unwell.
Reason (R): Loneliness or upset feelings can make a person feel unwell even in a clean place.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.
activities.explanation: The guarantee is false because loneliness can still cause unwell feelings, while the reason is true.

activities.prompt: How can a cleaner environment and supportive relationships together help a person stay healthy?
activities.answer: A cleaner environment supports health because clean air and water are important, and pollution from vehicles or factories can cause coughing or asthma. Keeping ourselves and our surroundings clean can also reduce contact with flies and mosquitoes found in dirty, unhygienic places. Supportive relationships matter too: lonely or upset feelings can make someone feel unwell even in a clean place, while happy time with friends and family helps keep the mind healthy. Therefore, good physical surroundings and emotional support work together.
points: Links clean surroundings with good physical health
Explains the effects of vehicle and factory pollution
Explains the effects of flies and mosquitoes
Shows how relationships support emotional health

activities.context: A boy feels pain, tiredness and dizziness, so his body does not seem to be working normally. activities.prompt: The boy later meets another person. What should the worker consider if his disease is communicable?

The disease cannot pass because symptoms are felt rather than seen.

why.The disease can pass only if the other p: Poor nutrition is not a condition for a disease to pass between people.
why.The disease cannot pass because symptoms: The difference between signs and symptoms does not decide whether a disease can spread.

activities.prompt:
Assertion (A): Poor nutrition can cause a disease.
Reason (R): Poor nutrition has no connection with the normal working of the body.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.

chapters.title: Electricity: Magnetic and Heating Effects
chapters.summary: In this chapter: lesson 1: electric current and magnetic effects; lesson 2: electromagnets and their strength; lesson 3: earth’s magnetic field and lifting electromagnets; lesson 4: the heating effect of electric current.

lessons.title: Lesson 1: Electric Current and Magnetic Effects

activities.prompt: Could electricity make a nail behave like a magnet?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: How current creates a magnetic effect
activities.body: Electric current can have a magnetic effect. When Sumana closed the circuit, the iron nail picked up iron paper clips. It was magnetic even without a separate magnet. A compass needle moved while current flowed, then returned when the current stopped. The region where a magnetic effect can be felt is called a magnetic field. Oersted discovered that electricity and magnetism are linked.
keyPoints: Current can create a magnetic effect.
A compass needle moves while current flows.
Electricity and magnetism are linked.
activities.explanation: This shows that electric current can affect magnets and compass needles.

activities.title: Light the bulb

tasks.then: Closing the switch completes the circuit, so current flows.
More cells for each bulb push more current through it.

activities.takeaway: Current flows only round a closed circuit; more cells push more current.
activities.explanation: Current flows only round a closed circuit; more cells push more current.

activities.prompt: A wire is beside a compass. What happens as current starts and stops?
steps: Current makes the wire have a magnetic effect on the compass needle.
It moves away from its original direction because current acts magnetically.
When current stops, the effect ends and the needle returns home.
This shows that electricity and magnetism are linked.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.title: What happened to the nail?
activities.prompt: When Sumana closed the circuit, what happened to the iron nail?
options: The nail picked up iron paper clips.
The nail pushed the paper clips away.
The nail picked up no paper clips.
The nail became a separate magnet.
activities.explanation: Closing the circuit made the nail pick up iron paper clips like a magnet.

activities.title: The nail became magnetic
activities.prompt: The iron nail was magnetic even though the model had no separate magnet.
activities.explanation: The iron nail was a magnetic material without a separate magnet.

activities.title: Name the magnetic region
activities.prompt: The region where a magnetic effect can be felt is called a ______.
activities.hint: This region has a special name in the lesson.
activities.explanation: A magnetic field is the region where a magnetic effect can be felt.

activities.title: Through which materials?
activities.prompt: Where can the magnetic effect of a magnet pass?
options: Only through the magnet itself.
Through non-magnetic materials between them.
Through the compass needle only.
Through no materials at all.
activities.explanation: The magnetic effect can pass through non-magnetic materials placed between magnets.

activities.title: Match each idea
activities.prompt: Match each idea with its correct meaning.
pairs: Has a magnetic effect on a compass needle
Region where a magnetic effect can be felt
Discovered that electricity and magnetism are linked
Uses the magnetic effect of electric current
activities.explanation: Each pair connects an important idea with its meaning.

activities.title: Effect of a current-carrying wire
activities.prompt: What effect does a current-carrying wire have on a compass needle?
options: It makes the needle move.
It makes the needle disappear.
It makes the needle stay still.
It makes the needle break.
activities.explanation: A current-carrying wire has a magnetic effect on the compass needle.

activities.title: Oersted's discovery
activities.prompt: What link did Hans Christian Oersted discover?
options: Electricity and heat are linked.
Electricity and sound are linked.
Electricity and magnetism are linked.
Magnetism and light are linked.
activities.explanation: Oersted discovered that electricity and magnetism are linked.

activities.title: Observe the compass needle
activities.prompt: Put the compass and current events in the correct order.
items: The compass needle moves away from its original direction.
The compass needle returns to its original direction.
activities.explanation: The needle moves while current flows and returns when the current stops.

activities.prompt: An iron nail is in a closed circuit with no separate magnet. What best explains what the nail does near iron paper clips?
options: It attracts the clips because current has a magnetic effect.
It pushes clips away because the iron nail is magnetic.
It attracts clips even after the current has stopped.
It attracts clips because a separate magnet is present.

why.It pushes clips away because the iron na: A magnet-like nail attracts clips instead of pushing them away.
why.It attracts clips even after the current: The nail picked up clips while current flowed, not after it stopped.
why.It attracts clips because a separate mag: The model had no separate magnet; current caused the effect.

activities.explanation: Current produced the magnetic effect that let the nail attract clips.

activities.prompt: One wire carries current; another does not. How should the test be set fairly?
options: Keep both setups the same, changing only the current.
Use different compasses, and change the current in both.
Place the current wire farther away from its compass.
Add a separate magnet beside the wire without current.

why.Use different compasses, and change the: Changing the compasses adds another difference and hides the cause.
why.Place the current wire farther away from: Changing the distance adds another difference besides current.
why.Add a separate magnet beside the wire wi: Adding a magnet changes the test instead of testing current alone.

activities.explanation: Only current changes, so any needle movement comes from current.

lessons.title: Lesson 2: Electromagnets and Their Strength

activities.prompt: How can we make an electromagnet stronger?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: How an Electromagnet Works
activities.body: An electric current can make a coil act like a magnet. Such a coil is called an electromagnet. Iron paper clips cling to the coil while current flows. They let go when the current stops. Putting an iron nail inside the coil makes it stronger. More current also makes a stronger magnetic field.
keyPoints: A current-carrying coil acts like a magnet.
An iron nail makes a coil stronger.
More current makes a stronger magnetic field.
activities.explanation: These are important ways to make and control an electromagnet.

activities.prompt: A child places an iron nail inside a powered coil and wonders why paper clips stay on it.
steps: Current flows through the coil, so it acts like an electromagnet.
An iron nail inside makes the coil behave like a stronger magnet.
That stronger magnet holds the paper clips while current flows.
When the current stops, the clips no longer cling to the coil.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.title: Making an Electromagnet Stronger
activities.body: An electromagnet has two poles, like a bar magnet. Most practical electromagnets use an iron core to become stronger. You can make the magnetic field stronger by using more current. A battery with more cells gives a larger current. Changing the current's direction reverses the electromagnet's poles.
keyPoints: An electromagnet has two poles.
An iron core makes most practical electromagnets stronger.
Reversing current reverses the poles.
activities.explanation: You can change an electromagnet's strength and pole positions.

activities.title: Clips and Current
activities.prompt: Iron paper clips keep clinging when the current stops.
activities.explanation: The clips no longer clung when the current stopped.

activities.title: Name the Electromagnet
activities.prompt: What is a current-carrying coil that behaves like a magnet called?
options: Electric coil
Electromagnet
Iron nail
Paper clip
activities.explanation: A current-carrying coil that behaves like a magnet is called an electromagnet.

activities.title: Match Each Change
activities.prompt: Match each change to its result.
activities.explanation: Current attracts the clips, while an iron nail strengthens the coil.

activities.title: Complete the Definition
activities.prompt: A current-carrying coil that behaves like a magnet is called an ______.
activities.hint: This coil behaves like a magnet while carrying current.
activities.explanation: The name describes a magnet made by passing current through a coil.

activities.title: More Current
activities.prompt: What happens when more current flows through the coil?
options: A stronger magnetic field forms.
The coil loses its magnetism.
The iron core disappears.
The coil changes into a nail.
activities.explanation: More current in the coil creates a stronger magnetic field.

activities.title: Watch the Clips
activities.prompt: Put these events in the correct order.
activities.explanation: The clips cling while current flows and release when it stops.

activities.title: Reversing the Current
activities.prompt: Changing the direction of current can reverse an electromagnet's poles.
activities.explanation: The poles reverse when the direction of the current changes.

activities.prompt: A coil carries current. Paper clips cling to it. The current stops. What happens to the clips?
options: The clips remain on the coil.
The clips fall away from the coil.
The clips become strong magnets.
The clips move toward the battery.

The clips no longer cling when the current stops.
This wrongly treats paper clips as electromagnets.
This wrongly assumes the battery attracts the clips.

activities.explanation: This wrongly assumes stopping current changes nothing.

activities.prompt: A battery with more cells powers a coil. What happens to the current and magnetic field?
options: The current becomes larger, and the field strengthens.
The current becomes smaller, and the field weakens.
The current stays same, and the field strengthens.
The current stops, and the field disappears.

why.The current becomes smaller, and the fie: This wrongly assumes more cells reduce the current.
why.The current stays same, and the field st: This wrongly assumes more cells do not increase current.
why.The current stops, and the field disappe: This wrongly assumes more cells stop the current.

activities.explanation: More cells give a larger current and a stronger magnetic field.
