lessons.title: Lesson 3: Earth’s Magnetic Field and Lifting Electromagnets

activities.prompt: What if we could use Earth’s magnetic field to lift metal?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: Earth’s Magnetic Field and Electromagnets
activities.body: Earth’s core contains liquid iron. Its movement creates electric currents. These currents make a magnetic field around Earth. This field helps many animals navigate. It also acts as a shield for life. Lifting electromagnets are strong electromagnets. Switching current ON lifts iron or steel objects. Switching it OFF releases them.
keyPoints: Moving liquid iron creates electric currents.
Electric currents create Earth’s magnetic field.
Lifting electromagnets lift iron or steel objects.
activities.explanation: This connects Earth’s moving core, animal navigation and lifting electromagnets.

activities.prompt: A crane must lift a steel lid. What should the operator do?
steps: The operator switches current ON, because the electromagnet lifts iron or steel.
The crane carries the lid while current stays ON, so lifting continues.
Current is switched OFF afterwards, because the disappearing field releases the lid.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.title: Controlling Lifting Magnets
activities.body: A crane operator switches an electromagnet’s current ON to lift iron or steel. Switching the current OFF makes its magnetic field disappear, so objects are released. Factories and scrap yards use these strong electromagnets to move heavy metal items efficiently. A moving magnet can also lead to an electric current. This connection between electricity and magnetism forms the basis of electric motors and power generators.
keyPoints: Current ON lifts iron or steel objects.
Current OFF removes the magnetic field and releases objects.
Electricity and magnetism are closely connected.
activities.explanation: Switching current controls lifting. Moving magnets also show a link between electricity and magnetism.

activities.title: Currents in Earth’s Core
activities.prompt: What creates electric currents inside Earth?
options: Movement of liquid iron
Movement of solid iron
Movement of outer rock
Movement of sea water
activities.explanation: Liquid iron moves inside Earth’s core. This movement creates electric currents.

activities.prompt: Many migratory birds use Earth’s magnetic field to navigate.
activities.explanation: Many migratory birds, fish and animals use this field for navigation.

activities.title: Lifting Electromagnet Uses
activities.prompt: Match each worker or place with its lifting electromagnet job.
pairs: Controls the current ON and OFF
activities.explanation: Crane operators control the current. Factories and scrap yards move heavy metal efficiently.

activities.title: Switching the Electromagnet
activities.prompt: The electromagnet lifts iron or steel objects when the current is ______.
activities.hint: Choose the state used to lift an object.
activities.explanation: The electromagnet lifts iron or steel objects when the current is ON.

activities.title: Electricity and Magnetism
activities.prompt: What forms the basis of electric motors and power generators?
options: Electricity and magnetism
Liquid iron and movement
Iron and steel objects
Factories and scrap yards
activities.explanation: The connection between electricity and magnetism forms the basis of both machines.

activities.prompt: A lifting electromagnet releases objects while its current is ON.
activities.explanation: The electromagnet lifts objects while current is ON. It releases them after current is OFF.

activities.title: Lifting an Iron Object
activities.prompt: Put the lifting electromagnet steps in order.
activities.explanation: Current ON creates the lifting action. Current OFF removes the field and releases the object.

activities.prompt: A scrap yard lifts steel beams. What should happen to release them?
options: Switch the current OFF, so the magnetic field disappears.
Switch the current ON, so the magnetic field disappears.
Move the crane farther away, so the beams fall slowly.
Turn the magnet over, so its field releases the beams.

why.Switch the current ON, so the magnetic f: Current ON keeps the lifting field; it does not remove the field.
why.Move the crane farther away, so the beam: Moving the crane does not remove the field that releases the beams.
why.Turn the magnet over, so its field relea: Turning the magnet over does not switch the current OFF.

activities.explanation: With current OFF, the field disappears and the steel beams are released.

activities.prompt: A fish travels elsewhere. What may help it find the way?
options: Earth’s magnetic field can guide its journey.
Earth’s electric currents can pull it home.
Earth’s core can carry the fish there.
Earth’s shield can keep the fish warm.

why.Earth’s electric currents can pull it ho: Currents in Earth’s core do not pull fish toward home.
Earth’s core is not a carrier that transports fish.
The magnetic field acts as a shield, not a warm covering.

activities.explanation: Many fish use Earth’s magnetic field to navigate.

lessons.title: Lesson 4: The Heating Effect of Electric Current

activities.prompt: Why does electricity make wires feel warm?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: Why Wires Become Warm
activities.body: When electric current passes through a conductor, the conductor gets heated. This warming is called the heating effect of electric current. Resistance is the opposition that current faces in a conductor. Different conductors have different resistance levels. Heat in a wire depends on its material, thickness, length and duration of current flow. Magnitude means how large the electric current is. Duration means how long current flows.
keyPoints: Resistance is opposition to electric current.
Current heats a conductor; this is the heating effect.
Heat depends on current magnitude and wire factors.
activities.explanation: This card explains the main ideas behind the heating effect of electric current.

activities.title: Light the bulb

tasks.then: Closing the switch completes the circuit, so current flows.
More cells for each bulb push more current through it.

activities.takeaway: Current flows only round a closed circuit; more cells push more current.
activities.explanation: Current flows only round a closed circuit; more cells push more current.

activities.prompt: A child sends current through a nichrome wire. Why does the wire feel warm?
steps: Current meets resistance in the wire, because the wire opposes its passage.
Current still passes through the conductor, because it faces only some opposition.
Passing current heats the conductor, because current has a heating effect.
The nichrome wire therefore feels warm, because this is the heating effect of electric current.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.prompt: What happened to nichrome wire when electric current passed through it?
options: It felt warm.
It felt cold.
It stayed unchanged.
It became wet.
activities.explanation: Passing current heated the nichrome wire, so it felt warm.

activities.prompt: When electric current passed through it, nichrome wire felt ______.
activities.hint: Describe how the wire felt.
activities.explanation: The current heated the nichrome wire, so it felt warm.

activities.prompt: Which wire has higher resistance when both have the same size and length?
options: Nichrome wire
Copper wire
Both wires equally
Neither wire
activities.explanation: Nichrome wire has higher resistance than copper wire of the same size and length.

activities.prompt: Match each item with its heating-effect fact.
pairs: Has higher resistance than copper wire of the same size and length
Amount of heat generated depends on it
One factor affecting heat in a wire
activities.explanation: Each pair shows a factor and the heating effect connected with it.

activities.prompt: Put these stages of the heating effect in order.
items: Electric current passes through a conductor
The warming is called the heating effect
activities.explanation: The conductor is heated first, and that warming is then named.

activities.prompt: Which group lists factors that affect heat in a wire?
options: Material, thickness, length and duration
Colour, thickness, length and duration
Material, colour, length and age
Material, thickness, size and age
activities.explanation: These are the material, thickness, length and duration factors listed for wire heat.

activities.prompt: A child tests current flow time. What must stay the same?
options: Wire material, thickness, length, and current strength.
Wire colour, thickness, length, and current strength.
Only wire length and current strength.
Only cell count and wire thickness.

why.Wire colour, thickness, length, and curr: This mistake treats colour as a factor in heating.
This mistake thinks length alone controls heating.
This mistake ignores material, length, and current strength.

activities.explanation: This keeps every other heat factor the same.

activities.prompt: One wire is nichrome; one is copper. Which setup fairly tests material?
options: Same thickness, length, current, and flow time.
Different thickness, length, current, and flow time.
Same material, thickness, length, and flow time.
Same material, thickness, length, and current.

why.Different thickness, length, current, an: Changing many factors makes the cause unclear.
why.Same material, thickness, length, and fl: Keeping material the same prevents a comparison of materials.
why.Same material, thickness, length, and cu: This ignores flow time, which also affects heat.

activities.explanation: Material changes between wires, while the other factors stay the same.

activities.prompt: Two cells heat a nichrome wire. What happens with only one cell?
options: The wire generates less heat with one cell.
The wire generates more heat with one cell.
The wire generates the same heat with one cell.
The wire generates no heat with one cell.

why.The wire generates more heat with one ce: This reverses the result of the experiment.
why.The wire generates the same heat with on: This assumes cell count does not affect the heat.
why.The wire generates no heat with one cell: This assumes one cell lets no current through the wire.

activities.explanation: The two-cell experiment generated more heat.

activities.prompt: A child claims wire thickness never changes heat. Why is this claim flawed?
options: Heat depends on thickness, not just current.
Heat depends only on thickness, not current.
Heat depends on current, so thickness cannot matter.
Heat depends on colour, so thickness cannot matter.

why.Heat depends only on thickness, not curr: This wrongly makes thickness the only heat factor.
why.Heat depends on current, so thickness ca: This wrongly removes thickness as a heat factor.
why.Heat depends on colour, so thickness can: This confuses wire colour with the listed heat factors.

activities.explanation: Thickness is one factor that affects heat.

activities.prompt: A wire warms during current flow. Which explanation fits the heating effect?
options: Resistance opposes current, while current heats the conductor.
Resistance stops current, while current cools the conductor.
Resistance pushes current, while current cools the conductor.
Resistance has no effect, while current cools the conductor.

why.Resistance stops current, while current: Current is opposed, not stopped, and passing it causes heating.
why.Resistance pushes current, while current: Resistance opposes current instead of pushing it forward.
why.Resistance has no effect, while current: Resistance does affect current, and current causes heating.

activities.explanation: Current faces resistance, and passing current causes heating.

lessons.title: Lesson 5: Voltaic Cells and How They Work

activities.prompt: What makes a simple battery create electricity?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: Meet a Voltaic Cell
activities.body: A Voltaic cell is also called a Galvanic cell. It uses metal rods called electrodes. These rods are partly dipped in an electrolyte. Current flows from the positive terminal, through the circuit, to the negative terminal. The chemicals get used up over time. Eventually, the cell stops working. In a lemon cell, copper wires and iron nails act as electrodes.
keyPoints: Voltaic and Galvanic are two names for the same cell.
Electrodes are partly dipped in electrolyte.
Chemicals get used up over time.
activities.explanation: This card introduces the parts, current path, and working life of a cell.

activities.prompt: A lemon cell uses copper wires and iron nails. Why can it make current, and what happens later?
steps: Copper wires and iron nails act as the metal electrodes.
The metals and liquid work together, so they generate electric current.
This current flows from the positive terminal through the circuit to the negative terminal.
The chemicals get used up, so the cell eventually stops working.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.title: Volta's Idea
activities.body: The Voltaic and Galvanic cells were named after two Italian scientists. Volta believed that electricity came from metals rather than from a frog. A combination of metals and liquid generates electric current. A lemon cell uses copper wires and iron nails as its metal electrodes.
keyPoints: Two Italian scientists gave the cells their names.
Volta believed electricity came from metals.
Metals and liquid generate electric current.
activities.explanation: These ideas connect the cell's names with the way it makes current.

activities.title: Another Name
activities.prompt: What is another name for a Voltaic cell?
options: A Galvanic cell
A metal rod
An electrolyte
A positive terminal
activities.explanation: A Voltaic cell is also known as a Galvanic cell.

activities.prompt: Current flows from the negative terminal to the positive terminal.
activities.explanation: Current flows from the positive terminal through the circuit to the negative terminal.

activities.prompt: The metal rods are partly dipped in the ______.
activities.hint: This liquid part of the cell holds the electrodes.
activities.explanation: The metal rods called electrodes are partly dipped in the electrolyte.

activities.title: What Makes Current?
activities.prompt: What combination generates electric current in these cells?
options: Only copper wire
Only iron nails
Metals and liquid
A metal and a frog
activities.explanation: The combination of metals and liquid generates the electric current.

activities.prompt: The chemicals in a cell stay unchanged for ever.
activities.explanation: The chemicals get used up over time, so the cell eventually stops working.

activities.title: Follow the Current
activities.prompt: Put the current's path in order.
activities.explanation: Current moves from the positive terminal through the circuit to the negative terminal.

activities.title: Match the Cell Facts
activities.prompt: Match each part with its correct description.
activities.explanation: Each pair shows a name, part, belief, or current path from the lesson.

activities.prompt: You want to test whether metals and liquid make current. Which setup is the fair test?
options: A lemon cell with copper wires and iron nails
A lemon with one copper wire and no iron nail
Two metal rods placed above a bowl of liquid
A bowl of liquid with no metal rods

why.A lemon with one copper wire and no iron: This mistake uses only one metal instead of testing a combination of metals.
why.Two metal rods placed above a bowl of li: This mistake keeps the metals away from the liquid.
why.A bowl of liquid with no metal rods: This mistake leaves out the metals needed with the liquid.

activities.explanation: This is right because it combines copper wires, iron nails, and liquid in a lemon cell.

activities.prompt: A cell has metal rods partly dipped in electrolyte. Why can this setup generate current?
options: The metals and liquid together generate the current.
The empty space between the rods generates current.
The outer ends of the rods generate the current.
The metal rods alone generate all the current.

why.The empty space between the rods generat: This mistake thinks the empty space between the rods makes current.
why.The outer ends of the rods generate the: This mistake thinks only the parts outside the liquid make current.
why.The metal rods alone generate all the cu: This mistake ignores the liquid needed with the metals.

activities.explanation: This is right because metals and liquid together generate electric current.

lessons.title: Lesson 6: Dry Cells and Rechargeable Batteries

activities.prompt: Could a battery be reused again and again?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: Batteries at a Glance
activities.body: Dry cells contain a thick paste instead of a liquid electrolyte. Its zinc container is the negative terminal. The metal cap over the carbon rod is the positive terminal. Dry cells are single-use and need disposal. Rechargeable batteries can be recharged and reused many times, saving money and reducing wastage. Lithium-ion is the most common rechargeable type. Solid-state batteries use solid materials instead of liquid or paste. Used batteries need e-waste recycling facilities.
keyPoints: Dry cells use thick paste and have zinc negative and metal-cap positive terminals.
Rechargeable batteries can be recharged and reused many times.
Used batteries should go to e-waste recycling facilities.
activities.explanation: This card shows how battery parts, uses and disposal differ.

activities.prompt: Your toy stops working because its dry cell is used up. You want to use a battery again many times without making more waste. What should you do?
steps: A dry cell contains a thick moist paste instead of a liquid electrolyte.
A dry cell is single-use, so it must be disposed of after it is used up.
A rechargeable battery can be recharged and reused many times.
Reusing it prevents wastage and saves money, so you should choose a rechargeable battery.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.prompt: Which part is the negative terminal of a dry cell?
options: Zinc container
Thick moist paste
Metal cap
Carbon rod
activities.explanation: The zinc container acts as the dry cell's negative terminal.

activities.prompt: A dry cell can be recharged and used again.
activities.explanation: A dry cell is single-use and must be disposed of after it is used up.

activities.prompt: A dry cell contains a thick moist ______ instead of a liquid electrolyte.
activities.hint: It replaces the liquid electrolyte in a dry cell.
activities.explanation: A dry cell contains a thick moist paste instead of a liquid electrolyte.

activities.prompt: The metal cap covering the carbon rod is the positive terminal.
activities.explanation: The metal cap covering the carbon rod acts as the positive terminal.

activities.prompt: Which statement about rechargeable batteries is true?
options: A dry cell can be reused many times.
A rechargeable battery can be reused many times.
A lithium-ion battery is single-use.
A solid-state battery uses moist paste.
activities.explanation: Rechargeable batteries can be recharged and reused many times. This saves money and reduces wastage.

activities.prompt: Match each device with the rechargeable battery used in it.
activities.explanation: Rechargeable batteries are used in watches, phones, laptops, inverters and electric vehicles.

activities.prompt: Which pair matches both clues: solid materials replace electrolytes; most common rechargeable type?
options: Lithium-ion battery; solid-state battery
Dry cell; lithium-ion battery
Solid-state battery; lithium-ion battery
Solid-state battery; dry cell
activities.explanation: Solid-state batteries use solid materials instead of liquid or paste. Lithium-ion is the most common rechargeable type.

activities.prompt: Used batteries should be taken to special ______ recycling facilities.
activities.hint: Name the special kind of recycling place for used batteries.
activities.explanation: Used batteries should be taken to special e-waste recycling facilities.

activities.prompt: A child has a dry cell and a rechargeable battery. The child wants to use a battery again many times. Which one should they choose?
options: The rechargeable battery.
The dry cell.
The zinc container.
The thick moist paste.

A dry cell is single-use and must be disposed of after use.
The zinc container is only the negative part, not a complete battery.
The thick moist paste is the electrolyte, not a complete battery.

activities.explanation: A rechargeable battery can be recharged and reused many times.

activities.prompt: A dry cell has a thick moist paste. A new design replaces liquid or paste with solid materials. What has changed in the new design?
options: Its electrolyte is now solid.
Its zinc container is now solid.
Its carbon rod is now solid.
Its metal cap is now solid.

This confuses the electrolyte with the zinc container.
This confuses the electrolyte with the carbon rod.
This confuses the electrolyte with the metal cap.

activities.explanation: The electrolyte changes from liquid or paste to solid materials.

lessons.title: Test practice
lessons.sceneAlt: A compass needle is placed inside a coil of wire to indicate the presence of electric current.
lessons.sceneCaption: A compass in an electric coil acts as a current indicator.

sceneCredit.text: Compass in coil by Zátonyi Sándor, (ifj.) Fizped, CC BY-SA 3.0, via Wikimedia Commons
sceneCredit.creator: Zátonyi Sándor, (ifj.) Fizped

activities.context: Sumana closed a circuit containing an iron nail and a wire. Although the model had no separate magnet, the nail picked up iron paper clips like a magnet. She brought a compass close to the model and saw the needle move away from its original direction while current flowed. When Sumana stopped the current, the needle returned to its original direction. She also placed a non-magnetic material between the magnet-like nail and the compass.
activities.prompt: If Sumana closes the circuit again, what should happen to the compass needle?
options: It would again turn away from the direction in which it was resting.
It would remain in its original direction because no current would flow.
It would turn farther in the same direction and stay there after the current stopped.
It would turn in the opposite direction and stay there even after the current stopped.

why.It would remain in its original directio: This wrongly assumes that current has no effect on the needle.
why.It would turn farther in the same direct: This confuses a temporary movement with a lasting change.
why.It would turn in the opposite direction: This predicts both the wrong direction and a permanent change.

activities.explanation: A resumed current produces the magnetic effect again.

activities.context: Sumana closed a circuit containing an iron nail and a wire. Although the model had no separate magnet, the nail picked up iron paper clips like a magnet. She brought a compass close to the model and saw the needle move away from its original direction while current flowed. When Sumana stopped the current, the needle returned to its original direction. She also placed a non-magnetic material between the magnet-like nail and the compass.
activities.prompt: With current flowing, what should happen if the non-magnetic material is left between the nail and the compass?
options: The needle should move away from its original direction because the magnetic effect can pass through the material.
The needle should remain in its original direction because the material blocks all magnetic effects.
The needle should move in the opposite direction because the material reverses the magnetic effect.
The needle should return to its original direction because the material stops the current.

why.The needle should remain in its original: This wrongly treats the material as a complete barrier.
why.The needle should move in the opposite d: This wrongly claims that the material reverses the effect.
why.The needle should return to its original: This confuses blocking magnetic effects with stopping electric current.

activities.explanation: A magnet-like nail can exert its magnetic effect through non-magnetic material.

activities.prompt:
Assertion (A): The compass needle moved away from its original direction while current was flowing.
Reason (R): A current-carrying wire has a magnetic effect on a compass needle.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.
activities.explanation: The magnetic effect of the current-carrying wire caused the needle to move.

activities.prompt:
Assertion (A): The magnetic effect of a magnet can pass through a non-magnetic material placed between magnets.
Reason (R): The region where a magnetic effect can be felt is called a magnetic field.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.
activities.explanation: Both statements are true, but the definition of a magnetic field does not explain the passing of the magnetic effect.

activities.prompt: What is the difference between a magnetic field and the magnetic effect of electric current?
activities.answer: A magnetic field is the region in which a magnetic effect can be felt. The magnetic effect of electric current is the production of that field by electric current. This is why a current-carrying wire can affect a compass needle: while current flows, the needle moves away from its original direction, and when the current stops, it returns. The word “production” identifies the process, while “region” identifies the place where the magnetic effect is experienced.
points: Defines a magnetic field as a region.
Defines the magnetic effect of electric current.
Uses the compass needle to show the effect.
Compares the two ideas clearly.
activities.explanation: Compare your answer with the points a marker looks for.

activities.context: A student made a coil and connected it to a battery. When electric current flowed through the coil, several iron paper clips clung to it. When the student stopped the current, the clips no longer clung to the coil. The student then put an iron nail inside the coil, which made it behave like a stronger magnet. Finally, the student reversed the direction of the current.
activities.prompt: What would happen to the paper clips if the student stopped the electric current again?
options: The clips would no longer cling to the coil.
The clips would remain attached because the iron nail was inside the coil.
The clips would cling more tightly after the current stopped.
The clips would stay attached if the coil had an iron core.

why.The clips would remain attached because: An iron nail makes the coil stronger while current is flowing.
why.The clips would cling more tightly after: A stopped current does not strengthen the magnetic effect.
why.The clips would stay attached if the coi: An iron core does not keep the clips attached without current.

activities.explanation: The clips lost their attachment when the current stopped before.

activities.context: A student made a coil and connected it to a battery. When electric current flowed through the coil, several iron paper clips clung to it. When the student stopped the current, the clips no longer clung to the coil. The student then put an iron nail inside the coil, which made it behave like a stronger magnet. Finally, the student reversed the direction of the current.
activities.prompt: What happened to the electromagnet's poles when the student reversed the direction of the current?
options: The two poles exchanged places.
The two poles remained in the same places.
The two poles merged into one pole.
The poles disappeared.

why.The two poles remained in the same place: Reversal does not leave the poles in their original positions.
An electromagnet continues to have two poles.
Reversing current does not remove the poles.

activities.explanation: Changing current direction reverses the electromagnet's poles.

activities.prompt:
Assertion (A): An electromagnet has two poles, just like a bar magnet.
Reason (R): The poles of an electromagnet can be reversed by changing the direction of the current.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.
activities.explanation: The reason describes reversing the poles, not why an electromagnet has two poles.

activities.prompt:
Assertion (A): Inserting an iron nail inside the coil causes it to stop behaving like a magnet.
Reason (R): Inserting an iron nail inside the coil makes it behave like a stronger magnet.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.
activities.explanation: The assertion is false because the nail makes the coil stronger rather than removing its magnetic behaviour.

activities.prompt: Explain why the iron paper clips clung to the coil while the current was flowing but not after it was stopped.
activities.answer: When electric current flows through the coil, the coil behaves like a magnet. The iron paper clips are therefore attracted to it and cling to the coil. If the current is stopped, the coil no longer attracts the clips, so they no longer cling to it. The iron nail helps make the coil behave like a stronger magnet, but the paper clips still depend on current flowing through the coil.
points: Current makes the coil behave like a magnet.
The clips cling because the coil attracts them.
Stopping the current removes the magnetic effect.
The nail strengthens the coil but does not replace the need for current.
activities.explanation: Compare your answer with the points a marker looks for.

activities.context: At a scrap yard, a crane operator needs to move heavy iron objects. The crane is fitted with a lifting electromagnet. The operator switches the current ON, and the electromagnet lifts the iron objects. When the objects must be released, the operator switches the current OFF, so the magnetic field disappears and the objects are released. This efficient method helps the scrap yard move heavy metal items.
activities.prompt: What would happen if the current remained ON while the crane moved the iron objects?
options: The crane could not move them because an OFF electromagnet has no lifting effect.
The objects would continue to be lifted throughout the move.
The objects would be released as soon as the crane began moving.
The objects would stick more firmly because movement increases attraction.

why.The crane could not move them because an: This describes the effect of switching the current OFF, not leaving it ON.
why.The objects would be released as soon as: This wrongly assumes that movement releases the objects.
why.The objects would stick more firmly beca: This wrongly assumes that movement makes the magnetic attraction stronger.

activities.explanation: This is correct because the electromagnet lifts iron objects whenever the current is ON.

activities.context: At a scrap yard, a crane operator needs to move heavy iron objects. The crane is fitted with a lifting electromagnet. The operator switches the current ON, and the electromagnet lifts the iron objects. When the objects must be released, the operator switches the current OFF, so the magnetic field disappears and the objects are released. This efficient method helps the scrap yard move heavy metal items.
activities.prompt: Why is a lifting electromagnet useful to the crane operator in the scrap yard?
options: It can handle heavy metal items in a controlled way.
It removes the need for electric current.
It makes iron objects become magnetic even when the current is OFF.
It can move the items without producing a magnetic effect.

why.It removes the need for electric current: This wrongly assumes that lifting electromagnets do not need current.
why.It makes iron objects become magnetic ev: This wrongly assumes that iron objects attract without current.
why.It can move the items without producing: This wrongly assumes that the lifting action is not magnetic.

activities.explanation: This is correct because the operator controls the lifting by switching the current ON and OFF.

activities.prompt:
Assertion (A): Earth’s magnetic field helps protect life on Earth.
Reason (R): It acts as a shield around Earth.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.
activities.explanation: Both statements are true, and the shield effect explains how the field helps protect life.

activities.prompt:
Assertion (A): Lifting electromagnets are suitable only for light metal items.
Reason (R): Factories and scrap yards use lifting electromagnets to move heavy metal items efficiently.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.
activities.explanation: The reason is true, but it contradicts the assertion because these electromagnets move heavy items.

activities.prompt: Explain the difference between Earth’s magnetic field and a lifting electromagnet.
activities.answer: Earth’s magnetic field surrounds Earth and is generated by electric currents. Movement of liquid iron inside Earth’s core creates these currents. The field helps many migratory birds, fish and animals navigate, and it acts as a shield that helps protect life on Earth. A lifting electromagnet is a strong electromagnet used for a different purpose. It lifts iron or steel objects when the current is ON. The crane operator can switch the current OFF, causing the magnetic field to disappear and the objects to be released.
points: Movement of liquid iron creates electric currents inside Earth.
The currents generate Earth’s magnetic field.
The field helps animals navigate and helps protect life.
A lifting electromagnet lifts metal objects when current is ON and releases them when it is OFF.
activities.explanation: Compare your answer with the points a marker looks for.

activities.context: A student connects a nichrome wire and a copper wire of the same size and length so current can pass through each. Both wires become warm, but the nichrome wire becomes warmer because it offers more resistance. The student then wonders what will happen if the wire experiment is repeated with two cells. Later, the student notices that the glowing filament in an incandescent lamp is heated by current flowing through it.
activities.prompt: If the current and wire size are kept the same but nichrome replaces copper, what should the student expect?
options: The nichrome wire would reach a higher temperature than the copper wire.
The copper wire would reach a higher temperature than the nichrome wire.
Both wires would reach exactly the same temperature.
Neither wire would become warm because current faces no opposition.

why.The copper wire would reach a higher tem: This reverses the known comparison of their resistance.
why.Both wires would reach exactly the same: It ignores that resistance differs and heat depends on material.
why.Neither wire would become warm because c: It denies both resistance and the heating effect of current.

activities.explanation: Nichrome has greater resistance than copper of the same size and length.

activities.context: A student connects a nichrome wire and a copper wire of the same size and length so current can pass through each. Both wires become warm, but the nichrome wire becomes warmer because it offers more resistance. The student then wonders what will happen if the wire experiment is repeated with two cells. Later, the student notices that the glowing filament in an incandescent lamp is heated by current flowing through it.
activities.prompt: Why does the incandescent lamp in the case give off light?
options: Heating its filament causes the filament to glow.
The current keeps the filament cool, although it still glows.
Resistance stops the current completely, and this makes the filament glow.
The filament glows even when current does not flow through it.

why.The current keeps the filament cool, alt: The given explanation involves heating rather than cooling.
why.Resistance stops the current completely,: Resistance opposes current rather than stopping it completely.
why.The filament glows even when current doe: The filament's glow depends on current heating it.

activities.explanation: Electric current heats the filament, and the heating makes it glow.

activities.prompt:
Assertion (A): A nichrome wire heats more than a copper wire of the same size and length when the same current is used.
Reason (R): A nichrome wire has higher resistance than a copper wire of the same size and length.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.
activities.explanation: Both statements are true, and the higher resistance explains the greater heating of the nichrome wire.

boss.title: Chapter challenge: Electricity: Magnetic and Heating Effects

activities.prompt: What happened when Sumana closed the circuit?
options: The nail picked up iron paper clips.
The nail became a compass needle.
The compass stayed in its direction.
The coil lost its magnetic effect.
activities.explanation: Closing the circuit let current flow. The iron nail picked up clips like a magnet.

activities.prompt: A current-carrying wire can move a compass needle.
activities.explanation: The needle moved away from its original direction. It returned when the current stopped.

activities.prompt: An iron nail inside a coil helps it behave like a stronger ______.
activities.hint: The iron core makes its magnetic effect stronger.
activities.explanation: Inserting the iron nail made the coil behave like a stronger magnet.

activities.prompt: Match each part or change with its effect.
pairs: Makes the coil a stronger magnet
activities.explanation: An electromagnet uses current to behave like a magnet. Its strength and poles depend on current.

activities.prompt: Put the lifting electromagnet’s steps in order.
items: The electromagnet lifts the metal objects.
activities.explanation: Switching current ON lifts metal objects. Switching it OFF removes the magnetic field and releases them.

activities.prompt: Match each cell or battery with its correct description.
pairs: Also known as a Galvanic cell
activities.explanation: Rechargeable batteries can be reused. Lithium-ion is most common, while solid-state batteries use solid electrolytes.

activities.prompt: Nichrome wire has lower resistance than copper wire of the same size and length.
activities.explanation: Nichrome has higher resistance than copper of the same size and length.

activities.prompt: What creates electric currents inside Earth’s core?
options: Heating of nichrome wire
Chemicals in a lemon cell
Movement of liquid iron
Movement of copper wires
activities.explanation: Movement of liquid iron creates currents. These currents generate a magnetic field around Earth.

activities.prompt: Put the current’s path in order.
activities.explanation: Current flows from the positive terminal through the circuit to the negative terminal.

boss.sceneCaption: A compass in an electric coil acts as a current indicator.

chapters.title: Exploring Forces
chapters.summary: In this chapter: 5.1 and 5.2 — what is a force and what can it do?; 5.3 — force as an interaction between objects; 5.4.1 — contact forces, muscular force and friction; 5.4.2 — non-contact forces.

lessons.title: 5.1 and 5.2 — What Is a Force and What Can It Do?

activities.prompt: What surprising things can happen when something pushes or pulls?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: What is a force?
activities.body: Force means a push or a pull on an object. A force can make a resting object move. It can change a moving object’s speed or direction. It can also change an object’s shape. Without the action of force, speed, direction and shape do not change. At rest, forces may balance one another.
keyPoints: Force is a push or a pull.
A force can change movement or shape.
Forces on a resting object may balance.
activities.explanation: A force can affect how an object moves and what it looks like.

activities.prompt: Why can a sideways hit change a moving ball's direction?
steps: A child hits a moving ball from the side.
The hit pushes the ball, so it applies a force.
A force can change the direction of a moving object.
Therefore, the ball may travel in a new direction after the hit.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.prompt: Which words define force?
options: Push or pull
Push only
Pull only
Rest or move
activities.explanation: Force means a push or a pull on an object.

activities.prompt: A force can make an object that is at rest begin to move.
activities.explanation: A push or pull can make a resting object begin to move.

activities.prompt: What can a force change about a moving object?
options: Its speed or direction
Its colour or sound
Its weight or size
Its age or name
activities.explanation: A force can change the speed or direction of a moving object.

activities.prompt: Put these steps in order.
activities.explanation: A force acting on a resting object can make it begin to move.

activities.prompt: Which statement about forces on an object at rest is correct?
options: The forces may balance one another
The forces always move the object
The forces always change its shape
The forces always change its speed
activities.explanation: When an object is at rest, the forces on it may balance one another.

activities.prompt: Speed, direction and shape do not change without the action of force.
activities.explanation: A change in speed, direction or shape needs the action of a force.

activities.prompt: A moving ball is hit from the side. It changes direction. What explains this?
options: The hit applied force, and force can change direction.
The hit applied force, and force can change shape.
The hit applied force, and force can change speed only.
The hit applied force, but force cannot change direction.

why.The hit applied force, and force can cha: The child confuses changing direction with changing shape.
The child thinks force can change speed but not direction.
why.The hit applied force, but force cannot: The child thinks a force cannot change an object's direction.

activities.explanation: This is right because a hit applies force, which can change direction.

activities.prompt: A child presses an inflated balloon. Its shape changes. What explains this?
options: The press applied force, and force can change shape.
The press applied force, and force can change direction.
The press applied force, and force can change speed.
The press applied force, but force cannot change shape.

why.The press applied force, and force can c: The child confuses changing shape with changing direction.
The child confuses changing shape with changing speed.
why.The press applied force, but force canno: The child thinks force can affect only moving objects.

activities.explanation: This is right because pressing applies force, and force can change shape.

activities.prompt: A child pushes a moving toy car from behind. Its speed changes. What explains this?
options: The push applied force, and force can change speed.
The push applied force, and force can change direction.
The push applied force, and force can change shape.
The push applied force, but force cannot change speed.

why.The push applied force, and force can ch: The child confuses changing speed with changing direction.
The child confuses changing speed with changing shape.
why.The push applied force, but force cannot: The child thinks force cannot change a moving object's speed.

activities.explanation: This is right because pushing applies force, and force can change speed.

activities.prompt: A toy car is at rest. A pull makes it move. What explains this?
options: The pull was a force that made the car begin moving.
The pull was a force that changed the car's speed.
The pull was a force that changed the car's direction.
The pull was a force that changed the car's shape.

why.The pull was a force that changed the ca: The child confuses beginning motion with changing speed.
The child confuses beginning motion with changing direction.
The child thinks pulling must always change an object's shape.

activities.explanation: This is right because pulling can make a resting object move.

activities.prompt: A child wants to test if pressing changes an inflated balloon's shape. Which test is fair?
options: Observe its shape, press it, then observe it again.
Observe the balloon's shape without ever pressing it.
Press the inflated balloon but never observe its shape.
Observe the balloon before pressing but never observe after.

why.Observe the balloon's shape without ever: The child thinks observing without pressing can test pressing.
why.Press the inflated balloon but never obs: The child thinks applying force alone is enough without checking shape.
why.Observe the balloon before pressing but: The child thinks one shape check is enough to show a change.

activities.explanation: This is right because both shape checks test the effect of pressing.

lessons.sceneCaption: Kicking a ball shows a force changing an object’s motion.

lessons.title: 5.3 — Force as an Interaction Between Objects

activities.prompt: What happens to your hand when you push a table?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: Force Needs Two Objects
activities.body: A force is a push or pull on an object. An interaction means two objects act on each other. At least two objects must interact for force to occur. When you push a table, your hand and table each feel a force from the other. The unit of force is the newton. Its symbol is N.
keyPoints: A force is a push or pull.
Two objects must interact for force to occur.
The newton, written N, is the unit of force.
activities.explanation: Forces happen through interactions between objects.

activities.prompt: A child pushes a table and wonders why the hand feels force.
steps: The hand and table interact because force needs two objects.
The hand pushes the table because a push is a force.
The table pushes the hand because both objects feel force.
When the push stops, both forces end because the interaction has ended.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.title: Spot the Force
activities.prompt: Which action shows a force?
options: Pushing a table
Looking at a table
Counting the tables
Choosing a table
activities.explanation: A push is a force. Your hand and table interact during it.

activities.title: Name the Unit
activities.prompt: The unit of force is the ______.
activities.hint: This unit has the symbol N.
activities.explanation: The SI unit of force is the newton. Its symbol is N.

activities.title: Match Each Action
activities.prompt: Match each situation with its result.
pairs: The force on your hand disappears
The two objects no longer experience the force
activities.explanation: The objects feel forces during interaction. These forces disappear when interaction ends.

activities.title: Why Does Your Hand Feel a Force?
activities.prompt: Which explanation best fits your hand feeling a force?
options: The hand and table act on each other.
The table acts on the hand alone.
The hand acts without the table.
The newton acts on both objects.
activities.explanation: Your hand and table interact. Each object feels a force from the other.

activities.title: Order the Force Events
activities.prompt: Put these events in order.
items: Your hand and table feel forces from each other
The force on your hand disappears
activities.explanation: The forces appear during the push. The force on your hand disappears when you stop.

activities.prompt: A pull is a force. A child pulls a suitcase. What should the child's hand feel?
options: The child's hand feels a force from the suitcase.
The child's hand feels no force while pulling it.
The suitcase feels no force from the pulling hand.
The child's hand feels force only after the pull ends.

why.The child's hand feels no force while pu: This wrongly denies force on the hand during the interaction.
why.The suitcase feels no force from the pul: This wrongly denies force on the suitcase during the interaction.
why.The child's hand feels force only after: This wrongly places the force after the interaction has ended.

activities.explanation: The hand and suitcase each feel force from the other.

activities.prompt: Each pull involves at least two objects. Two children pull opposite ends of a rope. What happens to both hands?
options: Only one child's hand feels a force from the rope.
Each child's hand feels force only from their own pull.
Each child's hand feels a force from the rope.
Neither child's hand feels a force from the rope.

why.Only one child's hand feels a force from: This wrongly thinks only one object can feel force.
why.Each child's hand feels force only from: This ignores that the other object also acts on each hand.
why.Neither child's hand feels a force from: This wrongly denies force on both interacting objects.

activities.explanation: Each child feels the rope's force during the interaction.

activities.prompt: A push is a force. A child pushes a football with a foot. What should the foot feel during the push?
options: The foot feels no force because the football moves.
The foot feels a force from the football.
The foot feels force only after the push ends.
The football feels force, but the foot feels none.

why.The foot feels no force because the foot: This wrongly thinks only the moving object feels force.
why.The foot feels force only after the push: This wrongly places the force after the interaction ends.
why.The football feels force, but the foot f: This wrongly denies force on the foot during the interaction.

activities.explanation: The foot and football each feel force from the other.

activities.prompt: A hand can feel force during a push. A child pushes a toy box. Which action fairly tests when the force disappears?
options: Push two different toy boxes at different times without any comparison.
Move the toy box away before pushing and check the hand.
Push the toy box after the hand already feels force.
Push the same toy box, then stop and check the hand.

why.Push two different toy boxes at differen: Different objects and times do not make a fair comparison.
why.Move the toy box away before pushing and: Without a push, there is no force during the first part.
why.Push the toy box after the hand already: This misses the change because the force is already present.

activities.explanation: It compares the hand during pushing and after the interaction ends.

activities.prompt: Pushing involves two interacting objects. A child pushes a cupboard. Why is the claim that only the cupboard feels force flawed?
options: The cupboard feels no force during the push.
The hand also feels a force from the cupboard.
The hand can push without any interaction.
The cupboard feels force only after the push ends.

why.The cupboard feels no force during the p: This wrongly denies the hand's push on the cupboard.
why.The hand can push without any interactio: This wrongly treats one object as enough for force.
why.The cupboard feels force only after the: This wrongly places the force after the interaction ends.

activities.explanation: Each object feels a force from the other during interaction.

activities.prompt: A push is a force. A child says one bag can push by itself. Why is this claim flawed?
options: A bag can create push without an interaction.
A push begins when the bag moves by itself.
A push needs another object for the interaction.
A bag keeps pushing even without another object.

why.A bag can create push without an interac: This wrongly treats one object as enough to cause force.
why.A push begins when the bag moves by itse: This wrongly makes movement alone the cause of force.
why.A bag keeps pushing even without another: This wrongly imagines force continuing without another object.

activities.explanation: A force needs at least two objects interacting with each other.

lessons.sceneCaption: Kicking a ball shows a force changing an object’s motion.

lessons.title: 5.4.1 — Contact Forces, Muscular Force and Friction

activities.prompt: How do touches, muscles, and surfaces change the way objects move?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: Contact Forces and Friction
activities.body: Contact forces need physical contact. Contact can be direct, when you use your hands or other body parts. It can be indirect, when you use a stick or rope. Muscular force is a contact force. Muscles contract and elongate during many activities. Friction acts when an object moves or tries to move over another surface. It acts opposite to movement and is greater on rough surfaces.
keyPoints: Contact forces need physical contact.
Direct contact uses body parts; indirect contact uses a stick or rope.
Friction opposes movement and is greater on rough surfaces.
activities.explanation: These ideas help you understand contact, muscular force and friction.

activities.prompt: A child pushes a box with a hand and pulls a cart with a rope. Which contact is direct?
steps: Direct contact uses hands, so the hand touching the box is direct.
Indirect contact uses a rope, so the rope pulling the cart is indirect.
Both actions need physical contact for the force to reach the object.
Muscular force helps because the child’s muscles contract and elongate.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.prompt: Which activity shows indirect contact?
options: Using your hand to press a wall
Using a stick to move a box
Using your hand to lift a bag
Using your foot to kick a ball
activities.explanation: A stick gives indirect contact because it connects you to the box without direct contact.

activities.prompt: You can push a cart indirectly by using a ______.
activities.hint: This tool can link you to the cart.
activities.explanation: A rope is used for indirect contact when you pull or push through it.

activities.prompt: Match each force or contact type with its description.
activities.explanation: Each pair shows an important idea about contact forces and friction.

activities.prompt: Which surface has greater friction?
options: A smooth surface
A rough surface
A surface with no irregularities
activities.explanation: Friction is greater on rough surfaces than on smooth surfaces.

activities.prompt: An object moves to the right. Which way does friction act?
options: Towards the left
Towards the right
Straight upwards
It depends on the surface
activities.explanation: Friction acts opposite to the direction of the object's movement.

activities.prompt: Put the friction story in order.
items: The object moves or tries to move
activities.explanation: Friction appears when touching surfaces move, and it opposes the movement.

activities.prompt: Muscles contract and elongate to produce force. A child’s hands are away from a bag. Can the hands lift the bag this way?
options: No; the hands must touch the bag.
Yes; muscle force works without touch.
No; only friction can provide lifting force.
Yes; the bag can move without contact.

This mistake thinks muscle force can act on the bag without contact.
why.No; only friction can provide lifting fo: This mistake treats friction as the force that lifts the bag.
This mistake allows an object to move without contact.

activities.explanation: This is right because physical contact is needed for direct force.

activities.prompt: A rope can pass a pull from a hand to a cart. Which action shows this indirect contact?
options: The hand pulls the rope, and the rope pulls the cart.
The hand pulls the cart directly without using rope.
The rope stays still while the cart moves by itself.
The cart pulls the hand without touching the rope.

why.The hand pulls the cart directly without: This mistake ignores the rope and shows direct contact.
why.The rope stays still while the cart move: This mistake thinks the cart can move through an untouched rope.
why.The cart pulls the hand without touching: This mistake removes the rope and reverses who pulls whom.

activities.explanation: This is right because a rope can provide indirect contact.

activities.prompt: Tiny irregularities cause friction where surfaces touch. A box on the floor tries to slide right. Which result is most likely?
options: Friction acts against the trying motion.
Friction acts with the trying motion.
Friction disappears when the surfaces touch.
Friction comes only from the object’s speed.

This mistake gives friction the wrong direction.
why.Friction disappears when the surfaces to: This mistake thinks touching surfaces remove friction.
why.Friction comes only from the object’s sp: This mistake thinks speed creates friction instead of surface irregularities.

activities.explanation: This is right because friction acts opposite to the trying movement.

activities.prompt: The same toy moves over a rough floor and a smooth floor. Which observation fits the friction fact?
options: It slows more on the rough floor.
It slows more on the smooth floor.
It moves the same on both floors.
It slides more easily on the rough floor.

This mistake reverses the comparison between rough and smooth surfaces.
This mistake ignores that friction depends on the surfaces.
why.It slides more easily on the rough floor: This mistake thinks greater friction makes sliding easier.

activities.explanation: This is right because friction is greater on rough surfaces.

activities.prompt: Two blocks have different shapes. Which test best shows whether surface roughness affects friction?
options: Slide the same block over rough and smooth floors.
Slide each different block over one rough floor.
Slide one block over rough floors and another over smooth floors.
Slide the same block over two similar rough floors.

why.Slide each different block over one roug: This mistake changes the blocks and never compares rough with smooth.
why.Slide one block over rough floors and an: This mistake changes both the block and the surface.
why.Slide the same block over two similar ro: This mistake keeps both surfaces rough, so roughness is not compared.

activities.explanation: This is right because it changes the surface while keeping the block same.

activities.prompt: Friction acts when an object moves or tries to move. A child says, "A box has no friction before it moves." Which reply is best?
options: The box can have friction while it tries to move.
The box has friction only after it starts sliding.
The box has friction only after it changes direction.
The box cannot have friction while staying still.

why.The box has friction only after it start: This mistake thinks friction needs actual movement first.
why.The box has friction only after it chang: This mistake thinks a direction change must happen before friction.
why.The box cannot have friction while stayi: This mistake thinks staying still always means no friction.

activities.explanation: This is right because friction acts even when an object tries to move.

lessons.sceneAlt: A child pushes a vegetable cart through a busy market in downtown Maracaibo.
lessons.sceneCaption: A child pushes a vegetable cart, showing muscular force and friction through direct contact.

sceneCredit.text: Child working selling vegetables in downtown Maracaibo by Wilfredor, CC0, via Wikimedia Commons

lessons.title: 5.4.2 — Non-Contact Forces

activities.prompt: How can a magnet move something without ever touching it?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: Forces Without Touching
activities.body: Forces can act without objects touching. A magnet attracts magnetic objects and pushes or pulls them. Like poles repel, while unlike poles attract. The push or pull is magnetic force. Rubbing certain objects builds up electrical charges on their surfaces. Charges that do not move by themselves are static charges. A charged object can attract suitable uncharged objects. Electrostatic force can act without touching.
keyPoints: Non-contact forces act without touching.
Like poles repel, and unlike poles attract.
Rubbing certain objects builds up static charges.
activities.explanation: Magnetic and electrostatic forces can work without touching.

activities.prompt: A child holds a magnet near a steel paper clip without touching it. The clip slides toward the magnet. Why?
steps: The magnet and clip never touch, yet the pull is still felt.
The clip is magnetic material, so the magnet attracts it.
This push or pull exerted by the magnet is magnetic force.
Therefore, the clip moves even though nothing touches it.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.title: What Is a Non-Contact Force?
activities.prompt: Which statement is true about non-contact forces?
options: They need objects to touch.
Their effects can be felt without touching.
They only act on charged objects.
They work only when objects move.
activities.explanation: Non-contact forces act without touching, so their effects can still be felt.

activities.title: Magnetic Attraction
activities.prompt: A magnet attracts objects made of magnetic materials.
activities.explanation: A magnet attracts objects made of magnetic materials.

activities.title: Name the Magnetic Force
activities.prompt: The push or pull exerted by a magnet is called ______ force.
activities.hint: Name the force exerted by a magnet.
activities.explanation: Magnetic force is the push or pull exerted by a magnet.

activities.title: Like Magnetic Poles
activities.prompt: What happens when like magnetic poles are brought close together?
options: They repel each other.
They attract each other.
They lose their poles.
They become static charges.
activities.explanation: Like magnetic poles repel each other, so they push away.

activities.title: Match Forces and Effects
activities.prompt: Match each phrase with its correct effect.
activities.explanation: Each pair shows a force or effect described in this lesson.

activities.title: How Electrostatic Attraction Can Happen
activities.prompt: Put these steps in order.
items: Electrical charges build up on their surfaces.
The charges do not move by themselves.
The charged object attracts a suitable uncharged object.
activities.explanation: Rubbing builds up charges, which can then attract suitable uncharged objects.

activities.title: Electrostatic Force
activities.prompt: Which statement about electrostatic force is correct?
options: It can act when objects do not touch.
It is the push or pull exerted by a magnet.
It makes like magnetic poles attract each other.
It makes unlike magnetic poles repel each other.
activities.explanation: Electrostatic force can act without touching. It is the force exerted by a charged body.

activities.prompt: A steel paper clip is held near a magnet without touching it. The clip moves toward the magnet. Why?
options: The magnet pulls the steel clip with magnetic force.
The clip pulls the magnet because the air pushes it.
The magnet and clip stick because they are touching.
The paper clip moves because its static charge attracts.

why.The clip pulls the magnet because the ai: This mistake assumes moving air pushes the clip toward the magnet.
why.The magnet and clip stick because they a: This mistake assumes the clip and magnet actually touch.
why.The paper clip moves because its static: This mistake mixes up static charge with magnetic attraction.

activities.explanation: This is right because the magnet attracts magnetic material with magnetic force.

activities.prompt: Two magnets have unlike poles facing each other. What happens as the gap gets smaller?
options: They pull together because unlike magnetic poles attract.
They push apart because unlike magnetic poles repel.
They pull together because every magnet attracts every magnet.
They stay still because magnetic force needs direct contact.

why.They push apart because unlike magnetic: This mistake reverses the rule for unlike poles.
why.They pull together because every magnet: This mistake generalizes attraction to all pairs of magnetic poles.
why.They stay still because magnetic force n: This mistake assumes force cannot act without touching.

activities.explanation: This is right because unlike magnetic poles attract each other.

lessons.sceneAlt: Two hands hold like poles of bar magnets apart, demonstrating that they repel each other.
lessons.sceneCaption: Like magnetic poles repel each other without touching.

sceneCredit.text: Feeling magnetic repulsion by Pieter Kuiper, Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons
sceneCredit.creator: Pieter Kuiper

lessons.title: 5.5 — Weight and Its Measurement

activities.prompt: Why do some objects feel heavier in one place than another?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: Understanding weight
activities.body: Weight is the force with which the Earth pulls an object towards itself. It shows how strongly the Earth pulls that object. The SI unit of weight is the newton, written as N. A spring balance measures weight or force. Its spring stretches when the Earth pulls a hanging object. An object's mass stays the same everywhere, but its weight can change from place to place.
keyPoints: Weight measures the Earth's pull on an object.
The newton is the SI unit of weight.
A spring balance measures weight or force.
Weight can change between places, but mass stays the same.
activities.explanation: The spring balance is the key measuring device in this lesson.

activities.prompt: The same toy moves to another place. What stays the same, what may change, and why?
steps: The same toy keeps the same mass in both places.
The Earth may pull it with different strength.
Weight shows how strongly the Earth pulls.
So its mass stays the same, but its weight may change.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.prompt: What does an object's weight show?
options: How fast it moves
How much heat it holds
How strongly Earth pulls it
How much space it takes up
activities.explanation: Exactly. Weight shows how strongly the Earth pulls an object.

activities.prompt: The SI unit of weight is the newton, written as N.
activities.explanation: Correct. The newton is the SI unit of weight.

activities.prompt: A spring balance can measure ______ or force.
activities.hint: Look for the device that shows an object's pull from Earth.
activities.explanation: Good choice. A spring balance measures weight or force.

activities.prompt: Which device measures weight or force?
options: thermometer
barometer
spring balance
speedometer
activities.explanation: Well done. This device measures weight or force.

activities.prompt: Match each idea with the correct word.
pairs: Device for measuring weight or force
Quantity that stays the same everywhere
activities.explanation: You matched each idea with its correct science word.

activities.prompt: Put these steps in order when a spring balance measures an object.
items: The Earth pulls the hanging object.
The amount of stretching shows the object's weight.
activities.explanation: Correct order. The pull causes stretching, and the balance shows the weight.

activities.prompt: A spring balance's stretching shows an object's weight. Two different objects are tested. What does more stretching show?
options: It shows a greater weight.
It shows a greater mass.
It shows a smaller weight.
It shows no change in weight.

This mistake confuses weight with mass.
This mistake reverses what more stretching shows.
This mistake ignores that the stretching changed.

activities.explanation: This is right because more stretching shows a greater weight.

activities.prompt: A spring stretches because Earth pulls the hanging object. Two objects hang from one spring. What does more stretching show?
options: The more-stretched object has more weight.
The less-stretched object has more weight.
Both objects have equal weights.
Their weights cannot be compared here.

why.The less-stretched object has more weigh: This mistake reverses the link between weight and stretching.
This mistake assumes different objects stretch one spring equally.
This mistake ignores a clear difference in stretching.

activities.explanation: More weight means a stronger pull, which stretches the spring more.

activities.prompt: A spring balance measures weight or force. One child compares two objects. Which test is fairest?
options: Use the same spring balance for both objects.
Use a different spring balance for each object.
Change the spring before testing the second object.
Measure one object, then guess the other.

why.Use a different spring balance for each: This mistake changes the measuring device during the comparison.
why.Change the spring before testing the sec: This mistake changes the spring instead of keeping it the same.
why.Measure one object, then guess the other: This mistake replaces the second measurement with a guess.

activities.explanation: This is right because one balance gives a fair stretching comparison.

activities.prompt: The balance has a maximum reading of 10 N. Its smallest readable value is 0.2 N. What happens with a weight above 10 N?
options: The balance cannot show that weight.
The balance will show a value above 10 N.
The balance will show exactly 10 N.
The balance will stop showing any reading.

why.The balance will show a value above 10 N: This mistake treats a weight above the maximum as readable.
This mistake mistakes the maximum reading for the object's weight.
why.The balance will stop showing any readin: This mistake guesses an effect that the facts do not give.

activities.explanation: This is right because 10 N is the balance's maximum measurable weight.

activities.prompt: Weight can change from place to place. The same toy is weighed in two places. What must be true about its mass?
options: The toy has the same mass in both places.
The toy has different masses in the two places.
The toy has more mass where its weight is larger.
The toy has no mass in either place.

why.The toy has different masses in the two: This mistake wrongly allows mass to change with place.
why.The toy has more mass where its weight i: This mistake wrongly connects greater weight with greater mass.
This mistake treats mass as something that can disappear.

activities.explanation: This is right because an object's mass stays the same everywhere.

activities.prompt: A balance's stretching shows an object's weight. Two objects are tested. A child says more stretch proves more mass. What mistake did the child make?
options: The child confused weight with mass.
The child reversed the stretching comparison.
The child said both objects have equal weight.
The child ignored Earth's pull on the objects.

why.The child reversed the stretching compar: This mistake treats a weight reading as proof about mass.
why.The child said both objects have equal w: This mistake ignores the clear difference in stretching.
why.The child ignored Earth's pull on the ob: This mistake assumes Earth's pull does not affect stretching.

activities.explanation: This is right because the balance shows weight, not mass.

lessons.title: 5.6 — Floating and Sinking

activities.prompt: Why do some things bob on water while others sink?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: Floating and sinking
activities.body: Some objects float on water, while others sink to the bottom. Water pushes upwards on a bottle pushed into it. This upward force is called upthrust or buoyant force. Gravity pulls an object downwards. An object floats when gravity and buoyant force are equal. The upward force equals the weight of displaced liquid. Pumice floats because it is less dense than water.
keyPoints: Some objects float, while others sink.
Upthrust pushes upwards, while gravity pulls downwards.
Equal forces help an object float.
Density affects buoyant force.
activities.explanation: These ideas explain why some objects float and others sink.

activities.title: Float or sink?

tasks.then: It is now denser than water, so it sinks.

activities.takeaway: Things lighter than water for their size float; denser things sink.
activities.explanation: Things lighter than water for their size float; denser things sink.

activities.prompt: A child pushes a bottle into water and lets it float. Why?
steps: Water pushes upwards, so the bottle feels an upthrust force.
Earth's gravity also acts, pulling the bottle downwards.
The two forces are equal, so the bottle can float.
The displaced water and bottle have equal weights, showing the balance.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.title: Where does a sinking object go?
activities.prompt: What happens to an object that sinks?
options: It moves to the bottom.
It stays on the surface.
It rises upwards.
It loses all weight.
activities.explanation: An object that sinks moves to the bottom of the liquid.

activities.title: Name the upward force
activities.prompt: The upward force applied by a liquid is called ______.
activities.hint: This force is also called buoyant force.
activities.explanation: The upward force applied by a liquid is called upthrust.

activities.title: Match the ideas
activities.prompt: Match each idea with its correct partner.
activities.explanation: Upthrust and buoyant force name the same upward force. Equal forces help an object float.

activities.title: What affects upthrust?
activities.prompt: Which factor affects the buoyant force?
options: The colour of the liquid.
The density of the liquid.
The shape of the container.
The time of day.
activities.explanation: The density of the liquid is one factor affecting buoyant force.

activities.title: The floating process
activities.prompt: Put these stages in order.
items: An object is immersed in a liquid.
Upward force equals the weight of displaced liquid.
Equal object and displaced-liquid weights mean floating.
activities.explanation: An immersed object displaces liquid. The upward force depends on the displaced liquid's weight. Equal weights allow floating.

activities.title: What does upthrust equal?
activities.prompt: An immersed object feels an upward force equal to what?
options: The weight of the object.
The weight of the displaced liquid.
The colour of the liquid.
The weight of the container.
activities.explanation: The upward force equals the weight of the displaced liquid.

activities.prompt: A bottle is pushed into water and into oil. What happens each time?
options: Each liquid pushes the bottle upwards.
Each liquid pulls the bottle downwards.
Only water pushes the bottle upwards.
Only oil pushes the bottle upwards.

This mistake treats gravity as a force from the liquid.
This mistake believes only water can give an upward force.
This mistake believes only oil can give an upward force.

activities.explanation: Water gives an upward force to the pushed bottle.

activities.prompt: To test liquid density's effect on upthrust, which setup is fairest?
options: Use the same bottle at the same depth in different liquids.
Use different bottles at the same depth in one liquid.
Use the same bottle at different depths in one liquid.
Use different bottles at different depths in different liquids.

why.Use different bottles at the same depth: Changing bottles adds another difference to the test.
why.Use the same bottle at different depths: Changing depth does not keep the test fair for density.
why.Use different bottles at different depth: Changing bottles and depth adds extra differences.

activities.explanation: Only the liquid changes, so density's effect can be compared.

activities.prompt: Gravity pulls every object downwards. Why can an object still float?
options: Gravity and upthrust can balance, so the object can float.
Gravity does not act on objects that are placed in liquids.
Upthrust always pulls objects towards the bottom of liquids.
Water removes gravity from every object that can float.

why.Gravity does not act on objects that are: This wrongly says Earth's gravity stops acting in liquids.
why.Upthrust always pulls objects towards th: This reverses the upward direction of the buoyant force.
why.Water removes gravity from every object: This wrongly says water cancels Earth's gravitational force.

activities.explanation: Equal gravity and upthrust allow an object to float.

lessons.sceneAlt: A young man in Tanzania kicks a ball while playing with others.
