activities.context: A moving ball was travelling along a path when it was hit. After the hit, the ball changed direction. An inflated balloon was then pressed, and its shape changed. A drawer was also opened by pulling it. Later, an autorickshaw driver turned the steering handle, and the vehicle changed direction. These actions took place one after another, and the question was which changes showed the action of force.
activities.prompt: If the moving ball were hit again, what could happen next?
options: Its direction of travel could change.
Its direction of travel would stay exactly the same.
Its speed and direction would both remain unchanged.
Its direction would change only after it had become stationary.

why.Its direction of travel would stay exact: A force need not always change direction.
why.Its speed and direction would both remai: A force can change speed or direction, so neither must stay unchanged.
why.Its direction would change only after it: Direction can change while the ball is still moving.

activities.explanation: Correct: a hit applies a force that can change direction.

activities.context: A moving ball was travelling along a path when it was hit. After the hit, the ball changed direction. An inflated balloon was then pressed, and its shape changed. A drawer was also opened by pulling it. Later, an autorickshaw driver turned the steering handle, and the vehicle changed direction. These actions took place one after another, and the question was which changes showed the action of force.
activities.prompt: Why does turning the steering handle let the autorickshaw change direction?
options: Turning the handle applies a force, and force can change direction.
The handle changes direction without any push or pull.
The autorickshaw changes direction only because its speed changes.
The driver applies force only to change the handle's shape.

why.The handle changes direction without any: Direction does not change without the action of force.
why.The autorickshaw changes direction only: Changing speed is not the only way a force can act.
why.The driver applies force only to change: Applying force to a handle does not mean it only changes shape.

activities.explanation: Correct: turning involves applying force, which can change direction.

activities.prompt:
Assertion (A): The moving ball changed its direction when it was hit.
Reason (R): The hit applied a force to the ball.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.
activities.explanation: Both statements are true, and the force from the hit explains the change in direction.

activities.prompt:
Assertion (A): The rubber band changed its shape when it was stretched.
Reason (R): An object's shape can change without the action of force.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.
activities.explanation: Stretching applies force and changes the shape, but the reason is false.

activities.prompt: Explain how the effect of force on a moving object differs from its effect on an object at rest.
activities.answer: An object at rest is not moving, while a moving object has motion. A force can make the resting object begin to move. For a moving object, force can change its speed or the direction in which it travels. A force can also change an object's shape, whether the object is at rest or moving. Although the effects of force can be different, they all involve a push or pull acting on an object. When an object is at rest, the forces on it may balance one another, so it need not begin to move.
points: Defines an object at rest and a moving object.
Explains that force can start motion.
Explains that force can change speed and direction.
Mentions balancing forces on an object at rest.
activities.explanation: Compare your answer with the points a marker looks for.

activities.prompt:
Assertion (A): A table feels a force when a hand pushes it.
Reason (R): The hand and table are interacting, and each object feels a force from the other.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.
activities.explanation: The reason explains the table's force because both objects feel a force during their interaction.

activities.prompt:
Assertion (A): A hand keeps feeling a force after the person stops pushing a table.
Reason (R): The hand and table no longer interact after pushing stops, so their force interaction ends.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.
activities.explanation: The statement is false because the force on the hand disappears when pushing stops, while the reason is true.

activities.prompt: Explain why pushing a table makes the hand feel a force and why this changes when pushing stops.
activities.answer: A force needs an interaction involving at least two objects. When a hand pushes a table, the hand and table act on each other, so each object feels a force from the other. The hand therefore feels a force while the pushing continues. When the person stops pushing, the hand-table interaction ends. The force on the hand disappears, and the two objects no longer experience the force from that interaction.
points: A force requires at least two interacting objects.
The hand and table each feel a force from the other.
The hand feels a force while pushing continues.
The force disappears when the interaction ends.
activities.explanation: Compare your answer with the points a marker looks for.

activities.context: A child pulls a toy cart using a rope. The child’s hands do not touch the cart, but the rope provides physical contact with it. The child’s muscles contract and elongate to produce muscular force. The cart moves over a rough floor, and friction acts opposite to its movement. If the floor were smooth, the amount of friction would be smaller.
activities.prompt: What would most likely happen if the child replaced the rough floor with a smooth one?
options: The cart would tend to slide more easily because friction would be lower.
The cart would tend to move less easily because friction would be lower.
The cart would keep moving at exactly the same ease because friction does not depend on the surfaces.
The cart would move less easily because smooth surfaces produce greater friction.

why.The cart would keep moving at exactly th: The second option reverses the effect of lower friction.
why.The cart would move less easily because: The third option denies the effect of the nature of surfaces.

activities.explanation: Smooth surfaces produce less friction than rough surfaces.

activities.context: A child pulls a toy cart using a rope. The child’s hands do not touch the cart, but the rope provides physical contact with it. The child’s muscles contract and elongate to produce muscular force. The cart moves over a rough floor, and friction acts opposite to its movement. If the floor were smooth, the amount of friction would be smaller.
activities.prompt: What would change if the child pushed the cart directly with their hands instead of using the rope?
options: The method of contact would change from indirect to direct.
No contact force would act because the cart would be moving.
The muscular force would disappear because the hands touch the cart.
The method would remain indirect because the cart is moving.

why.No contact force would act because the c: Replacing the rope with hands changes the contact method.
why.The muscular force would disappear becau: The second option wrongly says that contact forces stop acting on moving objects.
why.The method would remain indirect because: The third option wrongly claims that direct contact removes muscular force.

activities.explanation: Hands touching the cart make the contact direct.

activities.prompt:
Assertion (A): The rope allows force to be applied to the cart without the child’s hands touching it directly.
Reason (R): The rope provides indirect physical contact between the child and the cart.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.
activities.explanation: Both statements are true, and the second explains how the rope allows the force to be applied.

activities.prompt:
Assertion (A): Friction acts in the same direction as the movement of an object.
Reason (R): Friction acts opposite to the direction of the object’s movement.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.
activities.explanation: The assertion is false, while the reason correctly states the direction of friction.

activities.prompt: How does direct contact differ from indirect contact when a force is applied?
activities.answer: Direct contact means that the person applying the force touches the object using hands or another body part. Indirect contact means that the person does not touch the object directly but uses something such as a stick or rope, which provides physical contact with the object. In both cases, a contact force is involved because the force acts during physical contact. Muscular force is an example of a contact force because muscles contract and elongate to produce it.
points: Direct contact uses hands or another body part.
Indirect contact uses a stick or rope.
Both methods involve physical contact.
Muscular force is a contact force.
activities.explanation: Compare your answer with the points a marker looks for.

activities.context: While clearing a table, a child rubbed a plastic ruler on a cloth. Electrical charges built up on the ruler’s surface, so it became a charged object. The ruler attracted small pieces of suitable material without being touched. Nearby, a magnet was attracting magnetic objects, while two magnets with like poles faced each other and remained apart.
activities.prompt: What would happen if the charged ruler were brought close to an uncharged object made of a suitable material?
options: It would pull the object toward the ruler.
It would push the object away from the ruler.
It would have no effect on the object.
It would affect the object only after touching it.

why.It would push the object away from the r: Electrostatic force can act without touching.
The force is attraction rather than repulsion.
why.It would affect the object only after to: The objects do not need to touch for the force to act.

activities.explanation: A charged object attracts certain suitable uncharged objects.

activities.context: While clearing a table, a child rubbed a plastic ruler on a cloth. Electrical charges built up on the ruler’s surface, so it became a charged object. The ruler attracted small pieces of suitable material without being touched. Nearby, a magnet was attracting magnetic objects, while two magnets with like poles faced each other and remained apart.
activities.prompt: If one magnet were turned so that unlike poles faced each other, what would happen next?
options: The magnets would move toward each other.
The magnets would move farther apart.
The magnets would stop affecting each other.
The magnets would attract only after touching.

The force can act without contact.
why.The magnets would stop affecting each ot: Turning the magnet changes the poles facing each other.
why.The magnets would attract only after tou: Attraction does not require the magnets to touch.

activities.explanation: Unlike magnetic poles attract.

activities.prompt:
Assertion (A): A magnet pulls an object made of a magnetic material toward itself.
Reason (R): The object is made of a magnetic material, which a magnet attracts.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.
activities.explanation: The reason directly explains why the magnet attracts the object.

activities.prompt:
Assertion (A): A magnet’s two like poles pull toward each other.
Reason (R): The push or pull exerted by a magnet is called magnetic force.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.
activities.explanation: Like poles repel rather than attract, although the statement about magnetic force is true.

activities.prompt: Explain the difference between magnetic force and electrostatic force.
activities.answer: Magnetic force is the push or pull exerted by a magnet. A magnet attracts objects made of magnetic materials, while like magnetic poles repel each other and unlike magnetic poles attract each other. Electrostatic force is the force exerted by a charged body. It can act even when objects do not touch. For example, a charged object attracts certain uncharged objects made of suitable materials, and opposite kinds of charges attract each other.
points: Defines magnetic force correctly.
Defines electrostatic force correctly.
Explains the effect of like and unlike magnetic poles.
Explains attraction involving charged or suitable uncharged objects.
activities.explanation: Compare your answer with the points a marker looks for.

boss.title: Chapter challenge: Exploring Forces

activities.prompt: In science, what does force mean?
options: A push on an object
A pull on an object
A push or pull on an object
A change in an object
activities.explanation: A force is a push or pull on an object. Both pushing and pulling are forces.

activities.prompt: When an object is at rest, forces on it may be balancing one another.
activities.explanation: Balancing forces can keep an object at rest. The forces may be acting together.

activities.prompt: The SI unit of force is the ______.
activities.hint: This unit is also used to measure weight.
activities.explanation: The newton is the SI unit of force. Its symbol is N.

activities.prompt: Match each force effect with its example.
activities.explanation: Forces can change how fast an object moves, where it moves, and its shape. Each pair shows one effect.

activities.prompt: Which statement about force is correct?
options: One object can create force alone
Two objects must interact for force
Force needs no interaction
Only living things can push or pull
activities.explanation: A force needs an interaction between at least two objects. Each object feels a force from the other.

activities.prompt: Friction acts in the same direction as the movement of an object.
activities.explanation: Friction acts opposite to the direction of the object's movement. It acts when an object moves or tries to move.

activities.prompt: Put these events in order when you push a table and then stop.
items: Your hand and the table interact
The force on your hand disappears
activities.explanation: The objects interact during pushing, and your hand feels the force. When pushing stops, the interaction and force end.

activities.prompt: Which statement about weight and mass is correct?
options: Weight always stays the same
Mass changes at every place
Weight can change from place to place
Mass measures the Earth's pull
activities.explanation: Weight can change from place to place because it depends on Earth's pull. Mass remains the same at every place.

activities.prompt: What is the upward force applied by a liquid called?
options: Friction force
Magnetic force
Buoyant force
Contact force
activities.explanation: The upward force applied by a liquid is called upthrust or buoyant force. It can help an object float.

chapters.title: Pressure, Winds, Storms, and Cyclones
chapters.summary: In this chapter: lesson 1: pressure and liquids; lesson 2: pressure exerted by air; lesson 3: how winds form; lesson 4: high-speed winds and air pressure.

lessons.title: Lesson 1: Pressure and Liquids

activities.prompt: What happens to water pressure as a pipe gets deeper?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: Understanding Pressure
activities.body: Pressure is the force acting on each unit of surface area. A small area gives higher pressure. A larger area lowers it. Broad straps spread a bag’s weight and feel comfortable. Narrow straps act on a smaller shoulder area. The SI unit is the newton per square metre, also called a pascal. Liquids exert pressure in all directions.
keyPoints: Smaller area means higher pressure.
Larger area means lower pressure.
Liquids exert pressure in all directions.
activities.explanation: This card explains pressure and how area changes it.

activities.prompt: Why do broad bag straps feel more comfortable than narrow straps?
steps: Narrow straps make the bag's weight act on a smaller shoulder area.
Pressure is the force acting on each unit of surface area.
A smaller application area produces a higher pressure.
Broad straps spread the weight, so they feel more comfortable.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.prompt: Which strap choice acts on a smaller shoulder area?
options: Narrow straps
Wide straps
Soft straps
Heavy straps
activities.explanation: Narrow straps make the bag’s weight act on less shoulder area.

activities.prompt: Broad straps feel more comfortable because they spread the bag’s weight.
activities.explanation: Spreading the weight over a larger area makes broad straps more comfortable.

activities.prompt: Pressure is the force acting on each unit of surface ______.
activities.hint: Think about the surface where the force acts.
activities.explanation: Pressure describes force acting on each unit of surface area.

activities.prompt: Why is a nail easier to drive through its pointed end?
options: The pointed end has a wider area.
The pointed end has no pointed tip.
The pointed end has a smaller area.
The pointed end has a broad surface.
activities.explanation: The pointed end has a smaller area, so it produces higher pressure.

activities.prompt: Match each item to its effect.
activities.explanation: Each item acts on a smaller area or spreads weight more widely.

activities.prompt: One overhead tank is higher than another. What happens to pressure at the higher tank’s taps?
options: The higher tank has less pressure.
The higher tank has more pressure.
The higher tank has equal pressure.
The higher tank has no pressure.
activities.explanation: Putting an overhead tank at a height increases pressure at the taps.

activities.prompt: A bag's narrow straps act on a small shoulder area. How does the pressure compare with broad straps?
options: The pressure will be higher.
The pressure will be lower.
The pressure will stay the same.
The pressure will disappear.

This mistake thinks spreading weight lowers pressure in narrow straps.
This mistake thinks pressure does not depend on the area.
This mistake thinks reducing the area removes the bag's weight.

activities.explanation: Narrow straps use a smaller area, so they produce higher pressure.

activities.prompt: The same push is used on a nail's pointed end and its flat end. Which end enters the wood more easily?
options: The pointed end, because the push covers less area.
The flat end, because the push covers less area.
The pointed end, because the push covers more area.
The flat end, because the push covers more area.

why.The flat end, because the push covers le: This mistake reverses the link between area and pressure.
why.The pointed end, because the push covers: This mistake thinks a larger application area gives higher pressure.
why.The flat end, because the push covers mo: This mistake gets both the area and pressure effect wrong.

activities.explanation: The pointed end has a smaller application area, giving higher pressure.

activities.prompt: Two balloons are fitted below two water pipes. One pipe has a taller water column. Which balloon bulges more?
options: The balloon under the taller pipe bulges more.
The balloon under the shorter pipe bulges more.
Both balloons bulge equally because the pipes are similar.
Both balloons bulge equally because the water has weight.

why.The balloon under the shorter pipe bulge: This mistake thinks the shorter column produces more pressure.
why.Both balloons bulge equally because the: This mistake assumes similar pipes give equal pressure at different heights.
This mistake thinks any water weight gives equal bulges.

activities.explanation: A taller water column produces more pressure where the balloon bulges.

activities.prompt: An overhead tank is raised farther above the taps. What happens to the pressure at those taps?
options: The pressure at the taps increases.
The pressure at the taps decreases.
The pressure at the taps stays the same.
The pressure at the taps disappears.

This mistake reverses the effect of raising the tank.
This mistake thinks the tank's height does not affect pressure.
This mistake thinks raising the tank removes the water's pressure.

activities.explanation: Putting the overhead tank higher increases the pressure at the taps.

activities.prompt: A child says broad straps feel better because they lower pressure. Which test checks this claim fairly?
options: Use one bag with narrow straps and broad straps.
Use two bags with only broad straps.
Use two bags with only narrow straps.
Use one bag but change the bag's contents.

Two bags may have different weights, so the test is not fair.
This tests bags with the same strap type, not strap width.
why.Use one bag but change the bag's content: Changing the contents changes the weight, so the test is not fair.

activities.explanation: Keeping the bag and weight the same makes the strap test fair.

lessons.title: Lesson 2: Pressure Exerted by Air

activities.prompt: Why does a balloon swell all around when we blow it up?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: Understanding Air Pressure
activities.body: The atmosphere is the envelope of air around Earth. It reaches many kilometres above Earth's surface. Air pushes on every object in all directions. This push is pressure. The pressure around us is called atmospheric pressure. Air pressure is measured in millibars or hectopascals. One millibar and one hectopascal each equal 100 Pa. Our bodies are not crushed because internal pressure balances atmospheric pressure.
keyPoints: Air pushes on all objects in every direction.
Atmospheric pressure is the pressure of surrounding air.
Internal pressure balances atmospheric pressure inside our bodies.
activities.explanation: Air surrounds us and pushes in every direction.

activities.prompt: Why does lifting a paper plate feel harder with unfolded chart paper?
steps: Air pushes on the covered plate from all around.
The larger sheet increases the area where air pushes.
More air push means more effort is needed to lift.
So lifting feels harder with the unfolded chart paper.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.prompt: What is the atmosphere?
options: An envelope of air around Earth
A layer of water around Earth
A solid shell around Earth
A cloud above Earth's surface
activities.explanation: The atmosphere is the envelope of air that surrounds Earth.

activities.prompt: Air exerts pressure on only some objects.
activities.explanation: Air exerts pressure on all objects, not just some of them.

activities.prompt: The pressure of the air around us is called ______ pressure.
activities.hint: Use the name given for the pressure around us.
activities.explanation: The pressure of the surrounding air is called atmospheric pressure.

activities.prompt: What happens when you lift a paper plate covered with unfolded chart paper?
options: More effort is needed.
The plate becomes lighter.
The chart paper falls off.
The plate starts floating.
activities.explanation: The unfolded chart paper makes lifting the plate need more effort.

activities.prompt: What happens to air's push when the covering sheet has a larger area?
options: The push vanishes.
The push increases.
The push stays fixed.
The push becomes weak.
activities.explanation: Air's push increases when the area of the covering sheet increases.

activities.prompt: Match each situation with what happens.
pairs: An envelope of air around Earth
A balloon's mouth is left open
activities.explanation: Air pushes in every direction, so balloons expand everywhere. Open mouths let air escape. Higher surrounding pressure helps a sucker stick.

activities.prompt: Why does a sucker stick to a surface?
options: Surrounding air pressure is higher.
Inside air pressure is higher.
The surface pulls it upwards.
The sucker has become heavier.
activities.explanation: The surrounding air pressure is higher than the pressure inside the sucker.

activities.prompt: One millibar and one hectopascal each equal ______ Pa.
activities.hint: Use the value given for both units.
activities.explanation: One millibar and one hectopascal each equal 100 Pa.

activities.prompt: A balloon’s mouth is left open. What happens to its size?
options: It becomes smaller because air escapes.
It becomes larger because air escapes.
It stays the same because air escapes.
It becomes flat because air escapes.

Escaping air does not make a balloon grow.
Air escapes, so the balloon cannot stay the same.
This assumes escaping air must make the balloon flat.

activities.explanation: Air leaving the open mouth lets the balloon shrink.

activities.prompt: How can you test whether a bigger sheet makes lifting harder?
options: Keep the plate fixed and change only the sheet area.
Change both the plate and sheet each time you test.
Keep the sheet fixed and change only the plate.
Change the lifting speed and keep the sheet area.

why.Change both the plate and sheet each tim: Changing two things cannot show which change caused the result.
why.Keep the sheet fixed and change only the: This changes the plate instead of the sheet area.
why.Change the lifting speed and keep the sh: Speed is not the variable being tested here.

activities.explanation: Changing only sheet area tests its effect on lifting effort.

lessons.title: Lesson 3: How Winds Form

activities.prompt: What makes wind start and change direction?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: Wind and Pressure
activities.body: Wind forms when air moves because pressure is different in two places. In a balloon model, air moves from the inflated balloon to the uninflated one. It stops when both balloons have equal pressure. Near land and sea, daytime heating and nighttime cooling create pressure differences. These differences make land and sea breezes, and a bigger pressure difference makes moving air faster.
keyPoints: Air moves between balloons until pressure is equal.
Land and sea breezes mainly result from pressure differences.
A bigger pressure difference makes moving air faster.
activities.explanation: Pressure differences make air move and create wind.

activities.prompt: Two balloons are joined by a tube. One is inflated, and one is uninflated. What will happen to the air?
steps: Air moves because the inflated balloon has greater pressure.
The air keeps moving because the two pressures remain unequal.
The air stops flowing when both balloons have equal pressure.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.title: The Balloon Model
activities.prompt: Air moves from the inflated balloon into the ______ balloon.
activities.hint: Choose the balloon that starts with less air.
activities.explanation: The air moves from the inflated balloon into the uninflated balloon.

activities.title: Equal Pressure
activities.prompt: Air stops flowing when both balloons have equal pressure.
activities.explanation: Correct! The pressure becomes equal in both balloons, so the air stops.

activities.title: Land and Sea Breezes
activities.prompt: Match each clue with the correct statement about land and sea breezes.
pairs: Air flows from the high-pressure sea region towards the land
The water is warmer than the land
Wind blows from the land towards the sea and forms a land breeze
Pressure differences over land and sea
activities.explanation: During the day, sea air moves towards land. At night, land air moves towards the sea. Pressure differences mainly cause these breezes.

activities.title: The Air Movement
activities.prompt: Put the balloon steps in the correct order.
items: Air moves from the inflated balloon towards the uninflated balloon.
The pressure becomes equal in both balloons.
activities.explanation: Air first moves between the two balloons. The pressure then becomes equal, so the air stops flowing.

activities.title: The Main Cause
activities.prompt: What mainly causes land and sea breezes?
options: differences in air pressure over land and sea
differences in surface heating over land and sea
differences in water depth over land and sea
differences in land height over land and sea
activities.explanation: Land and sea breezes mainly result from pressure differences over land and sea.

activities.title: Pressure and Air Speed
activities.prompt: What happens when the pressure difference becomes bigger?
options: The moving air becomes slower.
The moving air becomes warmer.
The moving air becomes faster.
The moving air becomes still.
activities.explanation: A bigger pressure difference makes moving air faster. You spotted the key connection.

activities.prompt: During the day, land heats faster than water. The sea has higher pressure. Which way will the air move?
options: It will move from the sea towards the land.
It will move from the land towards the sea.
It will move from both areas straight upwards.
It will move in circles around the water.

why.It will move from the land towards the s: This reverses the daytime direction of the airflow.
why.It will move from both areas straight up: This mistakes vertical movement for pressure-driven airflow.
why.It will move in circles around the water: This invents a circular airflow instead of a pressure-driven flow.

activities.explanation: During the day, air flows from the high-pressure sea towards the land.

activities.prompt: At night, the water is warmer than the land. Which wind should form?
options: A land breeze will blow from the land to the sea.
A sea breeze will blow from the sea to the land.
No breeze will form between the land and sea.
A land breeze will blow from the land to the hills.

why.A sea breeze will blow from the sea to t: This uses the daytime direction instead of the nighttime direction.
why.No breeze will form between the land and: This ignores pressure differences between land and sea.
why.A land breeze will blow from the land to: This mistakes land-to-sea flow for land-to-hills flow.

activities.explanation: At night, land-to-sea airflow is called a land breeze.

activities.prompt: A bigger pressure difference can make moving air faster. Which test best checks this idea?
options: Keep the distance equal and change the pressure difference.
Change the distance and keep the pressure difference equal.
Use different distances and different pressure differences.
Change both distance and pressure difference each time.

why.Change the distance and keep the pressur: This changes distance as well, so pressure difference is not tested alone.
why.Use different distances and different pr: This changes two things, so the cause is not clear.
why.Change both distance and pressure differ: This changes two things, so the cause is not clear.

activities.explanation: The test changes pressure difference while keeping the setup fair.

lessons.title: Lesson 4: High-Speed Winds and Air Pressure

activities.prompt: What happens to air pressure when winds rush past us?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: Wind and Air Pressure
activities.body: When you blow between two balloons, you create a low-pressure area. The higher surrounding air pressure pushes the balloons towards each other. Blowing harder makes them approach faster. High-speed winds are accompanied by reduced air pressure. Near a house, pressure above the roof may become lower than pressure below it. A large pressure difference can blow away a weak roof.
keyPoints: Blowing between balloons creates low pressure.
Higher surrounding pressure pushes the balloons together.
High-speed winds reduce air pressure.
activities.explanation: Air pressure differences explain many moving balloons and roof dangers.

activities.prompt: A strong storm is near a house. Should someone open its doors and windows?
steps: High-speed winds create low pressure over houses, including above their roofs.
Pressure above a roof can be lower than pressure below it.
A large pressure difference can blow a weak roof away.
Opening doors and windows reduces pressure difference and helps protect the house.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.title: Protecting Houses During Storms
activities.body: Strong winds can lower the pressure above a house’s roof. This may make roof pressure lower than pressure below it. If the pressure difference becomes large, a weak roof may be blown away. Opening doors and windows during strong storms reduces the pressure difference around the house. It helps protect the house.
keyPoints: Roof pressure may become lower than pressure below it.
A large pressure difference may blow away a weak roof.
Opening doors and windows reduces the pressure difference.
activities.explanation: Opening doors and windows can help protect houses during strong storms.

activities.prompt: What pushes the two balloons towards each other?
options: Higher surrounding air pressure
Lower surrounding air pressure
Reduced surrounding pressure
Low pressure inside balloons
activities.explanation: Great choice! Higher surrounding pressure pushes the balloons together.

activities.prompt: Blowing harder makes the balloons approach each other faster.
activities.explanation: Yes! Harder blowing makes the balloons approach each other faster.

activities.prompt: Blowing between the balloons creates a ______-pressure area.
activities.hint: This pressure is lower than the pressure around the balloons.
activities.explanation: Well done! The blowing creates a low-pressure area between the balloons.

activities.prompt: What can help protect a house during a strong storm?
options: Opening doors and windows
Keeping doors and windows shut
Closing only the front door
Opening only the roof space
activities.explanation: Correct! Opening doors and windows helps protect the house.

activities.prompt: Put these events in the order they happen in the balloon example.
items: Push the balloons together with surrounding air pressure
activities.explanation: Perfect order! Blowing creates low pressure, and surrounding pressure pushes the balloons together.

activities.prompt: Opening doors and windows during strong storms increases the pressure difference around a house.
activities.explanation: Good thinking! Opening doors and windows reduces the pressure difference around the house.

activities.prompt: Two balloons hang near each other. Air is blown between them. What happens next?
options: They move closer because the surrounding air pressure pushes them together.
They move farther because the blown air pushes both balloons outward.
They stay still because blowing between balloons does not change pressure.
They stay still because only faster wind can change air pressure.

why.They move farther because the blown air: This mistake treats the blown air as pushing both balloons outward.
why.They stay still because blowing between: This mistake thinks blowing does not create a low-pressure area between the balloons.
why.They stay still because only faster wind: This mistake thinks only faster wind can change air pressure between the balloons.

activities.explanation: Higher surrounding air pressure pushes them together, so moving closer is right.

activities.prompt: High-speed wind passes over a house. What may happen to its weak roof?
options: It may blow away when the air pressure difference becomes large.
It may stay safe when the air pressure difference becomes large.
It may fall inward when the air pressure below becomes lower.
It may stay safe when the air pressure above becomes higher.

why.It may stay safe when the air pressure d: This mistake ignores that large pressure differences can blow weak roofs away.
why.It may fall inward when the air pressure: This mistake reverses the pressure order above and below the roof.
why.It may stay safe when the air pressure a: This mistake assumes higher pressure above makes a weak roof safer.

activities.explanation: Large pressure differences can blow weak roofs away, making this outcome right.

lessons.title: Lesson 5: Storms, Thunderstorms, and Lightning

activities.prompt: What makes storm clouds flash and rumble?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: How Storms Form
activities.body: Warm, moist air rises because it is lighter. Cooler air flows in to replace it. Rising air cools, and moisture forms water droplets and clouds. Heavier drops fall as rain, hail, or snow. Strong winds rubbing particles together build electric charges in clouds. These charges can become very large. Lightning heats nearby air, which expands and produces thunder. A storm with lightning and thunder is a thunderstorm.
keyPoints: Rising warm, moist air forms droplets and clouds.
Heavier drops fall as rain, hail, or snow.
Lightning heats air, which expands and produces thunder.
activities.explanation: Storms form through rising air, cooling, and falling drops.

activities.prompt: Warm air rises over a playground. Why can a breeze move toward the playground?
steps: Warm, moist air rises over the playground because it is lighter.
Cooler air moves inward from nearby high-pressure areas to replace it.
The rising warm air and incoming cooler air keep moving in a loop.
Therefore, a continuous wind circulation can form near the playground.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.prompt: What kind of air rises to begin storm formation?
options: Warm, moist air
Cooler air
Heavier drops
Water droplets
activities.explanation: Warm, moist air rises because it is lighter.

activities.prompt: What forms as rising air cools and moisture condenses?
options: Water droplets and clouds
Ice particles and static charges
Thunder sounds and strong winds
Rain, hail, and heavy snow
activities.explanation: Cooling makes moisture condense into water droplets and clouds.

activities.prompt: A storm consists of strong winds accompanied by ______.
activities.hint: Name the weather that comes with strong winds.
activities.explanation: A storm has strong winds accompanied by rain.

activities.prompt: Match each cause with its result.
activities.explanation: Rubbing builds charges, while large charges stop air's insulation. Cooling forms droplets and clouds, and heating air produces thunder.

activities.prompt: Put the storm-forming changes in order.
activities.explanation: Rising air cools first. Then moisture condenses, droplets and clouds form, and heavier drops fall.

activities.prompt: Why does lightning produce thunder?
options: Heats nearby air, making it expand
Cools nearby air, making it contract
Turns nearby moisture into rain
Rubbing particles together in clouds
activities.explanation: Lightning heats nearby air. The hot air expands, and this produces thunder.

activities.prompt: Warm air rises over a beach. Nearby cooler air is in a high-pressure area. What will happen next?
options: The cooler air will flow toward the beach.
The cooler air will stay far from the beach.
The cooler air will rise above the warm air.
The cooler air will move away from the beach.

why.The cooler air will stay far from the be: This wrongly thinks cool air does not move inward.
why.The cooler air will rise above the warm: This wrongly treats cooler air as lighter rising air.
why.The cooler air will move away from the b: This wrongly thinks cool air moves away from rising air.

activities.explanation: Cooler air moves in to replace the rising warm air.

activities.prompt: Warm air keeps rising over one field. What can form as surrounding cooler air keeps moving in?
options: Still air forms because the rising warm air has left.
Heavy rain forms before any cooler air moves inward.
A continuous wind circulation forms around the rising area.
Clouds form even though the rising air never cools.

why.Still air forms because the rising warm: Rising and cooler air keep moving in a continuous loop.
why.Heavy rain forms before any cooler air m: This wrongly thinks rising warm air ends the circulation.
why.Clouds form even though the rising air n: This wrongly thinks clouds need no cooling or condensation.

activities.explanation: This wrongly thinks heavy rain needs cooler air to arrive first.

activities.prompt: Warm, moist air rises into a cold layer. Soon the air looks cloudy. Why?
options: Rising air pulls ice particles into the cloudy mass.
Cooling makes its moisture condense into water droplets.
Strong winds rub particles together to make the cloud.
Heavy drops fall down and leave the air cloudy.

why.Rising air pulls ice particles into the: Cooling condenses moisture into droplets, and droplets form clouds.
why.Strong winds rub particles together to m: This confuses cloud formation with rubbing particles for electric charge.
why.Heavy drops fall down and leave the air: This wrongly thinks falling drops are needed to make clouds.

activities.explanation: This wrongly thinks rising air collects ice instead of condensing moisture.

activities.prompt: At great height, low temperatures turn cloud droplets into ice particles. What precipitation may follow?
options: New warm, moist air may fall into the cold cloud.
Strong winds may fall out of the cold cloud.
Thunder and lightning may fall out of the cold cloud.
Rain, hail, or snow may fall from the cloud.

why.New warm, moist air may fall into the co: Heavier drops come down as rain, hail, or snow.
why.Strong winds may fall out of the cold cl: This wrongly thinks new warm air can fall into the cold cloud.
why.Thunder and lightning may fall out of th: This wrongly treats falling precipitation as strong wind.

activities.explanation: This wrongly treats lightning and thunder as falling precipitation.

activities.prompt: Strong winds rub particles together inside a cloud. What happens when its charge becomes very large?
options: Lightning may occur, and its heat may produce thunder.
Thunder may occur first, and its charge may stop lightning.
Rain may occur first, and its heat may produce lightning.
Clouds may occur first, and their charge may cool the air.

why.Thunder may occur first, and its charge: This reverses the link between lightning, heating, and thunder.
why.Rain may occur first, and its heat may p: This wrongly links lightning to rain and thunder to raindrops.
why.Clouds may occur first, and their charge: This wrongly links lightning to cloud formation and cooling.

activities.explanation: The large charge breaks insulation, so lightning heats air and makes thunder.

activities.prompt: A storm has strong winds and rain. It has thunder but no lightning. A child calls it a thunderstorm. What is wrong?
options: A thunderstorm must have only thunder and heavy rain.
A thunderstorm must have both lightning and thunder.
A thunderstorm must have only lightning and strong winds.
A thunderstorm can have thunder without any lightning.

why.A thunderstorm must have only thunder an: This wrongly uses rain instead of lightning.
why.A thunderstorm must have only lightning: This wrongly uses wind instead of thunder.
why.A thunderstorm can have thunder without: This wrongly thinks thunder alone is enough for a thunderstorm.

activities.explanation: A thunderstorm must have both lightning and thunder.

lessons.title: Lesson 6: Cyclones and Safety

activities.prompt: What makes a cyclone spin, grow, and become dangerous?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: How Cyclones Form
activities.body: Cyclones are large storms that form over warm ocean water. Moist air rises, and its vapour condenses into raindrops. This releases heat. The Earth’s rotation makes moving air spin. The calm centre is called the eye. Near land, winds grow stronger. Cyclones can flood coastal areas and places farther inland. During a cyclone, stay updated and move quickly to a designated shelter.
keyPoints: Cyclones form over warm ocean water.
The calm centre is called the eye.
Cyclone safety includes updates and shelter.
activities.explanation: Learn how cyclones form, change near land, and require safe action.

activities.prompt: A family hears that a cyclone is approaching their coastal town. What should they do, and why?
steps: They check weather reports because warnings are important during a cyclone.
They expect higher winds because the cyclone is moving towards land.
They quickly move to the designated shelter, as advised during a cyclone.
Thus, they stay updated and remain sheltered, following the safety advice.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.prompt: Which part of a cyclone is calm?
options: the eye
the rising air
the spinning air
the condensing vapour
activities.explanation: The calm centre of a cyclone is called its eye.

activities.prompt: People should keep updated about weather reports and warnings during a cyclone.
activities.explanation: Weather reports and warnings give people important cyclone information.

activities.prompt: When water vapour condenses, heat is released back into the ______.
activities.hint: This is where released heat returns.
activities.explanation: Heat is released back into the atmosphere when vapour condenses.

activities.prompt: Match each cause or part with its result.
pairs: Moist air over warm ocean water
activities.explanation: Each pair shows an important cause, change, or part of a cyclone.

activities.prompt: What should you do during a cyclone?
options: Go to the coast and watch it
Stay outside to check the winds
Move quickly to a designated shelter
Wait beside the sea for calm
activities.explanation: During a cyclone, move quickly to a designated cyclone shelter.

activities.prompt: Put these stages in order.
items: Moist air rises over warm ocean water.
Heat is released into the atmosphere.
activities.explanation: Rising moist air leads to condensation. Condensation releases heat.

activities.prompt: A cyclone is approaching land. What can happen?
options: Its moist-air supply increases
Its wind speeds become higher
Its calm eye becomes stormy
Its raindrops change into vapour
activities.explanation: A cyclone moving towards land produces higher wind speeds.

activities.prompt: The wall of seawater pushed by a cyclone can flood only coastal areas.
activities.explanation: It can flood coastal areas and places farther inland.

activities.prompt: A cyclone moves towards land. What is its centre like, and what happens to its winds?
options: The centre is calm, and winds become faster near land.
The centre is calm, and winds become weaker near land.
The centre spins strongly, and winds become faster near land.
The centre spins strongly, and winds become weaker near land.

why.The centre is calm, and winds become wea: This child mixes up calm centres with weaker winds near land.
why.The centre spins strongly, and winds bec: This child confuses the calm centre with strong spinning.
This child gets both the calm centre and wind change wrong.

activities.explanation: The centre is calm, and approaching land produces higher wind speeds.

activities.prompt: A cyclone reaches land after moving over the sea. What happens to its strength and nearby land?
options: It weakens when moist air is cut off, and flooding can spread.
It weakens when moist air is cut off, and flooding cannot spread.
It strengthens when moist air is cut off, and flooding can spread.
It strengthens when moist air is cut off, and flooding cannot spread.

why.It weakens when moist air is cut off, an: This child wrongly thinks flooding cannot spread beyond the coast.
why.It strengthens when moist air is cut off: This child wrongly thinks cutting off moist air strengthens a cyclone.
This child wrongly thinks cutting off moist air strengthens it and stops flooding.

activities.explanation: Cutting off moist air weakens it, while a seawater wall can flood nearby land.

lessons.sceneCaption: A canvas haversack with narrow leather shoulder straps, metal buckles, and a cord lanyard.

activities.context: A student carries a bag with narrow straps and notices that the straps press strongly into the shoulders. The student changes to broad straps, making the bag feel more comfortable. At home, the student also checks a pipe connected to an overhead tank and wonders why water pressure at the taps changes when the tank is raised.
activities.prompt: What should the student expect when using narrow straps instead of broad straps?
options: The pressure on the shoulders will be higher because the weight acts on a smaller area.
The pressure on the shoulders will be lower because the weight is spread over a larger area.
The pressure on the shoulders will remain the same because the weight is unchanged.
The pressure on the shoulders will be lower because liquids exert pressure in all directions.

why.The pressure on the shoulders will be lo: Broad straps spread the weight over a larger area.
why.The pressure on the shoulders will remai: Keeping the weight unchanged does not keep the pressure unchanged when the area changes.
why.The pressure on the shoulders will be lo: Liquids exert pressure in all directions, but this does not explain the straps.

activities.explanation: Narrow straps make the bag’s weight act on a smaller shoulder area.

activities.context: A student carries a bag with narrow straps and notices that the straps press strongly into the shoulders. The student changes to broad straps, making the bag feel more comfortable. At home, the student also checks a pipe connected to an overhead tank and wonders why water pressure at the taps changes when the tank is raised.
activities.prompt: Why does the bag feel more comfortable after the student changes to broad straps?
options: Broad straps spread the bag’s weight over a larger area, so the pressure is lower.
Broad straps make the bag’s weight act on a smaller area, so the pressure is higher.
Broad straps increase the height of the water column in the tank.
Broad straps make liquids exert pressure in only one direction.

why.Broad straps make the bag’s weight act o: A larger application area produces lower pressure.
why.Broad straps increase the height of the: Straps do not affect the height of a water column.
why.Broad straps make liquids exert pressure: Liquids exert pressure in all directions, regardless of the straps.

activities.explanation: Broad straps spread the bag’s weight.

activities.context: A student carries a bag with narrow straps and notices that the straps press strongly into the shoulders. The student changes to broad straps, making the bag feel more comfortable. At home, the student also checks a pipe connected to an overhead tank and wonders why water pressure at the taps changes when the tank is raised.
activities.prompt: What will happen to the pressure at the taps if the overhead tank is put at a greater height?
options: The pressure at the taps will increase because the water column is taller.
The pressure at the taps will decrease because the water column is taller.
The pressure at the taps will stay the same because the tank holds the same water.
The pressure at the taps will increase because equal heights of water produce equal bulges.

why.The pressure at the taps will decrease b: The greater height of the tank increases the pressure at the taps.
why.The pressure at the taps will stay the s: The same amount of water does not remove the effect of a taller column.
why.The pressure at the taps will increase b: Equal bulges apply to equal heights of water, not to raising the tank.

activities.explanation: A taller water column produces more pressure at the bottom of a pipe.

activities.prompt:
Assertion (A): A bag with broad straps feels more comfortable than a bag with narrow straps.
Reason (R): Broad straps spread the bag’s weight over a larger area, which lowers the pressure.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.
activities.explanation: Both statements are true, and the larger area over which the weight acts explains the greater comfort.

activities.prompt: Explain why broad straps can make a bag more comfortable than narrow straps.
activities.answer: Pressure is the force that acts on each unit of surface area. Narrow straps make a bag’s weight act on a smaller area of the shoulders, so the pressure is higher. Broad straps spread the bag’s weight over a larger area, so increasing the area over which the force acts lowers the pressure. The SI unit of pressure is newton per square metre, and the SI unit of pressure is also called a pascal. Therefore, broad straps can feel more comfortable because they reduce the pressure on the shoulders.
points: Defines pressure as force per unit of surface area.
Explains that narrow straps use a smaller area.
States that spreading the weight lowers pressure.
Gives the SI unit as newton per square metre and pascal.
activities.explanation: Compare your answer with the points a marker looks for.

activities.context: At a school fair, a student blew up a balloon and left its mouth open while talking to a friend. The balloon gradually became smaller. Nearby, a paper plate was covered with an unfolded chart paper, and a visitor found that lifting it required more effort. When the visitor covered the plate with a larger sheet, the air pushed down more strongly. The student also wondered why the balloon had become round rather than remaining flat.
activities.prompt: If the visitor used a smaller covering sheet on the paper plate, what would happen?
options: Lifting the plate would require less effort.
Lifting the plate would require more effort because pressure acts in every direction.
Lifting the plate would require the same effort because atmospheric pressure surrounds everything.
The plate would lift by itself because the air would push it upward.

why.Lifting the plate would require more eff: Pressure acting in every direction does not make the covering area larger.
why.Lifting the plate would require the same: Reducing the covering area reduces the air’s push and the effort needed.
why.The plate would lift by itself because t: The air does not act only upward on the covered plate.

activities.explanation: A smaller covering area gives a smaller push from the air.

activities.context: At a school fair, a student blew up a balloon and left its mouth open while talking to a friend. The balloon gradually became smaller. Nearby, a paper plate was covered with an unfolded chart paper, and a visitor found that lifting it required more effort. When the visitor covered the plate with a larger sheet, the air pushed down more strongly. The student also wondered why the balloon had become round rather than remaining flat.
activities.prompt: Why did the inflated balloon become round rather than flat on one side?
options: Air pushes outward in every direction, so the balloon expands all around.
Air pushes mainly upward, so only the top expands.
Air pushes mainly downward, so only the bottom expands.
Air pushes only where the balloon is held, so its shape depends on the hand.

why.Air pushes mainly upward, so only the to: An upward push alone would not explain expansion all around.
why.Air pushes mainly downward, so only the: A downward push alone would not explain expansion all around.
why.Air pushes only where the balloon is hel: Air is not limited to pushing only where the balloon is held.

activities.explanation: Air’s pressure acts in every direction.

activities.prompt:
Assertion (A): An inflated balloon expands everywhere.
Reason (R): Air exerts pressure in all directions.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.
activities.explanation: Air pressure acts in every direction, causing the inflated balloon to expand all around.

activities.prompt:
Assertion (A): A balloon remains fully inflated when its mouth is left open.
Reason (R): Air escapes from a balloon whose mouth is left open.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.
activities.explanation: The reason is true and shows that the open balloon loses air instead of remaining fully inflated.

activities.prompt: Explain why an inflated balloon becomes round and what happens when its mouth is left open.
activities.answer: An inflated balloon becomes round because the air inside pushes outward in every direction. Since air exerts pressure in all directions, the balloon expands everywhere instead of growing only on one side. If the balloon’s mouth is left open, air escapes from it. As the air inside moves out, the balloon becomes smaller. Thus, the balloon’s round shape and its shrinking both result from the action of air and the way an open mouth allows air to leave.
points: Air exerts pressure in every direction.
The pressure makes the balloon expand all around.
An open mouth allows air to escape.
The balloon becomes smaller as air leaves.
activities.explanation: Compare your answer with the points a marker looks for.

activities.context: Air moves from the inflated balloon into the uninflated balloon. Air stops flowing when pressure becomes equal in both balloons. At a coast, land heats faster than water during the day, so air flows from the high-pressure sea region toward the land. At night, the water is warmer than the land, and wind blows from land to sea, forming a land breeze. Land and sea breezes mainly result from pressure differences over land and sea.
activities.prompt: After air has moved between the two balloons, what will happen when their pressures become equal?
options: The airflow will end after both balloons reach the same pressure.
The airflow will continue until the uninflated balloon is empty.
The airflow will reverse and return to the inflated balloon.
The airflow will become faster before it stops.

why.The airflow will continue until the unin: This option ignores the equal-pressure stopping condition.
why.The airflow will reverse and return to t: The given movement is from the inflated balloon to the uninflated balloon.
why.The airflow will become faster before it: Equal pressure stops the airflow rather than making it faster.

activities.explanation: Equal pressure is the condition for the airflow to stop.

activities.context: Air moves from the inflated balloon into the uninflated balloon. Air stops flowing when pressure becomes equal in both balloons. At a coast, land heats faster than water during the day, so air flows from the high-pressure sea region toward the land. At night, the water is warmer than the land, and wind blows from land to sea, forming a land breeze. Land and sea breezes mainly result from pressure differences over land and sea.
activities.prompt: During a coastal night, in which direction should the wind blow, and what is it called?
options: It moves toward the sea, and it is a land breeze.
It moves toward the land, and it is a land breeze.
It moves toward the sea, and it is not a land breeze.
It moves toward the land, and it is not a land breeze.

why.It moves toward the land, and it is a la: This gives the wrong direction for the nighttime wind.
why.It moves toward the sea, and it is not a: The nighttime wind in this direction is called a land breeze.
why.It moves toward the land, and it is not: This gives both the wrong direction and the wrong classification.

activities.explanation: At night, the wind blows from the land toward the sea and forms a land breeze.

activities.prompt:
Assertion (A): Land and sea breezes mainly result from pressure differences over land and sea.
Reason (R): During the day, land heats faster than water, and air flows from the high-pressure sea region toward the land.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.
activities.explanation: The daytime example shows how heating and pressure differences are connected to air flow over land and sea.

activities.prompt: Explain how daytime and nighttime land and sea breezes are different.
activities.answer: During the day, land heats up faster than water, and the sea region has higher pressure than the land. Air therefore flows from the sea toward the land. At night, the water is warmer than the land, so wind blows from the land toward the sea. This nighttime wind is called a land breeze. Both are mainly caused by pressure differences over land and sea, but they blow in opposite directions at different times of day.
points: During the day, land heats faster than water.
Air flows from the high-pressure sea region toward the land.
At night, wind blows from land toward the sea.
The nighttime wind is called a land breeze.
activities.explanation: Compare your answer with the points a marker looks for.

activities.context: During a strong storm, high-speed winds pass over a house. The wind creates a low-pressure area above the roof, so the pressure above the roof can be lower than the pressure below it. If the pressure difference is large, a weak roof may be blown away. People can protect the house by opening doors and windows, which reduces the pressure difference around it.
activities.prompt: During a strong storm, what should a person do if the pressure difference around the house is increasing?
options: Let air enter the house through the doors and windows.
Keep the house closed so the pressure difference cannot change.
Open the windows but leave the doors shut.
Wait until the wind stops before doing anything.

why.Keep the house closed so the pressure di: Keeping the house closed does not follow the stated protection method.
why.Open the windows but leave the doors shu: Opening only the windows may not reduce the pressure difference as needed.
why.Wait until the wind stops before doing a: Waiting does not protect the house during the storm.

activities.explanation: Opening doors and windows reduces the pressure difference around the house.

activities.context: During a strong storm, high-speed winds pass over a house. The wind creates a low-pressure area above the roof, so the pressure above the roof can be lower than the pressure below it. If the pressure difference is large, a weak roof may be blown away. People can protect the house by opening doors and windows, which reduces the pressure difference around it.
activities.prompt: What may happen to a weak roof when high-speed winds create a large pressure difference above and below it?
options: The roof may be lifted away by the wind.
The roof will become stronger.
The roof will remain unchanged.
The roof will attract the surrounding air.

The pressure difference can threaten the roof rather than strengthen it.
A large pressure difference can damage or remove the roof.
why.The roof will attract the surrounding ai: The stated effect is a possible lifting away of the roof.

activities.explanation: A weak roof may be blown away when the pressure difference is large.

activities.prompt:
Assertion (A): Opening doors and windows during strong storms helps protect a house.
Reason (R): Opening doors and windows reduces the pressure difference around a house.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.
activities.explanation: Reducing the pressure difference explains how opening doors and windows helps protect the house.

activities.prompt: Explain why high-speed winds can blow away a weak roof and what can be done to protect the house.
activities.answer: High-speed winds are accompanied by reduced air pressure. When these winds pass over a house, they create a low-pressure area above the roof. The pressure above the roof can therefore be lower than the pressure below it. This pressure difference can affect the roof, and a weak roof may be blown away when the difference is large. Opening doors and windows during strong storms helps protect the house because it reduces the pressure difference around the house.
points: High-speed winds create a low-pressure area over the house.
The pressure above the roof can be lower than the pressure below it.
A large pressure difference may blow away a weak roof.
Opening doors and windows reduces the pressure difference.
activities.explanation: Compare your answer with the points a marker looks for.

boss.title: Chapter challenge: Pressure, Winds, Storms, and Cyclones

activities.title: Choose the comfier straps
activities.prompt: Which strap design spreads a bag’s weight more widely?
options: Narrow straps
Broad straps
Short straps
Thin straps
activities.explanation: Broad straps feel more comfortable because they spread the bag’s weight.

activities.title: Liquid pressure
activities.prompt: Liquids exert pressure in all directions.
activities.explanation: Yes, liquids push on surfaces in every direction.

activities.title: Name the pressure unit
activities.prompt: The SI unit of pressure is also called a ______.
activities.hint: Use the unit name given for the SI unit of pressure.
activities.explanation: The SI unit is the newton per square metre, also called a pascal.

activities.title: Match each example
activities.prompt: Match each item with its result.
activities.explanation: Pressure depends on force and area. A smaller area gives higher pressure.

activities.title: Air pressure examples
activities.prompt: Match each item with the correct result.
activities.explanation: Air pushes in all directions. Its pressure around us is called atmospheric pressure.

activities.title: Balloons in moving air
activities.prompt: Why do two balloons move closer when air is blown between them?
options: The pressure between them lowers.
The pressure between them rises.
The pressure between them stays equal.
activities.explanation: Blowing between the balloons lowers the pressure there. Higher surrounding pressure pushes them together.

activities.title: From storm to thunder
activities.prompt: Put these storm events in the correct order.
items: Strong winds rub particles and develop charges.
The cloud charge becomes very large.
Air stops insulating the opposite charges.
The air expands and produces thunder.
activities.explanation: Charges build up until lightning occurs. Heated air expands and produces thunder.

activities.title: A cyclone over land
activities.prompt: A cyclone keeps its full strength after reaching land.
activities.explanation: After reaching land, a cyclone loses strength when its moist-air supply is cut off.

chapters.title: Particulate Nature of Matter
chapters.summary: In this chapter: what matter is made of; forces and the solid state; the liquid state; the gaseous state.

lessons.title: What Matter Is Made Of

activities.prompt: What are the tiny building blocks hiding inside the things around us?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: Tiny Building Blocks
activities.body: Matter is made of a very large number of extremely small particles. These particles are too small to see with an ordinary microscope. Breaking chalk into powder changes only the size of its specks. Each tiny chalk grain is still made of chalk. Sand and clay also consist of many smaller constituent particles.
keyPoints: Matter contains extremely small particles.
Ordinary microscopes cannot show these particles.
Chalk powder still contains tiny chalk grains.
activities.explanation: This shows that all matter has tiny building blocks, even when we cannot see them.

activities.prompt: A child grinds chalk into very fine powder. What is still inside the powder?
steps: Grinding makes the chalk specks smaller because it breaks the larger pieces.
Each grain is chalk, because grinding only changes the specks' size.
The smallest particles cannot be broken down further.
Chalk's basic building blocks are called constituent particles.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.title: The Smallest Pieces
activities.body: Grinding chalk can make its specks still smaller. Each tiny chalk grain is still made of chalk. The smallest chalk particles cannot be broken down further. These basic building blocks of chalk are called constituent particles. A tiny sugar grain contains millions and millions of constituent particles.
keyPoints: Finer grinding makes chalk specks smaller.
The smallest chalk particles cannot break down further.
A tiny sugar grain contains millions of constituent particles.
activities.explanation: Even tiny pieces of matter contain enormous numbers of basic particles.

activities.title: What Is Matter Made Of?
activities.prompt: What is all matter made of?
options: Extremely small particles
Large visible pieces
A few separate grains
One indivisible solid
activities.explanation: Matter contains a very large number of extremely small particles.

activities.title: Can We See Particles?
activities.prompt: An ordinary microscope cannot show the tiny particles that make matter.
activities.explanation: These particles are too small to see with an ordinary microscope.

activities.title: Changing Chalk
activities.prompt: Breaking chalk into powder changes only the ______ of its specks.
activities.hint: Think about what becomes smaller when chalk is powdered.
activities.explanation: Grinding makes the specks smaller, but each tiny grain is still chalk.

activities.title: Match Each Example
activities.prompt: Match each material with the correct particle fact.
pairs: Each tiny grain is still chalk
activities.explanation: Chalk and sugar both contain many tiny particles, even when we cannot see them.

activities.title: Chalk's Building Blocks
activities.prompt: What are the basic building blocks of chalk called?
options: Constituent particles
Visible chalk grains
Ordinary microscopes
Large chalk pieces
activities.explanation: The smallest chalk particles are called constituent particles.

activities.title: From Chalk to Tiny Particles
activities.prompt: Put these steps in the correct order.
items: Reach particles that cannot break further
activities.explanation: Finer grinding makes the chalk specks smaller until they cannot break down further.

activities.title: Dissolved Sugar
activities.prompt: Which statement about dissolved sugar is correct?
options: Cannot be seen; can be tasted.
Cannot be seen; cannot be tasted.
Can be seen; can be tasted.
Can be seen; cannot be tasted.
activities.explanation: Dissolved sugar cannot be seen, but its presence can be tasted.

activities.prompt: A child grinds a piece of chalk into very fine powder. What will the powder contain?
options: The powder will contain smaller particles, and every grain will be chalk.
The powder will contain new particles, because breaking changes the chalk.
The powder will contain larger particles, because grinding joins the specks.
The powder will contain no particles, because chalk disappears after crushing.

why.The powder will contain new particles, b: This wrongly assumes that breaking chalk creates a new material.
why.The powder will contain larger particles: This wrongly assumes that grinding joins small specks together.
why.The powder will contain no particles, be: This wrongly assumes that crushing makes matter disappear.

activities.explanation: This is right because grinding changes only the size, not the chalk.

activities.prompt: A child says grinding chalk creates new particles because its appearance changes. Which test best checks this claim?
options: Compare whole chalk with ground chalk to see if both remain chalk.
Count chalk specks before grinding, but do not compare their contents.
Check only whether the ground chalk has a different appearance.
Use an ordinary microscope to look for chalk's smallest particles.

why.Count chalk specks before grinding, but: This wrongly counts pieces without checking whether they remain chalk.
why.Check only whether the ground chalk has: This wrongly uses appearance to decide whether new particles formed.
why.Use an ordinary microscope to look for c: This wrongly assumes an ordinary microscope can show the tiny particles.

activities.explanation: This is right because both whole and ground chalk are still chalk.
