lessons.title: Forces and the Solid State

activities.prompt: Why do solids keep their shape, and what makes them flow when heated?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: Particles and Attractions
activities.body: Matter is made of particles. Attractive forces hold these particles together. These forces are called interparticle attractions. Their strength depends on the substance and particle distance. Solids have a definite shape and volume. Their particles are tightly packed and strongly attracted. Strong attractions keep particles in fixed positions. Weakening these attractions can turn a solid into a liquid.
keyPoints: Attractive forces hold particles together.
Solids have a definite shape and volume.
Weakening attractions can turn a solid into a liquid.
activities.explanation: Attractions help explain why matter behaves differently in different states.

activities.prompt: A wax bar changes into liquid. Why can its particles no longer stay in fixed positions?
steps: The bar was solid, so its particles were tightly packed and strongly attracted.
Strong attractions kept the particles in fixed positions.
As the bar became liquid, its interparticle attractions weakened.
Therefore, the particles no longer had to stay in fixed positions.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.prompt: Which statement about the particles of matter is correct?
options: Particles attract each other.
Particles always stay fixed.
Particles are always far apart.
Particles need no attractions.
activities.explanation: Attractive forces hold the particles of matter together.

activities.prompt: Match each solid-state idea with its correct description.
activities.explanation: Strong attractions keep solid particles together in fixed positions.

activities.prompt: Strong attractions keep solid particles in ______ positions.
activities.hint: This word means the particles stay in their places.
activities.explanation: Strong attractions keep solid particles in fixed positions.

activities.prompt: Why do solid particles stay in fixed positions?
options: Weak attractions keep them in place.
Strong attractions keep them in place.
Large distances separate them.
Empty spaces hold them still.
activities.explanation: Strong attractions hold solid particles in fixed positions.

activities.prompt: Matter's particles move farther apart. What may happen next?
options: Interparticle attractions may weaken greatly.
Interparticle attractions may grow stronger.
The solid must keep its definite shape.
The particles may become more tightly packed.
activities.explanation: Even a small increase in distance can weaken interparticle forces greatly.

activities.prompt: Put these events in the correct causal order.
activities.explanation: Greater distance weakens attractions. Weakened attractions can make a solid become liquid.

activities.prompt: Attraction strength depends on the substance and distance. Two different solids have equally spaced particles. What can we predict?
options: Their attraction strengths may be different.
Their attraction strengths must be equal.
One solid must always attract more strongly.
Their attraction strengths must both be zero.

why.Their attraction strengths must be equal: This mistake ignores that the substance can affect attraction strength.
why.One solid must always attract more stron: This mistake assumes one substance always has stronger attraction.
why.Their attraction strengths must both be: This mistake wrongly treats all solids as having no attraction.

activities.explanation: Different substances can have different strengths of interparticle attraction.

activities.prompt: Solids have a definite shape and volume. Why does a solid brick keep both?
options: Tight packing and strong attractions keep its particles fixed.
Tight packing and weak attractions keep its particles fixed.
Loose packing and strong attractions keep its particles fixed.
Tight packing and strong attractions keep its particles moving freely.

why.Tight packing and weak attractions keep: This mistake uses weak attractions instead of strong ones.
why.Loose packing and strong attractions kee: This mistake wrongly treats loose particles as a feature of solids.
why.Tight packing and strong attractions kee: This mistake reverses the effect of strong attractions on fixed positions.

activities.explanation: Solid particles are tightly packed, and strong attractions keep them fixed.

activities.prompt: Attraction strength depends on substance and particle distance. How can we test the distance effect fairly?
options: Use one solid and change only particle distance.
Use two solids and change only particle distance.
Use one solid and change everything together.
Use one solid and keep particle distance unchanged.

why.Use two solids and change only particle: This mistake changes the substance as well as the distance.
why.Use one solid and change everything toge: This mistake gives two factors different values at once.
why.Use one solid and keep particle distance: This mistake keeps the factor we want to test unchanged.

activities.explanation: Changing only distance tests its effect without changing the substance.

lessons.sceneAlt: A microscope image shows kitchen-salt crystals illuminated in blue and yellow.
lessons.sceneCaption: Kitchen-salt crystals photographed under a microscope in blue and yellow light.

sceneCredit.text: Kitchen salt crystals by Misiek1962, CC BY 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons
sceneCredit.creator: Misiek1962

lessons.title: The Liquid State

activities.prompt: What makes water flow into new shapes while keeping its amount?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: How a Liquid Behaves
activities.body: Particles are the small parts that make up a liquid. They move freely within a limited space. A liquid has no fixed shape, so it takes the shape of its container. Volume means the amount of liquid. A liquid has a definite volume, so its water level stays at 200 mL after pouring.
keyPoints: A liquid takes the shape of its container.
The particles of a liquid move freely.
A liquid keeps the same volume when poured.
activities.explanation: Liquids can flow, but their volume stays the same.

activities.prompt: Water is poured from a round jug into a square box. What changes, and what stays?
steps: Liquids have no fixed shape, so the water takes the box's shape.
Its volume stays 200 mL, because liquids have a definite volume.
Particles move freely in the limited space, so the water fills the box.
Therefore, the shape changes, but the volume stays the same.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.title: Particles, Water and Boiling
activities.body: Attractions between particles are slightly weaker in liquids than in solids. A finger can pass through water without permanently breaking it. The water is temporarily displaced while the finger passes through. After the finger is removed, the water returns to its position. The boiling point is the temperature at which a liquid turns into vapour.
keyPoints: Attractions between particles are weaker in liquids.
Water returns after a passing finger is removed.
A liquid turns into vapour at its boiling point.
activities.explanation: Liquid particles can move, and their attractions are weaker than in solids.

activities.prompt: A liquid keeps the same shape in every container.
activities.explanation: A liquid has no fixed shape. It takes the shape of its container.

activities.prompt: Which property does a liquid always have?
options: A definite volume
A fixed shape
A fixed particle position
A permanent hole
activities.explanation: A liquid has a definite volume. It can change shape without changing volume.

activities.prompt: A finger can pass through water without permanently breaking it.
activities.explanation: The water is only temporarily displaced. It returns after the finger is removed.

activities.prompt: Put the events in the correct order.
items: A finger passes through the water.
The water returns to its position.
activities.explanation: Passing the finger displaces the water. The water returns after the finger leaves.

activities.prompt: Match each liquid property with its description.
pairs: Takes the shape of its container
activities.explanation: Each description shows an important property of a liquid.

activities.prompt: Which sentence correctly compares attractions between particles?
options: They are slightly weaker in liquids than in solids.
They are slightly stronger in liquids than in solids.
They are exactly the same in liquids and solids.
They are much stronger in liquids than in solids.
activities.explanation: Attractions between particles are slightly weaker in liquids than in solids.

activities.prompt: A child pours 200 mL of water into a tall cup. What shape will it take?
options: It will take the tall cup's shape.
It will stay in a round shape.
It will keep its old shape.
It will have no shape at all.

This mistake thinks a liquid keeps its first shape.
This mistake thinks a liquid keeps the shape it had before.
This mistake confuses having no fixed shape with having no shape.

activities.explanation: This is right because liquids take the shape of their container.

activities.prompt: Compared with a solid, why can liquid particles move past one another?
options: There are no attractions between particles.
The attractions stop particles from moving.
The attractions between particles are slightly weaker.
The attractions between particles are much stronger.

why.There are no attractions between particl: This mistake treats slightly weaker as completely absent.
why.The attractions stop particles from movi: This mistake thinks attractions prevent particles from moving.
why.The attractions between particles are mu: This mistake thinks liquids have stronger attractions than solids.

activities.explanation: Liquids have slightly weaker attractions than solids.

activities.prompt: Water is poured into a wide plate. What should happen to its volume?
options: It should become smaller than 200 mL.
It should become larger than 200 mL.
It should change to fit the plate.
It should stay the same at 200 mL.

This mistake thinks a wider container removes water.
This mistake thinks a wider container adds water.
This mistake thinks volume must match the container's shape.

activities.explanation: This is right because the volume stays 200 mL after pouring.

activities.prompt: A child says a container's shape changes the amount of water. Which test is fair?
options: Use two different amounts in one container.
Fill one container and leave another empty.
Pour 200 mL into two differently shaped containers.
Pour water into a container with a hole.

why.Use two different amounts in one contain: This mistake changes the amount instead of changing only shape.
why.Fill one container and leave another emp: This mistake changes the amount instead of changing only shape.
This mistake changes the container condition, so it is not a fair test.

activities.explanation: This is right because changing shape should not change volume.

lessons.sceneAlt: Cold water flows and splashes as it is poured into a glass.
lessons.sceneCaption: Pouring water clearly shows a liquid flowing and taking the shape of its container.

lessons.title: The Gaseous State

activities.prompt: Why does smoke spread everywhere inside a jar?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: How Gases Behave
activities.body: Smoke spreads throughout a gas jar. It contains tiny particles suspended in the air. Gas particles move freely in all directions. Their attractions to one another are negligible, meaning very small. Gases occupy all the space available and take the shape of the vessel containing them. Liquids and gases are classified as fluids. The movement of smoke helps us observe the movement of gas particles.
keyPoints: Gases fill all available space.
A gas takes the shape of its vessel.
Gas particles move freely in all directions.
Attractions between gas particles are negligible.
Liquids and gases are classified as fluids.
activities.explanation: These ideas help you understand why a gas spreads and changes shape.

activities.prompt: Why does smoke from one spot fill a whole gas jar?
steps: Smoke contains tiny particles, so their movement can be seen.
Gas particles move freely, so they leave their starting place.
They occupy all available space, so smoke spreads outward.
Therefore, smoke fills the entire gas jar.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.prompt: Which statement is true about gases?
options: They keep one fixed shape.
They take the shape of their vessel.
Their particles stay still.
Their particles attract each other strongly.
activities.explanation: A gas takes the shape of the vessel containing it.

activities.prompt: A gas keeps the same shape in every vessel.
activities.explanation: A gas takes the shape of each vessel that contains it.

activities.prompt: Match each thing with its correct description.
pairs: takes the shape of its vessel
activities.explanation: Each pair shows an important fact about gases and smoke.

activities.prompt: Smoke contains tiny particles suspended in the air.
activities.explanation: The tiny particles in smoke remain suspended in the air.

activities.prompt: Gases tend to occupy all the ______ available to them.
activities.hint: Think of smoke filling a gas jar.
activities.explanation: Gases tend to occupy all the space available to them.

activities.prompt: Which set gives three correct facts about gases?
options: They fill all space. Their particles stay fixed. Their attractions are strong.
They fill all space. Their particles move freely. Their attractions are negligible.
They keep fixed shapes. Their particles move one way. Their attractions are strong.
They take vessel shapes. Their particles stay fixed. Their attractions are strong.
activities.explanation: Gases fill available space, and their particles move freely with negligible attractions.

activities.prompt: Attractions between gas particles are strong.
activities.explanation: Attractions between gas particles are negligible, meaning very small.

activities.prompt: Liquids and gases are classified as fluids.
activities.explanation: Your book classifies both liquids and gases as fluids.

activities.prompt: Smoke enters an empty gas jar. What will happen next?
options: It will spread throughout the whole jar.
It will stay only where it first entered.
It will settle quickly at the jar's bottom.
It will form one round layer in the middle.

why.It will stay only where it first entered: This assumes gas particles cannot move away from the start.
why.It will settle quickly at the jar's bott: This assumes smoke particles stop and gather below.
why.It will form one round layer in the midd: This assumes a gas keeps one shape inside a vessel.

activities.explanation: Smoke spreads to fill the entire space in a gas jar.

activities.prompt: Two open jars touch at their open ends. What will happen to their gases?
options: The gases will stay in separate parts.
The gases will mix through the open ends.
The gases will join into one solid.
The gases will move farther from each other.

This assumes gas particles cannot enter the other jar.
This wrongly imagines that mixing must create a solid.
why.The gases will move farther from each ot: This mistakes mixing for gas particles pushing each other away.

activities.explanation: Free movement and negligible attractions let the two gases mix.

lessons.title: How the Spacing Changes

activities.prompt: What happens to the space inside a syringe when you push the plunger?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: Changing the space between particles
activities.body: Gas particles normally have a lot of space between them. Pushing a syringe plunger reduces the air volume. This pushes gas particles closer together. External pressure can also reduce the space between gas particles. When the plunger is no longer pushed, the particles spread out again. Water is practically incompressible, meaning its volume hardly changes when squeezed. Sugar solution has less volume than the combined volume of sugar and water.
keyPoints: Gas particles have a lot of space between them.
Pushing the plunger brings gas particles closer.
An unpushed plunger allows gas particles to spread out.
activities.explanation: Notice how pushing and releasing the plunger changes particle spacing.

activities.prompt: What happens to gas when a syringe plunger is pushed and released?
steps: You push the plunger, so the air volume inside the syringe decreases.
The smaller space forces gas particles to come closer together.
Because the plunger is no longer pushed, gas particles spread out again.
So changing the plunger changes the space between gas particles.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.prompt: What happens to the air volume when you push the syringe plunger?
options: The volume decreases.
The volume increases.
The volume stays unchanged.
The volume disappears.
activities.explanation: Pushing the plunger reduces the air volume inside the syringe.

activities.prompt: Pushing the plunger forces gas particles to come closer.
activities.explanation: The plunger forces gas particles to come closer together.

activities.prompt: Gas particles have a lot of ______ between them in their natural state.
activities.hint: Think about what separates the particles.
activities.explanation: Gas particles naturally have a lot of space between them.

activities.prompt: External pressure can reduce the space between gas particles.
activities.explanation: External pressure can reduce the space between gas particles.

activities.prompt: Match each action with its result.
activities.explanation: Each action changes particle spacing or air volume.

activities.prompt: Put these events in order for pushing and then releasing a syringe plunger.
items: The plunger is no longer pushed
activities.explanation: Pushing brings particles closer. Releasing the plunger lets them spread out.

activities.prompt: Match each observation with what the lesson says about it.
pairs: Some space exists between water particles
The sand settles and occupies space
They cannot move from place to place
activities.explanation: Sugar solution has less volume because water particles have some space. Sand settles down, while solid particles cannot move.

activities.prompt: Which statement correctly compares water with gas particles?
options: Water is practically incompressible; gas particles have much space.
Water is easily compressed; gas particles have very little space.
Water has very little space; gas particles are closely packed.
Water stays completely fixed; gas particles are always squeezed.
activities.explanation: Water is practically incompressible, while gas particles have a lot of space naturally.

activities.prompt: A soft air-filled ball is squeezed. What happens to its gas particles?
options: The gas particles spread farther apart.
The gas particles stay very far apart.
The gas particles come closer together.
The gas particles stay very close together.

This mistakes external pressure for releasing the plunger.
This assumes pressure cannot reduce the space between particles.
why.The gas particles stay very close togeth: This assumes pressure cannot bring the particles closer.

activities.explanation: External pressure reduces the space between gas particles.

activities.prompt: Which test best checks whether water can be squeezed?
options: Measure different amounts of water under pressure.
Measure sugar solution before and after pressure.
Measure water and sand before and after pressure.
Measure the same water before and after pressure.

why.Measure different amounts of water under: Different amounts do not give a fair test of the same water.
why.Measure sugar solution before and after: Sugar solution is not the same as the water being tested.
why.Measure water and sand before and after: Sand is a solid, not the water being tested.

activities.explanation: Comparing the same water shows whether its volume changes under pressure.

lessons.title: How Particles Move

activities.prompt: How do tiny smells travel all the way around a room?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: Particles Are Always Moving
activities.body: Particles always move in water and air. Pink streaks spread from each permanganate grain. Eventually, the water becomes uniform pink, meaning the same colour throughout. Heating water makes particles move faster. Fragrance particles spread through a whole room. Soap lifts oil from fabric so it washes away. Sand is insoluble because its particles are held strongly together.
keyPoints: Water and air particles are always moving.
Heat increases particle movement.
Particles can spread throughout water or air.
activities.explanation: Particles are always moving, even when you cannot see them.

activities.title: Heat the water

tasks.then: Below 0 degrees water is ice: its particles can only jiggle in place.
At 100 degrees water boils and its particles fly apart as steam.

activities.takeaway: Heating gives particles more energy: held in place in ice, sliding in water, flying apart as steam.
activities.explanation: Heating gives particles more energy: held in place in ice, sliding in water, flying apart as steam.

activities.prompt: Why does potassium permanganate make the whole water pink?
steps: Water particles are always in motion.
Because these particles move, pink streaks spread from each grain.
As the streaks spread, the whole bulk of water becomes uniformly pink.
Thus, particle movement explains the spreading pink colour.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.title: How Particles Spread
activities.body: Different materials show particle movement in different ways. In water, pink streaks spread from each permanganate grain. The whole water eventually becomes one pink colour. In a room, fragrance particles spread everywhere, and air particles keep moving. Heat increases particle movement, so hot water's particles move faster. Sand does not dissolve because its particles stay strongly joined. Soap lifts oil away from fabric, helping it wash away.
keyPoints: Moving particles can spread through water or air.
Heating increases their movement.
Strongly joined particles can make a material insoluble.
activities.explanation: Spreading happens because particles keep moving.

activities.title: Heating Particles
activities.prompt: What happens when heat is provided to water particles?
options: They move more slowly
They move much faster
They stop moving
They stay still
activities.explanation: Providing heat increases the movement of particles.

activities.title: Particles Never Stop
activities.prompt: Water particles are always in motion.
activities.explanation: Water particles are always in motion.

activities.title: Hot Water Particles
activities.prompt: Hot water makes particles move ______ than water at room temperature.
activities.hint: Think about what heat does.
activities.explanation: Water particles move faster in hot water than at room temperature.

activities.title: Match the Particle Facts
activities.prompt: Match each material with what the lesson says about it.
activities.explanation: Each material shows the particle behaviour described in the lesson.

activities.title: Why Does the Water Become Pink?
activities.prompt: Why does the whole bulk of water eventually become a uniform pink colour?
options: Pink streaks spread from each grain
The sand settles at the bottom
The soap lifts oil away
The air particles move constantly
activities.explanation: Pink streaks spread out from each grain of potassium permanganate.

activities.title: The Effect of Heat in Order
activities.prompt: Put this heat-related sequence in the correct order.
items: Water particles move faster in hot water
activities.explanation: Providing heat increases movement, so particles move faster in hot water.

activities.prompt: A scent bottle opens in a warm room. What happens next?
options: The particles will spread throughout the whole room.
The particles will stay beside the bottle forever.
The particles will turn into air particles.
The particles will gather in one warm corner.

why.The particles will stay beside the bottl: This wrongly assumes that fragrance particles cannot move.
why.The particles will turn into air particl: This wrongly suggests that fragrance particles become air particles.
why.The particles will gather in one warm co: Heat increases movement, so particles would not gather together.

activities.explanation: Heat increases particle movement, so fragrance particles spread through the room.

activities.prompt: Pink streaks spread through water. Why does the water look the same?
options: The particles move and spread the colour evenly.
The sand particles hold the colour together.
The heat makes the pink colour lighter.
The soap lifts the pink grains away.

why.The sand particles hold the colour toget: This wrongly treats sand as the source of the pink colour.
Heating increases movement, but no fact says pink becomes lighter.
Soap helps with oil, not with spreading this pink colour.

activities.explanation: Moving particles spread the pink streaks until the water is uniform.

activities.prompt: Fine sand is stirred into water. What is most likely to happen?
options: The sand stays separate because its particles hold together.
The sand dissolves because its particles move faster.
The sand floats because its particles are heated.
The sand becomes soap and washes away.

why.The sand dissolves because its particles: Moving particles do not make strongly held sand particles dissolve.
why.The sand floats because its particles ar: No fact says heating sand particles makes them float.
Soap helps lift oil, not change sand into soap.

activities.explanation: Sand is insoluble because its particles are held together strongly.

activities.prompt: An oily shirt is washed with soap. What change shows that soap helped?
options: Oil lifts off the fabric and washes away.
Oil stays firmly inside the fabric.
Oil changes into pink streaks.
Oil becomes a separate sand layer.

This wrongly assumes soap keeps oil inside the fabric.
This wrongly connects soap with spreading pink streaks.
This wrongly connects soap with changing oil into sand.

activities.explanation: Soap lifts oil off the fabric so it can wash away.

activities.prompt: Which test best checks if heat changes water particle movement?
options: Compare water at different temperatures under the same conditions.
Compare different water amounts at the same temperature.
Add sand to one glass and compare the results.
Use soap in one glass and compare the results.

why.Compare different water amounts at the s: Changing the amount does not test the effect of heat.
why.Add sand to one glass and compare the re: Adding sand changes another factor, not only heat.
why.Use soap in one glass and compare the re: Using soap changes another factor, not only heat.

activities.explanation: Changing only temperature tests the effect of heat.

activities.context: A student has a piece of chalk that has broken into several small pieces. The student grinds the pieces more finely to make chalk powder. Later, sugar is stirred into a drink until it dissolves. The dissolved sugar cannot be seen, although its presence can be tasted. The student wonders whether grinding and dissolving make the original materials disappear or create something different.
activities.prompt: If the student grinds the chalk more finely, what would happen next?
options: Each speck would be smaller, while still being made of chalk.
The chalk would change into a different material.
Each speck would contain no particles at all.
The chalk particles would become visible under an ordinary microscope.

why.The chalk would change into a different: Grinding does not change chalk into another material.
why.Each speck would contain no particles at: Every tiny grain still consists of chalk.
why.The chalk particles would become visible: Ordinary microscopes cannot reveal these particles.

activities.explanation: Finer grinding only reduces speck size.

activities.context: A student has a piece of chalk that has broken into several small pieces. The student grinds the pieces more finely to make chalk powder. Later, sugar is stirred into a drink until it dissolves. The dissolved sugar cannot be seen, although its presence can be tasted. The student wonders whether grinding and dissolving make the original materials disappear or create something different.
activities.prompt: What should the student do to reduce the chalk to its smallest possible particles?
options: Keep grinding until the specks reach the limit at which further grinding cannot divide them.
Use an ordinary microscope to reveal the final chalk particles.
Dissolve the chalk so that it produces the smallest particles.
Stop after the first grinding because the resulting specks are already final.

why.Use an ordinary microscope to reveal the: Ordinary microscopes cannot reveal these particles.
why.Dissolve the chalk so that it produces t: The given process for chalk is grinding, not dissolving.
why.Stop after the first grinding because th: The first ground specks need not be the smallest.

activities.explanation: Further grinding divides the specks until the limit.

activities.prompt:
Assertion (A): If chalk is ground more finely, its specks become smaller.
Reason (R): Grinding reduces the size of chalk specks without changing what they are made of.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.
activities.explanation: The reason directly explains that grinding changes the size of chalk specks.

activities.prompt:
Assertion (A): Dissolved sugar can be seen as separate grains.
Reason (R): A tiny sugar grain contains millions and millions of constituent particles.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.
activities.explanation: The assertion is false because dissolved sugar cannot be seen, while the reason is true but does not explain it.

activities.prompt: Explain how grinding chalk changes the chalk, and what happens when the smallest particles are reached.
activities.answer: Grinding chalk changes only the size of its pieces. When chalk is broken into powder, each tiny chalk grain is still made of chalk. Finer grinding can break the specks into still smaller particles. This can continue until the smallest chalk particles are reached, and these cannot be broken down further. These basic building blocks are called constituent particles. Therefore, grinding does not turn chalk into a different material; it only separates it into smaller pieces, ending with particles that cannot be divided again.
points: Grinding changes the size of chalk specks.
Every tiny chalk grain is still made of chalk.
The smallest particles are called constituent particles.
The smallest chalk particles cannot be broken down further.
activities.explanation: Compare your answer with the points a marker looks for.

activities.context: A student is examining a solid object. Its particles are tightly packed and strongly attracted, so the object has a definite shape and volume. The student wonders what would happen if the particles were moved farther apart. The task is to decide whether the solid would keep its fixed positions or whether it could become a liquid.
activities.prompt: If the distance between the particles increases, what is likely to happen to the solid?
options: The interparticle attractions would weaken greatly, allowing the material to change into a liquid.
The interparticle attractions would become stronger, making the particles stay fixed.
The particles would remain tightly packed because the distance change would have no effect.
The solid would keep its definite shape and volume regardless of the distance change.

why.The interparticle attractions would beco: Incorrect: attractions do not become stronger when distance increases.
why.The particles would remain tightly packe: Incorrect: even a small distance increase can weaken the attractions.
why.The solid would keep its definite shape: Incorrect: weakening attractions can allow the solid to become a liquid.

activities.explanation: Correct: increased distance can weaken interparticle attractions greatly.

activities.context: A student is examining a solid object. Its particles are tightly packed and strongly attracted, so the object has a definite shape and volume. The student wonders what would happen if the particles were moved farther apart. The task is to decide whether the solid would keep its fixed positions or whether it could become a liquid.
activities.prompt: Why could the solid change into a liquid if the particles are moved farther apart?
options: A greater distance can weaken the attractions that hold the particles in fixed positions.
A greater distance makes the attractions stronger and causes the particles to separate.
The particles remain fixed only when they are loosely packed together.
The definite shape and volume prevent a solid from changing state.

why.A greater distance makes the attractions: Incorrect: increasing distance weakens rather than strengthens attractions.
why.The particles remain fixed only when the: Incorrect: solid particles are tightly packed, not loosely packed.
why.The definite shape and volume prevent a: Incorrect: the solid can change when its attractions are weakened.

activities.explanation: Correct: interparticle attractions depend on distance between particles.

activities.prompt:
Assertion (A): If the distance between particles increases, their interparticle attractions can weaken.
Reason (R): Even a small increase in distance can weaken interparticle forces greatly.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.
activities.explanation: The reason directly explains why increasing the distance can weaken the attractions.

activities.prompt:
Assertion (A): Increasing the distance between particles always strengthens interparticle attractions.
Reason (R): Even a small increase in distance can weaken interparticle forces greatly.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.
activities.explanation: The statement is false, but the reason is true and shows that increasing distance weakens attractions.

activities.prompt: Explain why a solid has a definite shape and volume, and what could happen if the distance between its particles increased.
activities.answer: The particles of a solid are tightly packed and strongly attracted. These strong interparticle attractions keep the particles in fixed positions. This fixed arrangement gives the solid a definite shape and volume. However, even a small increase in the distance between particles can weaken the attractions greatly. If the attractions are weakened, the solid can become a liquid because its particles are no longer held in the same fixed arrangement.
points: Particles are tightly packed.
Particles are strongly attracted.
Strong attractions keep particles fixed.
Weakened attractions can change the solid into a liquid.
activities.explanation: Compare your answer with the points a marker looks for.

activities.context: At home, a learner pours 200 mL of water into a different container. The water level is still 200 mL, although the shape of the water changes to match the container. The learner then pushes a finger into the water and takes it out. The water is only displaced for a short time and then returns to its position.
activities.prompt: What happens immediately when the finger is pushed into the water?
options: The water is shifted aside for a short time.
The water is permanently split into separate parts.
The water takes a permanent shape like the finger.
The water disappears from the container.

why.The water is permanently split into sepa: A temporary displacement does not permanently divide the water.
why.The water takes a permanent shape like t: Liquid takes the shape of its container, not the shape of the finger.
Displacing the water does not remove it from the container.

activities.explanation: Pushing the finger shifts the water temporarily.

activities.context: At home, a learner pours 200 mL of water into a different container. The water level is still 200 mL, although the shape of the water changes to match the container. The learner then pushes a finger into the water and takes it out. The water is only displaced for a short time and then returns to its position.
activities.prompt: What should the learner expect after taking the finger out of the water?
options: The water will move back to where it was before the finger entered.
The water will remain divided into two parts.
The water will stay in the position caused by the finger.
The water will keep the shape of the finger.

why.The water will remain divided into two p: A temporary displacement does not leave a permanent separation.
why.The water will stay in the position caus: The water is displaced only while the finger is present.
why.The water will keep the shape of the fin: A liquid takes the shape of its container, not a permanent shape like the finger.

activities.explanation: The water returns to its position after the finger is removed.

activities.prompt:
Assertion (A): A liquid has a definite volume.
Reason (R): The water level remains at 200 mL when the water is poured into another container.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.
activities.explanation: The unchanged 200 mL reading supports the fact that the liquid retains a definite volume.

activities.prompt:
Assertion (A): Liquids have no fixed shape.
Reason (R): The boiling point is the temperature at which a liquid turns into vapour.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.
activities.explanation: Both statements are true, but the boiling point does not explain why a liquid has no fixed shape.

activities.prompt:
Assertion (A): Passing a finger through water permanently breaks the water.
Reason (R): Passing a finger through water temporarily displaces the water.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.
activities.explanation: The displacement is temporary because the water returns after the finger is removed.

activities.prompt: How do the movement of liquid particles and interparticle attractions help explain the shape of a liquid?
activities.answer: Liquid particles are free to move within a limited space. Interparticle attractions in a liquid are slightly weaker than they are in a solid. Because the particles can move freely, they can arrange themselves to match the shape of the container. Therefore, a liquid has no fixed shape, but it does have a definite volume. The limited space means the liquid keeps its amount within a definite volume even when its shape changes.
points: Liquid particles move freely within a limited space.
Interparticle attractions are slightly weaker than in solids.
A liquid has no fixed shape.
A liquid retains a definite volume.
activities.explanation: Compare your answer with the points a marker looks for.

activities.context: During a classroom demonstration, a little smoke is released into a gas jar. The smoke quickly reaches every part of the jar. A student notices that the smoke moves in many directions rather than staying in one place. The smoke does not keep a separate shape inside the jar. As more space becomes available, the smoke continues spreading through it.
activities.prompt: If the same smoke were released into a larger gas jar, what would you predict?
options: It would spread into the extra space as well.
It would stay only in the smaller region.
It would collect at the bottom of the larger jar.
It would keep the shape of the smaller jar.

why.It would stay only in the smaller region: Smoke would not remain limited to the smaller region.
why.It would collect at the bottom of the la: This mistake treats smoke as something that settles instead of spreading.
why.It would keep the shape of the smaller j: A gas takes the shape of its current vessel.

activities.explanation: Gases tend to occupy all the space available to them.

activities.context: During a classroom demonstration, a little smoke is released into a gas jar. The smoke quickly reaches every part of the jar. A student notices that the smoke moves in many directions rather than staying in one place. The smoke does not keep a separate shape inside the jar. As more space becomes available, the smoke continues spreading through it.
activities.prompt: If the gas were transferred into a vessel with a different shape, what shape would it have?
options: It would match the new vessel.
It would remain in the shape of the first jar.
It would form a layer at the bottom.
It would have no shape and remain in the centre.

why.It would remain in the shape of the firs: A gas does not keep the shape of an earlier vessel.
This mistake treats the gas like a liquid that settles at the bottom.
why.It would have no shape and remain in the: A gas spreads through the available space rather than remaining in the centre.

activities.explanation: A gas takes the shape of the vessel containing it.

boss.title: Chapter challenge: Particulate Nature of Matter

activities.prompt: What happens when chalk is ground more finely?
options: Its specks become smaller.
Its specks become another substance.
All the chalk disappears.
Its specks stop being matter.
activities.explanation: Finer grinding breaks chalk specks into smaller particles. Each tiny grain is still made of chalk.

activities.prompt: Solid particles move freely in all directions.
activities.explanation: Strong attractions keep solid particles in fixed positions. They do not move from place to place.

activities.prompt: Which statement about a liquid is correct?
options: It has no fixed shape but has fixed volume.
It has a fixed shape but no fixed volume.
It has a fixed shape and fixed volume.
It has no fixed shape and no fixed volume.
activities.explanation: A liquid has no fixed shape and takes the shape of its container. It has a definite volume.

activities.prompt: Dissolved sugar breaks into particles that cannot be broken ______.
activities.hint: The particles have reached their smallest form.
activities.explanation: Dissolved sugar breaks into particles that cannot be broken down further. These are constituent particles.

activities.prompt: Match each state of matter with its property.
pairs: No fixed shape but a fixed volume
activities.explanation: Solids have a definite shape and volume. Liquids have fixed volume, while gases take the shape of their vessel.

activities.prompt: What happens when a syringe plunger is pushed in?
options: Gas particles lose their movement.
Gas particles come closer together.
Gas particles become strongly attracted.
Gas particles take a fixed shape.
activities.explanation: Pushing the plunger reduces the space between gas particles. External pressure can also reduce this space.

activities.prompt: Water particles move faster in hot water than at room temperature.
activities.explanation: Providing heat increases the movement of particles. Water particles therefore move faster in hot water.

activities.prompt: Put these chalk stages in the order described.
items: Constituent particles cannot be broken further
activities.explanation: Grinding makes the chalk specks smaller. The basic constituent particles cannot be broken down further.

activities.prompt: Passing a finger through water temporarily ______ the water.
activities.hint: The water moves aside while your finger is present.
activities.explanation: Passing a finger through water temporarily displaces the water. The water returns after the finger is removed.

activities.prompt: How does the volume of sugar solution compare with separate sugar and water?
options: It is less than the combined volume.
It is equal to the combined volume.
It is greater than the combined volume.
It has no volume at all.
activities.explanation: The volume of sugar solution is less than the combined volume. This shows some space between water particles.

chapters.title: Nature of Matter
chapters.summary: In this chapter: mixtures and their components; air as a mixture; types of mixtures and pure substances; elements and their particles.

lessons.title: Mixtures and Their Components

activities.prompt: What happens to the ingredients when they get mixed together?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: Meet Mixtures
activities.body: Air, water and food are examples of matter. A mixture forms when substances are mixed and each keeps its properties. These substances are called components. The components do not react chemically. A non-uniform mixture has components that can be seen separately. A uniform mixture has components that cannot be seen separately. An alloy has components mixed very uniformly. Brass is an alloy made from copper and zinc.
keyPoints: Each substance in a mixture keeps its properties.
Components do not react chemically.
Alloys are uniform mixtures, such as brass.
activities.explanation: Learning the clues helps you identify different mixtures.

activities.prompt: A child looks at brass and tries to pick out copper and zinc pieces. Why can this not work?
steps: Brass is an alloy, so its components are mixed very uniformly.
A uniform mixture has components that cannot be seen separately.
Therefore, the child cannot pick out separate copper and zinc pieces.
The components still keep their properties and do not react chemically.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.title: Find the Alloy
activities.prompt: Which one is an alloy?
options: Brass
Air
Water
Food
activities.explanation: Brass is an alloy. Its components are copper and zinc.

activities.title: Name the Substances
activities.prompt: In a mixture, the substances are called ______.
activities.hint: Each substance keeps its properties.
activities.explanation: The substances in a mixture are called components.

activities.title: Visible Components
activities.prompt: Which describes a non-uniform mixture?
options: Its components can be seen separately.
Its components cannot be seen separately.
Its components react chemically.
Each component loses its properties.
activities.explanation: A non-uniform mixture has components that can be seen separately.

activities.title: Match the Ideas
activities.prompt: Match each mixture word with its description.
activities.explanation: Each component keeps its properties. An alloy has components mixed very uniformly.

activities.title: Brass Components
activities.prompt: Which pair makes brass?
options: Copper and zinc
Air and water
Water and food
Food and air
activities.explanation: Brass is an alloy made from copper and zinc.

activities.title: Always True
activities.prompt: Which statement is always true about the substances in a mixture?
options: Each keeps its properties.
They react chemically.
They can all be seen separately.
They are mixed very uniformly.
activities.explanation: Each substance keeps its properties when the mixture forms.

activities.prompt: Brass mixes copper and zinc evenly. What can the child see separately?
options: The copper and zinc cannot be seen separately.
The copper and zinc can be seen separately.
Only the copper can be seen separately.
The copper and zinc react and form a new substance.

why.The copper and zinc can be seen separate: This confuses very uniform mixing with visible separate parts.
This wrongly treats one component as the only visible component.
why.The copper and zinc react and form a new: This wrongly assumes that mixing causes a chemical reaction.

activities.explanation: This is right: uniform brass has components that cannot be seen separately.

activities.prompt: Water and pieces of food are mixed. The components can be seen separately. What kind of mixture is this?
options: A non-uniform mixture, because its components can be seen separately.
A uniform mixture, because its components can be seen separately.
A non-uniform mixture, because its components react chemically.
A uniform mixture, because its components cannot be seen separately.

why.A uniform mixture, because its component: This confuses uniform mixing with components that can be seen.
why.A non-uniform mixture, because its compo: This wrongly adds a chemical reaction that mixture components lack.
why.A uniform mixture, because its component: This says the opposite of what visible separate components show.

activities.explanation: This is right because visible separate components make a non-uniform mixture.

activities.prompt: Water and food are mixed, and each substance keeps its properties. Has a mixture formed?
options: A mixture, because the mixed substances keep their properties.
A new substance, because mixing always changes the substances.
No matter, because the substances still keep their properties.
A mixture, because the substances react chemically together.

why.A new substance, because mixing always c: This wrongly assumes that mixing always changes the substances.
why.No matter, because the substances still: This wrongly thinks water and food stop being matter when mixed.
why.A mixture, because the substances react: This wrongly assumes that mixed substances react chemically.

activities.explanation: This fits the rule: a mixture forms when substances keep their properties.

activities.prompt: A brass item contains copper and zinc. Neither component can be seen separately. What kind of mixture is it?
options: A uniform mixture, because its components cannot be seen separately.
A non-uniform mixture, because its components cannot be seen separately.
A uniform mixture, because its components react chemically.
A non-uniform mixture, because each component keeps its own properties.

why.A non-uniform mixture, because its compo: This contradicts the rule for components that cannot be seen.
why.A uniform mixture, because its component: This wrongly adds a chemical reaction between mixture components.
why.A non-uniform mixture, because each comp: This wrongly uses kept properties to decide visual uniformity.

activities.explanation: This is right because its components cannot be seen separately.

activities.prompt: Brass mixes copper and zinc very uniformly. A child calls it non-uniform because they differ. Is the child right?
options: The claim is wrong because brass components cannot be seen separately.
The claim is right because copper and zinc are different substances.
The claim is wrong because brass components react chemically.
The claim is right because brass contains two different components.

why.The claim is right because copper and zi: This wrongly thinks different substances must make a non-uniform mixture.
why.The claim is wrong because brass compone: This wrongly claims that mixture components react chemically.
why.The claim is right because brass contain: This wrongly assumes that two components must make a non-uniform mixture.

activities.explanation: This is right: uniform brass components cannot be seen separately.

lessons.sceneAlt: A solid brass sample appears alongside separate pieces of zinc and copper, the two components used to make the alloy.
lessons.sceneCaption: Brass is an alloy made by mixing copper and zinc uniformly.

sceneCredit.creator: Splarka

lessons.title: Air as a Mixture

activities.title: Air as a Mixture
activities.body:
Air is a uniform mixture of several gases.

Most living beings need oxygen to stay alive.

Oxygen helps in combustion.
keyPoints: Nitrogen makes up about 78% of air and does not support combustion.
Water vapour can become tiny water droplets on a cool surface.
activities.explanation: Now try some questions.

activities.prompt: What hidden gases and tiny particles are floating in the air around us?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.prompt: A cup of lime water turns milky after standing in air. Why does this happen?
steps: Lime water is calcium hydroxide dissolved in water.
The air contains carbon dioxide, as the activity shows.
Carbon dioxide reacts with calcium hydroxide and makes lime water milky.
Therefore, the milky lime water shows that carbon dioxide is present in the air.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.prompt: Most living beings need oxygen to stay alive.
activities.explanation: Oxygen is needed by most living beings to stay alive.

activities.prompt: Match each substance with its property.
activities.explanation: Each gas or substance has a property shown in the lesson. These properties help us identify them.

activities.prompt: Put these steps in the correct order.
items: The solution is called lime water
Carbon dioxide makes lime water milky
activities.explanation: First, calcium oxide reacts with water. Next, calcium hydroxide forms and gives lime water.

activities.prompt: Why does lime water turn milky when carbon dioxide is added?
options: Water vapour forms droplets.
It supports combustion.
Carbon dioxide reacts.
It settles as dust.
activities.explanation: Carbon dioxide reacts with calcium hydroxide. This makes lime water milky.

activities.prompt: Which group contains only things found in air?
options: oxygen, nitrogen, calcium oxide, lime water
oxygen, nitrogen, water vapour, dust
oxygen, nitrogen, lime water, soot
oxygen, nitrogen, water vapour, lime water
activities.explanation: Air contains oxygen, nitrogen, water vapour, and suspended dust. Lime water and calcium oxide are not parts of air.

activities.prompt: A fire is moved into a jar filled with nitrogen. What is likely to happen?
options: The fire keeps burning because nitrogen also supports combustion.
The fire stops burning because nitrogen does not support combustion.
The fire stops burning because nitrogen turns the air milky.
The fire keeps burning because nitrogen cools the flame.

why.The fire keeps burning because nitrogen: This wrongly assumes that nitrogen supports combustion.
why.The fire stops burning because nitrogen: This wrongly connects nitrogen with the lime water reaction.
why.The fire keeps burning because nitrogen: This wrongly thinks that nitrogen cools and helps a fire.

activities.explanation: Nitrogen does not support combustion, so the fire cannot keep burning.

activities.prompt: Lime water is left open to air. It turns milky. What best explains this change?
options: Carbon dioxide in air reacts with calcium hydroxide.
Oxygen in air makes calcium hydroxide turn milky.
Nitrogen in air makes calcium hydroxide turn milky.
Water vapour in air makes calcium hydroxide turn milky.

why.Oxygen in air makes calcium hydroxide tu: This wrongly blames oxygen, which is linked with combustion here.
why.Nitrogen in air makes calcium hydroxide: This wrongly blames nitrogen for the reaction that makes lime water milky.
why.Water vapour in air makes calcium hydrox: This wrongly blames water vapour, which can form droplets on cool surfaces.

activities.explanation: Carbon dioxide reacts with calcium hydroxide and makes lime water milky.

activities.prompt: A student says, “Nitrogen is about 78% of air, so nitrogen is the only gas.” What is the best reply?
options: About 78% leaves room for other gases in the mixture.
About 78% means every part of air is nitrogen.
About 78% means nitrogen supports every fire.
About 78% means lime water comes from nitrogen.

why.About 78% means every part of air is nit: This mistakes a large part for the whole mixture.
why.About 78% means nitrogen supports every: This wrongly treats nitrogen as a supporter of combustion.
why.About 78% means lime water comes from ni: This wrongly links nitrogen with the lime water reaction.

activities.explanation: Air is a mixture of several gases, so nitrogen is not all of it.

lessons.sceneAlt: A solid brass sample appears alongside separate pieces of zinc and copper, the two components used to make the alloy.
lessons.sceneCaption: Brass is an alloy made by mixing copper and zinc uniformly.

sceneCredit.text: Brass by Splarka, Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons
sceneCredit.creator: Splarka

lessons.title: Types of Mixtures and Pure Substances

activities.prompt: What makes a mixture different from a pure substance?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: Mixtures and pure substances
activities.body: A mixture has components mixed together. These components may themselves be mixtures. In science, all components must be pure substances. A pure substance has no other substance present in it. It cannot be separated into other kinds of matter by physical processes. It consists of the same type of particles.
keyPoints: The components of a mixture may themselves be mixtures.
All components of a mixture must be pure substances.
A pure substance has the same type of particles.
activities.explanation: A pure substance contains one kind of particle and no other substance.

activities.prompt: A seller adds a cheaper substance to a product. Is it pure?
steps: This is adulteration because the added substance is cheaper.
Adulteration means illegally adding a cheaper or poor-quality substance.
A pure substance has no other substance present in it.
The added substance is present, so the product is not pure.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.title: Classifying and separating mixtures
activities.body: Mixtures can be grouped according to the physical states of their components. Examples include gas-and-liquid, solid-and-gas, liquid-and-liquid, and solid-and-liquid mixtures. Scientific separation is done to obtain pure substances. Adulteration means illegally adding cheaper or poor-quality substances to a product.
keyPoints: Mixtures can be grouped by the physical states of their components.
Scientific separation obtains pure substances.
Adulteration adds cheaper or poor-quality substances illegally.
activities.explanation: Different mixtures can be separated to obtain pure substances.

activities.prompt: In science, all components of a mixture must be ______ substances.
activities.hint: Use the word that describes a substance without another substance.
activities.explanation: Pure substances contain no other substance present in them.

activities.prompt: Which one is a gas-and-liquid mixture?
options: Aerated water
Sand and water
Carbon particles in air
Oil with water
activities.explanation: Aerated water and oxygen dissolved in water are gas-and-liquid mixtures.

activities.prompt: Match each mixture with its type.
activities.explanation: Each example shows the physical states of the components in that mixture.

activities.prompt: Which statement describes a pure substance correctly?
options: It has no other substance.
It has different particles.
It can be separated physically.
It contains added materials.
activities.explanation: A pure substance has no other substance present in it. It consists of the same type of particles.

activities.prompt: A pure substance can be separated into other kinds of matter by physical processes.
activities.explanation: No. A pure substance cannot be separated into other kinds of matter by physical processes.

activities.prompt: Which action is adulteration?
options: Adding cheaper substances illegally
Separating a mixture scientifically
Grouping components by state
Using one type of particle
activities.explanation: Adulteration means illegally adding cheaper or poor-quality substances to a product.

activities.prompt: A seller adds a cheaper substance to a product. What has happened?
options: The product has been adulterated.
The product has become purer.
The product has been separated.
The product is still pure.

Adding another substance does not make a product purer.
Adulteration means adding substances, not separating them.
A pure substance has no other substance present in it.

activities.explanation: Adding a cheaper substance illegally is adulteration.

activities.prompt: Oil and water are both liquids. Which mixture group will they form?
options: It will be a liquid-and-liquid mixture.
It will be a solid-and-liquid mixture.
It will be a solid-and-gas mixture.
It will be a gas-and-liquid mixture.

This wrongly treats one liquid component as a solid.
This wrongly treats both liquid components as solid and gas.
This wrongly treats one liquid component as a gas.

activities.explanation: Oil and water are both liquids, so both components are liquid.

activities.prompt: Acetic acid and water form a clear solution. Is this mixture pure?
options: No, because water is also present in the mixture.
No, because clear solutions always have one substance.
No, because pure substances always look clear.
No, because water and acetic acid form one substance.

why.No, because clear solutions always have: This wrongly treats appearance as proof of purity.
why.No, because pure substances always look: This wrongly assumes that clear means pure.
why.No, because water and acetic acid form o: This wrongly assumes two substances become one substance.

activities.explanation: A pure substance has no other substance present in it.

activities.prompt: Sand and water are mixed. How can the scientist obtain pure substances?
options: Use scientific separation to obtain the pure substances.
Leave the mixture unchanged because it already looks pure.
Add more water so the mixture becomes pure.
Shake the mixture so the sand becomes water.

why.Leave the mixture unchanged because it a: A mixture is not pure just because it looks unchanged.
why.Add more water so the mixture becomes pu: Adding another substance does not make the mixture pure.
why.Shake the mixture so the sand becomes wa: Shaking does not turn sand into water or purify the mixture.

activities.explanation: Scientific separation of a mixture obtains pure substances.

lessons.sceneAlt: Water, oil and beans are shown together as a mixture.
lessons.sceneCaption: Water, oil and beans together form a mixture containing two immiscible liquids.

sceneCredit.text: Mixture of water, oil and beans by LuciodeMoraes, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons
sceneCredit.creator: LuciodeMoraes

lessons.title: Elements and Their Particles

activities.prompt: What happens to water’s particles when electricity passes through them?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: Meet Elements and Atoms
activities.body: An element is a building block of matter. Each element is made of identical particles called atoms. The particles of one element differ from those of every other element. An element cannot be broken down into simpler substances. Water contains two elements: hydrogen and oxygen. Its particles stay the same during changes of state.
keyPoints: Each element contains identical particles called atoms.
Different elements have different particles.
Water contains hydrogen and oxygen.
activities.explanation: Every element is a building block of matter, and each has its own kind of atom.

activities.prompt: A puddle of water slowly dries. Does the water change into different elements?
steps: Water changes into vapour as the puddle dries.
This is a state change, so the particles stay the same.
Because the particles stay the same, no new elements form.
Therefore, this change does not create different elements.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.title: Atoms, Molecules and Metals
activities.body: Two or more atoms can join to form a molecule of an element. An element cannot be broken down into simpler substances. Gold, silver, magnesium, iron and aluminium are metals. Each element has identical particles called atoms. But its particles differ from every other element.
keyPoints: Atoms can join to form a molecule of an element.
An element cannot be broken into simpler substances.
Gold, silver, magnesium, iron and aluminium are metals.
activities.explanation: Each element has its own atoms, and some atoms can join to form molecules.

activities.prompt: Which two elements are present in water?
options: hydrogen and oxygen
hydrogen and gold
oxygen and iron
gold and silver
activities.explanation: Water contains the elements hydrogen and oxygen. Both are needed to describe water correctly.

activities.prompt: Elements are the building blocks of all ______.
activities.hint: Everything around you is made from this.
activities.explanation: Every element is a building block of matter. Elements make up all matter.

activities.prompt: Match each element with the clue linked to it.
activities.explanation: A pop sound indicates hydrogen. A brighter flame indicates oxygen. Gold is a metal.

activities.prompt: Put the steps for finding the gases from water in order.
items: Pass an electric current through water.
Break water into hydrogen and oxygen.
Use a pop sound to identify hydrogen.
Use a brighter candle flame to identify oxygen.
activities.explanation: Electric current breaks water into two gases. Their clues help identify hydrogen and oxygen.

activities.prompt: Which statement about the particles of elements is correct?
options: The particles of each element are identical.
The particles of all elements are identical.
One element contains two types of particle.
Elements do not contain particles.
activities.explanation: Each element has identical particles. However, different elements have different particles.

activities.prompt: Collected gases give a pop sound and a brighter candle flame. Which elements are present?
options: Hydrogen and oxygen
Only hydrogen
Only oxygen
Only gold
activities.explanation: A pop sound indicates hydrogen. A brighter candle flame indicates oxygen.

activities.prompt: One collected gas gives a pop sound. Another makes a candle flame brighter. What is present?
options: Hydrogen and oxygen are present.
Hydrogen and water vapour are present.
Only hydrogen is present.
Only water vapour is present.

The child wrongly thinks the bright flame shows water vapour.
The child ignores the evidence from the brighter flame.
The child wrongly thinks the gases are unchanged water.

activities.explanation: The pop shows hydrogen, and the brighter flame shows oxygen.

activities.prompt: Someone says boiling a pan of water makes hydrogen and oxygen. What corrects this claim?
options: No, boiling changes state without breaking water down.
Yes, boiling breaks water into hydrogen and oxygen.
Yes, boiling changes the water particles.
Yes, boiling turns water into a new element.

why.Yes, boiling breaks water into hydrogen: The child wrongly thinks boiling does what electric current does.
why.Yes, boiling changes the water particles: The child confuses a state change with a particle change.
why.Yes, boiling turns water into a new elem: The child wrongly thinks boiling can create an element.

activities.explanation: Boiling changes only water's state, so its particles stay the same.

activities.prompt: Two samples each have identical atoms. The atoms in one sample differ from those in the other. Can either be broken into simpler substances?
options: No, both are elements and cannot be broken down.
No, but only the second sample can be broken down.
Yes, because their atoms are joined in molecules.
Yes, because different elements can break down.

why.No, but only the second sample can be br: The child wrongly thinks different atoms make an element breakable.
why.Yes, because their atoms are joined in m: Joining atoms in molecules does not mean the element can break down.
why.Yes, because different elements can brea: The child wrongly thinks elements can become simpler substances.

activities.explanation: Different element particles cannot be broken into simpler substances.

lessons.sceneAlt: A Hofmann voltameter demonstrates the electrolysis of water into separate hydrogen and oxygen gases.
lessons.sceneCaption: This apparatus shows electric current splitting water into hydrogen and oxygen gases.

lessons.title: Compounds and Chemical Combinations

activities.prompt: Could two elements join and become something completely new?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: What is a compound?
activities.body: A compound forms when different elements combine in fixed amounts. Ratios show how many atoms of each element combine. Its elements cannot be separated by physical means. Water has a 2:1 ratio of hydrogen to oxygen. Sodium chloride has a 1:1 ratio. Heating Sample A, an iron and sulphur mixture, produces iron sulphide. It has different properties and is not attracted by a magnet.
keyPoints: Compounds use fixed ratios of elements.
Elements in compounds cannot be separated by physical means.
Heating iron and sulphur produces iron sulphide.
activities.explanation: Compounds form when elements combine in fixed ratios.

activities.prompt: A child heats iron and sulphur, then uses a magnet. What happens?
steps: Heating Sample A produces iron sulphide because iron and sulphur combine.
This product has different properties because it differs from both starting elements.
A magnet will not attract it because iron sulphide is not attracted.
Therefore, the magnet cannot pull in the iron sulphide.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.prompt: In water, what is the ratio of hydrogen atoms to oxygen atoms?
options: Two hydrogen atoms for every one oxygen atom
One hydrogen atom for every two oxygen atoms
One hydrogen atom for every one oxygen atom
Two hydrogen atoms for every two oxygen atoms
activities.explanation: Water has a 2:1 ratio of hydrogen atoms to oxygen atoms.

activities.prompt: Water has a ______:1 ratio of hydrogen atoms to oxygen atoms.
activities.hint: Use the hydrogen count in the ratio.
activities.explanation: Water has two hydrogen atoms for every one oxygen atom.

activities.prompt: Match each compound with its elements or linked products.
activities.explanation: Water, sodium chloride and sugar contain the listed elements. Heating sugar gives carbon and water. Heating Sample A gives iron sulphide from its iron and sulphur.

activities.prompt: Which substance can be separated from water by evaporation?
options: Dissolved sodium chloride
Carbon and water
Iron sulphide
Iron and sulphur
activities.explanation: Dissolved sodium chloride can be separated from water by evaporation.

activities.prompt: Which change explains the different properties of iron sulphide?
options: Heating Sample A produces iron sulphide.
The iron and sulphur remain completely separate.
The sulphur slowly disappears during the heating.
The magnet attracts the new iron sulphide.
activities.explanation: Heating Sample A produces iron sulphide. Its properties differ from iron and sulphur.

activities.prompt: Put these steps in order.
items: Sample A is an iron and sulphur mixture
activities.explanation: Sample A is heated. This produces iron sulphide.

activities.prompt: Sample A is heated until iron sulphide forms. What will the magnet do?
options: It will pull iron from the iron sulphide.
It will not attract the iron sulphide.
It will pull sulphur from the iron sulphide.
It will turn iron sulphide into iron.

why.It will pull iron from the iron sulphide: This mistake assumes iron sulphide behaves like separate iron.
why.It will pull sulphur from the iron sulph: This mistake assumes sulphur stays separate inside iron sulphide.
This mistake assumes a magnet changes iron sulphide.

activities.explanation: Iron sulphide is not attracted by a magnet.

activities.prompt: Elements form compounds in fixed ratios. Can any amount of iron and sulphur combine?
options: No, the elements must combine in a fixed ratio.
Yes, any amount of iron and sulphur can combine.
No, iron and sulphur must stay as separate elements.
Yes, each amount can form a different compound.

why.Yes, any amount of iron and sulphur can: This mistake assumes compounds allow any amount of elements.
why.No, iron and sulphur must stay as separa: This mistake assumes the elements never combine into a compound.
why.Yes, each amount can form a different co: This mistake assumes each amount gives a different compound.

activities.explanation: Compounds form when elements combine in fixed ratios.

activities.prompt: Sugar contains carbon, hydrogen and oxygen. Why would filtering fail to get carbon and water?
options: Sugar's elements cannot be separated by a physical method.
Carbon and water cannot form when sugar is heated.
Filtering makes sugar into a different compound.
Sugar does not contain carbon, hydrogen, or oxygen.

why.Carbon and water cannot form when sugar: This mistake denies the products formed when sugar is heated.
why.Filtering makes sugar into a different c: This mistake assumes filtering changes which elements are present.
why.Sugar does not contain carbon, hydrogen,: This mistake denies that sugar contains carbon, hydrogen, and oxygen.

activities.explanation: Sugar is a compound, so filtering cannot separate its elements.

lessons.sceneAlt: A colourful school molecular model shows one oxygen atom joined to two hydrogen atoms in water.
lessons.sceneCaption: A water model clearly shows hydrogen and oxygen combined in a fixed 2:1 ratio.

sceneCredit.creator: Ljeto

lessons.title: Uses of Matter and Minerals

activities.prompt: What are minerals made of, and how do we use them?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: Matter, minerals and materials
activities.body: Matter has mass and takes up space. Light, heat, electricity, thoughts and emotions are not made of matter. Iron and aluminium build bridges, buildings and vehicles. Wood, steel and concrete are mixtures used as building materials. Most rocks are mixtures of minerals. Most minerals are compounds containing more than one element. Native minerals are pure elements rather than compounds.
keyPoints: Matter has mass and takes up space.
Most minerals contain more than one element.
Native minerals are pure elements.
activities.explanation: This lesson connects matter, minerals and useful materials.

activities.prompt: A builder needs a strong and durable bridge. Should pure iron or stainless steel be used?
steps: Stainless steel is stronger than pure iron, so it fits the need for strength.
It is also more durable, so it fits the need for long use.
Iron is already used for bridges, so this choice fits building uses.
Therefore, stainless steel is the better choice for the bridge.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.prompt: Which material is said to be the lightest on Earth?
options: Graphene aerogel
Pure iron
Stainless steel
Cement
activities.explanation: Graphene aerogel is said to be the lightest material on Earth.

activities.prompt: Most rocks are single, pure elements.
activities.explanation: Most rocks are mixtures of minerals.

activities.prompt: Cement is made from ______, quartz, alumina and iron oxide.
activities.hint: A mineral listed beside quartz.
activities.explanation: Calcite is one of the materials used to make cement.

activities.prompt: Which statement about most minerals is correct?
options: Most are compounds.
Most are pure elements.
Every mineral is pure.
Rocks are minerals.
activities.explanation: Most minerals are compounds containing more than one element.

activities.prompt: A builder wants a metal stronger and more durable than pure iron. Which material fits?
options: Stainless steel
Graphene aerogel
Cement
Calcite
activities.explanation: Stainless steel is stronger and more durable than pure iron.

activities.prompt: Which set contains only mixtures used as building materials?
options: Wood, steel and concrete
Iron, aluminium and calcite
Graphene aerogel, cement and quartz
Calcite, quartz and pure iron
activities.explanation: Wood, steel and concrete are mixtures used as building materials.

activities.prompt: Stainless steel is stronger than pure iron. Which test would fairly check this claim?
options: Test only stainless steel and record the result.
Test only pure iron and record the result.
Test both metals with the same strength test.
Use a different strength test for each metal.

why.Test only stainless steel and record the: This omits pure iron, so the comparison is not fair.
why.Test only pure iron and record the resul: This omits stainless steel, so the comparison is not fair.
why.Use a different strength test for each m: Different tests may give different results, so the comparison is not fair.

activities.explanation: Using the same test for both metals gives a fair comparison.

activities.prompt: Most rocks are mixtures of minerals. A learner says rocks are pure elements. Why is the claim flawed?
options: Most rocks contain one mineral and no mixture.
Most rocks contain compounds made from one element.
Most rocks contain no minerals of any kind.
Most rocks are mixtures of minerals, not pure elements.

why.Most rocks contain one mineral and no mi: This confuses a mixture of minerals with a single pure mineral.
why.Most rocks contain compounds made from o: This mistakes a compound for something containing only one element.
why.Most rocks contain no minerals of any ki: This wrongly says that rocks contain no minerals.

activities.explanation: This correctly separates mixtures of minerals from pure elements.

activities.prompt: Most rocks are mixtures of minerals. What does this suggest about most minerals?
options: Most are pure elements rather than compounds.
Most are compounds containing more than one element.
Most contain only one element or no elements.
All are mixtures made from different rocks.

why.Most are pure elements rather than compo: This confuses native minerals with most minerals.
why.Most contain only one element or no elem: This wrongly makes compounds contain only one element or none.
why.All are mixtures made from different roc: This reverses the relationship between rocks and minerals.

activities.explanation: Most minerals are compounds containing more than one element.
