lessons.title: Test practice
lessons.sceneAlt: A solid brass sample appears alongside separate pieces of zinc and copper, the two components used to make the alloy.
lessons.sceneCaption: Brass is an alloy made by mixing copper and zinc uniformly.

sceneCredit.text: Brass by Splarka, Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons
sceneCredit.creator: Splarka

activities.context: A student mixes copper and zinc very uniformly to make brass. The student then combines water with pieces of food. The water and food are both matter, and the food pieces remain visible in the water. The student leaves both mixtures unchanged and thinks about how their components are arranged.
activities.prompt: The student wants the water and food to have the same kind of even appearance as brass. What should the student do?
options: Mix the water and food until their components cannot be seen separately.
Leave the food pieces visible because the mixture already has an even appearance.
Allow the food and water to react chemically so that they become new substances.
Stop combining them because substances in a mixture no longer keep their properties.

why.Leave the food pieces visible because th: Visible food pieces show that the mixture is not uniform.
why.Allow the food and water to react chemic: The components of a mixture do not react chemically with one another.
why.Stop combining them because substances i: Each substance in a mixture keeps its own properties.

activities.explanation: This would make the water and food a uniform mixture.

activities.context: A student mixes copper and zinc very uniformly to make brass. The student then combines water with pieces of food. The water and food are both matter, and the food pieces remain visible in the water. The student leaves both mixtures unchanged and thinks about how their components are arranged.
activities.prompt: Why does the student describe brass as an alloy rather than as a non-uniform mixture?
options: Because copper and zinc in it are combined very evenly, so its components cannot be seen separately.
Because copper and zinc react chemically to form one new substance.
Because the components in brass can be seen separately.
Because brass contains only one kind of component.

why.Because copper and zinc react chemically: The components of a mixture do not react chemically.
why.Because the components in brass can be s: A non-uniform mixture has components that can be seen separately.
why.Because brass contains only one kind of: Brass is made from copper and zinc, so it has more than one component.

activities.explanation: This matches the definition of an alloy and a uniform mixture.

activities.prompt:
Assertion (A): Brass is an alloy.
Reason (R): Its copper and zinc components are mixed very uniformly.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.
activities.explanation: The reason directly explains why brass meets the definition of an alloy.

activities.prompt:
Assertion (A): Copper and zinc are components of brass.
Reason (R): Air, water and food are examples of matter.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.
activities.explanation: Both statements are true, but being examples of matter does not explain the components of brass.

activities.prompt: Explain how the appearance of the water and food mixture in the case would change if the student mixed the components until they could not be seen separately.
activities.answer: At first, the water and food form a non-uniform mixture because the food pieces can be seen separately. If the student mixes them until the components cannot be seen separately, the mixture becomes uniform. The substances remain components, so each keeps its own properties, and they do not react chemically with one another. The brass is already an alloy because its copper and zinc were mixed very uniformly. Thus, changing how thoroughly the water and food are mixed changes whether the mixture is uniform or non-uniform.
points: Initially, the food pieces can be seen separately.
The changed mixture is uniform.
The components keep their properties and do not react chemically.
Brass is already an alloy.
activities.explanation: Compare your answer with the points a marker looks for.

activities.context: During a class activity, students investigated the air in their classroom. They mixed calcium oxide with water, forming calcium hydroxide, and used its solution, called lime water. When it stood exposed to the air, the lime water turned milky, showing that carbon dioxide was present. On a cool surface, tiny droplets appeared. One group also noticed dust remaining suspended in the air, while another asked how the air quality could be described.
activities.prompt: After the lime water stood exposed to the air, what happened, and why?
options: It became milky because carbon dioxide in the air reacted with calcium hydroxide.
It stayed unchanged because nitrogen does not support combustion.
It became milky because oxygen helps in combustion.
It became dusty because dust can remain suspended in the air.

why.It stayed unchanged because nitrogen doe: Nitrogen's lack of support for combustion does not explain the change.
why.It became milky because oxygen helps in: Oxygen's role in combustion does not make lime water milky.
why.It became dusty because dust can remain: Suspended dust does not cause lime water to become milky.

activities.explanation: Carbon dioxide reacts with calcium hydroxide and makes lime water milky.

activities.context: During a class activity, students investigated the air in their classroom. They mixed calcium oxide with water, forming calcium hydroxide, and used its solution, called lime water. When it stood exposed to the air, the lime water turned milky, showing that carbon dioxide was present. On a cool surface, tiny droplets appeared. One group also noticed dust remaining suspended in the air, while another asked how the air quality could be described.
activities.prompt: Which method would best help the students describe the quality of the air?
options: Use the AQI, because it is a tool for describing air quality.
Use only the visible dust, because it gives a complete description of air quality.
Use the milky appearance of lime water, because it describes all air quality.
Use the droplets on the cool surface, because they describe all air quality.

why.Use only the visible dust, because it gi: Visible dust shows an airborne pollutant but does not fully describe air quality.
why.Use the milky appearance of lime water,: Milky lime water shows that carbon dioxide is present.
why.Use the droplets on the cool surface, be: Droplets on a cool surface show the presence of water vapour.

activities.explanation: The AQI is a tool for describing air quality.

activities.prompt:
Assertion (A): Exposed lime water can turn milky.
Reason (R): Carbon dioxide reacts with calcium hydroxide and makes lime water milky.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.
activities.explanation: The reaction with carbon dioxide directly explains the milky appearance.

activities.prompt:
Assertion (A): Nitrogen does not support combustion.
Reason (R): About 78% of the air is nitrogen.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.
activities.explanation: The percentage describes how much nitrogen is present, not why it does not support combustion.

activities.prompt: Explain how the lime-water activity, the cool-surface observation, and the suspended dust support the idea that air is a mixture.
activities.answer: The lime-water activity showed that carbon dioxide was present in the air, because carbon dioxide reacts with calcium hydroxide and makes lime water milky. The cool-surface observation showed the presence of water vapour, since it can become tiny water droplets on a cool surface. These observations involve different substances in the same air, supporting the idea that air is a uniform mixture of several gases. The suspended dust showed that particles can remain in the air; dust and soot are examples of airborne pollutants.
points: Carbon dioxide makes exposed lime water milky.
Water vapour can form tiny droplets on a cool surface.
Different substances were observed in the air.
Air is described as a uniform mixture of several gases.
activities.explanation: Compare your answer with the points a marker looks for.

activities.context: A student visits a shop and notices that the keeper has added a cheaper, poor-quality substance to a product. The student explains that this is adulteration. The keeper says that separation is unnecessary because every mixture contains only pure substances. Looking at sand mixed with water, the student says that its components have different physical states. The student also identifies acetic acid in water as a liquid-and-liquid mixture.
activities.prompt: The keeper says separation is unnecessary. What should the student do?
options: Explain that scientific separation is used to obtain pure substances.
Agree that adding a substance is the same as scientifically separating a mixture.
Explain that a pure substance can be split into other kinds of matter by physical processes.
Agree that a mixture cannot contain pure substances as its components.

why.Agree that adding a substance is the sam: Adding a substance is not the same as separating a mixture.
why.Explain that a pure substance can be spl: A pure substance cannot be separated into other kinds of matter by physical processes.
why.Agree that a mixture cannot contain pure: The components of a mixture must be pure substances.

activities.explanation: Scientific separation is done to obtain pure substances.

activities.context: A student visits a shop and notices that the keeper has added a cheaper, poor-quality substance to a product. The student explains that this is adulteration. The keeper says that separation is unnecessary because every mixture contains only pure substances. Looking at sand mixed with water, the student says that its components have different physical states. The student also identifies acetic acid in water as a liquid-and-liquid mixture.
activities.prompt: If scientific separation removes only some of the sand from the sand-and-water mixture, what should the student expect?
options: The sample is still a solid-and-liquid mixture because some solid sand remains with liquid water.
The sample is a pure substance because scientific separation has been used.
The sample is a liquid-and-liquid mixture because the remaining sand is no longer counted.
The sample is a solid-and-gas mixture because water becomes a gas during separation.

why.The sample is a pure substance because s: Using scientific separation does not mean that every other substance has been removed.
why.The sample is a liquid-and-liquid mixtur: The remaining sand is still a solid, so the mixture is not liquid-and-liquid.
why.The sample is a solid-and-gas mixture be: The sand-and-water mixture has liquid water, not a gas component.

activities.explanation: Some sand remains as a solid component beside liquid water.

activities.prompt:
Assertion (A): The components of a mixture may themselves be mixtures.
Reason (R): This is possible because all components of a mixture must be pure substances.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.
activities.explanation: The assertion is true, but the proposed reason is false because mixture components must be pure substances.

activities.prompt:
Assertion (A): Aerated water and oxygen dissolved in water are gas-and-liquid mixtures.
Reason (R): Their gas component and liquid component have different physical states.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.
activities.explanation: Both statements are true, and the different physical states explain the classification.

activities.prompt: Explain how the state-based groups of mixtures are different, using examples from the lesson.
activities.answer: Mixtures can be grouped according to the physical states of their components. Aerated water and oxygen dissolved in water are gas-and-liquid mixtures because one component is a gas and the other is a liquid. Acetic acid in water and oil with water are liquid-and-liquid mixtures because both components are liquids. Sand and water form a solid-and-liquid mixture, while carbon particles in air form a solid-and-gas mixture.
points: Mixtures are grouped by component states.
Gas-and-liquid examples are given.
Liquid-and-liquid and solid-and-liquid examples are distinguished.
Solid-and-gas carbon particles in air are identified.
activities.explanation: Compare your answer with the points a marker looks for.

activities.context: A student passed an electric current through water and collected the gases produced. During testing, one gas gave a pop and the other made a candle flame brighter. The student knew that water contains elements and wondered how water could be separated into gases that were not water vapour. The lesson explained that elements are made of atoms, and that atoms from different elements are not identical.
activities.prompt: After hearing the pop during testing, which gas should the student identify?
options: Hydrogen
Oxygen
Water vapour
Magnesium

why.Oxygen: Oxygen is identified by the brighter-flame result, not the pop.
why.Water vapour: The collected breakdown gases were stated not to be water vapour.
why.Magnesium: Magnesium is a metal and was not one of the gases produced.

activities.explanation: Hydrogen is correctly identified because a pop indicates its presence.

activities.context: A student passed an electric current through water and collected the gases produced. During testing, one gas gave a pop and the other made a candle flame brighter. The student knew that water contains elements and wondered how water could be separated into gases that were not water vapour. The lesson explained that elements are made of atoms, and that atoms from different elements are not identical.
activities.prompt: If water changed to another state and then changed back before the electric current was passed, what should remain true?
options: Its particles would remain the same throughout both state changes.
Its particles would be replaced by those of another element.
It would contain one element instead of hydrogen and oxygen.
It would stop being made of atoms.

why.Its particles would be replaced by those: A state change does not replace water's particles with those of another element.
why.It would contain one element instead of: Water contains hydrogen and oxygen regardless of its state.
Elements are always made of atoms, including during changes of state.

activities.explanation: The particles of water remain the same during changes of state.

activities.prompt:
Assertion (A): The collected gases are not water vapour.
Reason (R): An electric current broke the water down into hydrogen and oxygen.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.
activities.explanation: The breakdown into hydrogen and oxygen explains why the collected gases are not water vapour.

boss.title: Chapter challenge: Nature of Matter

activities.prompt: Which description fits a uniform mixture?
options: Its components cannot be seen separately.
Its components react chemically together.
Its components have different proportions each time.
Its components can be seen separately.
activities.explanation: A uniform mixture has components that cannot be seen separately. Air is one example.

activities.prompt: The components of a mixture react chemically with one another.
activities.explanation: The components of a mixture do not react chemically with one another. Each keeps its properties.

activities.prompt: Brass is an alloy made from copper and ______.
activities.hint: This metal is mixed with copper to make brass.
activities.explanation: Brass is an alloy made from copper and zinc. Its components are mixed very uniformly.

activities.prompt: Match each mixture with its type.
activities.explanation: Mixtures can be grouped according to the physical states of their components.

activities.prompt: Which statement describes a pure substance?
options: It contains different kinds of particles.
It can be separated by physical processes.
It contains only one type of particle.
It contains another substance.
activities.explanation: A pure substance has no other substance present. It consists of the same type of particles.

activities.prompt: Water has a 2:1 ratio of hydrogen atoms to oxygen atoms.
activities.explanation: Different elements combine in fixed ratios to form a compound. Water has this ratio.

activities.prompt: The solution of calcium hydroxide in water is called ______ water.
activities.hint: Carbon dioxide makes this solution look milky.
activities.explanation: The solution is called lime water. Carbon dioxide makes lime water milky.

activities.prompt: Match each substance with a correct fact about it.
pairs: Is not attracted by a magnet
activities.explanation: Each substance has the stated elements or properties. Elements are the building blocks of all matter.

boss.sceneCaption: Brass is an alloy made by mixing copper and zinc uniformly.

chapters.title: Amazing World of Solutes, Solvents, and Solutions
chapters.summary: In this chapter: lesson 1: mixtures, solutions, solutes and solvents; lesson 2: solubility, saturation and temperature; lesson 3: gases dissolving in water; lesson 4: floating, sinking and density.

lessons.title: Lesson 1: Mixtures, Solutions, Solutes and Solvents

activities.prompt: What makes some mixes spread out while others settle apart?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: What makes a solution?
activities.body: A mixture can be uniform, with components evenly spread, or non-uniform. A uniform mixture of salt or sugar and water is a solution. The solid is the solute, and the liquid is the solvent. For two liquids, the smaller amount is the solute. The larger amount is the solvent. In sugar syrup, water is the solvent. Oral Rehydration Solution helps treat dehydration.
keyPoints: A uniform mixture is a solution.
The solute dissolves in the solvent.
In sugar syrup, water is the solvent.
activities.explanation: These ideas help you identify mixtures, solutions, solutes, and solvents.

activities.prompt: Why does sugar seem to disappear when it is stirred into water?
steps: The sugar dissolves in the water and spreads evenly.
This even spread shows that the mixture is uniform.
In this solution, sugar is the solute and water is the solvent.
So stirring produces a uniform solution, not separate sugar.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.prompt: What is a salt and sugar mixture in water?
options: Uniform
Non-uniform
Separated
Layered
activities.explanation: Its components are evenly spread throughout the mixture.

activities.prompt: In a solution of salt and water, the solid is called the ______.
activities.hint: This dissolves in the liquid.
activities.explanation: The solid in a solution of a solid and liquid is the solute.

activities.prompt: In sugar syrup, which liquid is the solvent?
options: Water
Sugar
Salt
Sawdust
activities.explanation: Water remains the solvent in sugar syrup, even with plenty of sugar.

activities.prompt: Which is used to treat dehydration?
options: Oral Rehydration Solution
Sawdust and water
Salt and sugar
Sugar syrup
activities.explanation: Oral Rehydration Solution treats dehydration by keeping the body hydrated.

activities.prompt: Put the steps for salt dissolving in water in order.
activities.explanation: The solute dissolves in the solvent and forms a solution.

activities.prompt: A child mixes salt with water. Another child mixes sawdust with water. Which mixture will have its parts spread evenly?
options: The salt and water parts will spread evenly.
The sawdust and water parts will spread evenly.
Both pairs of parts will spread evenly.
Neither pair of parts will spread evenly.

why.The sawdust and water parts will spread: This mistake treats sawdust and water as if they were uniform.
This mistake assumes every solid and liquid mixture is uniform.
why.Neither pair of parts will spread evenly: This mistake ignores that salt and water do spread evenly.

activities.explanation: Salt and water form a uniform mixture, so their parts spread evenly.

activities.prompt: A cook makes sugar syrup. The syrup has a large amount of sugar. Which component is the solvent?
options: The water is the solvent because it holds the sugar.
The sugar is the solvent because there is a large amount.
The sugar is the solvent because it dissolves in water.
The water is the solvent because it looks clearer.

why.The sugar is the solvent because there i: This mistake assumes the larger amount must always be the solvent.
why.The sugar is the solvent because it diss: This mistake confuses the dissolving sugar with the solvent holding it.
why.The water is the solvent because it look: This mistake uses colour instead of the sugar syrup rule.

activities.explanation: Sugar syrup has water as its solvent, even with much sugar.

activities.prompt: A child mixes salt and sugar until they spread evenly. Water is added and the cup is stirred. What should happen next?
options: The salt and sugar will spread evenly, making a solution.
The salt and sugar will stay separate, making a non-uniform mixture.
Only the salt will dissolve, while the sugar stays at the bottom.
The water will become the solute because the cup is stirred.

why.The salt and sugar will stay separate, m: This mistake assumes adding water will stop the salt and sugar spreading.
why.Only the salt will dissolve, while the s: This mistake assumes only one solid can spread through the water.
why.The water will become the solute because: This mistake swaps the solvent and solute roles in a solution.

activities.explanation: Salt and sugar in water form a uniform mixture, which is a solution.

activities.prompt: A child mixes sawdust and water, and the parts do not spread evenly. Can the water be called the solvent in this mixture?
options: No, because sawdust and water do not form a solution.
Yes, because water is the liquid in this mixture.
Yes, because every liquid is the solvent in a mixture.
No, because sawdust is the larger part of the mixture.

why.Yes, because water is the liquid in this: This mistake mistakes a non-uniform mixture for a solid and liquid solution.
why.Yes, because every liquid is the solvent: This mistake wrongly thinks every liquid in a mixture is its solvent.
why.No, because sawdust is the larger part o: This mistake uses amount instead of checking whether a solution forms.

activities.explanation: No solution forms, so the solvent rule does not apply.

lessons.title: Lesson 2: Solubility, Saturation and Temperature

activities.prompt: How does temperature change what dissolves in water?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: Dissolving Salt in Water
activities.body: Salt dissolves in water to form a solution. If you add too much salt, some settles at the bottom. The water has reached its limit. This is a saturated solution. An unsaturated solution can dissolve more solute. Concentration shows how much solute is in a fixed amount of solution. Solubility is the maximum amount that dissolves. Water at 70 °C dissolves more baking soda than water at 50 °C.
keyPoints: Saturation means no more solute dissolves, and extra solute settles.
An unsaturated solution can dissolve more solute.
Solubility is the maximum amount of solute that dissolves in a fixed quantity.
activities.explanation: These ideas help you understand how much salt water can dissolve.

activities.prompt: Why does extra salt settle at the bottom after the water has dissolved enough?
steps: First, salt dissolves completely in water and forms a solution.
Then, adding more salt gives the water more solute to dissolve.
Water has a limit, so it cannot dissolve all the extra salt.
Therefore, undissolved salt settles, and the solution becomes saturated.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.title: Comparing Concentration and Solubility
activities.body: Concentration tells you how much solute is present in a fixed amount of solution. A dilute solution has less solute. A concentrated solution has more solute. These words need each other for comparison. Solubility is the maximum amount of solute that dissolves in a fixed quantity. Water at 70 °C dissolves more baking soda than water at 50 °C. Most substances become more soluble as temperature rises.
keyPoints: Concentration compares how much solute a solution contains.
Dilute and concentrated need each other for comparison.
Most substances become more soluble as temperature rises.
activities.explanation: Concentration compares solutions, while solubility describes the maximum amount dissolved.

activities.prompt: What forms when salt dissolves completely in water?
options: a salt pile
a solution
a separate solid
an empty container
activities.explanation: Dissolved salt and water form a solution.

activities.prompt: Salt and water together form a ______.
activities.hint: It forms when salt dissolves completely.
activities.explanation: A solution forms when salt dissolves completely in water.

activities.prompt: At a given temperature, an unsaturated solution can dissolve more solute.
activities.explanation: An unsaturated solution has room to dissolve more solute.

activities.prompt: Match each solution description to its name.
activities.explanation: Each description shows the limit or amount of dissolved solute.

activities.prompt: Which water dissolves more baking soda?
options: Water at 70 °C
Water at 50 °C
Both waters dissolve the same amount
Neither water dissolves baking soda
activities.explanation: Water at 70 °C dissolves more baking soda than water at 50 °C.

activities.prompt: Put the stages of adding salt to water in order.
activities.explanation: Extra salt remains undissolved after the water reaches its limit.

activities.prompt: A solution can still dissolve more solute at a given temperature. A child adds more solute. What should happen?
options: The added solute should dissolve.
The added solute should settle immediately.
The solution should stop dissolving any solute.
The solution should become less concentrated.

why.The added solute should settle immediate: This assumes the solution has already reached its limit.
why.The solution should stop dissolving any: This describes saturation, but the solution is unsaturated.
why.The solution should become less concentr: Adding solute does not remove the solute already present.

activities.explanation: This is right because an unsaturated solution can dissolve more solute.

activities.prompt: Salt has dissolved until no more can dissolve. Some extra salt settles at the bottom. What does this solution contain?
options: A saturated solution and undissolved salt.
An unsaturated solution and undissolved salt.
A dilute solution and undissolved salt.
A saturated solution and undissolved water.

why.An unsaturated solution and undissolved: Unsaturated means more solute can still dissolve.
Dilute describes less solute, not what settles.
why.A saturated solution and undissolved wat: Water does not settle here; the solute is undissolved salt.

activities.explanation: This is right because dissolution stopped and extra salt settled.

activities.prompt: Two glasses contain the same amount of solution. One has less solute than the other. How should the glasses be compared?
options: The less-solute glass is dilute beside the more-solute glass.
The less-solute glass is concentrated beside the more-solute glass.
Both glasses are dilute because each contains some solute.
Both glasses are concentrated because each contains some solute.

why.The less-solute glass is concentrated be: This reverses the meanings of dilute and concentrated.
why.Both glasses are dilute because each con: Some solute in each glass does not make both solutions dilute.
why.Both glasses are concentrated because ea: Some solute in each glass does not make both solutions concentrated.

activities.explanation: This is right because dilute has less solute than the other.

activities.prompt: A child says, “The solubility of salt is the amount already dissolved in this glass.” What is the flaw?
options: It uses the current amount instead of the maximum amount.
It uses the settled amount instead of the maximum amount.
It uses the water amount instead of the maximum solute amount.
It uses the solution amount instead of the maximum solute amount.

why.It uses the settled amount instead of th: This confuses undissolved solute with the maximum that can dissolve.
why.It uses the water amount instead of the: This confuses the water with the solute whose amount matters.
why.It uses the solution amount instead of t: This confuses the whole solution with the solute whose amount matters.

activities.explanation: This is right because solubility means the maximum amount that dissolves.

lessons.sceneCaption: Salt crystals grown in a saturated salt solution.

lessons.title: Lesson 3: Gases Dissolving in Water

activities.prompt: How do gases hide inside water?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: Gases in Water
activities.body: Many gases, including oxygen, dissolve in water. Oxygen dissolves only a little. Dissolved oxygen helps aquatic life to survive. The gas mixture in water is uniform because the gases dissolve evenly. Gas solubility usually falls when temperature rises. Cold water can hold more oxygen. In a solution, the components cannot be seen separately. A non-uniform mixture has visible parts.
keyPoints: Oxygen dissolves in water to a small extent.
Cold water can hold more oxygen.
Solutions have components that cannot be seen separately.
activities.explanation: Even dissolving and temperature help explain what water can hold.

activities.prompt: An aquarium's water is warmed. Why might aquatic life receive less dissolved oxygen?
steps: The aquarium's water becomes warmer.
Gas solubility generally decreases as temperature increases.
Cold water can dissolve more oxygen than warm water.
Therefore, less dissolved oxygen is available to sustain aquatic life.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.prompt: Which gas dissolves in water?
options: Oxygen
Sawdust
Sand
Water
activities.explanation: Many gases dissolve in water, including oxygen.

activities.prompt: Cold water can dissolve more ______ than warmer water.
activities.hint: Think about the gas that helps aquatic life.
activities.explanation: More oxygen can dissolve in cold water.

activities.prompt: Match each part of the lesson with its correct description.
activities.explanation: Each pair matches a fact about gases, mixtures, or objects in water.

activities.prompt: Why is the mixture of gases in water uniform?
options: Because the gases dissolve evenly
Because sawdust floats above it
Because sand sinks below it
Because oxygen dissolves greatly
activities.explanation: The mixture is uniform because the gases dissolve evenly.

activities.prompt: Put this temperature-and-solubility sequence in order.
activities.explanation: Gas solubility generally decreases as temperature increases.

activities.prompt: A solution and a non-uniform mixture are compared. Which components can be seen separately?
options: Components in the solution
Components in the mixture
Components in both samples
Components in neither sample
activities.explanation: Solution components cannot be seen separately. Non-uniform mixture components can be seen separately.

activities.prompt: Many gases dissolve in water, including oxygen. Cold and warm water are compared. Which can dissolve more oxygen?
options: The cold water can dissolve more oxygen.
The warm water can dissolve more oxygen.
Both waters can dissolve exactly the same oxygen.
Only warm water can dissolve any oxygen.

This reverses the effect of higher temperature on solubility.
why.Both waters can dissolve exactly the sam: This ignores that solubility generally decreases as temperature rises.
This wrongly suggests that warm water cannot dissolve oxygen.

activities.explanation: Cold water can dissolve more oxygen, so this is right.

activities.prompt: A gas dissolves evenly in water. What will a child see?
options: An even mixture with no separate visible parts.
A visible gas layer floating on top.
A visible gas layer resting below.
Many tiny gas pieces inside the water.

This wrongly assumes the dissolved gas stays in a separate layer.
This wrongly assumes the dissolved gas gathers into a lower layer.
This wrongly assumes dissolved gas can be seen as separate pieces.

activities.explanation: The gases dissolve evenly, and their parts cannot be seen separately.

activities.prompt: Sawdust and sand are placed in water. Where will each material settle?
options: Sawdust stays above the sand.
Sand stays above the sawdust.
Both materials sink below the water.
Both materials float above the water.

This swaps the positions of floating sawdust and sinking sand.
This wrongly treats floating sawdust as if it were sand.
This wrongly treats sinking sand as if it were sawdust.

activities.explanation: Sawdust floats while sand sinks, so this arrangement is right.

activities.prompt: A pond's water becomes warmer than usual. What happens to its dissolved oxygen?
options: Less oxygen can dissolve, making aquatic life harder to sustain.
More oxygen can dissolve, making aquatic life easier to sustain.
Less oxygen can dissolve, making aquatic life easier to sustain.
More oxygen can dissolve, making aquatic life harder to sustain.

why.More oxygen can dissolve, making aquatic: This reverses the effect of higher temperature on gas solubility.
why.Less oxygen can dissolve, making aquatic: This mixes lower oxygen with the wrong effect on aquatic life.
why.More oxygen can dissolve, making aquatic: This mixes more oxygen with the wrong effect on aquatic life.

activities.explanation: Higher temperature lowers solubility, so less oxygen can support aquatic life.

activities.prompt: A child wants to test if temperature changes oxygen solubility. Which comparison is fair?
options: Compare cold water and warm water, keeping other things the same.
Compare cold water and warm water, while changing other things in both.
Compare two cold waters, while changing other things in both.
Compare two warm waters, while changing other things in both.

why.Compare cold water and warm water, while: Changing extra factors hides the effect of temperature.
why.Compare two cold waters, while changing: Comparing two cold waters does not test different temperatures.
why.Compare two warm waters, while changing: Comparing two warm waters does not test different temperatures.

activities.explanation: Keeping other things the same shows temperature's effect, so this is right.

activities.prompt: Gas dissolves in one bowl of water. Sawdust is placed in another. What can a child see in each bowl?
options: The first bowl looks even; sawdust stays visibly separate in the second.
The first bowl stays separate; the second bowl cannot be seen.
Both bowls look even, with no visible parts in either bowl.
Both bowls show visible parts, including the dissolved gas.

why.The first bowl stays separate; the secon: This wrongly treats dissolved gas as separate and sawdust as invisible.
why.Both bowls look even, with no visible pa: This wrongly treats the sawdust and water mixture as even.
why.Both bowls show visible parts, including: This wrongly assumes dissolved gas components can be seen separately.

activities.explanation: Dissolved gas parts cannot be seen, but sawdust remains visibly separate.

lessons.title: Lesson 4: Floating, Sinking and Density

activities.prompt: What makes some objects float while others sink in water?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: Floating, Sinking and Density
activities.body: Some objects float in water, while others sink. Husk particles float when rice is washed, but rice sinks to the bottom. Oil also floats on water. Density describes how much mass is packed into a unit volume. Objects that float are lighter than the liquid. Objects that sink are heavier than the liquid. Density is not the only factor that decides floating or sinking.
keyPoints: Some objects float, while others sink.
Density describes the mass in a unit volume.
Density is not the only factor affecting floating and sinking.
activities.explanation: You can use density to understand why some things float or sink.

activities.title: Float or sink?

tasks.then: It is now denser than water, so it sinks.

activities.takeaway: Things lighter than water for their size float; denser things sink.
activities.explanation: Things lighter than water for their size float; denser things sink.

activities.prompt: Why do rice husk particles float while rice sinks during washing?
steps: Rice husk particles are lighter than water, so they float.
Rice is heavier than water, so it sinks.
This difference shows how density describes heaviness.
During washing, floating husk particles separate from sinking rice.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.title: What Density Means
activities.body: Density is the mass present in a unit volume of a substance. It describes heaviness. A crowded bus has high density because many people are packed together. A bus with only a few people has low density. A forest with trees growing close together is called a dense forest. Density is not the only factor that decides whether an object floats or sinks.
keyPoints: Density is mass in a unit volume.
Crowded places can have high density.
A dense forest has trees growing close together.
activities.explanation: Density helps us describe how much mass is packed into a space.

activities.title: Washing Rice
activities.prompt: What happens to rice during washing?
options: Rice sinks to the bottom.
Rice stays above the water.
Rice changes into husk.
Rice dissolves in the water.
activities.explanation: Rice sinks to the bottom, while husk particles float on the surface.

activities.title: Oil and Water
activities.prompt: Oil sinks to the bottom when it is mixed with water.
activities.explanation: Oil floats on water when the two are mixed.

activities.title: Objects That Float
activities.prompt: Objects that float in a liquid are ______ than that liquid.
activities.hint: Use the opposite of heavier.
activities.explanation: Objects that float in a liquid are lighter than that liquid.

activities.title: High and Low Density
activities.prompt: Which statement is correct?
options: A crowded bus has high density.
A bus with few people has high density.
A dense forest has trees far apart.
A crowded bus has low density.
activities.explanation: Many people packed together give a crowded bus high density.

activities.title: Match Each Example
activities.prompt: Match each example with what happens or happens in the lesson.
activities.explanation: These examples show floating, sinking and high density.

activities.title: The Meaning of Density
activities.prompt: Which sentence gives the meaning of density?
options: It is mass in a unit volume.
It is the volume of an object.
It is the number of people in a bus.
It is the only factor in floating.
activities.explanation: Density is the mass present in a unit volume of a substance.

activities.prompt: Oil and water are mixed. What do you see in the container?
options: Water will stay above the oil in the container.
Water will stay below the oil in the container.
Oil and water will stay mixed at the same level.
Oil and water will form one completely mixed layer.

why.Water will stay above the oil in the con: Oil floats on water when the two are mixed.
why.Oil and water will stay mixed at the sam: It wrongly assumes oil and water remain mixed.
why.Oil and water will form one completely m: It wrongly assumes the two liquids form one layer.

activities.explanation: This reverses the known order of oil and water.

activities.prompt: One object floats in water, and another sinks. How do their weights compare with water?
options: The floating object is lighter; the sinking object is heavier than water.
The floating object is heavier; the sinking object is lighter than water.
Both objects weigh the same compared with the water.
Neither object's weight can be compared with the water.

why.The floating object is heavier; the sink: This reverses the meanings of floating and sinking.
why.Both objects weigh the same compared wit: It ignores how floating and sinking compare with the liquid.
why.Neither object's weight can be compared: It wrongly claims that the comparison is impossible.

activities.explanation: Floating means lighter than the liquid, while sinking means heavier.

activities.prompt: The bus keeps the same size. At noon, only a few people ride. Later, many people are packed inside. What happens to its density?
options: Density becomes higher because more mass is in the same volume.
Density becomes lower because more people make each person lighter.
Density stays the same because the bus keeps the same volume.
Density becomes higher because the bus gains more seats.

why.Density becomes lower because more peopl: This wrongly treats more packed people as lower density.
why.Density stays the same because the bus k: This wrongly ignores the extra mass in the same volume.
why.Density becomes higher because the bus g: This confuses adding passengers with adding seats.

activities.explanation: A crowded bus has more mass packed into the same volume.

lessons.title: Lesson 5: Measuring Mass and Volume

activities.prompt: How can we measure an object’s mass and space to uncover its secrets?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: Mass, Volume and Density
activities.body: Mass tells you the quantity of matter in an object. Volume tells you the space an object occupies. Density is mass in each unit of volume. Find density by measuring mass and volume. The tare or reset button returns the balance to zero. A measuring cylinder shows liquid volume. The curved liquid surface is the meniscus. Read colourless liquid at the meniscus bottom. Cubic metres (m³) is the SI unit of volume.
keyPoints: Mass is the quantity of matter in an object.
Volume is the space occupied by an object.
Density is the mass per unit volume.
activities.explanation: These ideas help you measure and compare objects.

activities.prompt: Two rectangular blocks have different masses. How can a child find which is denser?
steps: Measure each block's mass because density depends on mass.
Multiply each block's length, width and height because this gives volume.
Compare mass with volume because density is mass per unit volume.
The block with greater mass per unit volume has greater density.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.title: Finding Different Shapes' Volume
activities.body: For a cuboid, multiply length, width and height to find volume. For an irregular object, measure the initial water volume. Then measure the final water volume. Subtract the initial volume from the final volume. This gives the irregular object's volume.
keyPoints: A cuboid's volume is length multiplied by width and height.
An irregular object's volume is the change in water volume.
activities.explanation: These are two methods for finding volume.

activities.prompt: What does the tare or reset button do?
options: Shows the volume of liquid
Marks the curved liquid surface
Brings the reading to zero
Finds the mass per unit volume
activities.explanation: This button brings the balance reading to zero.

activities.prompt: Match each term with its correct meaning.
pairs: Quantity of matter present in an object
Mass per unit volume of a substance
activities.explanation: Each term is paired with its matching meaning.

activities.prompt: Density is the mass per ______ volume of a substance.
activities.hint: This means you measure mass for each part of the space occupied.
activities.explanation: Density compares mass with each unit of volume.

activities.prompt: Which method gives the volume of an irregular object?
options: Multiply length, width and height together
Subtract initial water volume from final volume
Divide object mass by unit volume
Add object mass to initial water volume
activities.explanation: The irregular object's volume is the final volume minus the initial volume.

activities.prompt: Put the steps for finding a cuboid's volume in order.
activities.explanation: The multiplication rule gives a cuboid's volume.

activities.prompt: Which calculation gives an object's density?
options: Unit volume divided by object mass
Object mass divided by unit volume
Object mass added to unit volume
Object mass multiplied by unit volume
activities.explanation: Density compares mass with unit volume.

activities.prompt: A child is using a balance to measure an object. The balance shows a non-zero reading before the object is added. What should the child do first?
options: Use the reset button to bring the reading to zero.
Add the object and keep the old reading.
Measure the object's volume before resetting.
Change the unit used for the balance reading.

The old reading would remain in the measured result.
why.Measure the object's volume before reset: Measuring volume does not bring the balance reading to zero.
why.Change the unit used for the balance rea: Changing the unit leaves the non-zero reading unchanged.

activities.explanation: The reset button brings the balance reading to zero.

activities.prompt: A pebble is fully placed in water in a measuring cylinder. The water level rises. How is the pebble's volume found?
options: Subtract initial water volume from final water volume.
Add initial water volume to final water volume.
Use final water volume without subtracting anything.
Use initial water volume without subtracting anything.

why.Add initial water volume to final water: Adding the initial volume does not isolate the pebble's volume.
why.Use final water volume without subtracti: The final volume includes the water and the pebble together.
why.Use initial water volume without subtrac: The initial volume does not include the space taken by the pebble.

activities.explanation: Subtracting the initial volume leaves the space taken by the pebble.

activities.prompt: One block has more mass and more volume than another block. What can the child conclude about their densities?
options: Their densities cannot be compared from this information alone.
The heavier block must have the greater density.
The lighter block must have the greater density.
Both blocks must have the same density.

why.The heavier block must have the greater: The child is using total mass instead of mass per unit volume.
why.The lighter block must have the greater: The child is using total mass instead of mass per unit volume.
Equal density does not require equal masses or equal volumes.

activities.explanation: Density depends on mass per unit volume, so both values are needed.

activities.prompt: Two samples have equal volumes, but one sample has more mass. What is the correct conclusion?
options: It has greater density because its mass is greater.
It has lower density because its mass is greater.
Both have equal density because their volumes match.
Density cannot be compared because their volumes match.

why.It has lower density because its mass is: Greater mass gives greater density, not lower density.
why.Both have equal density because their vo: Equal volumes do not make density equal when masses differ.
why.Density cannot be compared because their: Equal volumes do not prevent their densities from being compared.

activities.explanation: With equal volumes, the greater mass gives greater density.

lessons.title: Lesson 6: How Temperature and Pressure Affect Density

activities.prompt: What makes substances change density when they get hot or squeezed?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: Temperature, Pressure, and Density
activities.body: Density tells you how much matter is packed into a space. Heating usually makes particles move away and spread out. Volume increases while mass stays the same, so density decreases. Cooling reverses this for most substances. Pressure pushes gas particles closer, so gas volume falls and density rises. Pressure changes liquid density only a little, and solids even less. Water reaches its highest density at 4 °C.
keyPoints: Heating usually lowers density.
Cooling usually raises density.
Pressure strongly affects gas density.
Liquid density changes only a little with pressure.
Water reaches its highest density at 4 °C.
activities.explanation: This connects particle spacing, volume, mass, density, and pressure.

activities.prompt: A block is heated and then cooled. How does its density change?
steps: Heating makes the particles move away and spread out.
This makes the block's volume increase while its mass stays unchanged.
More volume with the same mass means the density decreases.
Cooling makes the density increase again, so the cool block is denser.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.prompt: What usually happens to the density of most substances when they are heated?
options: It decreases.
It increases.
It stays the same.
It becomes zero.
activities.explanation: Heating makes most substances less dense. You spotted the usual change.

activities.prompt: When a substance is heated, its particles tend to move away and ______ out.
activities.hint: Particles have more space between them.
activities.explanation: Exactly. The particles move away and spread out when heated.

activities.prompt: Match each change with its effect.
activities.explanation: You matched each change with its effect. Gas particles move closer as pressure rises.

activities.prompt: A gas experiences increased pressure. What happens to its particles and volume?
options: Particles move closer; volume decreases.
Particles move farther; volume increases.
Particles move closer; volume increases.
Particles stay still; volume increases.
activities.explanation: Yes. Closer particles occupy less space, so the gas volume falls.

activities.prompt: Put the changes caused by heating in order.
items: Particles move away and spread out.
activities.explanation: The changes follow in a clear chain. Heating leads to a larger volume and lower density.

activities.prompt: Which statement correctly describes water and ice?
options: Ice is lighter than liquid water; water reaches its maximum density at 4 °C.
Ice is denser than liquid water; water reaches its maximum density when frozen.
Ice has the same density as liquid water; pressure affects liquid density more strongly.
Ice is lighter than liquid water; water reaches its maximum density when frozen.
activities.explanation: Ice floats because it is lighter than liquid water. Water has its highest density at 4 °C.

activities.prompt: A child heats the same amount of material. What happens to its density?
options: Its density falls because its volume grows.
Its density rises because its volume grows.
Its density falls because its mass grows.
Its density stays same because particles move closer.

why.Its density rises because its volume gro: The child confuses volume increasing with density increasing.
why.Its density falls because its mass grows: The child wrongly thinks heating adds mass.
why.Its density stays same because particles: Heating makes particles move away, not closer.

activities.explanation: Heating increases volume without changing mass, so density decreases.

activities.prompt: Gas is pressed into a small space. What happens to its density?
options: Its density falls as its volume falls.
Its density stays same as particles spread out.
Its density rises as its volume falls.
Its density rises as its volume grows.

The child thinks lower volume must mean lower density.
why.Its density stays same as particles spre: The child wrongly says pressing makes particles spread out.
The child reverses the volume change caused by pressure.

activities.explanation: Pressure moves particles closer, lowering volume and raising density.

activities.prompt: Which test best compares how pressure affects liquids and solids?
options: Press both kinds equally and compare their density changes.
Press only the liquid and compare its density change.
Press both kinds unequally and compare their density changes.
Heat both kinds equally and compare their density changes.

why.Press only the liquid and compare its de: This test cannot compare liquids with solids.
why.Press both kinds unequally and compare t: Different pressures make the comparison unfair.
why.Heat both kinds equally and compare thei: Heating tests temperature, not the effect of pressure.

activities.explanation: Equal pressure is fair, and solids change less than liquids.

activities.prompt:
Assertion (A): In a solution of salt and water, salt is the solute.
Reason (R): Salt dissolves in the water and forms a solution.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.
activities.explanation: Both statements are true, and dissolving salt in water explains why salt is the solute.

activities.prompt:
Assertion (A): A mixture of sawdust and water is a solution.
Reason (R): The mixture of sawdust and water is non-uniform.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.
activities.explanation: The assertion is false, but the reason is true because a non-uniform mixture is not a solution.

activities.prompt: Explain how a uniform mixture of salt or sugar with water is different from a mixture of sawdust and water. Identify the solute and solvent when the mixture is a solution.
activities.answer: A salt-or-sugar mixture with water is a solution when the solid is evenly spread throughout the liquid. In that case, the solid is the solute and the liquid is the solvent. The solute dissolves in the solvent and forms the solution. A sawdust-and-water mixture is different because it is non-uniform: its components are not evenly spread. Therefore, it should not be called a solution. Uniformity, rather than simply having both a solid and a liquid present, decides whether the mixture is a solution.
points: Identifies an evenly spread mixture as a solution.
Names the solid as the solute.
Names the liquid as the solvent.
Explains that sawdust and water form a non-uniform mixture.
activities.explanation: Compare your answer with the points a marker looks for.

activities.context: A student pours water into a beaker and adds salt. At first, all the salt dissolves, so the mixture is a solution. When she adds still more salt, some salt remains undissolved and settles at the bottom. She then heats fresh water to 70 °C and finds that it dissolves more baking soda than water at 50 °C.
activities.prompt: What does the salt settling at the bottom of the beaker show?
options: The water has reached its limit for dissolving salt.
The solution is unsaturated because the salt is still visible.
The mixture contains less solute than any other salt solution.
The extra salt is helping make the solution concentrated.

why.The solution is unsaturated because the: Visible salt does not mean that more can still dissolve.
why.The mixture contains less solute than an: Undissolved salt does not determine the comparison.
why.The extra salt is helping make the solut: Concentration depends on the solute dissolved in the solution.

activities.explanation: Settling salt shows that the water cannot dissolve more.

activities.context: A student pours water into a beaker and adds salt. At first, all the salt dissolves, so the mixture is a solution. When she adds still more salt, some salt remains undissolved and settles at the bottom. She then heats fresh water to 70 °C and finds that it dissolves more baking soda than water at 50 °C.
activities.prompt: Before any salt settles, what will happen if the student adds more salt to the unsaturated solution?
options: The extra salt dissolves until the water reaches its limit.
All the extra salt must settle immediately.
The solution becomes dilute because more salt enters it.
The solution is saturated even before any more salt is added.

why.All the extra salt must settle immediate: Settling begins only after the limit is reached.
why.The solution becomes dilute because more: Adding more dissolved solute does not make a solution dilute.
why.The solution is saturated even before an: A solution is not saturated while it can still dissolve more.

activities.explanation: An unsaturated solution can dissolve more solute.

activities.prompt:
Assertion (A): A solution can be described as saturated when undissolved solute has settled.
Reason (R): The water has reached the limit of how much solute it can dissolve.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.
activities.explanation: The settled solute shows that the water has reached its dissolving limit.

activities.prompt:
Assertion (A): A dilute solution must contain the maximum amount of solute that can dissolve.
Reason (R): Dilute and concentrated are judged relative to another solution.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.
activities.explanation: A dilute solution contains less solute rather than the maximum amount.

activities.prompt: Explain the difference between a saturated and an unsaturated solution, and state what happens when more salt is added to each.
activities.answer: A saturated solution has reached the water's limit for dissolving solute at a given temperature. Once more salt is added, the extra salt cannot dissolve and settles at the bottom. An unsaturated solution has not reached that limit, so it can dissolve more solute at that temperature. If enough salt is added to an unsaturated solution, it may become saturated, and any further salt will remain undissolved and settle.
points: A saturated solution has reached the limit.
An unsaturated solution can dissolve more solute.
Undissolved salt settles after the limit is reached.
Adding enough salt can change an unsaturated solution into a saturated one.
activities.explanation: Compare your answer with the points a marker looks for.

activities.context: A learner visits a school pond and sees aquatic life in the water. She explains that dissolved oxygen helps sustain this life, even though oxygen dissolves only to a small extent. She says the mixture of gases in water is uniform because the gases dissolve evenly. After warming a sample of pond water, she notes that gas solubility generally decreases. She then cools it, so more oxygen can dissolve.
activities.prompt: The learner cools the warmed sample of pond water. What should she expect next?
options: The water can hold a greater amount of dissolved oxygen.
The water can hold less dissolved oxygen.
The amount of dissolved oxygen will remain exactly unchanged.
The water will hold an unlimited amount of dissolved oxygen.

why.The water can hold less dissolved oxygen: This reverses the stated relationship between temperature and gas solubility.
why.The amount of dissolved oxygen will rema: The stated solubility trend predicts a change when the water is cooled.
why.The water will hold an unlimited amount: Cold water still dissolves oxygen only to a small extent, not an unlimited amount.

activities.explanation: Cooling allows more oxygen to dissolve because gas solubility generally falls as temperature rises.

activities.context: A learner visits a school pond and sees aquatic life in the water. She explains that dissolved oxygen helps sustain this life, even though oxygen dissolves only to a small extent. She says the mixture of gases in water is uniform because the gases dissolve evenly. After warming a sample of pond water, she notes that gas solubility generally decreases. She then cools it, so more oxygen can dissolve.
activities.prompt: If the learner keeps warming the pond water, what should she expect next?
options: Less gas will generally dissolve, so dissolved oxygen may decrease.
More gas will generally dissolve, so dissolved oxygen may increase.
Gas solubility will remain unchanged as the water warms.
Less gas will generally dissolve, so dissolved oxygen may increase.

why.More gas will generally dissolve, so dis: This reverses the stated effect of increasing temperature on gas solubility.
why.Gas solubility will remain unchanged as: The case states that gas solubility generally decreases when water is warmed.
why.Less gas will generally dissolve, so dis: A decrease in solubility does not support a greater dissolved amount of oxygen.

activities.explanation: Gas solubility generally decreases as temperature rises, so less oxygen can remain dissolved.

activities.prompt:
Assertion (A): More oxygen can dissolve in cold water than in warmer water.
Reason (R): The solubility of gases generally decreases as temperature increases.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.
activities.explanation: The decrease in gas solubility at higher temperatures explains why cold water can dissolve more oxygen.

activities.prompt:
Assertion (A): The components of a solution cannot be seen separately.
Reason (R): A mixture of gases dissolved in water is non-uniform.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.
activities.explanation: The assertion is true, but gases dissolved evenly in water form a uniform mixture rather than a non-uniform one.

activities.prompt: Explain how temperature affects the amount of gas that dissolves in water.
activities.answer: The solubility of gases generally decreases when the temperature of water increases. This means that, as the water becomes warmer, less gas can generally dissolve in it. When the water is cooled, the opposite happens, so more oxygen can dissolve. Oxygen dissolves in water only to a small extent, but the dissolved oxygen helps to sustain aquatic life. Therefore, temperature can affect how much oxygen is available in the water.
points: Solubility generally decreases as temperature rises.
Warmer water can generally dissolve less gas.
Cooling allows more oxygen to dissolve.
Dissolved oxygen supports aquatic life.
activities.explanation: Compare your answer with the points a marker looks for.

activities.context: During a science activity, the student washed rice in a container. The student noticed that husk particles stayed at the surface while the rice grains collected at the bottom. Later, the student mixed oil and water in another container. The oil formed a layer above the water.
activities.prompt: What would most likely happen if the student added more rice grains to the washing water?
options: The extra grains would settle near the bottom with the other rice grains.
Most of the extra grains would remain at the surface with the husk particles.
The extra grains would stay evenly spread through the water.
The extra grains would rise above the container.

why.Most of the extra grains would remain at: Husk particles are lighter than water, so they remain at the surface.
why.The extra grains would stay evenly sprea: Even spreading is not expected because the grains sink.
why.The extra grains would rise above the co: Rice grains do not rise above the container.

activities.explanation: Rice grains are heavier than water, so they sink.

activities.context: During a science activity, the student washed rice in a container. The student noticed that husk particles stayed at the surface while the rice grains collected at the bottom. Later, the student mixed oil and water in another container. The oil formed a layer above the water.
activities.prompt: Why did the husk particles float while the rice grains sank?
options: The rice grains were heavier than water, while the husk particles were lighter.
The rice grains were lighter than water, while the husk particles were heavier.
Both the rice grains and husk particles were heavier than water.
Both the rice grains and husk particles were lighter than water.

why.The rice grains were lighter than water,: Sinking objects are heavier than the liquid.
why.Both the rice grains and husk particles: Husk particles float, so this option is incorrect.
Rice grains sink, so this option is incorrect.

activities.explanation: Floating objects are lighter than the liquid.

activities.context: During a science activity, the student washed rice in a container. The student noticed that husk particles stayed at the surface while the rice grains collected at the bottom. Later, the student mixed oil and water in another container. The oil formed a layer above the water.
activities.prompt: Why did the oil form a layer above the water?
options: Oil is lighter than water, so it floats above it.
Oil is heavier than water, so it stays below it.
Oil and water have the same density, so they mix evenly.
Oil is affected only by being packed closely together.

why.Oil is heavier than water, so it stays b: The result shows that oil does not stay below water.
why.Oil and water have the same density, so: Oil and water do not form evenly mixed layers in this case.
why.Oil is affected only by being packed clo: Packing is related to density but does not explain the oil layer here.

activities.explanation: The floating oil must be lighter than water.

activities.prompt:
Assertion (A): A crowded bus has high density.
Reason (R): Many people are packed together in the bus.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.
activities.explanation: The reason explains the high density because many people are packed into the same space.

activities.prompt:
Assertion (A): Oil forms a layer above water when the two are mixed.
Reason (R): Oil is heavier than water.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.
activities.explanation: The statement is true, but oil floats above water because it is lighter, not heavier.

boss.title: Chapter challenge: Amazing World of Solutes, Solvents, and Solutions

activities.prompt: In a solution of salt and water, what is the solvent?
options: Water
Salt
Sugar
Sand
activities.explanation: Water is the solvent because it dissolves the solid salt.

Volume decreases and density increases

Volume and mass both increase

chapters.title: Light: Mirrors and Lenses
chapters.summary: In this chapter: spherical mirrors and their types; images formed by spherical mirrors; curved mirrors and concentrated light; lenses and their images.

lessons.title: Spherical Mirrors and Their Types

activities.prompt: Why do the two sides of a shiny spoon reflect so differently?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: Meet Spherical Mirrors
activities.body: A spherical mirror is a curved mirror shaped like part of a hollow sphere. It is spherical when its reflecting surface is spherical. A concave mirror curves inwards, while a convex mirror curves outwards. The inner surface of a shiny spoon can form an inverted image. The outer surface forms an erect but smaller image. Spherical mirrors are made by grinding and polishing shaped flat glass.
keyPoints: Spherical mirrors have a spherical reflecting surface.
Concave mirrors curve inwards, while convex mirrors curve outwards.
A shiny spoon can show an inverted image from its inner surface.
activities.explanation: You can spot spherical mirrors by their curved reflecting surfaces.

activities.prompt: How can curved glass become either kind of spherical mirror?
steps: Grinding and polishing shape flat glass into a curved spherical form.
Spherical mirrors can curve inwards or outwards, so two types are possible.
Coating the outer curved surface produces a concave mirror.
Putting coating on the inner curved surface produces a convex mirror.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.prompt: Which statement describes a spherical mirror?
options: It has a flat reflecting surface.
It has a curved reflecting surface.
It has no reflecting surface.
It has a square reflecting surface.
activities.explanation: A spherical mirror is curved like part of a hollow sphere.

activities.prompt: A mirror is spherical when its reflecting surface is spherical.
activities.explanation: Yes. The shape of the reflecting surface gives the mirror its type.

activities.prompt: Match each description with the correct mirror or image.
activities.explanation: Inward curves belong to concave mirrors. Outward curves belong to convex mirrors.

activities.prompt: What image does the outer surface of a shiny spoon form?
options: An erect and smaller image.
An erect and larger image.
An inverted and smaller image.
An inverted and larger image.
activities.explanation: The outer surface forms an image that stays erect but becomes smaller.

activities.prompt: A coating on the outer curved surface produces a convex mirror.
activities.explanation: Not quite. A coating on the outer curved surface produces a concave mirror.

activities.prompt: Which method produces a concave mirror?
options: Coating the outer curved surface
Coating the inner curved surface
Leaving both curved surfaces plain
Polishing the flat surface only
activities.explanation: A reflective coating on the outer curved surface produces a concave mirror.

activities.prompt: A maker has curved glass and wants a concave mirror. Which coating plan works?
options: Coat the outer curved surface.
Coat the inner curved surface.
Grind and polish a flat sheet.
Polish the curved surface without coating.

This coating produces a convex mirror instead.
This shapes glass but does not choose the coated curved surface.
why.Polish the curved surface without coatin: Polishing without coating misses the step that makes the mirror.

activities.explanation: This coating produces a concave mirror.

activities.prompt: Two curved glass pieces are ready. Which test best reveals their mirror types?
options: Coat one inner surface and one outer surface.
Coat both inner surfaces, then compare them.
Coat both outer surfaces, then compare them.
Polish both surfaces, then compare them.

why.Coat both inner surfaces, then compare t: Both inner coatings make convex mirrors, so the test cannot separate them.
why.Coat both outer surfaces, then compare t: Both outer coatings make concave mirrors, so the test cannot separate them.
Polishing shapes the glass but does not set the mirror type.

activities.explanation: Inner coating makes a convex mirror, while outer coating makes a concave one.

lessons.title: Images Formed by Spherical Mirrors

activities.prompt: Why do some mirrors make your reflection look bigger or smaller?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: Mirror Images
activities.body: A concave mirror gives an erect (upright), enlarged image when its object is close. As the object moves farther away, the image becomes smaller. It also becomes inverted (upside down). A convex mirror always gives an erect, smaller image. A plane mirror gives an erect image of the same size. Concave mirrors are used in torch reflectors, vehicle headlights, and dentists' mirrors. Convex side-view mirrors give drivers a wider road view.
keyPoints: Concave mirrors can give erect, enlarged or inverted images.
Convex mirrors always give erect, smaller images.
Plane mirrors give erect images of the same size.
activities.explanation: Each mirror type forms a different kind of image.

activities.prompt: A child looks in a concave mirror, then steps away. What changes?
steps: The close object gives an erect, enlarged image because the mirror is concave.
As the object moves farther away, its image becomes inverted.
The enlarged image also becomes smaller as the object moves away.
Therefore, the image changes with the object's distance from a concave mirror.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.prompt: Which image is always formed by a convex mirror?
options: Erect and smaller
Erect and enlarged
Inverted and enlarged
Inverted and smaller
activities.explanation: A convex mirror always forms an erect image that is smaller than the object.

activities.prompt: A plane mirror forms an erect image of the same size as the object.
activities.explanation: A plane mirror forms an erect image with the same size as the object.

activities.prompt: A dentist uses a ______ mirror to get an enlarged view of teeth.
activities.hint: This mirror can give an enlarged image of a close object.
activities.explanation: A dentist uses a concave mirror to get an enlarged view of teeth.

activities.prompt: Match each mirror with its image property or special view.
activities.explanation: Dentists use concave mirrors, side-view mirrors are convex, and plane mirrors keep the same size.

activities.prompt: Vehicle side-view mirrors show the traffic behind as an inverted image.
activities.explanation: Vehicle side-view mirrors show the traffic behind as an erect image.

activities.prompt: An object moves farther from a concave mirror. What happens to its image?
options: It becomes upright.
It becomes larger.
It stays the same size.
It becomes inverted.
activities.explanation: As the object moves farther away, the concave mirror forms an inverted image.

activities.prompt: Put these events in order as the object moves farther from a concave mirror.
items: Object is close to the mirror
activities.explanation: The close object gives an erect, enlarged image before the image becomes inverted.

activities.prompt: Why are convex mirrors used as vehicle side-view mirrors?
options: A narrow view of the front
A close view of teeth
An enlarged view of a face
A wider view of the road behind
activities.explanation: A convex mirror gives drivers a much wider view of the road behind.

activities.prompt: A tooth is close to a concave mirror. What image appears?
options: An inverted, enlarged image.
An erect, enlarged image.
An erect, smaller image.
An inverted, smaller image.

This mistake uses the farther-away rule while the tooth is close.
This mistake thinks a concave image is always smaller.
This mistake mixes the inverted and smaller results from moving away.

activities.explanation: This is right because a close object gives an erect, enlarged image.

activities.prompt: How should you test distance changes in a concave mirror?
options: Move the object farther away and observe the image.
Cover the image and move the object farther away.
Replace the concave mirror with a convex one.
Keep the object still and make it larger.

why.Cover the image and move the object fart: This mistake hides the result, so the image cannot be watched.
why.Replace the concave mirror with a convex: This mistake changes mirror type, so distance is not tested alone.
why.Keep the object still and make it larger: This mistake changes object size instead of object distance.

activities.explanation: This is right because it changes distance and watches the image.
