lessons.title: Curved Mirrors and Concentrated Light

activities.prompt: Can a curved mirror gather sunshine into a tiny, fiery spot?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: How Curved Mirrors Change Light
activities.body: A spherical mirror's curved surface makes parallel rays converge or diverge. A plane mirror keeps reflected rays parallel. A concave mirror brings rays together, so they converge. A convex mirror makes rays spread apart, so they diverge. Every ray follows reflection laws. Mirrors and lenses can concentrate sunlight at one point. These solar concentrators can ignite paper, heat liquid to make steam, or melt steel.
keyPoints: Concave mirrors converge reflected rays.
Convex mirrors diverge reflected rays.
Concentrated sunlight can produce heat.
activities.explanation: Curved mirrors change whether reflected rays come together or spread apart.

activities.prompt: Why might a concave mirror's concentrated sunlight burn paper?
steps: Parallel sunlight hits the concave mirror.
The curved surface makes the reflected rays converge.
The converging rays concentrate sunlight at one point on the paper.
That concentrated light gives enough heat to ignite the paper.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.title: A Plane Mirror
activities.prompt: What happens to parallel rays after reflecting from a plane mirror?
options: They remain parallel.
They come closer together.
They spread apart.
They focus at one point.
activities.explanation: A plane mirror keeps parallel rays parallel after reflection.

activities.title: A Concave Mirror
activities.prompt: A concave mirror makes reflected rays come closer together.
activities.explanation: Yes. A concave mirror makes reflected rays converge.

activities.title: Rays from a Convex Mirror
activities.prompt: After reflection from a convex mirror, the rays ______ apart.
activities.hint: These rays move away from one another.
activities.explanation: Reflected rays from a convex mirror spread apart and diverge.

activities.title: Sunlight on Paper
activities.prompt: Why can reflected sunlight ignite paper?
options: It concentrates and produces enough heat.
It dims and produces less heat.
It changes colour and stays cool.
It stays parallel and produces no heat.
activities.explanation: Reflected sunlight becomes concentrated. The concentrated light produces enough heat.

activities.title: Match Each Reflection
activities.prompt: Match each mirror or surface to its ray behaviour.
activities.explanation: Concave surfaces bring rays together, while convex surfaces make them spread apart.

activities.title: A Spherical Mirror
activities.prompt: A spherical mirror can make parallel rays converge, but not diverge.
activities.explanation: A spherical mirror can make parallel rays converge or diverge.

activities.title: Uses of Concentrated Sunlight
activities.prompt: Which statement about concentrated sunlight is correct?
options: Concentrated sunlight heats liquid to make steam.
A convex mirror concentrates reflected rays.
A plane mirror spreads reflected rays apart.
Solar furnaces are used to cool steel.
activities.explanation: Concentrated sunlight heats liquid to make steam for electricity. Solar furnaces can melt steel.

activities.title: The Paper Experiment
activities.prompt: Put the steps for concentrating sunlight on paper in order.
items: Reflected sunlight concentrates at one point on paper.
The concentrated light produces enough heat.
activities.explanation: The light concentrates first. Then it produces enough heat to ignite the paper.

activities.prompt: Parallel sunlight hits a concave mirror. What happens to the reflected rays?
options: They stay parallel and do not meet.
They come closer and meet at one point.
They spread farther apart after reflection.
They turn into one single reflected ray.

This is the plane-mirror result, not the concave-mirror result.
why.They spread farther apart after reflecti: The child confuses a convex mirror with a concave mirror.
The child thinks converging rays turn into one ray.

activities.explanation: A concave mirror makes reflected rays come closer and converge.

activities.prompt: Parallel light reflects from a plane mirror. Do its rays then meet?
options: They stay parallel and do not meet.
They come closer and meet at one point.
They spread apart and move away.
They bend into a single bright ray.

The child confuses a plane mirror with a concave mirror.
The child confuses a plane mirror with a convex mirror.
The child thinks parallel rays become one ray.

activities.explanation: A plane mirror keeps reflected rays parallel.

lessons.title: Lenses and Their Images

activities.prompt: Why do lenses make objects look bigger, smaller, or upside down?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: How lenses make images
activities.body: A lens is transparent material with curved surfaces, usually made of glass or plastic. Light passes through it. A concave lens is thicker at its edges than in the middle. A convex lens is also called a converging lens because it brings light rays closer together. Close objects appear erect, or upright, and enlarged. Farther objects appear inverted, or upside down. Concave lens images are always erect and smaller.
keyPoints: Convex lenses bring light rays closer together.
Convex lens images change with distance.
Concave lens images are always erect and smaller.
activities.explanation: Lenses form images as light passes through them.

activities.prompt: A child looks at a small sign through one convex lens. The child first stands close, then steps farther away. How does the image change?
steps: The lens is convex, so it brings light rays closer together.
Near the sign, the image is erect and enlarged.
Farther away, the image becomes inverted and then smaller.
So the image changes from upright and large to inverted and small.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.title: A close object
activities.prompt: What happens when you view an object close to a convex lens?
options: It appears erect and enlarged.
It appears inverted and smaller.
It appears upright and smaller.
It appears upside down and enlarged.
activities.explanation: A close object appears erect and enlarged through a convex lens.

activities.title: Lens shape
activities.prompt: A concave lens is thicker at its edges than in its middle.
activities.explanation: This shape identifies a concave lens.

activities.title: Light through a lens
activities.prompt: Light passes through a lens, unlike a ______.
activities.hint: You can see through one, but not the other.
activities.explanation: A lens allows light to pass through it, unlike a mirror.

activities.title: Match the lenses
activities.prompt: Match each lens idea to the correct choice.
activities.explanation: These pairs connect each lens with its image or another name.

activities.title: Changes with distance
activities.prompt: Put the convex lens observations in order as the object moves farther away.
items: Close object appears erect and enlarged
activities.explanation: A convex image starts enlarged and upright. It later becomes inverted and smaller.

activities.prompt: A child holds a convex lens over a tiny printed word. The word is very close. How does it look?
options: Upright and larger than the word.
Inverted and larger than the word.
Upright and smaller than the word.
Inverted and smaller than the word.

This mixes up the close and far image rules.
This wrongly uses the rule for a concave lens.
This wrongly makes the close image inverted and smaller.

activities.explanation: Close objects form erect, enlarged images with a convex lens.

activities.prompt: A child moves a convex lens far away from a printed word. How does the word then look?
options: Inverted and smaller than the word.
Upright and larger than the word.
Upright and smaller than the word.
Inverted and larger than the word.

It keeps the upright, enlarged image seen up close.
It wrongly treats a convex lens like a concave lens.
It keeps the enlarged size but changes the upright position.

activities.explanation: Farther away, a convex image becomes inverted and then smaller.

activities.prompt: A child looks at a friend through a concave lens. How does the friend look?
options: Upright and smaller than the friend.
Inverted and smaller than the friend.
Upright and larger than the friend.
Inverted and larger than the friend.

It wrongly gives the usual inverted convex image.
It wrongly uses the close convex lens result.
It wrongly gives the distant convex lens result.

activities.explanation: Through a concave lens, objects always look erect and smaller.

activities.prompt: Three straight light rays enter a lens. Which result shows that the lens is convex?
options: The rays come closer together after passing through.
The rays spread farther apart after passing through.
The rays stay exactly parallel after passing through.
The rays stop moving after passing through.

why.The rays spread farther apart after pass: This is the usual effect of a concave lens.
why.The rays stay exactly parallel after pas: A flat glass plate does not make rays converge or diverge.
why.The rays stop moving after passing throu: A lens lets light pass through instead of stopping it.

activities.explanation: A convex lens brings converging light rays closer together.

activities.prompt: A child places a thin flat glass plate in straight light rays. What should happen next?
options: The rays pass through without converging or diverging.
The rays pass through and come closer together.
The rays pass through and spread farther apart.
The rays stop at the glass and do not pass.

why.The rays pass through and come closer to: Coming closer together is the effect of a convex lens.
why.The rays pass through and spread farther: Spreading farther apart is the effect of a concave lens.
why.The rays stop at the glass and do not pa: Light passes through the transparent glass plate.

activities.explanation: A thin flat glass plate does not make light converge or diverge.

activities.prompt: A student says a convex lens always makes objects look enlarged. Which observation proves the claim wrong?
options: Farther away, the image can become inverted and smaller.
Very close, the image can become inverted and smaller.
Through a concave lens, objects can look enlarged.
Through a flat plate, objects can look inverted.

why.Very close, the image can become inverte: Close to a convex lens, the image is erect and enlarged.
why.Through a concave lens, objects can look: A concave lens always makes objects look erect and smaller.
why.Through a flat plate, objects can look i: A flat plate does not make light converge or diverge.

activities.explanation: Farther away, a convex image becomes inverted and then smaller.

lessons.title: Uses of Lenses and Chapter Review

activities.prompt: How do tiny letters, distant stars, and our eyes become easier to see?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: Lenses at Work
activities.body: Lenses have many uses. A magnifying glass makes small letters look bigger. Telescopes and microscopes use lenses to work. The human eye contains a convex lens. A convex lens pulls light beams together. A concave lens pushes them apart. Convex lenses can make images bigger, smaller or the same size. Concave lenses always make images that stand upright and are smaller.
keyPoints: A magnifying glass makes small letters look bigger
Telescopes and microscopes use lenses
Convex lenses join light beams, while concave lenses spread them apart
activities.explanation: These uses show how lenses help people see and study.

activities.prompt: How do the eye and magnifying glass help with tiny print?
steps: A magnifying glass makes tiny letters look bigger, so reading becomes easier.
The eye contains a convex lens, so it also helps us see.
The eye’s convex lens converges light, while the magnifying glass enlarges letters.
Therefore, different lenses help us see in different ways.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.title: The Magnifying Glass
activities.prompt: Which statement about a magnifying glass is correct?
options: It makes small letters look bigger.
It makes small letters look smaller.
It makes small letters look clearer.
It makes small letters look wider.
activities.explanation: A magnifying glass makes small letters look bigger.

activities.title: A Concave Mirror
activities.prompt: A concave mirror always forms an image that is erect and diminished.
activities.explanation: A concave mirror can make images enlarged, diminished or the same size.

activities.title: Lenses and Their Uses
activities.prompt: Match each item with its use or feature.
activities.explanation: Each pair shows a use or feature given in the lesson.

activities.title: Images from a Concave Lens
activities.prompt: What does a concave lens always do to an image?
options: It makes an erect, diminished image.
It makes an enlarged, erect image.
It makes an inverted, enlarged image.
It makes a same-sized, erect image.
activities.explanation: A concave lens always forms an erect and diminished image.

activities.title: The Reflection Rule
activities.prompt: In every reflection, the angle of ______ always equals the angle of reflection.
activities.hint: Choose the angle named before the equals sign.
activities.explanation: The reflection rule states that the two angles are always equal.

activities.title: Observing the Stars
activities.prompt: Put the astronomers’ steps in the correct order.
items: Measure the positions of the stars and planets.
activities.explanation: The positions were measured from the reflected images.

activities.prompt: A convex mirror shows a small, erect image. Which lens does too?
options: a convex mirror
a concave lens
a convex lens
a concave mirror

why.a convex mirror: This is a mirror, but the question asks for a lens.
why.a convex lens: Convex lenses can form enlarged or same-sized images.
why.a concave mirror: This is a mirror, but the question asks for a lens.

activities.explanation: Concave lenses always form erect, diminished images.

activities.prompt: A child claims a convex mirror can enlarge an image. Which observation proves the claim wrong?
options: The image stays upright but becomes smaller.
The image stays upright but becomes larger.
The image becomes larger and upside down.
The image becomes smaller and upside down.

why.The image stays upright but becomes larg: This wrongly allows an enlarged image from a convex mirror.
why.The image becomes larger and upside down: This wrongly allows both enlarged and upside-down images.
why.The image becomes smaller and upside dow: The upside-down part is wrong for a convex mirror.

activities.explanation: Convex mirrors always form erect, diminished images.

activities.prompt: A concave lens shows a printed page. Which observation fits this lens?
options: The words stay upright but look smaller.
The words stay upright but look larger.
The words turn upside down but look smaller.
The words turn upside down but look larger.

This wrongly gives the concave lens an enlarged image.
why.The words turn upside down but look smal: Concave lens images always stay upright.
why.The words turn upside down but look larg: This wrongly gives the image both larger size and wrong direction.

activities.explanation: Concave lenses always form images that are upright and smaller.

activities.context: A student cleans a shiny spoon. The student notices that the polished hollow side shows an upside-down picture, while the polished outside gives an upright picture that looks reduced. A mirror maker grinds and polishes flat glass and then coats the outside of its hollow curve, making a mirror that bends toward the middle. The maker wonders what would happen if the coating were placed on the other curved side instead.
activities.prompt: If the maker places the reflective coating on the inner curved surface of the shaped glass, what kind of mirror results?
options: A convex mirror.
A concave mirror.
A concave mirror made by coating the inner curved surface.
A convex mirror made by coating the outer curved surface.

That result comes from coating the outer curved surface.
why.A concave mirror made by coating the inn: The inner-coating rule gives a convex mirror, not a concave mirror.
why.A convex mirror made by coating the oute: The outer-coating rule gives a concave mirror, not a convex mirror.

activities.explanation: Coating the inner curved surface produces a convex mirror.

activities.context: A student cleans a shiny spoon. The student notices that the polished hollow side shows an upside-down picture, while the polished outside gives an upright picture that looks reduced. A mirror maker grinds and polishes flat glass and then coats the outside of its hollow curve, making a mirror that bends toward the middle. The maker wonders what would happen if the coating were placed on the other curved side instead.
activities.prompt: What feature places the mirror made by the maker in the concave group?
options: Its reflecting surface has an inward curve.
Its reflecting surface has an outward curve.
Its reflecting surface has no curved shape.
Its reflecting surface curves in both directions at once.

why.Its reflecting surface has an outward cu: An outward curve describes a convex mirror.
why.Its reflecting surface has no curved sha: A spherical mirror has a curved reflecting surface, not a flat one.
why.Its reflecting surface curves in both di: This matches neither of the inward and outward curvature directions.

activities.explanation: A concave mirror has a reflecting surface that curves inwards.

activities.prompt:
Assertion (A): A reflective coating on the outer curved surface produces a concave mirror.
Reason (R): The reflecting surface of a concave mirror curves inwards.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.
activities.explanation: Both statements are true, and the inward curve identifies the reflective surface of the mirror produced by outer-side coating.

activities.prompt: Explain the difference between a concave mirror and a convex mirror.
activities.answer: A concave mirror and a convex mirror are both spherical mirrors because their reflecting surfaces are spherical. Their main difference is the direction in which the reflecting surface curves. A concave mirror curves inwards, whereas a convex mirror curves outwards. The place of the reflective coating is also important: coating the outer curved surface produces a concave mirror, and coating the inner curved surface produces a convex mirror. Therefore, the reflective surface and coating position determine which of these two mirror types is made.
points: Both are spherical mirrors.
A concave reflecting surface curves inwards.
A convex reflecting surface curves outwards.
Outer-side coating produces a concave mirror, while inner-side coating produces a convex mirror.
activities.explanation: Compare your answer with the points a marker looks for.

activities.prompt:
Assertion (A): A dentist can obtain an enlarged view of teeth by using a concave mirror close to the teeth.
Reason (R): A concave mirror gives an erect, enlarged image when the object is close to it.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.
activities.explanation: The reason directly explains how the concave mirror enlarges the close view of the teeth.

activities.prompt: Explain how the image formed by a concave mirror changes as a close object is moved farther away, and compare it with the image formed by a convex mirror.
activities.answer: A concave mirror forms an erect, enlarged image when the object is close to it. If the object is moved farther away, the image becomes inverted, and the previously enlarged image becomes smaller. A convex mirror, however, always forms an image that is erect and smaller than the object. Therefore, the size and orientation of the images differ: the close object gives a large, upright image in the concave mirror, while the convex mirror always gives an upright, reduced image.
points: A close object forms an erect, enlarged image in a concave mirror.
Moving the object farther away makes the image inverted.
The enlarged image becomes smaller as the object moves away.
A convex mirror always forms an erect, smaller image.
activities.explanation: Compare your answer with the points a marker looks for.

activities.context: At a school activity, Meera places a concave mirror in sunlight. The mirror brings the sunlight together, and the reflected sunlight becomes concentrated at one point on the paper. The paper catches fire because the concentrated light produces enough heat to ignite it. Meera also learns that mirrors and lenses can concentrate sunlight in solar concentrators. She wonders whether such concentrated sunlight could heat a liquid to make steam for generating electricity.
activities.prompt: If Meera replaces the concave mirror with a convex mirror, what should happen to the reflected rays?
options: The rays would fan outward and move farther apart.
The rays would remain parallel to one another.
The rays would come together at one point.
The rays would travel straight through the mirror.

why.The rays would remain parallel to one an: A plane mirror keeps reflected rays parallel.
why.The rays would come together at one poin: Convergence is the effect of a concave mirror.
why.The rays would travel straight through t: Light reflects from a mirror instead of passing through it.

activities.explanation: This is the effect of a convex mirror.

activities.context: At a school activity, Meera places a concave mirror in sunlight. The mirror brings the sunlight together, and the reflected sunlight becomes concentrated at one point on the paper. The paper catches fire because the concentrated light produces enough heat to ignite it. Meera also learns that mirrors and lenses can concentrate sunlight in solar concentrators. She wonders whether such concentrated sunlight could heat a liquid to make steam for generating electricity.
activities.prompt: What should Meera use if she wants to concentrate sunlight to heat a liquid?
options: Use a mirror-and-lens device designed for gathering sunlight.
Use a device that sends sunlight in many directions.
Use a plane mirror that keeps the light rays parallel.
Use a convex mirror that makes the reflected rays diverge.

why.Use a plane mirror that keeps the light: A plane mirror does not concentrate sunlight.
why.Use a convex mirror that makes the refle: A convex mirror makes reflected rays diverge.

activities.explanation: Such a device is a solar concentrator.

activities.prompt:
Assertion (A): Reflected rays from a concave mirror come closer together and converge.
Reason (R): The curved surface of a spherical mirror makes parallel rays converge or diverge.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.
activities.explanation: The curved surface of the concave mirror causes the parallel rays to converge.

activities.prompt:
Assertion (A): Concentrated sunlight can heat a liquid to make steam for generating electricity.
Reason (R): Every ray of light follows the laws of reflection.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.
activities.explanation: Both statements are true, but the laws of reflection do not explain heating the liquid with concentrated sunlight.

activities.prompt: Explain how the curved surface of a spherical mirror changes the behaviour of parallel light rays after reflection.
activities.answer: The curved surface of a spherical mirror changes the way parallel light rays behave after reflection. With a concave mirror, the reflected rays come closer together and converge. With a convex mirror, the reflected rays spread apart and diverge. Both kinds of mirror follow the laws of reflection, but their curved surfaces make the reflected parallel rays behave differently. The kind of mirror therefore determines whether the rays are brought together or separated.
points: The curved surface changes the reflected rays.
A concave mirror makes reflected rays converge.
A convex mirror makes reflected rays diverge.
Every reflected ray follows the laws of reflection.
activities.explanation: Compare your answer with the points a marker looks for.

activities.context: A student visits a school display where a convex lens and a concave lens are shown separately. The student first places a nearby object in front of the convex lens and notices that it appears upright and enlarged. When the object is moved farther away, the image changes. The student then looks through the concave lens and sees a smaller, upright image. A thin flat glass plate is also placed beside the lenses.
activities.prompt: What happens next when the student moves the object farther away from the convex lens?
options: The image stays upright and enlarged.
It turns upside down, and the image later becomes smaller.
The image stays upright but becomes smaller.
It turns upside down while staying enlarged.

This ignores the change caused by greater object distance.
why.The image stays upright but becomes smal: A convex image does not remain upright when the distance becomes greater.
why.It turns upside down while staying enlar: The image becomes smaller after it has first been enlarged.

activities.explanation: At a greater distance, the image becomes inverted and later smaller.

activities.context: A student visits a school display where a convex lens and a concave lens are shown separately. The student first places a nearby object in front of the convex lens and notices that it appears upright and enlarged. When the object is moved farther away, the image changes. The student then looks through the concave lens and sees a smaller, upright image. A thin flat glass plate is also placed beside the lenses.
activities.prompt: If the convex lens were replaced by the thin flat glass plate in the ray demonstration, what would happen?
options: The rays would still be brought closer together.
The rays would be spread farther apart.
The rays would pass through without being made to converge or diverge.
The rays would bounce back toward their source.

why.The rays would still be brought closer t: A flat plate does not bring converging rays closer together.
A flat plate does not make light diverge.
why.The rays would bounce back toward their: Light passes through the plate rather than bouncing back.

activities.explanation: This is the stated behavior of light passing through a thin flat glass plate.

activities.prompt:
Assertion (A): A convex lens is also called a converging lens.
Reason (R): An object close to a convex lens appears erect and enlarged.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.
activities.explanation: Both statements are true, but the appearance of a nearby object does not explain the alternative name.

activities.prompt:
Assertion (A): A thin flat glass plate makes light rays converge.
Reason (R): Light passes through a thin flat glass plate without being made to converge or diverge.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.
activities.explanation: The reason is true, but it shows that the assertion about convergence is false.

activities.prompt: Explain the difference between a convex lens and a concave lens.
activities.answer: A convex lens is a converging lens, while a concave lens is a diverging lens. A concave lens is thicker at its edges than in the middle, and both kinds of lens allow light to pass through them. With a nearby object, a convex lens makes it appear erect and enlarged. As the distance becomes greater, the image becomes inverted; it is first enlarged and then smaller in size. An object seen through a concave lens always appears erect and smaller.
points: Convex means converging; concave means diverging.
A concave lens is thicker at its edges.
A nearby object appears erect and enlarged through a convex lens.
A concave lens always gives an erect, smaller view.
activities.explanation: Compare your answer with the points a marker looks for.

activities.context: During a school astronomy activity, Bhāskara II’s astronomers used shallow bowls of water to observe stars and planets. They measured the positions of the objects from their reflected images. The student then examines a concave mirror, a convex mirror, and two lenses. One lens makes light beams converge, and the other makes them diverge. The student also uses a magnifying glass to read tiny print and compares the images formed by the optical devices.
activities.prompt: Why were the astronomers able to measure the positions of the stars and planets after using the shallow bowls?
options: Their reflected images allowed them to record where each object appeared.
The water always changed the objects into enlarged images.
The convex mirror always made the images erect and diminished.
The lenses converged the light beams before the positions were recorded.

why.The water always changed the objects int: A convex mirror always gives an erect, diminished image, but that does not explain the measurements.
why.The convex mirror always made the images: The convex mirror was used later, not for measuring the objects’ positions.
why.The lenses converged the light beams bef: Convergence is a property of a convex lens, not of the bowl method.

activities.explanation: Correct: the measurements were made from the reflected images.

activities.context: During a school astronomy activity, Bhāskara II’s astronomers used shallow bowls of water to observe stars and planets. They measured the positions of the objects from their reflected images. The student then examines a concave mirror, a convex mirror, and two lenses. One lens makes light beams converge, and the other makes them diverge. The student also uses a magnifying glass to read tiny print and compares the images formed by the optical devices.
activities.prompt: If the student uses a convex mirror instead of the concave mirror while comparing images, what result should be expected?
options: An erect image that is diminished.
An image that may be enlarged, diminished or the same size.
An enlarged image for every object.
An image that is erect and the same size as the object.

why.An image that may be enlarged, diminishe: Those are the possible image sizes of a concave mirror.
A convex mirror does not always give an enlarged image.
why.An image that is erect and the same size: A convex mirror always makes the image diminished, not the same size.

activities.explanation: Correct: a convex mirror always gives an erect, diminished image.

boss.title: Chapter challenge: Light: Mirrors and Lenses

activities.prompt: Which shape describes a concave mirror?
options: Curves inwards
Curves outwards
Stays completely flat
Has no reflecting surface
activities.explanation: A concave mirror has a reflecting surface that curves inwards.

activities.prompt: Spherical mirrors are made by shaping flat glass with grinding and polishing.
activities.explanation: Grinding and polishing shape flat glass into spherical mirrors.

activities.prompt: The inner surface of a shiny spoon can form an ______ image.
activities.hint: The image is turned upside down.
activities.explanation: The inner surface of a shiny spoon can form an inverted image.

activities.prompt: What happens when an object is close to a concave mirror?
options: Erect and enlarged
Erect and smaller
Inverted and enlarged
Inverted and smaller
activities.explanation: A close object gives a concave mirror an erect, enlarged image.

activities.prompt: Match each mirror or lens to its correct description.
activities.explanation: The pairs use each mirror or lens shape from the lesson.

activities.prompt: Put the stages of making steam with concentrated sunlight in order.
items: Steam is used for generating electricity
activities.explanation: Concentrated sunlight heats a liquid to make steam for generating electricity.

activities.prompt: A convex mirror forms an inverted image of an object.
activities.explanation: A convex mirror always forms an image that is erect and smaller.

activities.prompt: What does an object close to a convex lens appear like?
options: Erect and enlarged
Erect and smaller
Inverted and enlarged
Inverted and smaller
activities.explanation: An object close to a convex lens appears erect and enlarged.

activities.prompt: For every light ray, the angle of incidence equals the angle of reflection.
activities.explanation: The angle of incidence always equals the angle of reflection.

chapters.title: Keeping Time with the Skies
chapters.summary: In this chapter: watching the moon’s changing shapes; finding and explaining the moon; eclipses and natural cycles; how natural cycles became calendars.

lessons.title: Watching the Moon’s Changing Shapes

activities.prompt: Why does the Moon seem to change shape in the night sky?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: Meet the Moon’s Phases
activities.body: The spherical Moon shines by reflecting sunlight. From Earth, its bright part changes shape. These changes are called phases of the Moon. A full bright circle is the full Moon day, or Purnima. An invisible Moon marks the new Moon day, or Amavasya. After the new Moon, the bright side grows. The growing stage is waxing. The shrinking stage is waning. India calls them Shukla Paksha and Krishna Paksha.
keyPoints: Phases are the Moon’s changing shapes.
Full Moon day is Purnima; new Moon day is Amavasya.
Waxing means growth; waning means shrinking.
activities.explanation: This helps you connect each visible change with its name.

activities.prompt: Meera sees the Moon shining during the daytime. Her friend says it must make its own light. Why is the friend’s claim wrong?
steps: Meera sees the Moon shining even during the daytime.
The Moon is spherical and reflects sunlight, so its light comes from outside it.
Because it reflects sunlight, the Moon can shine without making its own light.
Therefore, the Moon’s daytime brightness comes from reflected sunlight.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.title: Name the Full Moon Day
activities.prompt: The Indian name for a full Moon day is ______.
activities.hint: Look for the name beside full Moon day.
activities.explanation: A full bright circle is called the full Moon day or Purnima.

activities.title: Match the Moon’s Names
activities.prompt: Match each Moon name or stage with its correct label.
activities.explanation: In India, these names help describe the Moon’s changing stages.

activities.title: After the New Moon
activities.prompt: After the new Moon, what happens to the bright side?
options: The bright side grows to a half circle.
The bright side slowly shrinks to a half circle.
The bright side stays hidden for a week.
The bright side changes into a bright star.
activities.explanation: After the new Moon, the bright side grows to a half circle in about a week.

activities.title: Order the Waning Changes
activities.prompt: Put the waning changes in the order given.
items: half circle after about a week
activities.explanation: The bright part shrinks from a full circle to a half circle in about a week.

activities.title: Name India’s Waxing Period
activities.prompt: In India, the waxing period is called ______ Paksha.
activities.hint: This name is for the period when the bright side grows.
activities.explanation: In India, the waxing period is called Shukla Paksha.

activities.title: Match India’s Two Periods
activities.prompt: Which pair correctly matches a period and its Indian name?
options: Shukla Paksha—waxing; Krishna Paksha—waning
Krishna Paksha—waxing; Shukla Paksha—waning
Amavasya—waxing; Purnima—waning
Purnima—waxing; Amavasya—waning
activities.explanation: Shukla Paksha means the waxing period, while Krishna Paksha means the waning period.

activities.prompt: The Moon is spherical and shines by reflecting sunlight. Meera sees it during the day. Why can she see it?
options: It makes its own light during the day.
It hides sunlight and becomes bright.
It reflects sunlight and stays visible.
It copies the light from the sky.

This wrongly says the Moon makes its own light.
This wrongly says hiding sunlight makes the Moon bright.
This wrongly treats sky light as the Moon’s source.

activities.explanation: The Moon shines by reflecting sunlight, so Meera can see it.

activities.prompt: On Purnima, the Moon shows a full bright circle. What should a child expect about one week later?
options: A smaller half circle, because the waning phase continues.
A larger half circle, because the waxing phase begins.
A full circle, because the bright shape never changes.
No visible Moon, because it vanishes after one week.

why.A larger half circle, because the waxing: A larger half circle is the waxing pattern, not the waning pattern.
why.A full circle, because the bright shape: A full circle contradicts the stated shrinking pattern.
why.No visible Moon, because it vanishes aft: This wrongly treats a shrinking bright part as whole-Moon disappearance.

activities.explanation: A full circle shrinks to a half circle in about a week during waning.

activities.prompt: Amavasya is the new Moon day, when the Moon is not visible. About a week later, what should a child expect?
options: A full circle that keeps growing larger.
A half circle with a shrinking bright side.
No visible Moon for another week.
A half circle with a growing bright side.

The fact predicts growth to a half circle, not a full circle.
why.A half circle with a shrinking bright si: Shrinking belongs to waning, but this starts after the new Moon.
The bright side starts growing after the new Moon.

activities.explanation: After the new Moon, the bright side grows to a half circle in about a week.

activities.prompt: The Moon’s changing shapes are called phases. After the new Moon, one child sees a growing bright side. Another sees a shrinking bright side. Which pair names their periods correctly?
options: First: Shukla Paksha; second: Krishna Paksha.
First: Krishna Paksha; second: Shukla Paksha.
First: Shukla Paksha; second: Shukla Paksha.
First: Krishna Paksha; second: Krishna Paksha.

why.First: Krishna Paksha; second: Shukla Pa: This swaps the growing and shrinking periods.
why.First: Shukla Paksha; second: Shukla Pak: This wrongly gives both children the waxing period.
why.First: Krishna Paksha; second: Krishna P: This wrongly gives both children the waning period.

activities.explanation: Growth is Shukla Paksha, and shrinking is Krishna Paksha in India.

activities.prompt: The Moon is spherical and shines by reflecting sunlight. Which test best shows this on a model?
options: Place a spherical model beside a bright window.
Shine sunlight on a spherical model in a dark room.
Put a spherical model inside a closed box.
Cover a spherical model with a dull cloth.

why.Place a spherical model beside a bright: This adds another light source, so it is not a fair test.
why.Put a spherical model inside a closed bo: This gives the model no sunlight to reflect.
why.Cover a spherical model with a dull clot: This blocks the sunlight before it reaches the model.

activities.explanation: The model reflects sunlight like the Moon, making this a fair test.

activities.prompt: The Moon is spherical. Its changing bright shapes are seen from Earth. A child says the Moon itself changes shape. Which observation best shows the flaw?
options: The Moon stays spherical while its bright part changes.
The Moon changes shape when its bright part grows.
The Moon becomes hidden when its bright part shrinks.
The Moon turns half each time it is bright.

why.The Moon changes shape when its bright p: This wrongly treats a changing bright part as a changing Moon.
why.The Moon becomes hidden when its bright: This confuses a shrinking bright part with the Moon becoming invisible.
why.The Moon turns half each time it is brig: The Moon itself does not turn into a half circle.

activities.explanation: The Moon stays spherical, so its changing bright part is the phase.

lessons.title: Finding and Explaining the Moon

activities.prompt: Why does the Moon seem to change shape each night?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: The Moon's Bright Shapes
activities.body: The Moon's shape itself does not change. It does not produce light of its own. The half facing the Sun receives sunlight and becomes bright. Only one half always faces Earth. When the Moon looks like a half circle, it is overhead at sunrise. A waxing Moon is easiest to spot at sunset. A waning Moon is easiest to spot at sunrise. It rises about 50 minutes later each day.
keyPoints: The Moon's shape itself does not change.
Sunlight brightens the half facing the Sun.
Only one half always faces Earth.
The Moon rises about 50 minutes later each day.
activities.explanation: The Moon is found by its changing brightness and rising times.

activities.prompt: A child sees a full Moon and wants to know where to look at sunrise the next day.
steps: On a full Moon day, the Moon is nearly opposite the Sun.
After the full Moon, it appears closer to the Sun at sunrise.
It shifts because the Moon rises about 50 minutes later each day.
So its position changes, although its own shape does not.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.prompt: Which statement about the Moon's light is true?
options: The Moon makes light of its own.
Sunlight makes the Sun-facing half bright.
The whole Moon glows by itself.
The dark half makes more light.
activities.explanation: The Moon does not produce light of its own. Sunlight makes the half facing the Sun bright.

activities.prompt: The shape of the Moon itself changes each night.
activities.explanation: The shape of the Moon itself does not change.

activities.prompt: After the full Moon, the Moon appears closer to the Sun at ______.
activities.hint: Think about the time just after the full Moon.
activities.explanation: After the full Moon, the Moon appears closer to the Sun at sunrise.

activities.prompt: When is a waning Moon easiest to spot?
options: at sunrise
at sunset
on a full Moon day
activities.explanation: A waning Moon is easiest to spot at sunrise.

activities.prompt: Why does the Moon show different bright shapes while its own shape stays the same?
options: Sunlight brightens the half facing the Sun.
The Moon changes its own shape each night.
The Earth blocks all sunlight from the Moon.
The Moon produces different kinds of light.
activities.explanation: The shape itself does not change. Sunlight brightens the half facing the Sun.

activities.prompt: Put these events in order from the Sun's light to brightness.
items: The half of the Moon faces the Sun.
activities.explanation: Sunlight reaches the half facing the Sun. That half then becomes bright.

activities.prompt: A child sees a full Moon today. What will the Moon appear to do at sunrise tomorrow?
options: It will appear farther from the Sun.
It will appear overhead at sunrise.
It will appear closer to the Sun.
It will stay in the same place.

This reverses what happens after a full Moon.
This describes the position of a half-circle Moon at sunrise.
This mistakes a changing position for an unchanged position.

activities.explanation: This is right because the Moon appears closer to the Sun after a full Moon.

activities.prompt: A child claims the Moon changes its own shape each night. Which test would fairly check this claim?
options: Watch the Moon's brightness over several nights.
Move a lamp closer to the Moon each night.
Ask someone what the Moon looks like.
Watch the Moon's shape over several nights.

why.Watch the Moon's brightness over several: This checks brightness instead of the Moon's shape.
why.Move a lamp closer to the Moon each nigh: This changes the test instead of checking the claim fairly.
This checks someone's answer instead of making an observation.

activities.explanation: This is right because it checks whether the Moon's own shape changes.

activities.prompt: A child sees one bright half of the Moon. Why is this half bright?
options: Sunlight lights the half facing the Earth.
The Moon makes its own bright light.
The Moon changes shape into a half.
Sunlight lights the half facing the Sun.

why.Sunlight lights the half facing the Eart: This confuses the half facing Earth with the sunlit half.
This wrongly says that the Moon produces its own light.
This mistakes the visible shape for a change in the Moon itself.

activities.explanation: This is right because sunlight makes the half facing the Sun bright.

lessons.sceneCaption: A waning gibbous Moon over Kolkata, photographed on the twentieth day after the new Moon.

lessons.title: Eclipses and Natural Cycles

activities.prompt: Why do eclipses sometimes miss the Moon?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: Why eclipses happen
activities.body: Earth’s shadow can fall on the Moon. This causes a lunar eclipse, and it can happen only on a full Moon day. A solar eclipse can happen only on a new Moon day. Eclipses do not happen every month because the Moon’s orbit, or path, is slightly tilted. The Moon’s changing phases form a natural cycle of almost a month. This cycle can also help keep time.
keyPoints: Earth’s shadow on the Moon causes a lunar eclipse.
A solar eclipse can happen only on a new Moon day.
Eclipses do not happen every month because the Moon’s orbit is slightly tilted.
activities.explanation: The shadow and the Moon’s day both help decide when an eclipse can happen.

activities.title: Line them up

tasks.then: The Moon is between the Sun and the Earth and blocks the Sun.
The Earth is in the middle, so its shadow falls on the Moon.

activities.takeaway: An eclipse happens when the Sun, Earth and Moon line up.
activities.explanation: An eclipse happens when the Sun, Earth and Moon line up.

activities.prompt: A child sees the full Moon turn dark. What caused this?
steps: Earth’s shadow fell on the Moon, so a lunar eclipse happened.
A lunar eclipse can happen only on a full Moon day.
Earth’s shadow does not cause the Moon’s regular phases.
So the Moon darkened because of an eclipse, not a phase change.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.title: Regular patterns in nature
activities.body: A natural cycle is a repeating pattern in nature. The Moon’s changing phases form a natural cycle of almost a month. This monthly cycle can also be used for keeping time. Day, night and the changing seasons are also regular natural events. These are patterns that happen again and again.
keyPoints: The Moon’s changing phases form a cycle of almost a month.
The monthly cycle can be used for keeping time.
Day, night and the changing seasons are regular natural events.
activities.explanation: Natural cycles are repeating patterns, and some of them help people keep time.

activities.title: Cause of a lunar eclipse
activities.prompt: What causes a lunar eclipse?
options: Earth’s shadow falling on the Moon
The Moon’s changing phases
The Moon’s slightly tilted orbit
The changing seasons
activities.explanation: A lunar eclipse happens when Earth’s shadow falls on the Moon.

activities.title: When can a lunar eclipse happen?
activities.prompt: A lunar eclipse can happen only on a ______ Moon day.
activities.hint: Think about the phase named in the lesson.
activities.explanation: A lunar eclipse can happen only on a full Moon day.

activities.title: Match each idea
activities.prompt: Match each idea on the left with its matching idea on the right.
pairs: Earth’s shadow falling on the Moon
Eclipses do not occur every month
A natural cycle of almost a month
activities.explanation: Each pair connects an eclipse, its cause, or the cycle of the Moon.

activities.title: Why not every month?
activities.prompt: Why do eclipses not occur every month?
options: Because the Moon’s orbit is tilted.
Because the Moon changes its phases.
Because day and night change.
Because the seasons change.
activities.explanation: The Moon’s orbit is slightly tilted, so eclipses do not occur every month.

activities.title: Choose the correct link
activities.prompt: Which statement correctly links an eclipse with a Moon day?
options: A solar eclipse can happen on a full Moon day.
A lunar eclipse can happen on a new Moon day.
A solar eclipse can happen on a new Moon day.
A lunar eclipse can happen every month.
activities.explanation: A solar eclipse can happen only on a new Moon day.

activities.title: Length of the Moon’s cycle
activities.prompt: The Moon’s changing phases form a natural cycle of almost a ______.
activities.hint: Think about how long the cycle lasts.
activities.explanation: The changing phases form a natural cycle of almost a month.

activities.prompt: The full Moon enters Earth’s shadow. What should the child expect?
options: A lunar eclipse is happening.
The Moon is changing phase.
A solar eclipse is happening.
Clouds are hiding the Moon.

This mistake confuses a phase change with an eclipse.
This mistake treats a solar eclipse as Earth-shadow related.
This mistake blames clouds instead of Earth’s shadow.

activities.explanation: Earth’s shadow on the Moon causes a lunar eclipse.

activities.prompt: A full Moon day has no eclipse. Is this possible?
options: Yes, because eclipses do not happen every month.
No, because every full Moon causes an eclipse.
No, because lunar eclipses happen every month.
Yes, because a solar eclipse changes Earth’s shadow.

why.No, because every full Moon causes an ec: This mistake assumes every full Moon must have an eclipse.
why.No, because lunar eclipses happen every: This mistake assumes eclipses follow a strict monthly pattern.
why.Yes, because a solar eclipse changes Ear: This mistake mixes up solar eclipses and Earth’s shadow.

activities.explanation: The tilted Moon orbit means eclipses do not occur every month.

activities.prompt: A family needs a natural cycle for keeping time. Which cycle fits?
options: The Moon’s nearly monthly phase cycle.
The Moon’s slightly tilted orbit.
Earth’s shadow on the Moon.
The shadow of a solar eclipse.

The tilted orbit explains missing eclipses, not keeping time.
Earth’s shadow causes a lunar eclipse, not a time cycle.
A solar eclipse is not the Moon’s monthly time cycle.

activities.explanation: The Moon’s monthly phase cycle can be used for keeping time.

lessons.sceneCaption: A total solar eclipse occurs when the Moon's shadow reaches Earth and blocks the Sun.

lessons.title: How Natural Cycles Became Calendars

activities.prompt: How did the Sun, Moon, and seasons help people build calendars?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: Natural Cycles and Time
activities.body: Earth’s rotation and the Sun’s cycle form the basis of a day. The Moon’s changing phases help define a month. Earth’s cycle of seasons can define a solar year. A lunar calendar uses the Moon’s cycle for months. Ancient people used twelve lunar months. A lunar year lasts 354 days. Solar calendars match years with seasons and adjust months to add up to 365 days.
keyPoints: The day comes from Earth’s rotation and the Sun’s cycle.
The Moon’s phases help define the month.
Solar calendars match years with seasons.
activities.explanation: Natural cycles helped people make calendars for days, months, and years.

activities.prompt: Twelve lunar months make a 354-day year. A solar year has 365 days. How can the calendar keep matching the seasons?
steps: A lunar year lasts 354 days because it has twelve lunar months.
A solar year uses months adjusted to add up to 365 days.
The eleven-day gap would move dates away from the seasons.
Therefore, add days to the months until each year totals 365 days.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.title: What Moves the Sun Across the Sky?
activities.prompt: The Sun’s daily apparent motion is mainly due to what?
options: Earth’s rotation
Moon’s phases
Earth’s seasons
The Moon’s cycle
activities.explanation: Earth’s rotation makes the Sun’s daily apparent motion. This movement helps form the basis of the day.

activities.title: The Mean Solar Day
activities.prompt: The average time between the Sun’s highest positions is the mean solar day.
activities.explanation: Yes. The mean solar day is the average time between the Sun’s highest positions.

activities.title: Lunar Months
activities.prompt: Ancient people created lunar calendars using ______ lunar months in a year.
activities.hint: This number comes from the ancient lunar calendar.
activities.explanation: Ancient lunar calendars used twelve lunar months in each year.

activities.title: Why Make Solar Calendars?
activities.prompt: Why were solar calendars created?
options: To match years with seasons
To measure Earth’s rotation
To show only Moon phases
To replace the idea of a day
activities.explanation: The need to match years with seasons led to the creation of solar calendars.

activities.title: Match the Cycle
activities.prompt: Match each calendar idea with its natural cycle.
pairs: Earth’s rotation and the Sun’s cycle
The need to match years with seasons
activities.explanation: Each calendar idea comes from a natural cycle or the need to match years with seasons.

activities.title: Days in Solar Months
activities.prompt: Solar calendars adjust their months to add up to how many days?
options: 354 days
365 days
12 days
activities.explanation: Months in solar calendars are adjusted to add up to 365 days.

activities.title: How Solar Calendars Developed
activities.prompt: Put these events in order.
items: Months adjusted to add up to 365 days
activities.explanation: Lunar calendars came first. The need to match seasons led to solar calendars and adjusted months.

activities.title: Solar or Lunar?
activities.prompt: Solar calendars were made so their months would add up to 354 days.
activities.explanation: Solar months add up to 365 days. A lunar year lasts 354 days.

activities.prompt: Earth stops rotating in a model. What should happen to the Sun’s daily apparent motion?
options: It should mostly stop each day.
It should keep moving as before.
It should move only once yearly.
It should move faster each day.

This assumes daily motion does not depend on rotation.
This mistakes the seasonal cycle for daily motion.
This assumes rotation makes the Sun move faster.

activities.explanation: Without rotation, the main cause of daily motion is gone.

activities.prompt: After twelve lunar months, compare the calendar with a solar year. Will both reach the same seasonal point?
options: No, because its year is eleven days shorter.
Yes, because twelve lunar months fill 365 days.
No, because each lunar month is longer.
Yes, because lunar and solar years always match.

why.Yes, because twelve lunar months fill 36: Twelve lunar months make 354 days, not 365 days.
Longer lunar months do not explain the eleven-day difference.
why.Yes, because lunar and solar years alway: Lunar and solar years do not have the same length.

activities.explanation: A 354-day year is eleven days shorter than 365 days.

lessons.title: Indian Luni-Solar Calendars and Sky Traditions

activities.prompt: How do the Moon, Sun, and changing seasons shape India’s traditional calendars?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: Calendars Guided by the Sky
activities.body: Ancient observers noticed repeating patterns and cycles in natural events. Uttarayan means the Sun’s apparent northward movement from December to June. Dakshinayan means its apparent southward movement from June to December. Luni-solar calendars mainly use Moon phases, but also adjust to match the seasons. Some add an extra month called Adhika Maasa. In Amant calendars, a new month starts after the new Moon.
keyPoints: The Sun appears northward from December to June.
The Sun appears southward from June to December.
Luni-solar calendars follow Moon phases and seasonal changes.
activities.explanation: These ideas explain how Indian calendars follow Moon phases, seasons, and the Sun.

activities.prompt: A family wants monthly dates to stay close to the same seasons. How can a luni-solar calendar do this?
steps: Twelve lunar months are nearly eleven days short of the solar year.
Luni-solar calendars mainly follow Moon phases but adjust to seasons.
Adding an extra Adhika Maasa can correct the seasonal gap.
So the calendar keeps its dates close to the seasons.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.prompt: The Sun’s apparent northward movement from December to June is called Uttarayan.
activities.explanation: Uttarayan is the Sun’s apparent northward movement from December to June.

activities.prompt: Which calendars mainly use Moon phases and adjust to match the seasons?
options: Luni-solar calendars
Only solar calendars
Only lunar calendars
Daily calendars
activities.explanation: Luni-solar calendars mainly use Moon phases. They also adjust to match the seasons.

activities.prompt: Match each name with its correct meaning.
activities.explanation: The pairs connect each movement or month-start rule with its correct name.

activities.prompt: Twelve lunar months fall nearly ______ days short of the solar year.
activities.hint: The gap is nearly eleven days.
activities.explanation: Twelve lunar months fall nearly 11 days short. Some calendars add Adhika Maasa.

activities.prompt: In a leap year, an extra day is added to Chaitra.
activities.explanation: In a leap year, an extra day is added to Chaitra.

activities.prompt: Which statement about the months of the Indian National Calendar is correct?
options: Every month has 30 days.
Months have 30 or 31 days.
Every month has 31 days.
activities.explanation: Its months have either 30 or 31 days. A leap year changes Chaitra.

activities.prompt: Twelve lunar months end nearly eleven days before the solar year. What happens if no seasonal adjustment is made?
options: Their dates drift earlier against the seasons.
Their dates stay fixed against the seasons.
Their dates drift later against the seasons.
Their dates change with every Moon phase.

why.Their dates stay fixed against the seaso: This assumes twelve lunar months already match the solar year.
why.Their dates drift later against the seas: This reverses the direction of the eleven-day shortfall.
why.Their dates change with every Moon phase: This confuses month construction with seasonal drift.

activities.explanation: This is right because the eleven-day gap makes dates drift against the seasons.

activities.prompt: A luni-solar calendar is nearly eleven days short after twelve lunar months. Why add an extra month?
options: To help match the calendar back with the seasons.
To make every lunar month begin after a new Moon.
To replace all twelve regular months with extra ones.
To make the solar year longer by eleven days.

why.To make every lunar month begin after a: This mistakes the Amant month-start rule for the extra month’s purpose.
why.To replace all twelve regular months wit: This wrongly assumes that extra months replace regular months.
why.To make the solar year longer by eleven: This wrongly assumes that the calendar can lengthen the solar year.

activities.explanation: This is right because an extra month helps correct the seasonal gap.

activities.prompt: The Indian National Calendar has 365 days and starts on 22 March. How does it differ from a luni-solar calendar?
options: It follows the Sun, while the other follows Moon phases.
It follows Moon phases, while the other follows seasons.
Both calendars begin every month after a full Moon.
Both calendars add an extra month in every year.

why.It follows Moon phases, while the other: This reverses their main time cycles and ignores seasonal adjustments.
why.Both calendars begin every month after a: This wrongly applies the Purnimant month-start rule to both calendars.
why.Both calendars add an extra month in eve: This wrongly assumes that every luni-solar calendar always adds a month.

activities.explanation: This is right because the Indian National Calendar is solar, while luni-solar calendars use Moon phases.

lessons.title: Festivals and Artificial Satellites

activities.prompt: Why do festival dates change, and how do satellites help us?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: Moon, Calendars and Satellites
activities.body: Many Indian festivals are linked to the phases of the Moon. Holi falls on the full Moon of Phalguna. Eid-ul-Fitr is celebrated after sighting the crescent Moon. Moon-based festivals can fall on different Gregorian calendar dates in successive years. Festivals following a solar sidereal calendar keep almost the same date each year. Most artificial satellites take roughly 100 minutes to orbit. Old satellites and rocket parts can become space debris.
keyPoints: Moon phases link many Indian festivals.
Solar sidereal festivals keep nearly the same yearly date.
Most artificial satellites take roughly 100 minutes to orbit.
activities.explanation: Moon phases can shift festival dates, while satellites orbit and create possible debris.

activities.prompt: A child sees Holi's date change between years and wonders why.
steps: Many Indian festivals follow Moon phases, so the Moon affects their timing.
Holi follows the full Moon of Phalguna, so its timing is Moon-based.
Because Moon-based festivals can fall on different Gregorian dates, Holi's date can change.
Therefore, the changed date is expected, not a calendar mistake.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.title: Useful Satellites and Space Debris
activities.body: Most artificial satellites take roughly 100 minutes to complete one orbit. They help with communication, navigation, weather monitoring and other work. Old satellites and rocket parts can become space junk or space debris. This lesson connects useful satellite work with possible debris.
keyPoints: Most satellite orbits take roughly 100 minutes.
Satellites help communication, navigation and weather monitoring.
Old satellites and rocket parts can become space debris.
activities.explanation: Satellites support useful work, while old parts can become space debris.

activities.title: Moon Connections
activities.prompt: What are many Indian festivals linked to?
options: The phases of the Moon
The sunrise times
Satellite orbits
Rocket launches
activities.explanation: The lesson links many Indian festivals to the phases of the Moon.

activities.title: Same Festival Date
activities.prompt: Festivals following a solar sidereal calendar happen on almost the same date each year.
activities.explanation: Festivals using this calendar keep nearly the same date each year.

activities.title: Satellite Orbit Time
activities.prompt: Most artificial satellites take roughly ______ minutes to complete one orbit.
activities.hint: The lesson gives an approximate time for one orbit.
activities.explanation: Most artificial satellites complete one orbit in roughly 100 minutes.

activities.title: Festival Connections
activities.prompt: Match each festival or calendar with its linked detail.
pairs: Different Gregorian dates in successive years
Almost the same date each year
activities.explanation: Holi and Eid-ul-Fitr follow Moon details, while solar sidereal festivals keep nearly the same date.

activities.title: Compare Festival Dates
activities.prompt: Put these steps in order to compare festival dates across successive years.
items: Note its Gregorian date in the current year.
Note its Gregorian date in the next year.
activities.explanation: Recording and comparing dates shows whether a festival date shifts.

activities.title: Regional Date Shift
activities.prompt: What can differ between eastern and western India and shift a festival date?
options: Sunrise times
Satellite orbits
Rocket launches
Satellite debris
activities.explanation: The sunrise time difference between eastern and western India can shift a festival date.

activities.title: Sources of Space Debris
activities.prompt: What can become space junk or space debris?
options: New communication satellites
Old satellites and rocket parts
The full Moon of Phalguna
Gregorian calendar dates
activities.explanation: Old satellites and rocket parts can become space junk or space debris.

activities.prompt: Holi has different Gregorian dates in two years. What best explains this?
options: It follows the full Moon of Phalguna each year.
It follows a solar sidereal calendar each year.
It follows a crescent Moon sighting each year.
It follows a fixed sunrise time each year.

why.It follows a solar sidereal calendar eac: This confuses a Moon-based festival with a solar sidereal calendar.
why.It follows a crescent Moon sighting each: This confuses Holi's full Moon with the crescent rule for Eid-ul-Fitr.
why.It follows a fixed sunrise time each yea: This confuses Moon-based timing with regional sunrise timing.

activities.explanation: Holi follows the full Moon of Phalguna, so its date can change.

activities.prompt: No one has seen the crescent Moon. Eid-ul-Fitr is due. What should the family do?
options: The family should wait for a crescent Moon sighting.
The family should wait for the full Moon of Phalguna.
The family should wait for a solar sidereal date.
The family should wait for one satellite orbit.

why.The family should wait for the full Moon: This confuses Eid-ul-Fitr's crescent sighting with Holi's full Moon.
why.The family should wait for a solar sider: This confuses Moon sighting with a solar sidereal calendar.
why.The family should wait for one satellite: This confuses a lunar festival with a satellite's orbit.

activities.explanation: Eid-ul-Fitr is celebrated after the crescent Moon is sighted.
