activities.context: During the daytime, Meera saw the Moon shining. She knew the Moon is spherical and shines by reflecting sunlight. She also noticed that its bright part changes shape. At one point, it looked like a full circle. Over the next two-week period, Meera watched the bright part become smaller and eventually reach a half circle. She wondered what these changing shapes were called.
activities.prompt: Why was Meera able to see the Moon shining during the daytime?
options: The Moon creates its own light.
Its light is sunlight reflected by the Moon.
The Moon reflects light from Earth.
The Moon is visible only when it has a full-circle bright part.

The Moon shines by reflecting sunlight rather than creating its own light.
The source of the Moon’s reflected light is sunlight, not Earth.
why.The Moon is visible only when it has a f: The Moon can be seen during the daytime even when it does not have a full-circle bright part.

activities.explanation: The Moon shines by reflecting sunlight, so it can be seen during the daytime.

activities.context: During the daytime, Meera saw the Moon shining. She knew the Moon is spherical and shines by reflecting sunlight. She also noticed that its bright part changes shape. At one point, it looked like a full circle. Over the next two-week period, Meera watched the bright part become smaller and eventually reach a half circle. She wondered what these changing shapes were called.
activities.prompt: If Meera observed the Moon on new Moon day, what change should she expect after about a week?
options: The bright side will grow until it reaches a half circle.
The bright part will shrink until it reaches a half circle.
The Moon will remain invisible.
The bright part will become a full circle immediately.

why.The bright part will shrink until it rea: A shrinking bright part belongs to the waning period.
On new Moon day the Moon is not visible, but its bright side later grows.
why.The bright part will become a full circl: The bright part grows to a half circle before becoming a full circle.

activities.explanation: After the new Moon, the bright side grows to a half circle in about a week.

activities.prompt:
Assertion (A): Meera could see the Moon during the daytime because it shines by reflecting sunlight.
Reason (R): The Moon is spherical and reflects sunlight.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.
activities.explanation: Both statements are true, and the reason explains why the Moon could be seen during the daytime.

activities.prompt:
Assertion (A): During Krishna Paksha, the bright part of the Moon grows after the new Moon.
Reason (R): In India, the waxing period is called Shukla Paksha.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.
activities.explanation: The statement is false because Krishna Paksha is the waning period, while the reason is true.

activities.prompt: Explain how the changing shapes of the Moon are described using the terms phases, waxing period, and waning period.
activities.answer: The changing shapes seen from Earth are called the phases of the Moon. The Moon is spherical and shines by reflecting sunlight, while the shape of its visible bright part changes. After the new Moon, the bright side grows to a half circle in about a week. During the waning period, the bright part shrinks from a full circle to a half circle in about a week. In India, the growing period is called Shukla Paksha and the shrinking period is called Krishna Paksha.
points: Calls the changing shapes the phases of the Moon.
States that the Moon is spherical and reflects sunlight.
Explains that the bright side grows after the new Moon.
Identifies Shukla Paksha as waxing and Krishna Paksha as waning.
activities.explanation: Compare your answer with the points a marker looks for.

activities.context: A student sees a half-circle Moon overhead at sunrise. The next morning, the student notices that the Moon rises about 50 minutes later than it did the day before. On another morning, the student sees the full Moon nearly opposite the Sun. In the evening, the Moon is easiest to spot when it is waxing. The student thinks that the Moon's changing shapes mean that the Moon itself is changing.
activities.prompt: What should the student do if the student wants to spot a waxing Moon?
options: Look for it at sunset.
Look for it only at sunrise.
Wait until the Moon is nearly opposite the Sun.
Look for it before sunrise.

Option 1 is wrong because sunrise is the easiest viewing time for a waning Moon.
why.Wait until the Moon is nearly opposite t: Option 2 is wrong because being nearly opposite the Sun describes the full Moon.
Option 3 is wrong because a waxing Moon is easiest to spot at sunset, not before sunrise.

activities.explanation: Option 0 is correct because a waxing Moon is easiest to spot at sunset.

activities.context: A student sees a half-circle Moon overhead at sunrise. The next morning, the student notices that the Moon rises about 50 minutes later than it did the day before. On another morning, the student sees the full Moon nearly opposite the Sun. In the evening, the Moon is easiest to spot when it is waxing. The student thinks that the Moon's changing shapes mean that the Moon itself is changing.
activities.prompt: Why should the student correct the idea that the Moon's own shape is changing?
options: Sunlight makes the half facing the Sun bright, changing the bright shape seen from Earth.
The Moon produces its own light, causing its shape to change each day.
The Moon's own shape changes because only one half always faces Earth.
The half facing the Sun becomes dark, so the visible bright shape changes.

why.The Moon produces its own light, causing: Option 1 is wrong because the Moon does not produce light of its own.
why.The Moon's own shape changes because onl: Option 2 is wrong because only one half facing Earth does not mean that the Moon's shape changes.
why.The half facing the Sun becomes dark, so: Option 3 is wrong because the half facing the Sun receives sunlight and becomes bright, not dark.

activities.explanation: Option 0 is correct because sunlight brightens the half facing the Sun while the Moon's own shape remains unchanged.

activities.prompt:
Assertion (A): The Moon can appear to have different shapes even though its own shape does not change.
Reason (R): Sunlight makes the half of the Moon facing the Sun bright, so the bright part seen from Earth can have a different shape.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.
activities.explanation: Both statements are true, and the lighting of the Moon explains why its apparent shape changes.

activities.prompt:
Assertion (A): A half-circle Moon is overhead at sunrise.
Reason (R): The Moon rises about 50 minutes later each day.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.
activities.explanation: Both statements are true, but the daily change in rising time does not explain why a half-circle Moon is overhead at sunrise.

activities.prompt: Explain why the Moon appears to change shape even though the Moon's own shape does not change.
activities.answer: The Moon does not produce light of its own, so sunlight is what makes it visible. The half of the Moon facing the Sun receives sunlight and becomes bright. As the Moon is seen in different positions relative to the Sun, the bright part visible from Earth can appear to have a changing shape. The Moon itself does not change shape. Also, only one half always faces Earth, but this is different from which half is lit by the Sun.
points: The Moon does not produce its own light.
The half facing the Sun receives sunlight.
The visible bright part can appear to change shape.
The Moon's own shape remains unchanged.
activities.explanation: Compare your answer with the points a marker looks for.

activities.context: A student plans a Moon-watching activity with classmates. On a full Moon day, they watch Earth’s shadow fall across the Moon, so a lunar eclipse occurs. Their project also records the Moon’s changing phases and uses the monthly cycle to keep time. The student wonders why eclipses do not happen every month and why the Moon still shows different phases even when no eclipse is visible.
activities.prompt: Why might the group not see an eclipse in every month, even though it follows the Moon’s monthly cycle?
options: The Moon’s orbit is slightly tilted.
The Moon’s phases are caused by Earth’s shadow.
The monthly cycle is mainly used for keeping time.
Day and night determine whether an eclipse can be seen.

why.The Moon’s phases are caused by Earth’s: Earth’s shadow does not cause the Moon’s changing phases.
why.The monthly cycle is mainly used for kee: Keeping time is a use of the monthly cycle, but it is not the reason eclipses are not monthly.
why.Day and night determine whether an eclip: Day and night are regular, but they do not explain why eclipses are not monthly.

activities.explanation: The tilted orbit is why eclipses do not happen every month.

activities.context: A student plans a Moon-watching activity with classmates. On a full Moon day, they watch Earth’s shadow fall across the Moon, so a lunar eclipse occurs. Their project also records the Moon’s changing phases and uses the monthly cycle to keep time. The student wonders why eclipses do not happen every month and why the Moon still shows different phases even when no eclipse is visible.
activities.prompt: If the Moon’s orbit were not tilted, what would most likely happen to eclipses?
options: They could occur every month.
They could never occur.
A lunar eclipse could happen only on a new Moon day.
A solar eclipse could happen only on a full Moon day.

The given facts do not show that removing the tilt would prevent all eclipses.
why.A lunar eclipse could happen only on a n: A lunar eclipse can happen only on a full Moon day.
why.A solar eclipse could happen only on a f: A solar eclipse can happen only on a new Moon day.

activities.explanation: The tilt is the reason eclipses do not happen every month.

activities.prompt:
Assertion (A): Earth’s shadow falling on the Moon causes a lunar eclipse.
Reason (R): This shadow effect can occur only on a full Moon day.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.
activities.explanation: Both statements are true, and the full Moon condition explains when the shadow can cause a lunar eclipse.

activities.prompt:
Assertion (A): Earth’s shadow causes the changing phases of the Moon.
Reason (R): Earth’s shadow falling on the Moon causes a lunar eclipse.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.
activities.explanation: The assertion is false because Earth’s shadow does not cause the Moon’s phases, while the reason is true.

activities.prompt: What is the difference between a lunar eclipse, a solar eclipse, and an ordinary change in the Moon’s phase?
activities.answer: A lunar eclipse happens when Earth’s shadow falls on the Moon, and it can happen only on a full Moon day. A solar eclipse can happen only on a new Moon day. The Moon’s changing phases form a natural cycle of almost a month, so different phases can appear without an eclipse. Eclipses do not happen every month because the Moon’s orbit is slightly tilted. Therefore, the monthly pattern of phases and the timing of eclipses are related ideas, but they are not the same event.
points: A lunar eclipse involves Earth’s shadow falling on the Moon.
A lunar eclipse can happen only on a full Moon day.
A solar eclipse can happen only on a new Moon day.
The monthly phase cycle and eclipses are not the same event.
activities.explanation: Compare your answer with the points a marker looks for.

activities.context: A community first used a lunar calendar, following the Moon’s phases and placing twelve lunar months in a year. Their lunar year lasted 354 days, so it did not add up to 365 days. They therefore created a solar calendar so their years would match Earth’s cycle of seasons, adjusting the months to total 365 days. The Sun’s daily apparent motion, mainly caused by Earth’s rotation, also helped them organize the day.
activities.prompt: If the community kept its original lunar calendar instead of creating a solar calendar, what would happen?
options: Its calendar year would not match the seasonal cycle.
The year would contain 365 days without any adjustment.
The Moon’s phases would stop providing the basis for a month.
Earth’s rotation would no longer make a day.

why.The year would contain 365 days without: Wrong: The lunar year had 354 days.
why.The Moon’s phases would stop providing t: Wrong: Moon phases still provide the month.
why.Earth’s rotation would no longer make a: Wrong: Earth’s rotation still forms the day.

activities.explanation: Correct: A 354-day year does not match the seasons.

activities.context: A community first used a lunar calendar, following the Moon’s phases and placing twelve lunar months in a year. Their lunar year lasted 354 days, so it did not add up to 365 days. They therefore created a solar calendar so their years would match Earth’s cycle of seasons, adjusting the months to total 365 days. The Sun’s daily apparent motion, mainly caused by Earth’s rotation, also helped them organize the day.
activities.prompt: What should the community do to make the months in its new solar calendar cover a full year correctly?
options: Make the calendar’s months total 365 days.
Leave the months at 354 days because the Moon controls the year.
Base each month only on the Sun’s highest position each day.
Use the Moon’s phases for each month and make no adjustment.

why.Leave the months at 354 days because the: Wrong: A lunar year has 354 days.
why.Base each month only on the Sun’s highes: Wrong: Days are not the basis of calendar months.

activities.explanation: Correct: Solar months are adjusted to total 365.

activities.prompt:
Assertion (A): The Sun’s daily apparent motion is mainly due to Earth’s rotation.
Reason (R): Earth’s rotation and the Sun’s cycle form the basis of the day.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.
activities.explanation: Earth’s rotation accounts for the Sun’s daily apparent motion and supports the day.

Sunlight passes through it
activities.explanation: The Moon shines by reflecting sunlight, so it can be visible during daytime.

activities.prompt: After the new Moon, the bright side grows to a half circle in about a week.
activities.explanation: This growth marks the early part of the waxing period.

activities.prompt: In India, the waning period is generally called ______ Paksha.
activities.hint: Use the Indian name for the waning period.
activities.explanation: The waning period is generally called Krishna Paksha in India.

activities.prompt: Match each Moon term with its correct name.
activities.explanation: These names describe the Moon's brightness and its changing phases.

activities.prompt: Put these Moon stages in order, starting with the new Moon.
activities.explanation: The bright part grows after the new Moon and shrinks after the full Moon.

activities.prompt: What causes a lunar eclipse?
options: Earth's shadow falls on the Moon
The Moon makes its own shadow
The Moon changes its shape
The Moon blocks Earth's sunlight
activities.explanation: A lunar eclipse happens when Earth's shadow falls on the Moon.

activities.prompt: Earth's shadow causes the phases of the Moon.
activities.explanation: Earth's shadow causes a lunar eclipse, not the Moon's phases.

activities.prompt: Match each festival or calendar with the correct detail.
pairs: Falls on the full Moon of Phalguna
Use Moon phases and adjust to seasons
Festivals following a solar sidereal calendar
Happen on almost the same date each year
activities.explanation: Moon phases and seasons help explain the dates of many festivals and calendars.

activities.prompt: A lunar year lasts ______ days.
activities.hint: Think of the length of twelve lunar months.
activities.explanation: Ancient lunar calendars used twelve lunar months in a year.

activities.prompt: Which work do artificial satellites help with?
options: Communication and navigation
Bookbinding and farming
Cooking and weaving
Painting and pottery
activities.explanation: Artificial satellites help with communication, navigation, weather monitoring and other work.

chapters.title: How Nature Works in Harmony
chapters.summary: In this chapter: nature, habitats and change; populations, communities and pollination; food chains and food webs; waste, migration and cascading change.

lessons.title: Nature, Habitats and Change

activities.prompt: Why do elephants sometimes visit farms and villages?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: Living Things and Their Homes
activities.body: A habitat is the place where an organism lives. An organism is a living thing. Every organism needs suitable conditions to survive. Plants and animals interact and adapt to their surroundings. Elephants may enter farms and villages when food is scarce and waterholes dry up. They can eat bananas and sugarcane. Wildlife corridors are marked routes for safe animal movement between forest areas.
keyPoints: A habitat is where a living thing lives.
Elephants may seek farm food when vegetation and water are scarce.
Wildlife corridors support safe movement between forest areas.
activities.explanation: These ideas show how living things, their surroundings, and changes are closely connected.

activities.prompt: Elephants enter a farm after rainfall and temperature change. Why might this happen?
steps: Changes in rainfall and temperature can affect vegetation.
Vegetation may become scarce, and waterholes may dry up.
Elephants may wander towards farms, where food can include bananas and sugarcane.
This chain shows that nature's elements are closely connected.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.prompt: What is a habitat?
options: the place where an organism lives
the food an organism eats
the work an organism does
the weather an organism likes
activities.explanation: A habitat tells you where a living thing lives.

activities.prompt: Elephants may wander towards farms when vegetation is scarce and waterholes dry up.
activities.explanation: Elephants may search for food when plants are scarce and waterholes dry up.

activities.prompt: A ______ is the place where an organism lives.
activities.hint: Think about where a living thing lives.
activities.explanation: The habitat is the home of an organism.

activities.prompt: Match each idea with its detail from the lesson.
pairs: the place where an organism lives
activities.explanation: Each pair connects an idea with its matching detail from the lesson.

activities.prompt: Marked wildlife corridors make animals enter human settlements.
activities.explanation: Corridors allow safe movement, so animals can avoid human settlements.

activities.prompt: Why are wildlife corridors useful to animals?
options: They provide food for wild animals.
They make forest loss happen faster.
They allow safe movement between forests.
They fill dry waterholes with water.
activities.explanation: Wildlife corridors let animals move safely between large forest areas.

activities.prompt: Put these events in the chain that can lead elephants towards farms.
items: Vegetation becomes scarce and waterholes dry up
activities.explanation: Changes in rainfall and temperature can affect vegetation. Scarce vegetation and dry waterholes can lead elephants towards farms.

activities.prompt: Rainfall changes. Plants become scarce, and waterholes dry up. What may elephants do?
options: They may wander towards farms to find food.
They may stay in forests and wait for plants.
They may enter villages only to find more water.
They may rest near farms until plants grow again.

why.They may stay in forests and wait for pl: This mistake thinks animals will wait instead of searching for food.
why.They may enter villages only to find mor: This mistake focuses on water and ignores the search for food.
why.They may rest near farms until plants gr: This mistake assumes elephants can wait without searching for food.

activities.explanation: Right, because scarce plants and dry waterholes can draw elephants to farms.

activities.prompt: Rainfall and temperature can affect vegetation. Which test would show temperature's effect alone?
options: Use the same plants and rainfall, but change temperature.
Use different plants, rainfall levels, and temperatures together.
Use the same plants, but change rainfall and temperature.
Use different temperatures, but change rainfall and plants.

why.Use different plants, rainfall levels, a: This mistake changes several things, so the cause is unclear.
why.Use the same plants, but change rainfall: This mistake changes rainfall too, so temperature's effect is unclear.
why.Use different temperatures, but change r: This mistake changes plants too, so temperature's effect is unclear.

activities.explanation: Right, because only temperature changes while plants and rainfall stay the same.

lessons.title: Populations, Communities and Pollination

activities.prompt: What happens when a habitat’s living and non-living parts work together?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: Living in a Habitat
activities.body: A habitat contains living beings and non-living things. Living beings are called biotic components. Non-living things are called abiotic components. A population is the same type of organism living in a habitat at a given time. A community has different populations sharing the same habitat. Pollination happens when wind, water and animals carry pollen between flowers.
keyPoints: Biotic components are living beings.
Abiotic components are non-living things.
Wind, water and animals carry pollen during pollination.
activities.explanation: These terms help you describe the parts of habitats and the groups living there.

activities.prompt: A pond has many fish and some plants. How can both live and grow there?
steps: Fish and plants are living beings in the pond habitat.
This makes them biotic components of the pond.
Food, oxygen, shelter and space help organisms grow in the pond.
Different organisms can use these resources in different ways, so their populations form a community.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.prompt: Both the pond and the forest contain living beings and non-living things. Which are biotic components?
options: Organisms
Oxygen
Water
Space
activities.explanation: Organisms are living beings, so they are biotic components.

activities.prompt: Biotic components are the non-living things in a habitat.
activities.explanation: Biotic components are living beings, while abiotic components are non-living things.

activities.prompt: Living beings in a habitat are called ______ components.
activities.hint: These components are alive.
activities.explanation: The living beings in a habitat are called biotic components.

activities.prompt: Match each item with its correct meaning.
activities.explanation: A pond gives resources, while biotic and abiotic components describe living and non-living parts.

activities.prompt: Each habitat has its own biotic components and physical conditions.
activities.explanation: Every habitat has its own living beings and physical conditions.

activities.prompt: If all organisms were alike, they would compete for different requirements.
activities.explanation: If all organisms were alike, they would compete for the same requirements.

activities.prompt: Match each item with the correct description.
pairs: Same type of organism in a habitat
Habitats with living and non-living things
Has its own biotic components and physical conditions
activities.explanation: These pairs connect populations, habitats and the helpers involved in pollination.

activities.prompt: Which list contains all the helpers that carry pollen between flowers?
options: Wind, water and animals
Food, oxygen and shelter
Biotic and abiotic components
Living and non-living things
activities.explanation: During pollination, wind, water and animals help carry pollen between flowers.

activities.prompt: A pond has plants and fish. Both use the pond's food, oxygen, shelter and space. What may happen if one population becomes very large?
options: The population may compete for the same pond resources.
The population may use resources in completely different ways.
The population may stop needing food and oxygen.
The population may become a non-living pond component.

why.The population may use resources in comp: This mistake treats different organisms as using resources in the same way.
why.The population may stop needing food and: This mistake thinks a population stops needing resources as it grows.
why.The population may become a non-living p: This mistake confuses living beings with non-living habitat parts.

activities.explanation: This is right because alike organisms compete for the same requirements.

activities.prompt: A pond has plants, fish, rocks and water. A child calls the rocks biotic components. Why is this claim wrong?
options: Rocks are non-living, so they are abiotic components.
Rocks are living, so they are biotic components.
Rocks share the habitat with every population.
Rocks provide oxygen for organisms to grow.

why.Rocks are living, so they are biotic com: This mistake treats non-living rocks as living beings.
why.Rocks share the habitat with every popul: This mistake thinks sharing a habitat makes a thing biotic.
why.Rocks provide oxygen for organisms to gr: This mistake treats oxygen support as a living component instead of a habitat resource.

activities.explanation: This is right because rocks are non-living abiotic components.

lessons.sceneAlt: Mangrove trees grow along the coast at Fish Eagle Point in Tanzania, creating a habitat for marine and terrestrial wildlife.
lessons.sceneCaption: Mangrove forests provide habitat for marine and terrestrial wildlife while protecting Tanzania’s shoreline from erosion.

lessons.title: Interactions and Ecosystems

activities.prompt: How could one small pond change the life around it?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: Living and Non-Living Parts
activities.body: Living things are biotic components. Non-living surroundings are abiotic components. These parts affect each other. Fish eat dragonfly larvae, so ponds with fish have fewer dragonflies. These insects help pollinate flowers near the ponds. Pollination helps nearby plants produce seeds. Plants and animals depend on one another for nutrition, respiration and reproduction. Together, biotic and abiotic components form an ecosystem.
keyPoints: Biotic and abiotic components affect each other.
Plants and animals depend on one another.
Biotic and abiotic components form an ecosystem.
activities.explanation: A habitat works through many linked interactions.

activities.title: Fish and Dragonflies
activities.prompt: Ponds with fish have fewer dragonflies than ponds without fish.
activities.explanation: Fish eat dragonfly larvae, so ponds with fish have fewer dragonflies.

activities.title: Fish Food
activities.prompt: What do fish eat in the pond study?
options: Dragonfly larvae
Flowers near ponds
Plant seeds
activities.explanation: Fish eat dragonfly larvae in the pond study.

activities.title: Needed for Survival
activities.prompt: Living organisms depend on ______ components for survival.
activities.hint: These components are the non-living parts of a habitat.
activities.explanation: Living organisms depend on abiotic components for survival.

activities.title: Connect the Pond Interactions
activities.prompt: Match each part with its connection in the pond study.
activities.explanation: The pond study shows how each interaction affects another part.

activities.title: Important Interactions
activities.prompt: Both biotic-biotic and biotic-abiotic interactions are important for survival.
activities.explanation: Living organisms interact with one another and with abiotic components.

activities.title: The Big Idea
activities.prompt: What does the pond study show about ecosystem parts?
options: Only living parts can change a habitat.
Only non-living parts can change a habitat.
Biotic and abiotic parts affect each other.
Living and non-living parts act alone.
activities.explanation: Biotic and abiotic components affect each other and together form an ecosystem.

lessons.sceneAlt: Hine’s emerald dragonfly larvae are kept in cages beside a pond where good water will not freeze.
lessons.sceneCaption: Hine’s emerald dragonfly larvae are placed in pond cages to protect them through winter.

lessons.title: Food Chains and Food Webs

activities.prompt: Who eats whom in a busy little meadow?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: Who Eats Whom?
activities.body: Plants make their own food by photosynthesis. They are producers, also called autotrophs, and occupy the first trophic level. Consumers cannot make their own food, so they depend on other organisms. Herbivores eat only plants, carnivores eat only animals, and omnivores eat both. In a grassland, grass is eaten by hares. Interlinked food chains form a food web.
keyPoints: Producers make food by photosynthesis.
Consumers depend on other organisms.
Food webs contain interlinked food chains.
activities.explanation: Follow the feeding links from plants to consumers.

activities.prompt: Which group makes its own food by photosynthesis?
options: Green plants
Hares and deer
Small carnivores
Consumers
activities.explanation: Plants make their own food by photosynthesis. These organisms are producers.

activities.prompt: Herbivores eat only plants.
activities.explanation: Herbivores are animals that eat only plants.

activities.prompt: Frogs occupy the second trophic level.
activities.explanation: Frogs are small carnivores. Small carnivores occupy the third trophic level.

activities.prompt: What do interlinked food chains form?
options: a trophic level
a food web
a producer
a herbivore
activities.explanation: Interlinked food chains form a network called a food web.

activities.prompt: Hares and deer occupy the ______ trophic level.
activities.hint: These animals are herbivores.
activities.explanation: Hares and deer occupy the second trophic level.

activities.prompt: Match each group with its name.
activities.explanation: Each pair joins an organism or group with its feeding role.

activities.prompt: Put these organisms in order from the first to the third trophic level.
activities.explanation: Green plants occupy the first level. Hares and deer occupy second, and small carnivores occupy third.

activities.prompt: Which list shows the first, second, and third trophic levels correctly?
options: Green plants, hares and deer, frogs
Hares and deer, green plants, frogs
Green plants, frogs, hares and deer
Frogs, hares and deer, green plants
activities.explanation: Green plants occupy the first trophic level. Hares and deer occupy second, and frogs occupy third.

lessons.sceneCaption: A red fox, an omnivore that eats berries, mice, voles, lemmings and arctic ground squirrels.

lessons.title: Waste, Migration and Cascading Change

activities.prompt: How do waste and migration connect to changes across an ecosystem?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: Nature Reuses Everything
activities.body: Living things make waste while they follow their life cycles. This waste includes dead matter and food waste. Microorganisms break down complex substances in dead plants and animals. Mushrooms are fungi that grow on dead matter. In nature, nothing is wasted because everything is reused. Migratory birds travel from different parts of the world to avoid harsh weather. Harsh means very difficult. They help keep ecosystems balanced as pollinators and seed dispersers.
keyPoints: Organisms produce dead matter and food waste.
Nature reuses waste through decomposers.
Migratory birds help balance ecosystems.
activities.explanation: Waste, migration and ecosystem balance are closely connected in nature.

activities.prompt: What do organisms produce during their life cycle?
options: waste
pollution
migration
balance
activities.explanation: Organisms produce waste during their life cycle.

activities.prompt: Microorganisms break down complex substances in dead plants and animals.
activities.explanation: Microorganisms help break down complex substances in dead plants and animals.

activities.prompt: Match each pond change with its result.
activities.explanation: Pollution can kill pond plants. A smaller fish population means fewer consumers remain.

activities.prompt: Migratory birds travel to avoid ______ weather.
activities.hint: This word means very difficult.
activities.explanation: Migratory birds travel from different parts of the world to avoid harsh weather.

activities.prompt: Put this frog-change chain in order.
activities.explanation: Harvesting reduced frogs and caused pests to rise. The Government banned frog-leg exports.

activities.prompt: How do migratory birds help keep ecosystems balanced?
options: as pollinators and seed dispersers
as pond plants and fish
as waste and fungi
as farm pests and insects
activities.explanation: Migratory birds act as pollinators and seed dispersers, helping balance ecosystems.

activities.prompt: Because nothing is reused in nature, waste builds up and stays unused.
activities.explanation: In nature, everything is reused, so nothing is wasted.

activities.prompt: How can banning frog-leg exports help farms?
options: It can protect frogs and lower pest numbers.
It can increase pollution around nearby farms.
It can cause harsher weather near farms.
It can make pond plants die much faster.
activities.explanation: Frog harvesting reduced frogs and caused pests to rise. Protecting frogs can help reduce pest numbers.

lessons.sceneAlt: Fungi grow on dead wood beside a revitalised creek bed in Šumava National Park.
lessons.sceneCaption: Fungi growing on dead wood illustrate how fungi live on and break down dead matter.

sceneCredit.text: Fungi growing on dead wood by Slunkopunk, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons
sceneCredit.creator: Slunkopunk

lessons.title: Balance, Benefits and Sustainable Nature

activities.prompt: How do living things share resources, and how can people protect nature?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: Living Together and Using Nature
activities.body: Organisms compete for shared resources like food, water, space and sunlight. Competition controls population size and keeps ecosystems balanced. In mutualism, both organisms benefit. In commensalism, one benefits while the other is unaffected. In parasitism, one benefits while the other is harmed. Forests and aquatic ecosystems give people useful resources. Careful use and protected areas help nature stay balanced. Sustainable farming can reduce interference in nature.
keyPoints: Competition helps keep ecosystems balanced.
Different organism relationships affect organisms differently.
Protected areas and sustainable farming support nature.
activities.explanation: These ideas connect competition, benefits and protecting nature.

activities.prompt: Which resource does an aquatic ecosystem provide to people?
options: Water
Timber
Fibres
Fertile soil
activities.explanation: Aquatic ecosystems provide people with water and food.

activities.prompt: In mutualism, both organisms benefit.
activities.explanation: Mutualism is a relationship in which both organisms benefit.

activities.prompt: In commensalism, one organism benefits while the other is ______.
activities.hint: This organism is not changed by the relationship.
activities.explanation: In commensalism, one organism benefits while the other remains unaffected.

activities.prompt: Match each relationship with its result.
pairs: One benefits while the other is unaffected
One benefits while the other is harmed
activities.explanation: Each relationship has a different effect on the two organisms.

activities.title: Nature Gives Us Many Benefits
activities.body: Forests give people fresh air, fertile soil, food, fibres, timber and medicines. Aquatic ecosystems provide people with water and food. Overusing or misusing natural resources disturbs nature’s balance. Industrial waste and untreated sewage damage water and habitats in the Sundarbans. Protecting habitats and choosing sustainable farming can help people use natural resources with less harm.
keyPoints: Forests provide many useful resources.
Aquatic ecosystems provide water and food.
Misusing resources can disturb nature’s balance.
activities.explanation: These resources benefit people, but their use needs care.

activities.prompt: How do the Sundarbans protect people?
options: Slow strong winds and waves
Control the ecosystem population size
Keep both organisms benefiting together
Leave one participating organism unaffected
activities.explanation: The Sundarbans protect people by slowing strong winds and waves.

activities.prompt: Mangrove trees in the Sundarbans are being cut for ______ and farming.
activities.hint: This comes from trees and is used as fuel.
activities.explanation: These mangrove trees are being cut for fuelwood and farming.

activities.prompt: Which action best supports sustainable farming?
options: Use organic and natural methods
Use synthetic fertilisers for years
Use pesticides for many years
Cut mangroves for more farming
activities.explanation: Organic and natural farming supports sustainable farming with less interference in nature.

lessons.sceneAlt: A bee interacts with a flower, with the plant providing food and the bee enabling reproduction.
lessons.sceneCaption: A bee and flower show mutualism: the plant provides food, while the bee enables reproduction.

lessons.sceneAlt: A herd of Asian elephants crosses a road through a wildlife corridor in Manas National Park.
lessons.sceneCaption: A herd of Asian elephants crosses a road through a corridor in Manas National Park.

activities.context: In several parts of India, elephants often enter farms and villages. When vegetation becomes scarce and waterholes dry up, the elephants may wander towards farms, where their search for food can include bananas and sugarcane. Changes in rainfall and temperature can affect vegetation, while cutting trees for roads and buildings makes forest loss worse. Ecologists have marked corridors that allow animals to travel safely between large forest areas without entering settlements.
activities.prompt: Why might the elephants in the case move towards farms and villages?
options: Scarcer vegetation and dry waterholes can make farm food more attractive.
Bananas and sugarcane are the only foods every elephant can eat.
Elephants enter farms because marked corridors lead directly into villages.
Cutting trees for roads guarantees that no elephant will visit a farm.

why.Bananas and sugarcane are the only foods: The passage does not say these foods are the only choices.
why.Elephants enter farms because marked cor: Corridors help animals avoid settlements rather than direct them into villages.
why.Cutting trees for roads guarantees that: Forest loss can worsen encounters with farms and villages.

activities.explanation: Vegetation and water are linked to where elephants search for food.

activities.context: In several parts of India, elephants often enter farms and villages. When vegetation becomes scarce and waterholes dry up, the elephants may wander towards farms, where their search for food can include bananas and sugarcane. Changes in rainfall and temperature can affect vegetation, while cutting trees for roads and buildings makes forest loss worse. Ecologists have marked corridors that allow animals to travel safely between large forest areas without entering settlements.
activities.prompt: What should be done with a marked wildlife corridor beside a human settlement?
options: Keep the route open so wildlife can pass safely without entering the settlement.
Fill the route with buildings to create more human habitats.
Direct all animals through the farms so they can find food.
Block the marked route because wildlife no longer needs to move.

why.Fill the route with buildings to create: Adding buildings would damage the purpose of a corridor.
why.Direct all animals through the farms so: Farm routes do not provide the safe movement described by corridors.
why.Block the marked route because wildlife: Wildlife still needs routes between large forest areas.

activities.explanation: Corridors allow safe movement without entering human settlements.

activities.prompt:
Assertion (A): Every marked corridor guarantees that elephants will never enter farms or villages.
Reason (R): Elephants often enter farms and villages in several parts of India.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.
activities.explanation: The assertion is false because corridors cannot guarantee this, while the reason is true.

activities.prompt: Explain why changes in vegetation, water availability, and forest loss can affect human habitats.
activities.answer: Vegetation, water, and wildlife are closely connected. Changes in rainfall and temperature can affect vegetation. When vegetation is scarce and waterholes dry up, elephants may wander towards farms to find food, including bananas and sugarcane. Cutting trees for roads and buildings also makes forest loss worse, so animals may lose their natural habitats and enter human habitats. Marked corridors help by allowing safe movement between large forest areas without entering settlements.
points: Changes in rainfall and temperature can affect vegetation.
Scarce vegetation and dry waterholes can lead elephants towards farms.
Forest loss can cause animals to enter human habitats.
Wildlife corridors support safe movement between forest areas.
activities.explanation: Compare your answer with the points a marker looks for.

activities.context: A school pond contains several populations, including organisms of the same type and organisms of different types. The pond provides food, oxygen, shelter and space for organisms to grow. Nearby, flowers receive pollen carried by wind, water and animals. Students also visit a forest, where living beings and non-living things form the habitat. They compare how different organisms in the pond use resources in different ways and examine the parts of the community.
activities.prompt: Why might organisms in the pond face stronger competition if they all began using resources in exactly the same way?
options: They would compete for the same requirements.
They would each need fewer resources.
They would divide the pond into separate habitats.
They would stop sharing the habitat because they are alike.

Using resources in one way would not necessarily reduce their needs.
why.They would divide the pond into separate: Different habitats would not form merely because resource use changed.
why.They would stop sharing the habitat beca: Organisms can still share a habitat even when they are alike.

activities.explanation: This is the correct result of organisms having the same requirements.

activities.context: A school pond contains several populations, including organisms of the same type and organisms of different types. The pond provides food, oxygen, shelter and space for organisms to grow. Nearby, flowers receive pollen carried by wind, water and animals. Students also visit a forest, where living beings and non-living things form the habitat. They compare how different organisms in the pond use resources in different ways and examine the parts of the community.
activities.prompt: If wind, water and animals were unavailable around the flowers, what would most likely happen?
options: Pollen would have less help reaching other flowers.
Pollen would move between flowers more quickly without a carrier.
Only water would continue carrying pollen between the flowers.
All three would still carry pollen because they are always present.

why.Pollen would move between flowers more q: Removing the carriers would not make pollen transfer faster.
why.Only water would continue carrying polle: Water would also be unavailable under the changed condition.
why.All three would still carry pollen becau: The carriers cannot continue helping if they are unavailable.

activities.explanation: These three agents help carry pollen between flowers.

activities.prompt:
Assertion (A): A habitat contains only one population.
Reason (R): Different populations can share the same habitat.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.
activities.explanation: The first statement is false because different populations can share a habitat, while the reason is true.

activities.prompt: Explain the difference between a population and a community, using the pond as an example.
activities.answer: A population is a group of the same type of organism living in a habitat at a given time. For example, all the organisms of one type in the pond form a population. A community includes all the different populations that share that same habitat. Thus, the pond’s community includes each population of organisms found there. The pond also has abiotic components, which are its non-living things, but these are not part of the community because a community consists of living populations.
points: Defines a population as the same type of organism at a given time.
Uses the pond to show that one type of organism forms a population.
Explains that a community contains different populations sharing one habitat.
Distinguishes abiotic components from the living populations.
activities.explanation: Compare your answer with the points a marker looks for.

boss.title: Chapter challenge: How Nature Works in Harmony

activities.prompt: Which pair shows one biotic and one abiotic component?
options: Fish and rocks
Water and sunlight
Rocks and water
Sunlight and oxygen
activities.explanation: Fish are living beings, so they are biotic. Rocks are non-living, so they are abiotic.

activities.prompt: Migratory birds travel to avoid harsh weather.
activities.explanation: Migratory birds travel from different parts of the world to avoid harsh weather.

activities.prompt: Green plants occupy the ______ trophic level.
activities.hint: Think about the beginning of a food chain.
activities.explanation: Producers, such as green plants, occupy the first trophic level.

activities.prompt: Match each feeding group with its meaning.
activities.explanation: These groups show how organisms get food in an ecosystem.

activities.prompt: Put these organisms in food-chain order.
activities.explanation: Producers come first, herbivores come next, and small carnivores occupy the third trophic level.

activities.prompt: What do identified wildlife corridors allow?
options: Safe movement of animals
More building materials
Less rainfall
Larger villages
activities.explanation: Corridors allow safe movement between large forest areas without entering human settlements.

activities.prompt: Ponds with fish have fewer dragonflies because fish eat dragonfly larvae.
activities.explanation: Fish eat dragonfly larvae. This connection shows how biotic components affect each other.

activities.prompt: Fish eat ______ larvae, so ponds with fish have fewer dragonflies.
activities.hint: These insects help pollinate flowers near ponds.
activities.explanation: Fish eat dragonfly larvae, reducing dragonfly numbers in ponds with fish.

activities.prompt: Match each interaction with its meaning.
pairs: One benefits while the other is unaffected
One benefits while the other is harmed
activities.explanation: These interactions show different ways organisms affect one another.

activities.prompt: Put these events in the correct order.
items: Vegetation becomes scarce and waterholes dry
Their search includes bananas and sugarcane
activities.explanation: Elephants may move towards farms when vegetation is scarce and waterholes dry. Their search can include crops.

chapters.title: Our Home: Earth, a Unique Life-Sustaining Planet
chapters.summary: In this chapter: earth is special and the planets around the sun; earth’s position in the solar system; the right size and magnetic shield of earth; connections that sustain life.

lessons.title: Earth Is Special and the Planets Around the Sun

activities.prompt: What makes Earth so special, and how do the planets differ?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: Why Earth Is Special
activities.body: Earth is special because life, as we know it today, exists and thrives here. Life lives in a thin surface layer. Mountains, rivers, forests, animals and people live there too. Earth gives us air to breathe and water to drink. We use Earth's rock and timber for homes, buildings and roads. Our solar system means the Sun and eight planets going around it.
keyPoints: Earth supports life as we know it today.
Earth gives us air, water, rock and timber.
Eight planets go around the Sun.
activities.explanation: Earth has special conditions that support life.

activities.prompt: Which planet has life, as we know it today?
options: Earth
Mars
Venus
Mercury
activities.explanation: Earth is the only planet where life, as we know it today, exists and thrives.

activities.prompt: Mountains, rivers, forests, animals and people live in a thin surface layer.
activities.explanation: All these parts of life live in Earth's thin surface layer.

activities.prompt: Our solar system has ______ planets going around the Sun.
activities.hint: Think of all the planets named in this lesson.
activities.explanation: Our solar system has eight planets going around the Sun.

activities.prompt: Match each planet with its description.
activities.explanation: Mercury is small and rocky, Venus is hottest, and Earth supports life today.

activities.prompt: Which statement about Venus is correct?
options: Venus is the hottest planet.
Venus is hottest only because it is close to the Sun.
Venus is made mostly of gases.
Venus has life today.
activities.explanation: Venus is hottest, but its closeness to the Sun is not the simple reason.

activities.prompt: Planets generally become colder as they move away from the Sun.
activities.explanation: Planets generally become colder as their distance from the Sun increases.

activities.prompt: Which pair contains only large planets made mostly of gases?
options: Jupiter and Saturn
Mercury and Venus
Earth and Mars
Mercury and Mars
activities.explanation: Jupiter and Saturn are both large planets made mostly of gases.

activities.prompt: Closeness to the Sun alone explains why Venus is the hottest planet.
activities.explanation: Venus is the hottest planet, but not simply because it is close to the Sun.

lessons.title: Earth’s Position in the Solar System

activities.prompt: What would happen if Earth lived closer to—or farther from—the Sun?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: Earth and the Habitable Zone
activities.body: Earth’s distance from the Sun helps it support life. This distance lets water remain liquid. The habitable zone is where water stays liquid. It is also called the Goldilocks zone. Closer to the Sun, Earth would be too hot, and water would evaporate. Farther away, Earth would be too cold, and water would freeze. Mars lies at this zone’s edge. No proof of life has yet been found on Mars.
keyPoints: Earth’s distance helps it support life.
The habitable zone is also called the Goldilocks zone.
Mars lies at the edge of the Sun’s habitable zone.
activities.explanation: Liquid water and a suitable distance from the Sun help life survive.

activities.prompt: Earth’s distance from the Sun is a major reason it can support life.
activities.explanation: This distance helps Earth keep water liquid. Liquid water is essential for life to evolve.

activities.prompt: What would happen if Earth were closer to the Sun?
options: Earth would become too cold.
Earth would become too hot.
Earth would keep the same heat.
activities.explanation: Closer to the Sun, Earth would be too hot. Its water would evaporate, and most life forms could not thrive.

activities.prompt: The ______ zone is the range where water remains liquid.
activities.hint: This is the suitable range for liquid water.
activities.explanation: This range is where water remains liquid. It is also called the Goldilocks zone.

activities.prompt: Proof of life has been found on Mars.
activities.explanation: No proof of life has yet been found on Mars.

activities.prompt: Match each term with its correct link.
pairs: Another name for the habitable zone
Most of its surface is covered with water
At the edge of the Sun’s habitable zone
activities.explanation: Most of Earth’s surface is covered with water. Mars lies at the habitable zone’s edge.

activities.prompt: What would happen if Earth were farther from the Sun?
options: Water would remain liquid.
Water would freeze.
Water would evaporate.
activities.explanation: Farther from the Sun, Earth would be too cold. Its water would freeze.

activities.prompt: Put these positions in order from nearest to farthest.
items: A position closer to the Sun
A position farther from the Sun
activities.explanation: A closer position makes Earth too hot. A farther position makes Earth too cold.

activities.prompt: Which statement about Mars is correct?
options: Mars lies outside the habitable zone.
Life on Mars has been proved.
Mars marks the habitable zone’s edge.
activities.explanation: Mars lies at the edge of the Sun’s habitable zone. No proof of life has yet been found on Mars.

lessons.title: The Right Size and Magnetic Shield of Earth

activities.prompt: How does Earth keep us safe from space?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: Earth’s Two Protections
activities.body: Earth’s right size allows it to support an atmosphere. Gases would escape from a smaller Earth into space. Mars has an atmosphere one hundred times thinner than Earth’s, while Mercury has no atmosphere. Oxygen lets living beings breathe, and the ozone layer blocks harmful ultraviolet rays. Movement of molten iron in Earth’s core may create its magnetic field. This field pushes many harmful space particles away.
keyPoints: Earth’s right size helps it support an atmosphere.
Ozone blocks harmful ultraviolet rays.
The magnetic field pushes many harmful space particles away.
activities.explanation: You can see how Earth’s size and magnetic field help protect life.

activities.prompt: Mars has an atmosphere one hundred times thicker than Earth’s.
activities.explanation: Mars has an atmosphere one hundred times thinner than Earth’s. It is not thicker.

activities.prompt: Mercury has ______ atmosphere at all.
activities.hint: This atmosphere is completely missing.
activities.explanation: Mercury has no atmosphere at all. The word “no” completes the sentence.

activities.title: Match Each Part
activities.prompt: Match each planet, gas, or layer with its feature or role.
pairs: one hundred times thinner atmosphere than Earth’s
activities.explanation: Mars has a much thinner atmosphere, while Mercury has none. Oxygen and ozone protect living beings.

activities.title: Making a Magnetic Field
activities.prompt: What may create Earth’s magnetic field?
options: Movement of molten iron in Earth’s core
Oxygen moving through the ozone layer
Rock spinning inside Earth’s atmosphere
Gases circling around Earth’s surface
activities.explanation: Moving molten iron in Earth’s core may create the magnetic field. This movement is inside Earth’s core.

activities.title: Earth’s Magnetic Shield
activities.prompt: Put these steps in order.
items: Molten iron moves in Earth’s core.
Many harmful space particles are pushed away.
activities.explanation: Molten iron moves first. This may create the magnetic field, which pushes particles away.

activities.prompt: An extremely large planet could pull living beings down with crushing force.
activities.explanation: An extremely large planet can pull living beings down with crushing force. That makes its pull dangerous.

activities.title: The Correct Protection Pair
activities.prompt: Which pair protects Earth in the correct way?
options: Ozone blocks ultraviolet rays; magnetic field pushes particles.
Ozone pushes particles; magnetic field blocks ultraviolet rays.
Ozone creates oxygen; magnetic field forms the ozone layer.
Ozone warms the core; magnetic field supports the atmosphere.
activities.explanation: Ozone blocks harmful ultraviolet rays. Earth’s magnetic field pushes many harmful space particles away.

lessons.title: Connections That Sustain Life

activities.prompt: How do air, water, and land connect to keep life going?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: Life and Earth’s Connected Parts
activities.body: Life depends on linked parts of Earth. Plants make food and release oxygen during photosynthesis. Humans, animals and plants use atmospheric oxygen for respiration. Water covers about seventy per cent of Earth’s surface. All Earth’s water forms the hydrosphere. Rocks, soils and minerals form the geosphere. Living beings and their homes form the biosphere.
keyPoints: Plants release oxygen during photosynthesis.
Living beings use atmospheric oxygen for respiration.
Water, rocks and living beings form connected parts of Earth.
activities.explanation: These links show how different parts of Earth support life.

activities.prompt: What do plants release when they make food by photosynthesis?
options: water
heat
freshwater
oxygen
activities.explanation: Plants make food by photosynthesis and release oxygen.

activities.prompt: Water covers about seventy per cent of Earth’s surface.
activities.explanation: This is the share of Earth’s surface covered by water.

activities.prompt: All of Earth’s ______ forms the hydrosphere.
activities.hint: Name the substance that makes up the hydrosphere.
activities.explanation: All of Earth’s water forms the hydrosphere.

activities.prompt: Match each part of Earth with its name.
activities.explanation: Each name describes a different part or variety within Earth.

activities.prompt: Which pair shows two jobs of water in animals?
options: temperature and hydration
rainfall and digestion
clouds and respiration
soil and photosynthesis
activities.explanation: Water regulates body temperature and keeps animals hydrated.

activities.title: Changes Can Affect Nature
activities.body: Nature works as a connected system. A change in one part can affect rainfall, soil, air quality and animals. Greenhouse gases in the atmosphere trap heat. Water vapour forms clouds and brings rain or snow. Freshwater helps crops grow and supports people. These links help us see how one change can affect many parts of nature.
keyPoints: A change in one part can affect several other parts.
Greenhouse gases trap heat in the atmosphere.
Water vapour helps form clouds and bring rain or snow.
activities.explanation: One change can affect many connected parts of nature.

activities.prompt: Put these steps in order.
items: Living beings use atmospheric oxygen for respiration.
activities.explanation: Photosynthesis makes food and releases oxygen. Living beings then use atmospheric oxygen for respiration.

activities.prompt: Which set lists effects that a change in nature can affect?
options: rainfall, soil, air quality, animals
clouds, snow, crops, people
oxygen, water, heat, freshwater
geodiversity, minerals, hydrosphere, biosphere
activities.explanation: A change in one part of nature can affect rainfall, soil, air quality and animals.

lessons.sceneCaption: This simple diagram introduces a leaf’s role in gas exchange.

lessons.title: Reproduction and the Continuity of Life

activities.prompt: How can reproduction help living things keep surviving?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: How Life Continues
activities.body: Reproduction keeps life going. Without it, plants and animals would eventually disappear. Genes are instructions stored inside cells. Asexual reproduction makes exact copies from one parent. Sexual reproduction combines instructions from two parents. A gamete carries half of a parent's genetic material. Fertilisation forms a zygote, which develops into a seed. This helps life adapt to changes and continue in new forms.
keyPoints: Reproduction keeps life going.
Asexual reproduction makes exact copies from one parent.
Sexual reproduction combines instructions from two parents.
activities.explanation: Reproduction helps living things continue in new forms.

activities.title: Where Genes Stay
activities.prompt: Which statement about genes is correct?
options: They are instructions stored outside cells.
They are instructions copied outside bodies.
They are instructions stored inside cells.
They are instructions found only in seeds.
activities.explanation: Genes are instructions stored inside the cells of living beings. Great choice!

activities.prompt: In asexual reproduction, one parent produces exact copies of itself.
activities.explanation: That is exactly what happens in asexual reproduction. Well spotted!

activities.prompt: Each ______ carries only half of its parent's genetic material.
activities.hint: It carries half of a parent's genetic material.
activities.explanation: Each gamete carries only half of its parent's genetic material.

activities.title: Match Each Word
activities.prompt: Match each word with its meaning.
pairs: Carries half of a parent's genetic material
activities.explanation: Genes guide cells, while reproduction helps life continue in new forms.

activities.title: Reproduction in Animals
activities.body: Animals have gametes called sperm and eggs. Each gamete carries only half of its parent's genetic material. In most mammals, the embryo develops inside the female's body. Sexual reproduction combines instructions from two parents. These combined instructions help life continue in new forms.
keyPoints: The gametes of animals are sperm and eggs.
Each gamete carries half of its parent's genetic material.
In most mammals, the embryo develops inside the female's body.
activities.explanation: Sperm and eggs are the gametes of animals.

activities.title: Sexual Reproduction and Gametes
activities.prompt: Which statement correctly describes sexual reproduction and its gametes?
options: Two parents combine, but each gamete carries all parental material.
One parent copies itself, and each gamete carries half its material.
Two parents combine, and each gamete carries half one parent's material.
One parent copies itself, and each gamete carries no parental material.
activities.explanation: Instructions from two parents combine. Each gamete carries only half of one parent's material.

activities.title: From a Gamete to a Seed
activities.prompt: Put these steps in order from a gamete to a seed.
items: Each gamete carries half of a parent's genetic material.
The zygote develops into a seed.
activities.explanation: Fertilisation forms a zygote, and the zygote develops into a seed.

lessons.title: Threats to Life and Ways to Protect Earth

activities.prompt: How can we protect Earth and the many lives that share it?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: Life Needs a Balanced Earth
activities.body: Humans are disturbing the balance that supports life. Climate change, biodiversity loss and pollution create a planetary crisis. Burning coal and oil releases greenhouse gases. Extra carbon adds heat, melts ice caps and can flood coastal cities. Destroying habitats makes plants and animals disappear. Waste, fertilisers and pollution can harm soil, water, crops and breathing. Earth’s four connected spheres need care.
keyPoints: Human actions disturb the balance supporting life.
Climate change, biodiversity loss and pollution threaten life.
Earth’s connected spheres need protection.
activities.explanation: Many human actions add harm to the systems that support life.

activities.prompt: Which one is part of the planetary crisis?
options: Climate change
Ice-cap melting
Coastal flooding
Natural habitats
activities.explanation: Climate change is one part of the planetary crisis.

activities.prompt: Burning coal and oil releases greenhouse gases into the atmosphere.
activities.explanation: Yes. Burning coal and oil releases greenhouse gases into the atmosphere.

activities.prompt: Extra carbon cannot be absorbed ______ enough, so more heat builds up.
activities.hint: Carbon cannot be taken in at the needed speed.
activities.explanation: Extra carbon cannot be absorbed fast enough. More heat therefore builds up.

activities.title: Pollution Can Harm Living Things
activities.body: Air pollution can damage crops, cause breathing problems and lead to acid rain. Factory, farm and plastic waste can make water unsafe for living things. Excess fertilisers and poor waste disposal can pollute soil. These harms happen because human actions disturb the balance supporting life. We can protect Earth by reducing pollution, protecting natural habitats and stopping waste from entering soil and water.
keyPoints: Air pollution harms crops, breathing and rainfall.
Different wastes can make water and soil unsafe.
Reducing pollution and protecting habitats can protect life.
activities.explanation: Pollution can harm people, plants, animals and their surroundings.

activities.prompt: Why can factory and plastic waste make water unsafe?
options: The waste adds pollution
The waste melts ice
The waste traps carbon
The waste changes habitats
activities.explanation: Factory, farm and plastic waste can make water unsafe for living things.

activities.prompt: Match each human action with its effect.
pairs: Water becomes unsafe for living things
activities.explanation: Each action has an effect on the atmosphere, habitats, water or soil.

activities.prompt: Put the chain of effects in order.
items: Extra carbon cannot be absorbed fast enough
Ice caps melt and coastal cities can flood
activities.explanation: The extra carbon adds heat, which can melt ice caps and flood coastal cities.

activities.prompt: Climate change means short-term changes in temperature, rainfall and weather.
activities.explanation: Climate change means long-term changes in temperature, rainfall and weather.

boss.title: Chapter challenge: Our Home: Earth, a Unique Life-Sustaining Planet

activities.title: The right distance
activities.prompt: What does Earth's distance from the Sun allow?
options: Water to remain liquid
Venus to stay cooler
Mercury to keep air
Mars to have thicker air
activities.explanation: Earth's distance lets water remain liquid, which supports life.

activities.title: A thin atmosphere
activities.prompt: Mars has an atmosphere ______ times thinner than Earth's.
activities.hint: Think about the scale of thinness.
activities.explanation: Mars's atmosphere is one hundred times thinner than Earth's.

activities.title: Planet clues
activities.prompt: Match each planet with a fact about it.
activities.explanation: Each clue describes one of these planets in our solar system.

activities.title: Destroying homes
activities.prompt: Which action can make plants and animals disappear?
options: Using a bicycle
Building a school
Playing a board game
Destroying natural habitats
activities.explanation: Destroying natural habitats can make plants and animals disappear.

activities.title: Rising sea levels
activities.prompt: Melting ice caps can raise sea levels and flood coastal cities.
activities.explanation: Melting ice caps can raise sea levels and flood coastal cities.

activities.title: Earth's connected parts
activities.prompt: Match each part of Earth with what it includes.
activities.explanation: These parts of Earth are connected and influence one another.

activities.title: The protective layer
activities.prompt: The ozone layer blocks harmful ______ rays.
activities.hint: Name the harmful rays blocked by ozone.
activities.explanation: The ozone layer blocks harmful ultraviolet rays from reaching Earth's surface.

activities.title: Before a new seed forms
activities.prompt: Put the sexual reproduction stages in order.
items: Each gamete carries half its parent's genetic material.
The zygote develops into a seed.
activities.explanation: Gametes join through fertilisation, creating a zygote that develops into a seed.
